items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: As mentioned on pp. 21–23 (Education) the strategy addresses AI literacy through systemic integration of AI and digital skills across the education system. The SmartLabs project equips pre-university schools with technological infrastructure and introduces programming from the first grade to build critical thinking and problem-solving skills. The strategy further commits to a national digital skills agenda that supports students in developing competencies to participate in ethical and sustainable AI development while also training teachers and school leaders to effectively use AI tools. This dual focus on student capacity and educator training embeds AI literacy institutionally and long term.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The strategy integrates AI and digital skills across the education system including initiatives such as the SmartLabs project which introduces programming from the first grade and embeds digital competencies throughout schooling (pp. 21–23).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The strategy promotes systemic integration of AI and digital skills in the education system and introduces initiatives like SmartLabs that provide technological infrastructure and programming education in schools (pp. 21–23). However it does not explicitly establish dedicated AI-specific institutions or degree programs.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: As mentioned on pp. 21–23 (Education) the strategy explicitly provides for the continuous training of teachers and school principals to ensure the effective use of AI-related technologies introduced through the SmartLabs project. It also commits to supporting educators in adopting AI tools and methods to improve pedagogical practices and professional development. These measures constitute concrete provisions for teacher training and resource support in AI education within the formal education system.

items.title: Law No. 124/2024 “On the Protection of Personal Data”
items.justification: Law No. 124/2024 safeguards children’s rights in AI contexts by regulating and limiting automated processing and profiling (Art. 20 pp. 12–13) requiring child-specific consent for online services under 16 (Art. 8(6) pg. 6) and mandating clear age-appropriate information.  While the law does not explicitly use the term “Artificial Intelligence” it covers automated and algorithmic processing (Art. 13(1)c) profiling and data protection by design/default which are directly applicable to AI systems used with or by minors.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law regulates automated processing profiling and algorithmic decision-making that apply to AI-related data processing (Art. 13(1)(c); Art. 20 pp. 12–13). It also requires child-specific consent for online services under 16 and clear age-appropriate information strengthening privacy protections when AI or automated systems process children’s data (Art. 8(6) p. 6).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The law introduces safeguards by restricting automated processing and profiling involving children and requiring consent and age-appropriate transparency which can help mitigate manipulation or exploitation through algorithmic systems (Art. 20; Art. 8(6)). However it does not explicitly regulate AI uses such as targeted advertising or harmful AI-generated content directed at children.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The law requires data protection by design and by default and regulates automated processing and profiling involving children which indirectly applies to AI systems processing children’s data (Art. 13(1)(c); Art. 20). However it does not establish explicit AI-specific design obligations requiring systems to be safe or developmentally appropriate for children.

items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: As mentioned in Section 6 (Cultural Heritage and Tourism) the document addresses cultural and linguistic diversity by promoting AI applications that preserve digitize and enhance access to Albania’s cultural heritage. It highlights the use of image recognition and 3D reconstruction to digitally restore monuments and artifacts as well as machine learning tools to catalog and translate historical documents. The strategy also supports multilingual virtual guides and augmented reality experiences ensuring inclusive access for diverse domestic and international audiences while strengthening cultural identity and global visibility.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes AI applications that support cultural and linguistic diversity including tools for digitizing and translating historical documents and the development of multilingual virtual guides and augmented reality experiences to make cultural heritage accessible to diverse audiences (Section 6). These measures encourage AI systems that are responsive to different languages and cultural contexts while strengthening cultural identity and global accessibility.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes AI applications that preserve cultural heritage and support multilingual access contributing to the protection of cultural and linguistic diversity (Section 6). However it does not establish explicit safeguards or regulatory measures aimed at preventing AI systems from perpetuating cultural stereotypes erasing linguistic diversity or privileging dominant cultures. The approach is therefore supportive rather than explicitly risk-preventive.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: The document addresses environmental impact by recognizing both the strategic opportunity and the sustainability risks associated with AI development. As mentioned on p. 18 (Regional Leadership and Specialized Focus) it encourages Albania to differentiate itself through “Green AI” promoting environmentally sustainable AI solutions as a competitive advantage. At the same time as noted on p. 19 (Resource Constraints and Sustainability) it acknowledges that AI systems are resource-intensive and may strain electricity and digital infrastructure if not carefully managed. The strategy warns that increased computing demands could conflict with environmental objectives unless sustainability considerations are integrated into AI development.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: As mentioned on p. 19 (Resource Constraints and Sustainability) the document acknowledges that AI systems are resource-intensive and may strain electricity infrastructure potentially conflicting with environmental objectives. It also highlights the importance of focusing on “Green AI” as noted on p. 18 (Regional Leadership and Specialized Focus). However it does not establish concrete regulatory provisions or binding measures specifically aimed at preventing excessive energy consumption or e-waste. The approach is strategic and cautionary rather than prescriptive.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: As mentioned on p. 18 (Regional Leadership and Specialized Focus) the document promotes the development of “Green AI” as a strategic differentiator. On p. 19 (Resource Constraints and Sustainability) it acknowledges that AI systems are energy-intensive and may strain electricity infrastructure if not managed sustainably. However it does not set out concrete measures specifically targeting data center efficiency renewable energy integration advanced cooling technologies or hardware optimization. The commitment remains strategic rather than technically prescriptive.

items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: On p. 39 the document addresses fairness and non-discrimination by emphasizing equality justice and respect for human dignity as foundational principles of trustworthy AI. It recognizes that bias may arise from data algorithms or applications and may result in discriminatory outcomes based on characteristics such as race gender ethnicity or religion. To mitigate these risks it calls for the establishment of guidelines and standards for data collection and analysis algorithm design and testing and evaluation and auditing processes. The framework stresses transparency explainability accountability and alignment with human rights as safeguards against discriminatory impacts.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly promotes equality justice and non-discrimination as core principles of trustworthy AI (p. 39). It recognizes that bias in data algorithms or applications can lead to harmful or disproportionate impacts on groups defined by race gender ethnicity or religion. It calls for guidelines and standards in data collection algorithm design testing and auditing to mitigate discriminatory outcomes and emphasizes transparency accountability and alignment with human rights to ensure fair and equitable AI results.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly recognizes that bias may arise from data algorithms or applications and may produce discriminatory outcomes based on characteristics such as race gender ethnicity or religion. To mitigate these risks it calls for guidelines and standards for data collection and analysis algorithm design and testing and evaluation and auditing processes alongside safeguards such as transparency explainability accountability and alignment with human rights (p.39).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document calls for guidelines and standards covering data collection and analysis algorithm design and testing and evaluation and auditing processes to address bias in AI systems. By emphasizing that bias may arise from data algorithms or applications it promotes proactive identification and mitigation of discrimination risks across different stages of the AI lifecycle supported by principles of transparency explainability accountability and human rights alignment (p.39).

items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: On p. 38 the document addresses Human Oversight and Determination by embedding it within “Governance and oversight” and “Responsibility.” It calls for regulatory frameworks that clearly define the roles and obligations of developers providers users and regulators across the AI lifecycle ensuring that AI systems remain subject to institutional control. It further requires oversight mechanisms audits traceability and impact assessments so that AI decisions can be reviewed and attributed. By mandating accountability of public institutions businesses and individuals for AI-related harms it affirms that ultimate decision-making authority and responsibility remain with human actors not autonomous systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document embeds human oversight within governance and responsibility frameworks requiring regulatory structures that define the roles and obligations of developers providers users and regulators across the AI lifecycle. It mandates oversight mechanisms audits traceability and impact assessments to ensure AI systems remain subject to institutional control and that ultimate decision-making authority and accountability remain with human actors (p. 38).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document emphasizes human oversight accountability and institutional control over AI systems requiring mechanisms such as audits traceability and impact assessments to review AI-enabled decisions (p. 38). While these provisions reinforce the role of human judgment and responsibility the document does not explicitly prohibit full automation in specific sensitive sectors such as law enforcement or healthcare.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The document calls for regulatory frameworks that clearly define the roles and obligations of developers providers users and regulators ensuring that responsibility for AI systems is assigned to identifiable human actors. It also requires accountability mechanisms and traceability making organizations and individuals responsible for AI-related outcomes and ensuring that human actors can oversee and intervene in AI operations (p. 38).

items.title: Digital Agenda of Albania 2022–2026
items.justification: The strategy aims to integrate advanced technologies explicitly including AI (p. 11) and frames digital education and training of public employees as an absolute prerequisite for their implementation and adaptation (p. 17). It further emphasises the digitisation of public-sector data and archives as a necessary condition for enabling such technologies (p. 17). In addition it recognises the growing importance of predictive analytics and AI in identifying potential governance challenges early (p. 15) whilst carrying out  actions  aimed  at  improving  the  digital  skills  of  civil  servants  and  employees  in  local  and  regional  government  and  public  administration (p. 36).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: various ministries and other institutions

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: National AI Strategy 2025–2030 (draft) (Albania)
items.justification: The document addresses reskilling and upskilling in the context of AI mainly through its Education and Workforce Development pillar and the Action Plan. It commits to AI-related upskilling and reskilling programs for individuals already in the workforce including civil servants and professionals to adapt to AI-driven labour changes (pg. 34–36). It foresees continuing education vocational training programs in AI and data science and lifelong learning pathways linked to employability (pg. 35–36). The Action Plan highlights retraining workers for higher-value roles as automation expands and integrates AI skills into national education and training strategies (pg. 42–44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The strategy commits to AI-related upskilling and reskilling programs for individuals already in the workforce including civil servants and professionals to help them adapt to labour market changes driven by AI (pp. 34–36). It also foresees continuing education vocational training in AI and data science and lifelong learning pathways linked to employability with the Action Plan emphasizing retraining workers for higher-value roles as automation expands (pp. 35–36; pp. 42–44).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The document refers to financial support instruments such as scholarships and grants for studies and research in AI and support for training programs as part of workforce development (pp. 35–36). However it does not clearly establish direct financial incentives targeted specifically at workers participating in reskilling programs.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Law No. 124/2024 “On the Protection of Personal Data”
items.justification: The law addresses explainability through Art. 14–15 (pg 11–13) on information duties requiring notice of automated decision-making and “meaningful information about the logic involved'. Art. 22 (pg 18–19) regulates automated decision-making and profiling granting the right to human intervention and to contest decisions.Art. 24–26 (pg 20–23) require records of processing and risk assessments supporting auditability and oversight.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Commissioner for the Right to Information and Protection of Personal Data

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The law requires information duties regarding automated decision-making including providing meaningful information about the logic involved (Arts. 14–15 pp. 11–13) which promotes transparency about how automated systems function.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The law obliges controllers to provide “meaningful information about the logic involved” in automated decision-making and profiling particularly where decisions produce legal or similarly significant effects (Art. 14–15 pg 11–13; Art. 22 pg 18–19).This applies to high-stakes contexts such as employment or credit decisions and includes the right to human intervention and to contest the outcome.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes the right to receive “meaningful information about the logic involved” in automated decision-making and profiling (Art. 14–15 pg 11–13; Art. 22 pg 18–19). It also guarantees the right to human intervention and to contest decisions. These provisions ensure individuals can obtain explanations and understand key factors behind decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects.

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Angola)
items.justification: The Draft Law on AI addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence mainly through criminal liability provisions. Article 76 criminalizes the intentional use of AI systems to violate fundamental rights promote discrimination or hatred through algorithms or harm democratic processes and public order. Article 77 increases penalties when crimes are committed using advanced technologies such as “deepfakes or bots” that manipulate public opinion. Article 51 requires AI-generated news content to include visible identifiers to ensure information accuracy. These provisions target malicious uses of AI that spread disinformation or incite harm.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence explicitly excludes military AI from its scope stating that development and use of AI for military purposes are regulated under a separate legal framework (Article 4). Personal or family AI use and scientific research are also excluded confirming that defence and security are explicitly outside this law’s remit.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Draft on Artificial Intelligence partially addresses this issue through criminal provisions. Article 76 criminalizes the intentional use of AI systems to promote discrimination incite hatred through algorithms or harm democratic processes and public order. Article 77 further increases penalties when crimes are committed using technologies such as “deepfakes or bots” used to manipulate public opinion. However the law focuses mainly on punishment after misuse rather than preventive safeguards or technical restrictions preventing AI systems from generating or amplifying misinformation or harassment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence includes limited obligations related to information integrity but does not establish comprehensive platform moderation requirements. Article 51 requires news services using AI to ensure the accuracy of information and to include visible identifiers for AI-generated content. Article 53 requires social-bot providers to control information quality and prevent abuses that manipulate public opinion.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence provides mechanisms for accountability and compensation but does not create specific victim protection regimes for misinformation harms. Article 31 establishes the right for individuals to submit complaints against AI providers and pursue legal action if grievances are not addressed. Additionally Article 80 establishes strict civil liability requiring developers or suppliers of AI systems to compensate damages caused to third parties.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Personal Data Protection Law (Draft) (2025) (Angola)
items.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data '2025 Version' guarantees Access to Redress and Remedy by granting data subjects the right to request explanations of AI decisions contest outputs and demand human intervention (Article 37 Section II). Article 33 prohibits harmful fully automated decisions and requires disclosure of criteria upon request. Articles 26–32 ensure rights to access rectification deletion and complaints to a supervisory authority reinforcing avenues for remedy.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data '2025 Version' explicitly excludes certain data processing activities related to national defense public security internal or external state intelligence and Activities of investigation and repression of criminal offenses from its scope (Article 4 n.º 2 letters a–d). These activities are instead governed by specific legislation which must respect proportionality and necessity principles but are not covered by the general data protection law.

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data '2025 Version' grants individuals affected by AI systems the right to contest decisions request explanations and demand human intervention (Article 37). It also establishes responsibilities for entities operating AI systems (Article 38) and sets sanctions for violations (Article 73). However it does not explicitly establish or detail judicial mechanisms for seeking remedies meaning the framework addresses some aspects of redress but does not mandate formal judicial procedures.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Angola)
items.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence requires AI developers to ensure fairness among users preventing discrimination based on gender age ethnicity region belief or economic status (Article 23). Risk assessments must identify potential biases and verify ethical compliance (Article 33). Critical AI requires audited data labeling to improve fairness and accuracy (Article 42). Criminal penalties apply for AI used to discriminate or incite hate (Article 76).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence explicitly excludes military AI from its scope stating that development and use of AI for military purposes are regulated under a separate legal framework (Article 4). Personal or family AI use and scientific research are also excluded confirming that defence and security are explicitly outside this law’s remit.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence mandates AI developers and suppliers to ensure fairness among users prevent prejudice and discrimination and guarantee equitable access regardless of gender age ethnicity region belief or economic status (Article 23). Critical AI must undergo data labeling audits to enhance fairness (Article 42). Risk assessments further ensure ethical compliance and equitable outcomes (Article 33).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence requires AI risk assessments to identify potential biases or discrimination (Article 33) and criminalizes AI use intended to promote discrimination or incite hate (Article 76). Critical AI systems must follow audited data labeling rules to reduce bias ensuring outputs do not reinforce societal inequities (Article 42).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence obliges developers and suppliers to conduct risk assessments before deployment and upon significant changes (Article 33) implement data labeling audits for critical AI (Article 42) and adopt measures to prevent prejudice and discrimination at all stages (Article 23). Criminal liability enforces accountability for failure to mitigate bias (Article 76).

items.title: Personal Data Protection Law (Draft) (2025) (Angola)
items.justification: The draft addresses human oversight indirectly through safeguards on automated processing and AI systems. Chapter III Art. 33 regulates “automated individual decisions” limiting decisions based solely on automated processing and granting data subjects rights when affected by AI-driven processing. Articles 36–38 also defines profiling as automated evaluation of personal aspects and sets obligations and prohibited practices for entities developing or operating AI systems. While these provisions restrict fully automated decisions and establish accountability the draft does not define operational human-in-the-loop procedures or detailed oversight mechanisms for high-risk uses.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data '2025 Version' explicitly excludes certain data processing activities related to national defense public security internal or external state intelligence and Activities of investigation and repression of criminal offenses from its scope (Article 4 n.º 2 letters a–d). These activities are instead governed by specific legislation which must respect proportionality and necessity principles but are not covered by the general data protection law.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The draft frameworkChapter III Art. 33 limits solely automated decisions and recognizes rights of individuals affected by AI-based processing implying that automated outcomes should not be final without safeguards. Articles 36–38 also places responsibilities on AI developers/operators. However it does not explicitly require meaningful human control human authorization for high-risk decisions or define HITL/HOTL mechanisms to ensure AI assists rather than replaces human judgment in critical sectors.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Draft framework Articles 36–38 assigns responsibilities and obligations to entities that develop or operate AI systems and process personal data establishing accountability for compliance and harms. However it does not explicitly require the designation of specific responsible individuals (e.g. an AI officer) to oversee intervene in or be personally accountable for AI system decisions nor does it define oversight roles.

items.title: Personal Data Protection Law (Draft) (2025) (Angola)
items.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data (2025 Version) addresses Impact Assessments in the context of AI under Articles 36–38 (Section II) and Articles 43(1–9) (Chapter IV). Article 43(1–9) (Chapter IV) requires controllers to perform a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before any processing likely to result in high risks such as profiling or automated decision-making using AI systems. The DPIA must evaluate the nature scope context and purposes of processing identify risks to data subjects and define mitigation measures. Supervisory authority consultation is required before deployment if high residual risks remain.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4.2 of the Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data (2025 Version) explicitly excludes processing of personal data for purposes related to national defence public security internal and external intelligence and criminal investigation or prosecution. And according to 4.3 the processing of personal data referred to in the previous paragraph is governed by specific legislation which must provide for measures that are proportionate and strictly necessary for the pursuit of the public interest as well as the general principles of data protection and the rights of data subjects provided for in this law.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data (2025 Version) partially promotes proactive risk management. Article 36 requires controllers to implement technical and organizational measures to prevent risks arising from automated processing including profiling. Articles 37–38 establish obligations for security and confidentiality. Article 43(1–9) mandates a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before high-risk processing such as AI-based automated decisions and requires prior consultation with the supervisory authority if residual risks remain. However it does not address societal ethical or environmental impacts beyond data protection.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Personal Data Protection Law assigns obligations to data controllers who may include AI developers and users to assess and mitigate risks before initiating automated processing. Article 36 of the Draft Personal Data Protection Law explicitly prohibits the implementation and use of AI systems that compromise privacy exploit vulnerabilities or conduct illegitimate profiling of individuals based on social behavior or personality traits. Article 43(1–9) further requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for high-risk processing identifying potential harms and defining mitigation measures. However these provisions focus on data protection and privacy risks not broader societal impacts of AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: White Book on Information and Communication Technologies (2023–2027)
items.justification: The White Book on ICT (2023–2027 sec. 5.6.7.1 pp. 99–103) proposes workforce reskilling with AI competencies including the National Workforce Training Plan Young Smarts Program training for regulatory authorities scholarships university partnerships hackathons and ethical AI guidelines which promote both technical and ethical skills for public servants and the judiciary. Further p. 101 states that AI has the potential to improve the performance and efficiency of public services but few public sector institutions are currently leveraging it. It is imperative to invest in awareness-raising through pilot projects demonstrations and capacity building to implement and manage AI projects thus providing better public services. The Executive will engage local AI solution providers through innovation-friendly procurement processes organize training sessions and invest in hackathons awards and challenges to open opportunities for responsible AI applications in the public sector.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The White Book establishes a National Workforce Training Plan and the Young Smarts Program to develop AI competencies across the civil service and regulatory authorities including the judiciary. It outlines measures for workforce reskilling technical and ethical training and AI literacy (section 5.6.7.1 pp. 99–103).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The White Book proposes the creation of a National AI Council ethical AI networks and guidance structures establishing dedicated roles to foster responsible AI innovation provide expert advice and promote best practices across public institutions (section 5.6.7.1 pp. 99–103).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The White Book emphasizes continuous workforce reskilling technical and ethical training hackathons and partnerships with universities to develop AI competencies (section 5.6.7.1 pp. 99–103). However it does not specify formal recurring professional development requirements certifications or mandatory refresher programs for public servants or judiciary to systematically keep pace with AI advancements.

items.title: Personal Data Protection Law (Draft) (2025) (Angola)
items.justification: The draft law (Section II Articles 36–38; Chapter IV Articles 39–43) ensures Safety and Security by prohibiting manipulative AI practices requiring secure data management transparency and human oversight. It mandates data protection by design encryption breach notification and impact assessments to prevent risks to individuals’ rights and data integrity.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4.2 of the Draft Law on the Protection of Personal Data (2025 Version) explicitly excludes processing of personal data for purposes related to national defence public security internal and external intelligence and criminal investigation or prosecution. And according to 4.3 the processing of personal data referred to in the previous paragraph is governed by specific legislation which must provide for measures that are proportionate and strictly necessary for the pursuit of the public interest as well as the general principles of data protection and the rights of data subjects provided for in this law.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The draft law addresses aspects of AI reliability and accuracy through Articles 36–38 (Section II) and Articles 39–43 (Chapter IV) by requiring secure data handling transparency human oversight and pre-deployment impact assessments. These measures indirectly support reliability and accuracy but do not establish explicit numeric performance thresholds or formal quality benchmarks for AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The draft law addresses safeguards and risk mitigation indirectly through Articles 36–38 (Section II) and Articles 39–43 (Chapter IV) by requiring human oversight secure data handling transparency and data protection impact assessments. These measures help prevent harm from AI misuse or failures but do not explicitly mandate formal fallback procedures or emergency protocols for AI system malfunctions.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The draft law addresses pre-deployment evaluation indirectly through Articles 36–38 (Section II) and Articles 43(1–9) (Chapter IV) which require data protection impact assessments and documentation of data processing risks. These measures help assess AI system robustness; however the law does not explicitly mandate or mention about systematic pre-deployment testing validation or technical documentation throughout the AI system lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The draft law addresses security obligations in Articles 39–42 (Chapter IV Section I) requiring the data controller and processors to implement technical and organizational measures including pseudonymization encryption confidentiality integrity and resilience of systems.

items.title: Guide for the Integration of Artificial Intelligences in Education
items.justification: The document addresses AI literacy by explaining what AI is how it works and its limitations offering foundational knowledge for teachers and students (Presentation and Introduction pp. 5–7). It promotes critical understanding of algorithms bias and ethical risks (Secondary Education p. 13; Governance and data protection p. 20). It also includes explicit recommendations for developing responsible transparent and informed use of AI in the classroom strengthening digital and AI skills (Recommendations p. 16).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: PP. 16-17 establish an 'RTD' (Responsible Transparent and Documented) approach for teachers. This requires modeling AI use by openly declaring its support and documenting tools employed. Key lines of action include: 1) Professional Development: Programs covering technical skills and pedagogical strategies; 2) AI Literacy: Training students to use AI critically while valuing academic integrity; and 3) Institutional Support: Investment in infrastructure and ongoing training. However the guideline does not include any reference to state-led investment for educational resources and training.

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: Section 5 (pp. 20-21) mandates that AI data processing be 'consistent with international law.' It integrates Law 25326 guaranteeing rights to rectification updating and deletion of inaccurate or irrelevant data plus the right to object to processing for advertising. Critically page 25 establishes that individuals have the right 'not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing' that significantly affects them. This includes the right to obtain human intervention express their point of view and dispute the decision. By combining data protection with human oversight the framework ensures individuals maintain control and can challenge automated outcomes throughout the AI lifecycle
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Page 41 states that AI privacy policies must include 'the right to file a complaint with the Public Information Access Agency' (AAIP) and provide contact details regarding data processing. Furthermore page 44 requires organizations to 'enable communication channels' for user inquiries and complaints. However while the framework facilitates reporting to the data protection authority and requires internal channels it lacks explicit comprehensive state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms specifically designed to address broader AI-related grievances beyond personal data protection

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Page 37 recommends designating a person responsible for 'answering queries and responding to possible incidents.' Page 44 adds that organizations including the private sector (p. 43) should enable communication channels for inquiries and complaints emphasizing clear language and human assistance for vulnerable groups or those preferring non-digital contact. However while the framework promotes transparency and user support channels it does not establish explicit formal grievance or redress mechanisms specifically for individuals harmed by AI systems. It focuses on communication and incident response rather than providing a structured legal or administrative path for victim compensation or formal dispute resolution

items.title: Disposition 2/2023 – 'Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence'(Undersecretariat of Information Technologies Chief of the Cabinet of Ministers) (Argentina)
items.justification: Section 3 Principle 5: “Equidad y no discriminación” (p. 5) states that AI systems should “promote diversity and inclusion safeguard equity and avoid bias or discrimination based on gender ethnicity age or other characteristics.” The document also emphasises the need to identify and mitigate algorithmic bias throughout the AI lifecycle to ensure equitable and human-centred outcomes.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: It recommends that AI systems promote diversity and inclusion safeguard equity and avoid bias or discrimination based on gender ethnicity age or other traits. However it does not establish concrete mechanisms or measurable objectives to ensure fair outcomes or to monitor and correct biased results (p. 5)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: It recommends public entities developing or using AI to identify and mitigate algorithmic bias promoting fair and inclusive systems yet 'partially' was chosen since there are no technical methods specified to do so or accountability procedures for continuous bias assessment across the AI lifecycle.

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The Guide addresses gender equality noting AI can amplify discrimination (pp. 6–7). It identifies 'genders and dissidences' as vulnerable groups (p. 7). In 'Main problems and challenges' (pp. 16–18) it highlights gender and ethnic bias specifically in facial recognition (affecting women with darker skin) and language models. Under 'Transparency and Data Protection Principles' (p. 22) gender identity is categorized as sensitive data requiring special protection. Although the guideline acknowledges gender as a critical issue throughout these sections the audit reveals that it is not translated into specific actionable obligations within the final recommended principles
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: In the Introduction it identifies gender equity and genders and dissidences as areas vulnerable to unfair decisions (pp. 6–7). In Main problems and challenges of AI it explicitly highlights gender bias noting higher error rates for women in facial recognition and the reinforcement of stereotypes in language models grouped under ethnic and gender bias (pp. 16–18). Under 'Transparency and Data Protection Principles' (p. 22) gender identity is categorized as sensitive data requiring special protection. These sections frame bias prevention as a key objective but not directly as a principle.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: It sets out responsibilities such as proactive accountability risk assessments audits and bias reviews throughout the AI lifecycle (pp. 26–39). It highlights gender bias as a key risk (pp. 16–18) but the obligations are defined broadly to prevent discrimination and protect rights in general rather than as explicit gender oriented actions.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: Page 25 provides the right to control how people's data is collected. It establishes the right to human intervention allowing them to request a review by a physical person for decisions based on automated processing that significantly affect them such as profiling or credit assessments. Organisations are encouraged to ensure significant human intervention and are required to disclose their forms of human supervision in transparency sheets to avoid purely mechanical determinations (Page 47). The guide recommends appointing specific personnel responsible for manually monitoring system behaviour and providing human communication channels for users who prefer interacting with a person rather than a machine (Pages 37 and 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It emphasises that humans must retain the final decision-making authority especially when AI affects individual rights or public interests (Page 25). Page 47 provides the right 'not to be subject to a decision that produces adverse legal effects negatively affects him or her or has discriminatory effects based solely or partially on automated data processing including profiling and inference'. Yet the framework does not explicitly mention critical areas providing only a few examples.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The document includes impact assessments and risk management across the entire lifecycle of AI systems (pp. 28–32). A subsection titled “Impact assessments” explains that these studies help identify risks such as re-identification of individuals algorithmic bias and misuse of data (p. 29). The document also specifies which companies must develop risk management strategies and provides a risk matrix along with guidance for conducting AI impact assessments (p. 30). It further distinguishes between material and moral impact (p. 32) and emphasises that impact assessments should be conducted continuously during validation implementation operation and maintenance (pp. 31–32).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Section “Principle of proactive and demonstrated accountability” emphasizes that impact assessment is a cross-cutting principle and applies “to all stages of an Artificial Intelligence system’s lifecycle and includes impact assessment and risk management monitoring and detailed documentation of actions staff training specialised technical teams (also referred to as data protection officers) incident management audits and reviews among other measures” (p. 28). The recommendation from Stage 1 (p. 36) explicitly states: 'Evaluate the project's impact on personal data protection from the outset including risks and adverse impacts.'

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Impact assessments are mandatory for organizations processing large data volumes sensitive data or conducting profiling via automated processing. This applies to both large corporations and startups where processing poses privacy risks. The framework uses a risk matrix to categorize systems as high medium or low risk based on probability and impact. Notably sensitive data processing requires 'enhanced responsibility' involving superior security levels confidentiality and stricter access controls (p.29-32). However it is not entirely clear whether these comprehensive impact assessment requirements apply to all developers and users across the AI lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Draft Law on Regulatory Framework and Development of AI Systems
items.justification: Article 5 establishes in i) as one of the core principles of the law the 'Transparency in the algorithmic management of work' which provides the right of workers or their representatives to be informed on whether an automated system is used for monitoring or making decisions that affect them. These systems must be transparent and audited and be constantly supervised by humans. Art. 18 point (c) classifies as high-risk any AI system used for: 'recruitment selection screening candidate evaluation and decision-making regarding promotions or terminations of contractual employment relationships; the distribution of tasks; and the control and evaluation of the performance and behavior of the people affected by these applications
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 5 establishes in principle i): 'Transparency in the algorithmic management of work' granting workers and their representatives the right to be informed when automated systems are used for monitoring or decision-making. These systems must be transparent audited and under constant human oversight. Furthermore Art. 18 (c) classifies as high-risk any AI system used for recruitment candidate evaluation promotions or terminations. This classification also extends to systems managing task distribution and the evaluation of performance or behavior of those affected by these applications. This dual approach ensures both transparency and strict oversight in the workplace

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Article 5 directly addresses this in the pinciple i) which provides the right of workers or their representatives to be informed on whether an automated system is used for monitoring or making decisions that affect them. These systems must be transparent and audited and be constantly supervised by humans. Companies must report on the use of automated control or decision-making systems workers under these systems their legal representatives and the authorities.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The Guideline expands on how to achieve algorithmic transparency (promoted on p. 36 as part of the Principle of Transparency and Explainability) including a specific 'AI Systems Transparency Sheet' (pp. 43-45). This section focuses on system characteristics organizational information and technical details that define the technology provided to the user. As stated on page 43 'organizations' explicitly include the public sector. This ensures that transparency obligations apply to state-led implementations fulfilling the requirements for public accountability
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: Page 43 recommends including key organizational and technical details in a 'transparency sheet' such as the implementing entity system objectives and the problem being addressed. It also covers system functionalities operating modes and the contact information of the person responsible for implementation. While these requirements ensure granular transparency for individual systems the framework does not mention a public registry or national inventory of AI systems

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: Page 43 recommends detailing the system's risk level including input data types output data and data sources. However the framework does not establish differentiated obligations for high-risk systems and does not mandate Algorithmic Impact Assessments (AIA)

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: Pages 43 and 44 recommend disclosing whether the system interacts with citizens ensuring they are informed of its automated nature and the availability of human alternatives. Regarding communication and complaint channels (p. 44) the framework mandates that these be 'as clear and comprehensive as possible' using non-expert language. Furthermore it emphasizes establishing human-mediated communication to assist users and documenting all procedures

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The guidelines identify security risks such as cyberattacks data breaches and integrity compromises (p. 17). Security is a core principle for protecting personal and sensitive data against unauthorized access or loss (pp. 20 23). In Section 6 the framework mandates security measures for data processing (p. 33) including incident management protocols (p. 34). During the validation stage testing and monitoring are required to ensure data quality and mitigate risks (p. 37). Implementation requires security standards to ensure traceability and human accountability (p. 39). Finally the framework establishes that security monitoring and control are essential during the final stages of the AI lifecycle (p. 41
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Section 6 details security measures for personal data processing within the AI lifecycle (p. 33) specifically mandating a 'Security incident management protocol' (p. 34). On page 37 the framework emphasizes that monitoring and recording tests during the validation stage are vital for ensuring data quality security and risk mitigation. During implementation security standards are required to ensure system actions and decisions remain traceable including the identification of responsible personnel (p. 39). These requirements establish a continuous security framework from data ingestion through to final system deployment

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Section 6 details security measures for personal data processing within the AI lifecycle (p. 33) specifically mandating a 'Security incident management protocol' (p. 34). The main objective is to implement technical and organizational measures to protect personal data against unauthorized access disclosure alteration and destruction. Furthermore the framework considers the Security Incident Management Protocol a key principle within the broader scope of impact assessment measures

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: During verification and validation (p. 37) models must be tested to evaluate performance and impact. To enhance transparency the framework suggests publishing an ethical commitment statement detailing individuals responsible for critical roles. It emphasizes that monitoring and recording tests are vital to ensure data quality security and risk mitigation (p. 37). Finally the framework identifies documentation and reporting as essential actions for the testing phase (p. 38

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Regarding the operation and maintenance stage (p. 42) the framework recommends reporting ethical or security incidents to the relevant authority considering the affected sector and the rights involved. While it notes that incidents include 'external attacks' the framework does not explicitly mention cyberattacks model manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Guide for Public and Private Entities on Transparency and Protection of Personal Data for Responsible Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: In Section 4 (pp. 16–19) the framework identifies 'lack of transparency' as a key risk noting that 'AI models can be complex and opaque making it difficult to understand how decisions are made.' Consequently if data algorithms and internal processes remain unknown a transparency deficit occurs. To mitigate this Section 5 (pp. 20-26) establishes the 'Principles related to transparency' stating: 'Individuals must have the opportunity to request explanations and information from the AI controller or relevant public sector institutions.' (p.21). This confirms that the right to an explanation regarding decisions made by AI systems is an integral part of the framework's mandate
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: According to the 'Principles related to transparency' (page 21) individuals must have the opportunity to request explanations and information from the AI controller or relevant public sector institutions about decisions or services provided by AI systems. Regarding the public sector citizens have the right to request information from the agency responsible for implementing a system that integrates Artificial Intelligence (page 22)

items.title: National Strategy against Disinformation (Armenia)
items.justification: According to the strategy the private sector is key in combating disinformation by developing AI- and machine learning-based tools.  Closer cooperation between governments and platforms on algorithms advertising and co-regulation can enhance resilience against large-scale disinformation.(page 22 2.4 Engagement and mobilization of private sector )
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The ministries the National Security Service the Government Staff as well as other governmental bodies and organizations are mentioned

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Amendments to the Criminal Code of the Republic of Armenia
items.justification: The Draft Law broadens the conceptual scope of child pornography extending its definition to encompass materials generated by means of artificial intelligence

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
