thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

items.title: Australian Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Schools
items.justification: The Framework integrates AI literacy by requiring schools to teach students how generative AI works its limitations potential biases and appropriate ethical use. Page 7 (Principle 1.2) states that schools must “engage students in learning about generative AI tools and how they work including their potential limitations and biases.” It also links AI literacy to critical thinking academic integrity safe data use and awareness of risks ensuring students develop informed ethical and practical competencies.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Framework states it does not address other forms of AI including predictive AI or broader national security applications (p.3)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Framework does not prescribe curriculum reforms but encourages integrating learning about generative AI through instruction critical thinking and responsible use (Principle 1.2 p.7). It expects students to learn how AI works its limitations and ethical considerations which implies curriculum-related adjustments but no formal curriculum reform is mandated.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Framework emphasises that teachers must have access to clear information and guidance (Principle 3.1 p. 6) and that generative AI should support teachers' expertise (Principle 1.3). It also states that teachers must help students learn how AI works and manage risks. These provisions indicate a need for teacher capability building and resources to teach AI effectively.

items.title: Gen AI Strategies for Australian Higher Education: Emerging Practice
items.justification: The document embeds AI literacy by requiring institutions to build student and staff capability to “use gen AI tools effectively and ethically” (Foreword p.1). Sections on Student support (pp.26–30) and Staff engagement (pp.32–36) call for training modules guidance workshops and resources to develop skills critical understanding and ethical use. It emphasises literacy in academic integrity modules curriculum review and assessment design (pp.43–51).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The toolkit calls for curriculum and assessment review to integrate gen AI literacy including revising learning outcomes embedding ethical AI use and transforming assessment design (pp.43–51). However this only applies to the tertiary level not the primary/secondary.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The document does include measures related to AI education but not in the sense of establishing formal AI degree programs or institutions. Instead it focuses on integrating generative AI training and literacy into existing higher education structures. For example it recommends providing GenAI training modules and other training resources for students and staff updating academic integrity modules to include ethical AI use and offering professional development opportunities to increase capabilities as responsible AI users (pp.26-36).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: It explicitly requires providers to offer gen AI training modules resource hubs staff induction professional development workshops and ongoing support for ethical and effective AI use (pp. 32-36). These measures directly address teacher and staff AI capability building.

items.title: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024
items.justification: The Act amends the Criminal Code to create offences for using a carriage service to transmit sexual material of an adult without consent regardless of whether the material is unaltered or “created or altered in any way using technology”. A note clarifies this expressly includes material edited or generated using digital technology “including artificial intelligence” such as realistic but false “deepfakes” (p. 4). Aggravated offences apply where the offender created or altered the material (p. 5).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Act criminalises the use of a carriage service to transmit sexual material without consent including material “created or altered in any way using technology (including artificial intelligence)” (s 474.17A(1)–(2) p. 4). A statutory note clarifies that this includes realistic but false “deepfake” material (Note to s 474.17A p. 4). An aggravated offence applies where the offender created or altered the material using digital technology (s 474.17AA(5) p. 6). These provisions directly address AI-facilitated harassment and violence but the Act does not address broader misinformation or hate speech.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes criminal offences for transmitting sexual material of a person without consent including material created or altered using digital technology such as AI (s. 474.17A(1)-(2) pp. 3-4). Individuals who use a carriage service to transmit such material may face imprisonment of up to 6 years with aggravated offences carrying up to 7 years (s. 474.17A(1)-(2) pp. 4-6). These provisions provide legal protection under the law and enable redress through criminal prosecution of perpetrators. However the Act does not establish rights to redress against platforms.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly covers sexual material “created or altered…using digital technology (including artificial intelligence)” including deepfakes and criminalises transmitting such material without consent (s 474.17A(1)–(2)  p. 4). An aggravated offence applies where the offender created or altered the material (s 474.17AA(5) p. 6). These provisions directly aim to deter and punish non-consensual sexual deepfakes and similar tech-facilitated sexual abuse which disproportionately manifests as gender-based harassment and violence.

items.title: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL)
items.justification: Although the ACL is technologically neutral and does not refer to AI it is valid and meaningful for the indicator when read in light of the Government Treasury’s discussion paper Review of AI and the Australian Consumer Law (https://storage.googleapis.com/files-au-treasury/treasury/p/prj3726058ed26a734ddd6e6/public_assets/c2024-584560-dp.pdf). As an official interpretive material it clarifies that consumers of AI-enabled goods and services can rely on existing guarantees and seek compensation (pp. 2 11) while noting challenges due to AI (p. 12). The ACL itself outlines remedies in Sections 259–260 and permits claims for damages under Section 236. The framework can be used due to the interpretative materials extending its scope to remedies for AI-enabled goods/services.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Although the ACL is technologically neutral and does not explicitly refer to AI it addresses access to redress and remedies when read together with the Government Treasury’s discussion paper Review of AI and the Australian Consumer Law (https://storage.googleapis.com/files-au-treasury/treasury/p/prj3726058ed26a734ddd6e6/public_assets/c2024-584560-dp.pdf). The paper clarifies that existing mechanisms apply to AI-enabled goods and services including compensation where guarantees are breached (pp. 2 11) while noting challenges due to AI (p. 12) and confirming the adequacy of the framework (p. 6). However it does not establish new AI-specific judicial mechanisms; the ACL provides only general remedies under Sections 259–260 and 236.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Although the ACL does not explicitly refer to AI it must be read together with the Government Treasury’s discussion paper Review of AI and the Australian Consumer Law (https://storage.googleapis.com/files-au-treasury/treasury/p/prj3726058ed26a734ddd6e6/public_assets/c2024-584560-dp.pdf). The materials indicate that consumers who suffer loss or damage can make a complaint to a regulator (p. 12) thereby reflecting the use of existing state-based non-judicial mechanisms. However this is framed within the general consumer protection system of the ACL and is not specifically tailored to AI-related grievances thus parital.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Basic Online Safety Expectations Regulatory Guidance (July 2024)
items.justification: Adds an expectation that providers make the “best interests of the child” a primary consideration where services are likely accessed by children (s.6(2A)); requires robust default privacy/safety settings for children’s services (s.6(3)(b)); mandates safety risk assessments incl. child safety (s.6(3)(e)); requires age assurance and improved tech to prevent children’s access to Class 2 material (s.12(2)(a)(c)); enables eSafety to request child/adult user counts (s.20(5)). Specific steps must also be taken when the services use generative AI (s.8A) to mitigate risks and impacts for the child.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Determination is administered by the eSafety Commissioner under section 45 of the Online Safety Act 2021 Several provisions (eg s20(5)) explicitly authorise the Commissioner to request reports and enforce compliance with the Basic Online Safety Expectations

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems

Specific steps must also be taken when the services use generative AI (s.8A) to mitigate risks and impacts for the child.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Requires providers to minimise unlawful/harmful outputs from generative AI (s.8A) and reduce harmful amplification by recommender systems (s.8B) plus hate-speech and harmful content processes (s.6(3)(h)(i)). It doesn’t specifically address “targeted advertising.”

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: “Best interests of the child” as a primary consideration (s.6(2A)); child-safety risk assessments across design?post-deployment (s.6(3)(e)); age assurance (s.12(2)(a)); safety measures for generative AI and recommender systems (ss.8A–8B).

items.title: Australia's AI Ethics Principles
items.justification: The framework places particular emphasis on cultural diversity as a key safeguard in the design and deployment of AI systems. It encourages organisations to involve individuals from diverse cultural backgrounds alongside different disciplines and perspectives to ensure that AI systems reflect a broader range of social values and lived experiences (p. 4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: National framework for the assurance of artificial intelligence in government (2024) (Australia)
items.justification: The framework addresses environmental impact through the principle “Human societal and environmental wellbeing” which states that AI systems should benefit individuals society and the environment throughout their lifecycle (p. 13). It requires governments to define expected outcomes for people society and the environment and to assess likely impacts of AI use cases on people communities societal and environmental wellbeing to determine whether benefits outweigh risks (p. 13). It also refers more broadly to environmental wellbeing in the ministerial statement (p.1). Under contestability it also mentions hat When an AI system significantly impacts the environment there should be a timely process to allow people to contest it (p. 23).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
items.justification: The document addresses fairness and non-discrimination by requiring organisations to ensure AI systems serve all people regardless of attributes such as gender race age or disability and by recognising that bias can lead to unfair disadvantage or unlawful discrimination (pp. 4 7). Under Guardrail 10 organisations must engage stakeholders including marginalised groups identify potential bias and minimise negative effects of unwanted bias in AI systems (pp. 42–44). It also requires organisations to evaluate impacts on diversity inclusion and fairness and to mitigate discriminatory outcomes through governance processes and impact assessments (pp. 26 42–44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: It promotes fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems by requiring organisations to identify and mitigate bias and discrimination in AI development and deployment. It emphasises that AI systems should serve all people regardless of attributes such as gender race age or disability and recognises that bias can lead to unfair disadvantage or unlawful discrimination (p. 4). Under Guardrail 10 organisations must identify potential bias minimise negative effects of unwanted bias and ensure AI systems do not undermine diversity inclusion and fairness (pp. 42–44). It requires stakeholder engagement evaluation of impacts on affected groups and the documentation of processes to prevent discriminatory outcomes in AI systems (pp. 26 42–44).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document includes provisions to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal bias and discrimination. It states that AI systems should serve all people regardless of attributes such as gender race age or disability and recognises that bias can lead to unfair disadvantage or unlawful discrimination (p. 4). Under Guardrail 10 organisations are required to identify potential bias minimise negative effects of unwanted bias and remove ethical prejudices from AI systems while evaluating impacts on diversity inclusion and fairness and engaging affected stakeholders (pp. 42–44). These measures aim to ensure AI systems do not produce discriminatory outcomes affecting protected groups.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns obligations to organisations developing and deploying AI systems to identify assess and mitigate bias across the AI lifecycle. Under Guardrail 10 organisations must identify potential bias minimise negative effects of unwanted bias and remove ethical prejudices from AI systems (pp. 42–44). It also requires stakeholder engagement and evaluation of potential harms to individuals and groups as well as the documentation of processes to ensure AI systems do not undermine diversity inclusion and fairness (pp. 42–44). These provisions require organisations to proactively address bias during the development and deployment of AI systems.

items.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
items.justification: The framework addresses gender equality through its emphasis on fairness inclusion and the mitigation of algorithmic bias. The document notes that AI systems can amplify discrimination against groups such as women and therefore requires organisations to identify and minimise unwanted bias (p.7). The standard also highlights that biased training data can produce discriminatory outcomes such as under-diagnosis or misdiagnosis of women (p.10) requiring risk assessments testing and oversight mechanisms to detect and mitigate such harms (Guardrails 2 pp.19–21).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The document includes provisions addressing the risk of AI systems perpetuating discrimination and bias including gender bias. It states that organisations should assess potential harms caused by AI systems to individuals groups and communities including discrimination against women (p. 7). It also highlights that biased or non-representative training data can lead to AI-enabled discriminatory outcomes for example when health diagnostic systems trained on historically male-dominated datasets lead to the under-diagnosis or misdiagnosis of women (p. 10). These sections recognise gender bias as a risk in AI systems and recommend assessing and addressing such harms during AI development and deployment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The framework assigns responsibilities to organisations developing and deploying AI systems to assess and mitigate harms including discrimination affecting groups such as women (p. 7). It highlights that biased or non-representative training data can lead to discriminatory outcomes (p. 10). More broadly the framework also assigns general responsibilities to organisations to manage risks of bias and discrimination through governance mechanisms (pp. 16–18) risk and impact assessments (pp. 19–21) and testing and monitoring of AI systems (pp. 25–28). It also calls for stakeholder engagement and evaluation of impacts with attention to diversity inclusion and fairness (pp. 42–44).

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
items.justification: The framework addresses Human Oversight and Determination through governance and operational guardrails requiring human supervision of AI systems. Guardrail 5 requires organisations to “enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight across the lifecycle” (pp. 29–30). The standard also requires leadership accountability and governance structures for AI oversight (Guardrail 1 pp. 16–18). Additionally Guardrail 7 requires processes allowing people affected by AI systems to challenge decisions or outcomes (pp. 34-35) ensuring human review and contestability of AI-driven decisions.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 5 requires organisations to “enable human control or intervention in an AI system to achieve meaningful human oversight across the lifecycle” ensuring humans can intervene to reduce unintended harms (pp. 29-30). The standard also emphasises a human-centred approach to AI deployment that prioritises human rights and decision-making (p. 4). Additionally Guardrail 1 requires leadership accountability and governance structures overseeing AI use (pp.16–18) reinforcing that AI systems support rather than replace human judgement.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The framework promotes human oversight but does not explicitly prohibit full automation in specific sensitive sectors (e.g. law enforcement or medicine). Instead it provides general governance guidance requiring human control or intervention mechanisms to achieve meaningful human oversight across the AI lifecycle (Guardrail 5 pp.29–30). It also notes that systems operating without meaningful human oversight can increase risks particularly where AI decisions affect individuals (p. 9). Thus the framework supports maintaining human judgement in high-risk contexts but does not impose sector-specific restrictions on automation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 1 requires organisations to establish an accountability process including appointing an overall owner for AI use and leadership roles responsible for AI governance and outcomes (pp.16–18). It states that leaders cannot delegate accountability for the safe and responsible deployment of AI systems and must maintain operational accountability and meaningful human oversight across the AI lifecycle (p. 17). These provisions ensure responsible individuals oversee and remain accountable for AI-enabled decisions.

items.title: National framework for the assurance of artificial intelligence in government (2024) (Australia)
items.justification: The framework embeds Impact Assessment processes across the AI lifecycle. It requires governments to assess impacts on people communities society and the environment (p.13 s.1.3) conduct human rights impact assessments (p.14) privacy impact assessments (p.18) and apply a risk-based assessment model throughout design deployment and operation (pp.8–9). It also outlines verification testing monitoring and evaluation obligations (pp.20–23).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework emphasises proactive open AI risk management requiring agencies to assess impacts on people communities society and the environment (p.13 s.1.3) conduct human rights impact assessments (p.14) and privacy impact assessments (p.18).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The framework instructs government users to undertake multiple assessment types (impact rights privacy risk) (pp.13–18). However obligations on developers are indirect and mostly addressed through procurement guidance not mandated assessments.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Transparency requirements include disclosing AI use and maintaining explainable records (pp.21–22). Contestability provisions require clear communication of rights and access to review mechanisms (p.23). However the framework does not explicitly mandate public access to assessment findings.

items.title: Checklist: Privacy Considerations when using commercially available AI products
items.justification: The checklist requires organisations deploying AI to assess compliance risks across key stages of the AI lifecycle. It directs entities to evaluate collection generation and inference of personal information (p.1) accuracy and oversight of AI outputs (p.2) transparency and accountability measures (p.2) and ongoing monitoring and assurance processes (p.2). These obligations collectively function as a structured privacy-focused impact assessment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The checklist requires organisations to assess risks relating to data collection use accuracy transparency and oversight before deploying AI systems (pp.1–2). However it focuses only on privacy impacts not broader societal or environmental consequences.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The checklist outlines structured assessment steps—collection generation disclosure accuracy oversight transparency and ongoing monitoring (pp.1–2)—functioning as a privacy impact assessment. However it does not mandate full societal or human-rights-based impact assessments.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Standard for AI Transparency Statements: Supporting the policy for responsible use of AI in government
items.justification: The document mandates agencies publish a publicly available AI transparency statement outlining their AI use (p.4 “Your responsibilities”) . It requires disclosure of AI intentions classifications public interaction without human intervention governance measures legislative compliance and protections against negative impacts (p.4). Agencies must publish statements on their public website and update them at least annually or when changes occur (p.4). Attachment A (pp.7–8) requires classification of AI usage patterns and domains.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: The Standard requires agencies to publish public AI Transparency Statements describing their approach to AI use governance impacts and accountability (p. 4 “Your responsibilities”). However it does not establish a single public registry nor require disclosure of all individual AI systems. Agencies may provide only high-level information and are not required to list use-case-level details (p. 5 “Implementing the AI transparency statements”).

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The Standard requires agencies to publicly disclose high-level information about AI use including public impacts governance measures risk-mitigation processes and whether AI may significantly affect individuals without human intervention (p. 4 “Your responsibilities”). It also requires disclosure of monitoring measures and compliance with the Policy for Responsible Use of AI (pp. 4–5). However it does not require disclosure of training data model architecture or the results of impact assessments; agencies are explicitly not required to provide use-case-level detail (p. 5).

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The Standard requires transparency statements to be public-facing while complying with applicable legislation and regulation including privacy and security obligations (p. 4 “Your responsibilities”). It acknowledges the need to protect the public from negative impacts and comply with legal requirements (p. 4). However it does not set out clear criteria specifying what information must be withheld for national security or privacy reasons (pp. 4–5).

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: The Standard explicitly requires 'Statements must use clear plain language that is consistent with the Australian Government Style Manual and avoid technical jargon' (p. 4). Agencies must explain how AI is used its purpose impacts on individuals and governance arrangements in an accessible way (pp. 4–5 “Your responsibilities” and “Implementing the AI transparency statements”). This directly supports clear public understanding of AI systems and their effects.

items.title: National framework for the assurance of artificial intelligence in government (2024) (Australia)
items.justification: The framework includes a dedicated “Procurement” section (p. 10) that requires agencies to embed AI ethics transparency human oversight and risk-based assurance into procurement documentation and contracts. It emphasises due diligence vendor accountability lifecycle performance testing and prevention of opaque or high-risk systems ensuring the safe acquisition of AI across government.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The framework includes AI-specific procurement guidance that extends beyond traditional IT procurement. It requires consideration of “AI ethics principles” “clearly established accountabilities” “transparency of data” and “proof of performance testing throughout an AI system’s life cycle” (p.10). It also highlights risks such as explainability of ‘black box’ systems privacy security and ongoing monitoring and review mechanisms (p.10) reflecting ethical social and technical considerations beyond standard IT procurement.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The framework references the relevant dimensions (fairness/bias audits in use cases (p.16); reliability/safety testing incl. red teaming and monitoring (p.20); procurement expecting proof of performance testing across the lifecycle (p.10) ). However it stops short of requiring vendors to demonstrate bias fairness and safety testing as a vendor obligation; instead it asks agencies to consider a vendor’s capability to support review ongoing monitoring/evaluation and incident response (p.10)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: The framework requires procurement to consider “transparency of data” and access to relevant information assets (p.10) and highlights risks of ‘black box’ AI systems including explainability challenges (p.10). It also requires disclosure of AI use and maintaining records of data and decisions for scrutiny (p.21). However it does not impose a formal mandate compelling vendors to disclose detailed data sources or model information to prevent black-box systems.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: Policy for the responsible use of AI in government (Australia)
items.justification: The policy recommends that APS agencies implement AI training for all staff within six months of commencement (p.12). It mandates competencies in AI literacy risk management responsible use and human oversight. Additionally specialized training is required for roles involved in the procurement development and deployment of AI systems. The document also integrates AI considerations into existing frameworks for privacy protective security record keeping and cyber-data management.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The policy explicitly excludes defence and national intelligence activities from its scope. Under the “National security carveouts” section it states that the policy “does not apply to the use of AI in the defence portfolio” and does not apply to the “national intelligence community (NIC)” including agencies such as ASIO ASD ASIS and others (p.8). It further notes that Defence and NIC entities may only voluntarily adopt elements of the policy where appropriate.

body.name: Digital Transformation Agency

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The policy recommends “AI fundamentals training for all staff” within 6 months and additional role-based training (p.12 enable and prepare – Staff training on AI) . It also promotes APS-wide capability uplift through whole-of-government capacity building (p.14). However it does not establish a specific government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants nor does it explicitly include members of the judiciary. Therefore it addresses foundational AI understanding for APS staff but not all aspects stated.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The policy strongly recommends “Additional training for staff in consideration of their roles and responsibilities such as those responsible for the procurement development training and deployment of AI systems” (p.12 enable and prepare – Staff training on AI). The policy mandates designation of accountable official(s) within 90 days to oversee implementation act as contact points and engage in whole-of-government AI coordination and forums (p.11 enable and prepare – Accountable officials). It also encourages APS-wide capability uplift (p.14). However it does not explicitly require dedicated AI teams or “AI champions” tasked with fostering a culture of innovation nor does it formalise expert advisory structures within each agency.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The policy strongly recommends AI fundamentals training for all staff and additional role-based training (p.12 enable and prepare – Staff training on AI). It also requires accountable officials to “keep up to date with changing requirements as they evolve over time” (p.11) and promotes adaptability and ongoing review (p.7 p.14). However it does not mandate structured ongoing professional development programs or specify continuous training cycles tied to AI’s rapid evolution.

items.title: AUSTRALIA’S AI ACTION PLAN
items.justification: The framework clearly addresses reskilling and upskilling of the existing workforce combining structured programs with on-the-job training. It frames this as part of a broader system-wide approach to skills development noting that “preparing our existing workforce… requires a system-wide approach… from schools… through to on-the-job training” (p. 14). It also points to programs and incentives aimed at strengthening digital and technological skills with AI identified as a central component (p. 5). More broadly the framework stresses that staying competitive in an AI-driven economy will require the workforce to “constantly retool and reskill” (p. 14).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Centre

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
items.justification: The framework promotes safe and secure AI deployment through ten guardrails addressing governance risk management testing and monitoring. Guardrail 2 requires organisations to implement risk and impact management processes to identify and mitigate harms from AI systems (pp. 19–21). Guardrail 3 requires data governance cybersecurity and system protection measures to manage risks related to data quality and vulnerabilities (pp. 22–24). Guardrail 4 requires testing AI models before deployment and monitoring system performance after deployment to detect unintended behaviour or harms (pp.25–28). These guardrails collectively support safe reliable and accountable AI systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 4 requires organisations to test AI models and systems before deployment and monitor them after deployment against clearly defined acceptance criteria and performance requirements to detect unintended behaviour and ensure reliable operation (pp. 25–28). The standard also requires organisations to establish measurable criteria (p. 26) to verify that identified risks and harms are adequately controlled. These provisions function as performance benchmarks ensuring AI systems operate reliably under stated conditions.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 2 requires organisations to establish risk and impact management processes to identify risks and implement controls to mitigate potential harms from AI systems (pp.19–21). Guardrail 4 requires testing AI models before deployment and monitoring them after deployment to detect unintended behaviour and respond appropriately (pp.25–26). The standard also emphasises implementing safeguards and corrective actions (p. 18) when risks or system deficiencies are identified to prevent or reduce harm and to document and implement a system of controls to safeguard against risks and potential harms from AI systems (p 21).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 4 requires organisations to test AI models and systems before deployment and monitor them after deployment to detect unintended behaviour and evaluate system performance (pp.25–28). The standard also requires maintaining records and AI system documentation to demonstrate compliance with the guardrails (Guardrail 9 pp. 39-41). These measures support validation traceability and robustness across the AI system lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 3 requires organisations to implement data governance privacy and cybersecurity measures to protect AI systems and manage risks related to data quality provenance and cyber vulnerabilities (pp.22–24). The standard also recommends evaluating and adapting existing cybersecurity practices and applying recognised security frameworks to AI systems to address emerging threats and system vulnerabilities. These measures aim to safeguard AI systems against misuse adversarial interference and other security risks throughout the AI lifecycle.

items.title: Voluntary AI Safety Standard
items.justification: Guardrail 6 (pp. 31–33) requires organisations to ensure transparency and explainability including informing users when AI is used and explaining system purpose and limitations. Guardrail 7 (pp. 34–35) supports contestability of AI-enabled decisions. Guardrail 9 (pp. 39–41) requires documentation and record-keeping to evidence compliance. Together these guardrails enhance transparency accountability and public trust.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 6 (pp. 31–33) promotes transparency and explainability by requiring organisations to inform users when AI is used and to communicate system purpose and limitations and Guardrail 8 (pp. 36–38) encourages transparency across the supply chain including information about data and models. It also notes as a key concept to define and document the requirements for each AI system relating to data quality data/modelprovenance and data preparation (p. 23).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Guardrail 6 (pp. 31–33) requires disclosure of AI involvement in decisions and Guardrail 7 (pp. 34–35) requires mechanisms for contestability and redress. While this implies explanation of decisions it does not impose any obligations to provide detailed explanations in specific high-stakes contexts.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Austrian Federal Government: Artificial Intelligence Mission Austria 2030 (AIM AT 2030)
items.justification: AI literacy is addressed by building AI-related knowledge and skills through education and training. The strategy first frames the need for such literacy by defining AI and its societal relevance (pg. 11). It then embeds literacy-type goals within the AI ecosystem pillar where Qualification education and training are listed as key fields of action for strengthening capacities to develop and use AI (Section 4.4 pg 37).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: An interministerial working group chaired by the BMK and BMDW

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Government aims to increase the AI skills of students and graduates. To this end AI skills must increasingly find their way into the curricula of universities and AI research is to be strengthened (Pg 53 Chapter 4.4). At the upper secondary level as part of the revision of the curricula an increased focus will be placed on STEM topics. (Pg 52).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Government will continue to quantitatively and qualitatively expand STEM and AI training places and focal points at vocational secondary schools (BHS) with regard to regional demand (Pg 52 Chapter 4.4). The Federal Government supports the expansion of AI education and training offers at universities and in cooperation with other (further) education and training institutions (Pg 53 Chapter 4.4).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Government will further increase media and digital skills in the field of teacher education by integrating AI topics specifically into existing education training and further education (Pg 38).

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Strategy Digital Skills Austria: Together into the Future
items.justification: A strategic measure addressing digital competencies and Artificial Intelligence commits to cross-ministerial measures that support Reskilling and Upskilling as AI spreads through the workplace. It foresees mapping ongoing initiatives across education administration and labour markets and developing expert recommendations (pg 61). Moreover this strategic objective is implemented through the government-funded “Digital Everywhere (Digital Überall)” program which provides basic digital competencies including AI with free nationwide workshops (pg 59).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...'
