Child sexual abuse materials safeguards (2.6) add AI-specific privacy protections to prevent misuse of children’s data.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses preventing AI-enabled exploitation or harm to children. Safety-by-Design (2.3 p.12-13) requires companies to anticipate detect and eliminate online harms including manipulative or harmful AI outputs through risk-based measures. Section 2.5 (p.14) mandates that content environments for children prevent exposure to unacceptable behaviours or harmful material. These obligations create enforceable standards that if breached support avenues for accountability and redress.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns clear obligations to AI developers and deployers to ensure systems are safe and age-appropriate. Safety-by-Design (2.3 p.12-13) requires developers to design for the evolving capacities of children ensure age-appropriate design and apply risk-based measures even when products are not child-specific. These duties create enforceable standards; if breached they support accountability and enable children and guardians to seek redress through established remedy mechanisms.

items.title: Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025-2030) (Cambodia)
items.justification: The document addresses the indicator of human oversight by requiring that processes involving artificial intelligence operate under human supervision (p. 15). This provision ensures that AI systems remain subject to human monitoring and control rather than operating autonomously. It also requires clear indicators when AI is the creator of content which promotes transparency and allows users to distinguish between human- and AI-generated outputs (p. 15). These measures support human determination over AI-driven processes and aim to maintain accountability reduce risks associated with AI use and strengthen trust in the deployment of AI technologies.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes human oversight by stating that processes involving artificial intelligence must operate under human supervision (p. 15). This requirement ensures that AI systems remain subject to human monitoring and control rather than functioning entirely autonomously. It also requires clear indicators when AI is the creator of content which supports transparency and accountability in AI use (p. 15). However while the provision establishes general human supervision and transparency principles it does not explicitly address maintaining human judgment in critical sectors or preventing AI from replacing human decision-making in areas with broad systemic implications.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document requires that processes involving artificial intelligence be conducted under human supervision (p. 15) which indicates that AI systems should not operate entirely without human oversight. This provision supports the principle that human monitoring should remain present when AI systems are used. However the document does not specifically prohibit full automation in sensitive sectors such as law enforcement healthcare or other high-risk domains where human intervention and ethical judgment are particularly necessary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Cambodia Digital Economy and Society Policy Framework 2021–2035
items.justification: Under the considerations for the future development the policy explicitly lists (3). Raising digital awareness and digital skills for civil servants at all levels including local administration. (p. 174).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Council for Digital Economy and Society (NC-DES)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The policy only lists (3). Raising digital awareness and digitalskills for civil servants at all levels including local administration as a future development being targeted (p. 174) thus not focusing on the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Digital Media and Information Literacy Competency Framework (DMIL) (Cambodia)
items.justification: P.1 emphasises that DMIL is 'increasingly necessary to equip individuals with pertinent knowledge skills attitudes and value' to protect themselves from risks (like disinformation and privacy violations) and critically to 'empower them to benefit from the opportunities that artificial intelligence brings.' (p. 11). P.3 mandates comprehensive policy measures to promote DMIL 'at all levels through professional trainings in formal education informal trainings and sectoral support programmes.' P.15 focuses on upgrading the skills of frontier technologies. Section 4 mandates the document to serve as the foundation for organising various upskilling and training initiatives.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The framework promotes upskilling and training by mandating policy measures to advance Digital Media and Information Literacy through professional training formal education informal learning and sectoral support programmes (p. 3). It also emphasizes upgrading skills related to frontier technologies (p. 15) and establishes the framework as a basis for organizing training and capacity-building initiatives (Section 4). However it does not specifically mention government-funded or subsidized programmes nor does it explicitly target workers adapting to AI-driven labor market changes.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Draft National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025-2030) (Cambodia)
items.justification: Strategy 5 Promoting Ethical and Responsible AI - aiming to build trust by establishing an appropriate governance framework to manage risks and address the negative impacts of AI. P.9 - Aim 5 is to Manage AI Risks by implementing social technical and regulatory measures to ensure ethical and responsible AI use. P.816 - acknowledges well-known anecdotal cases of AI being used in frauds and notes that the Draft Law on Personal Data Protection and the Draft Law on Cybersecurity are undergoing review which will apply to AI systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Priority 5 includes studying the preparation of a response mechanism for artificial intelligence incidents (5.7) and promoting risk assessments of AI use (5.5) which indicate an intention to address potential harms and failures. However it does not specify concrete safeguards defined fallback procedures or detailed emergency protocols for mitigating harm in cases of AI system failure or unexpected behavior.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Priority 5 promotes risk assessments of AI use by sectors and key institutions (5.5) the preparation of a National AI Governance Framework (5.1) and the compilation of technical resources to facilitate responsible AI development (5.3). These measures support oversight and robustness considerations. However the document does not explicitly require mandatory pre-deployment testing formal validation procedures or lifecycle documentation obligations to ensure technical robustness.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The strategy clarifies that existing cybersecurity and personal data protection rules apply to AI systems and calls for preparing strategies frameworks projects and legal documents that include responsibilities ethics security and safety protection and risk management related to artificial intelligence in the financial sector p. 14. It also promotes national risk assessments and the study of an AI incident response mechanism (strategic priority 5). However it does not establish specific AI focused security obligations explicitly addressing protection against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference targeting AI systems.

items.title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems (Canada)
items.justification: This document is a set of guidelines that informs the development and management of generative AI systems. It explicitly mentions 'the capability to generate realistic images and video or to impersonate the voices of real people' and AI systems that can enable deception (p. 1). The Code includes the resource of 'Implementation guide for managers of artificial intelligence systems' (https://shorturl.at/jfF2O) and encourages the creation of a risk management framework proportionate to the nature and risk profile of activities (p. 6).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The 'Implementation Guide for Managers of Artificial Intelligence Systems' provided as a resource refers to the objective of performing a comprehensive assessment of reasonably foreseeable potential adverse impacts including risks arising from the use of the system for misinformation and how these systems negatively impact marginalized groups (pp. 1-2 8). However it does not refer to hate speech or violence.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: Section 6.4.1 of the Directive on Automated Decision-Making states that the assistant deputy minister responsible for the program using the automated decision system or any other senior official named by the deputy head is responsible for 'informing clients of recourse options to challenge the administrative decision.' 6.4.1.1 states that the said entities are responsible for e]nsuring that recourse options are timely effective and easy to access.'
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Directive states that 'This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital (s. 8.1 p. 8). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.'

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat heads of agents of Parliament

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: S. 6.4.1 creates an administrative mechanism to handle AI-related grievances. S. 6.4.1 gives people the option to challenge an administrative decision that was made using an automated decision system and in 6.4.1.1 states that the this recourse must be timely effective and easy to access. However no provision provides detail as to the specific mechanisms regarding the provision of such recourse.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Bill C-216: An Act to enact the Protection of Minors in the Digital Age Act and to amend two Acts
items.justification: This proposed law creates a duty of care on digital service providers ('operators') to prevent or mitigate the effects of physical harm or incitement of harm; online sexual violence against minors; the creation of imagery of a minor that is sexually exploitative; the promotion and marketing of unlawful products or services to minors; mental health disorders; addictive behaviours; the use of accounts that have not been age verified; predatory/deceptive marketing practices (s. 4 p. 7). It also broadens the definition of intimate image under s. 162.1 of the Criminal Code to encompass deepfakes/images or videos created from scratch online (p. 16).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The law imposes a duty of care on digital service providers to prevent or mitigate harms affecting minors including online sexual violence the creation of sexually exploitative imagery of minors predatory or deceptive marketing practices the promotion of unlawful products to minors and the use of non–age-verified accounts (s. 3-4 p. 7). It also expands the definition of intimate images to include AI-generated deepfakes (p. 16) thereby addressing the misuse of AI to create harmful or exploitative content targeting children.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The law assigns a duty of care to digital service providers to prevent or mitigate harms affecting minors including online sexual violence sexually exploitative imagery predatory marketing and the use of non–age-verified accounts (s. 4 p. 7) and expands protections against AI-generated deepfake imagery (p. 16). However it does not explicitly require AI developers or deployers to design systems that are age-appropriate or beneficial for children as a general design obligation; its focus is harm prevention rather than proactive child-centred system design.

items.title: Guiding principles on diversity of content online (Canada)
items.justification: The Guiding Principles on Diversity of Content Online promote cultural and linguistic diversity by emphasizing access to and discoverability of content reflecting different cultures and perspectives including in local and Indigenous languages. They call for inclusive creation equitable access and transparency in algorithms that recommend diverse sources and minimize systemic bias. The principles and Theme 4 especially seek to recognize linguistic minorities within broader goals of digital inclusion and equity aiming to address barriers that limit participation in the digital space.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: Theme 1 bullet point 1 states: 'Content reflecting different cultures and perspectives including in local languages should be created and discoverable'. Theme 1 bullet point 2 states: 'Users should have access to local national and international sources of content including in local and Indigenous languages where applicable'. Theme 4 bullet point 2 states that 'Content recommendation algorithms should promote content reflecting different sources perspectives ideas and genres.'

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The Acknowledgments section under the point on Equity states that signatories ought to '[r]ecognize that some content and ideas that may be circulated on online platforms including hate racial prejudice disinformation and misinformation can have real and concrete consequences and that these can disproportionately affect Indigenous people and equity-deserving groups and persons including persons with disabilities racialized and local communities linguistic or religious minorities members of the LGBTQ2+ and gender diverse communities.' Theme 4 in the list of principles calls for transparent fair and diverse algorithms that respect privacy reduce bias and promote inclusive online content.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: Theme 4 bullet point 2 states that '[c]ontent recommendation algorithms should promote content reflecting different sources perspectives ideas and genres'. In effect this bullet point does not encourage nor obligate stakeholders to ensure that AI systems are trained on diverse datasets but it states that algorithms should be designed so as to promote diverse datasets and be adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts.

items.title: AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025-2027 (Canada)
items.justification: The document states that: 'The Government of Canada should minimize the environmental impact of its AI use by deploying AI appropriately and choosing solutions that demonstrate responsible environmental practices.' pp. 36-37 'ensuring that the benefits of AI do not come at the expense of our environment' p. 10.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The document states that it applies to departments and agencies covered by the Policy on Service and Digital (p. 7). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.' Instead organizations that are partially or wholly exempt from the Policy on Service and Digital including those that fall under the national security exemption are encouraged to comply with the AI Strategy as much as possible as a matter of good practice (p. 7).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The document states that: 'The Government of Canada should minimize the environmental impact of its AI use by deploying AI appropriately and choosing solutions that demonstrate responsible environmental practices.' pp. 36-37 'ensuring that the benefits of AI do not come at the expense of our environment' p. 10 while also emphasizing the need for environmental impact assessments (p. 16) specifically in case of AI procurement. Taken together these provisions prevent resource-intensive AI development and deployment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
thematicElements.justification: While the document recommends conducting environmental impact assessments (p. 16) specifically in case of AI procurement it is not an obligation nor does it include reporting obligations regarding energy usage.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The Directive provides structural tools (algorithmic impact assessments (s. 6.1) bias testing (s. 6.3) transparency (s. 6.2) recourse (s. 6.4) peer review (s. 6.3.7)) that can be leveraged to protect against discrimination in automated systems. Its integration of GBA-plus — a tool used to examine how policies programs and initiatives may differently impact various genders — is relevant to ensuring gender equality in particular is considered proactively in the design deployment and oversight of automated decision systems by the federal government.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Directive states that 'This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital (s. 8.1 p. 8). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.'

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.1 requires algorithmic impact assessments to be completed which measure the risk of a system's bias or discriminatory outcomes. Section 6.3 requires testing and monitoring AI systems for unintended bias. Section 6.3.8 and Appendix C require that Gender-based Analysis Plus be completed which is a tool to measure the risks that a system will discriminate based on gender.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Directive requires the completion of an algorithmic impact assessment (section 6.1) ongoing testing and monitoring (section 6.3) and the completion of Gender-based Analysis Plus (section 6.3.8 and Appendix C). It is also recommended at page 17 that AI systems be assessed for the possibility that they will have discriminatory impacts on the basis of age disability and race. These measures help prevent Canada's federal government use of AI systems from having biased and discriminatory outcomes with a specific focus on preventing discrimination based on gender age race and disability.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The requirement to engage in ongoing testing and monitoring (section 6.3) and to complete an algorithmic impact assessment  at the outset of using a system as well as when the functionality or scope of the AI system changes means that deployers are are required to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle. Section 6.3.5 of the Directive also requires training and input data to be relevant accurate and up-to-date as part of addressing a system's risk of bias and discrimination throughout the lifecycle of data collection to deployment though it does not explicitly mention the prevention of sources of bias in a system's input or training data.

items.title: Pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices (Canada)
items.justification: The guidance document provides guidance to manufacturers who are submitting new or amended applications for Class II-IV medical devices under Canada's medical device regulations. It provides guidelines for considerations that ought to inform the lifecycle of AI-based medical products. It states that bias should be part of the risk analysis as part of risk management and that Sex and Gender-based Analysis Plus ought to be used to identify how a product/initiative may impact diverse groups of people. The document refers to the need to consider various identity factors (sex gender race age etc.) when making decisions around the diversity of training and input data.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: In the Design section the guidelines state that bias should be considered in manufacturers’ risk analysis and encourage using Sex and Gender-based Plus Analysis to prevent unwanted bias. In the Policy statement section they require training and input data to reflect the target population. In the Data selection and management and Clinical validation sections manufacturers must justify dataset characteristics related to identity factors (e.g. sex gender race age). In the Testing and evaluation section they should provide evidence of how and why AI systems perform differently across subgroups to reduce bias.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document includes several measures addressing the prevention of bias and discrimination. In the Design section it requires manufacturers to consider bias in their risk analysis and encourages the use of Sex and Gender-based Plus Analysis to prevent unwanted bias. The Policy statement section calls for training and input data to reflect the intended population. The Data selection and management and Clinical validation sections require justification of dataset characteristics linked to identity factors (e.g. sex gender race age). The Testing and evaluation section encourages evidence on how and why AI systems perform differently across subgroups in order to mitigate bias.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document includes a clear pre-deployment obligation to test an automated decision system’s data and model for accuracy and unintended bias including impacts that may be unfair or violate human rights and freedoms (Section 6.3). However it does not fully specify end-to-end lifecycle duties (eg ongoing measurement and mitigation from data collection through deployment) or concrete bias-mitigation methods beyond this testing requirement.

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The Directive provides structural tools (algorithmic impact assessments (s. 6.1) bias testing (s. 6.3) transparency (s. 6.2) recourse (s. 6.4) peer review (s. 6.3.7)) that can be leveraged to protect against gender discrimination in automated systems. Its integration of GBA-plus — a tool used to examine how policies programs and initiatives may differently impact various genders — is particularly relevant to ensuring gender equality is considered proactively in the design deployment and oversight of automated decision systems by the federal government.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Directive states that 'This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital (s. 8.1 p. 8). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.'

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The Directive uses the Gender-based Analysis Plus a tool that is used to examine how policies programs and initiatives may differently impact various genders (s. 6.3.8; Appendix C).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Appendix C states that completion of Gender-Based Analysis Plus (GBA-Plus) involves the entity responsible for conducting an algorithmic impact assessment to consult one's department’s diversity and inclusion experts to ensure GBA-plus is applied. They must also assess how the automation project and its data may affect different population groups including based on gender age disability and race. They must also cite available data or note gaps. Finally they must include planned or existing measures to mitigate any risks identified through GBA-Plus or other assessments.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Playbook for Gender Equality in the Digital Age
items.justification: Developed by the Digital Inclusion Lab at Global Affairs Canada the purpose of the Playbook for Gender Equality in the Digital Age is to put forward a set of best practices to support gender equality in digital contexts. They note under Culture Point 9 that everyone needs to assure that algorithms and machine learning systems do not perpetuate historical patterns of gender-based discrimination and that the use of Artificial Intelligence to perpetrate sexual and gender based violence is adequately addressed.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The Playbook for Gender Equality in the Digital Age put forward a set of best practices to support gender equality in digital contexts. They note under Culture Point 9 that everyone needs to assure that algorithms and machine learning systems do not perpetuate historical patterns of gender-based discrimination and that the use of Artificial Intelligence to perpetrate sexual and gender based violence is adequately addressed.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The document addresses human oversight and determination in Appendix C (p. 13). Level I systems can make decisions and assessments without direct human involvement though humans must be involved in quality assurance and can intervene in decision-making where appropriate (p. 20). Level III and above require humans to make the final decisions (p. 20). Decisions must review the decision or recommendations for accuracy and appropriateness (p. 20).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Directive states that 'This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital (s. 8.1 p. 8). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.'

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.3.13 of the Directive states that the AI system must allow for human involvement and includes 4 levels of risk for higher risk systems such as those where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications (p. 7). Appendix C provides for Level I and II systems where decisions can be made without human involvement though human oversight is possible and is needed for quality assurance (p. 20). Level III and IV systems require human intervention for decisions and assessments allowing for human review for accuracy and appropriateness at all times (p. 20).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.3.13 of the Directive states that the AI system must allow for human involvement (p. 7). Appendix C provides for a two-tiered level of human involvement where Level I and II systems can make decisions without human oversight and Level III and IV systems require human oversight before any action is taken on the basis of a system's recommendations or decision (p. 20). The Directive does not have any outright prohibitions on the use of AI for certain very high-risk decisions and instead provides for differing levels of human oversight the higher risk a system is.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.3.13 of the Directive states that the AI system must allow for human involvement. Appendix C provides for a two-tiered level of human involvement where Level I and II systems can make decisions without human oversight and Level III and IV systems require human oversight before any action is taken on the basis of a system's recommendations or decision (p. 20).

items.title: Pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices (Canada)
items.justification: This document addresses human oversight and determination by requiring manufacturers to clearly define the intended user and how the device fits into clinical workflows including the degree of autonomy (i.e. the level of user intervention needed to perform a clinical function) (p. 9-10). It also emphasizes transparency and explainability (p. 12 and 23) so users can interpret outputs and includes human-centred information in labeling and instructions (p. 23-24). These elements help ensure that healthcare professionals understand oversee and appropriately use ML-enabled systems in practice.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document meaningfully promotes human oversight by requiring manufacturers to define intended users clarify integration into clinical workflows and specify the degree of autonomy and necessary user intervention (pp. 9–10). It further emphasizes transparency and explainability (pp. 12 23) and mandates human-centred labelling and instructions (pp. 23–24) supporting informed professional control. However it does not explicitly establish a general principle that AI must remain subordinate to human judgment in all critical or systemically impactful contexts.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document includes measures that limit unchecked automation in clinical contexts by requiring manufacturers to define the intended user specify the degree of autonomy and required user intervention (pp. 9–10) and ensure transparency and explainability so outputs can be meaningfully interpreted by healthcare professionals (pp. 12 23). It also mandates human-centred labelling and instructions (pp. 23–24) reinforcing professional oversight. However it does not explicitly prohibit full automation or categorically require human intervention in all sensitive sectors.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The core requirement of this document is the completion of an algorithmic impact assessment (s. 6.1 p. 4). The algorithmic impact assessment is a risk identification and mitigation tool that requires the completion of such an assessment when any automated decision-making system is used by the Canadian federal government. The AIA assesses risk areas (decision type algorithm data system design) and mitigation measures generating impact levels I-IV (p. 11-20). Components include: transparency requirements quality assurance human oversight training peer review recourse mechanisms and compliance with administrative law principles of fairness accountability and legality (p. 3 5-7).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital which in section 6.3 states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.'

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Woven throughout this document is a commitment to the promotion of a culture that proactively manages the risks related to AI. The completion of an algorithmic impact assessment means that the societal and ethical impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment. Section 6.3 illustrates this commitment requiring that 'before an automated decision system is in production testing the data information and underlying model for accuracy unintended biases and all factors that may unintentionally or unfairly impact the outcomes or violate human rights and freedoms' (p. 5). The Directive does not govern environmental considerations or impacts of AI.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The requirement to complete an algorithmic impact assessment as set out by section 6.1 requires the federal government users (though not necessarily developers) of AI to complete a comprehensive impact assessment that identify and mitigate potential risks of AI systems to individuals and society.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.1.1 of this document requires that completed algorithmic impact assessments be shared in an accessible format on the Open Government Portal but the provision des not provide the public with the right to access these findings.

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The Directive requires that the results of algorithmic impact assessments be published in an accessible format on the Open Government Portal prior to the production of any automated decision system (s. 6.1.1). Reporting requirements include publishing information on the effectiveness and efficiency of the automated decision system in meeting program objectives on the Open Government Portal (s. 6.5.1) as well as publishing information on this portal on how the use of the automated decision system is fair and transparent and does not violate human rights and freedoms (s. 6.5.2). Notably there is a list of Agents of Parliaments at s. 8.3.1 which are not required to publish algorithmic impact assessments or reporting information (s. 8.3.4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: No defence or security entity is listed as falling under the scope of the Directive so defence and security is explicitly excluded from the scope of the framework.

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat Heads of Agents of Parliament

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: The Directive requires publishing the results of algorithmic impact assessments (s. 6.1.1) and other reporting information (s. 6.5) but carves out exceptions such that certain government entities do not have to provide such information. Section 8 provides a list of federal government offices that are 'Agents of Parliament' and do not have to publish algorithmic impact assessments nor provide reporting information on the Open Government Portal (s. 8.3.4).

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The Directive requires publishing the results of algorithmic impact assessments (s. 6.1.1) and other reporting information (s. 6.5). This reporting information consists of the effectiveness and efficiency of the automated decision system in meeting program objectives (s. 6.5.1) as well as whether use of the automated decision system is fair and transparent and does not violate human rights and freedoms (s.6 .5.2). There are no specific requirements in the Directive to disclose the data used to train systems.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.2 of the Directive requires that notice be provided through all service delivery channels in use that an automated decision system will be used to make or assist in the making of a decision (s. 6.2.1) and that a meaningful explanation be provided to clients of how and why a decision was made (s. 6.2.3). Appendix C clarifies when such notice and explanations be provided and it requires that plain language be used. Appendix C states that systems of impact level III and above must direct clients to the explanation required under Explanation level I. Level II systems must provide an explanation to clients of how the system provided the output that it did which informs clients of how such systems might affect them.

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The Directive on Automated Decision-Making applies to automated decision systems both developed internally and procured from vendors (s.1.2). Section 6.2.4–6.2.6 establishes procurement-specific obligations: departments must determine appropriate software licences (including open source) obtain all released versions of software components and if using proprietary systems retain rights to access test audit and monitor the system (s.6.2.6.1–6.2.6.2). Departments remain responsible for completing the AIA regardless of whether the system is built or procured (s.6.1.1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: No defence or security entity is listed as falling under the scope of the Directive so defence and security is explicitly excluded from the scope of the framework.

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat Heads of Agents of Parliament

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The Directive extends procurement requirements beyond traditional IT by mandating AIAs for procured systems (s.1.2) requiring proprietary vendor access rights for auditing (s.6.2.6) and applying ethical/human rights testing obligations regardless of whether a system is built or procured. However it is framed as an automated decision-making directive rather than a dedicated procurement guideline document.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: Departments must test procured systems for accuracy unintended biases and human rights impacts before production (s.6.3.1) and conduct ongoing monitoring (s.6.3.2). However the obligation falls on departments not vendors directly — vendors are not independently required to demonstrate prior testing.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.2.6.1 explicitly requires that when using proprietary systems departments retain the right to access test monitor and audit all released versions including authorising external parties to review (s.6.2.6.2). Section 6.2.3 mandates meaningful explanations of how decisions are made.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: AI Strategy for the Federal Public Service 2025-2027 (Canada)
items.justification: The strategy addresses public sector skills development by proposing and developing an evergreen training plan for public servants including general training to build AI understanding and tailored training for specific roles with both technical and leadership skills (17). It benchmarks talent needs and existing skills to create learner personas and targeted training (17-18). It also includes a talent plan for recruitment and retention flexible career pathways and partnerships with educational institutions; co-op programs apprenticeships and internships support talent pipelines (18). These initiatives prepare the workforce to responsibly adopt AI and adapt to evolving roles promoting a culture of continuous learning and AI competence.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The document states that it applies to departments and agencies covered by the Policy on Service and Digital (p. 7). Section 6.3 of the Policy on Service and Digital states that 'This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.' Instead organizations that are partially or wholly exempt from the Policy on Service and Digital including those that fall under the national security exemption are encouraged to comply with the AI Strategy as much as possible as a matter of good practice (p. 7).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes specific measures under 'Priority 3: Talent and training' for a government-wide strategy to train upskill and retrain public servants on AI its applications and risks. Working with the Canadian School for Public Service the strategy mandates a training plan for all public servants tailored learning benchmarking of AI skills and initiatives for recruitment and retention. However it does not mention specific provisions for members of the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: While the program does not mention the creation of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation priority 3 states that the strategy will 'establish flexible data science career pathways for AI practitioners.' The strategy will 'create a talent pipeline' for data scientists through interchanges apprenticeships co-op programs and partnerships with AI institutes and research centres. In this way the strategy prioritizes the hiring of data scientists to recruit data science talent who will invariably at times be AI experts who can foster a culture of responsible AI adoption. The AI Centre of Excellent will also contribute to these efforts.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The strategy explicitly includes provisions requiring ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology. Under 'Priority 3: Talent and training' it commits to developing an evergreen training plan for public servants that adapts to AI advancements continuously. The plan includes general and role-specific training to build confidence in AI use risk management leadership and technical skills. This reflects recognition of the need to maintain workforce readiness amid fast AI developments.

items.title: Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy (Canada)
items.justification: The Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy led by the Government of Canada addresses reskilling and upskilling through its “Talent and Research” pillar. It supports institutions such as CIFAR Amii Mila and the Vector Institute to train and develop AI talent strengthening the national skills base. At the same time initiatives like the Global Innovation Clusters promote industry adoption enabling workers to build practical AI competencies. Together these measures support continuous workforce skill development across research and industry.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: CIFAR (coordination of research & talent programs) AI institutes (Amii Mila Vector Institute) Global Innovation Clusters (industry adoption)Standards Council of Canada (standards pillar) Digital Research Alliance of Canada (compute infrastructure)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The document outlines government-funded initiatives that directly support AI-related skills development including substantial public investment in training research and talent pipelines. Under the “Talent and Research” pillar funding supports institutions such as CIFAR Amii Mila and the Vector Institute to develop and train AI professionals while Global Innovation Clusters and AI Institutes facilitate industry adoption and applied skill-building. These measures constitute publicly funded upskilling and reskilling mechanisms enabling individuals and organizations to adapt to AI-driven labour market changes.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems (Canada)
items.justification: This document is a short code of conduct and set of guidelines that informs the development and management of generative AI systems. It encourages developers and managers of generative AI systems to achieve the outcomes of: accountability safety fairness and equity transparency human oversight and monitoring and validity and robustness. As of page 6 these principles are laid out in a table with the measures required for each principle. Page 8 states that comprehensive testing must be done to achieve system safety to test how the system could be used inappropriately or maliciously. Validity and robustness testing set out in pages 13-14 are essential parts of security and adversarial testing is a key requirement for this principle.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: In the point on safety this document states that systems should be subject to risk assessments and risk mitigation measures in order to ensure safe operation are put in place prior to deployment. Cybersecurity risks are also a key concern of these guidelines; pages 8 and 13-14 state that comprehensive testing and red-teaming must be undertaking to identify vulnerabilities in a system as well as how it can be used inappropriately or with malicious intent.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: At page 13-14 of this document the validity and robustness principle requires that there be 'a wide variety of testing methods across a spectrum of tasks and contexts prior to deployment to measure performance and ensure robustness' which means that this document addresses pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The validity and robustness point of this document states that generative AI systems should be secure against cyber attacks and the systems' behaviour in response to a range of task or situations to which they are likely to be expose should be understood (p. 13 14).

items.title: Directive on Automated Decision-Making (Canada)
items.justification: The Directive addresses transparency by requiring those using AI systems to complete approve and publish the algorithmic impact assessments regarding the deployment of AI (section 6.1 Appendix C). It also requires notice that decisions will be made or assisted by AI systems (section 6.2) and that meaningful explanations to clients be provided as to how and why the decision was made (s. 6.2.3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This directive applies to all institutions subject to the Policy on Service and Digital which in section 6.3 states that ' This policy does not apply to national security systems except where the Chief Information Officer of Canada is identified as the system business owner.

body.name: Treasury Board Secretariat

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Directive promotes transparency by mandating that deployers of AI systems complete approve and publish Algorithmic Impact Assessments related to the system’s deployment (section 6.1 Appendix C). Additionally Appendix C requires transparency around a system's input data its source and method of data collection; the criteria used to evaluate input data; and for higher risk level systems transparency is required for principal factors that led to a decision such as descriptions of decision trees or the scoring or weights of certain factors.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.2 and Appendix C include the obligation to provide meaningful explanations for AI systems' decisions but the Directive does not mention high risk or high stake contexts such as hiring or loan applications etc.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Section 6.2.3 of the Directive gives clients the right to meaningful explanations that explain how and why decisions were made using AI systems. Appendix C requires transparency around a system's input data its source and method of data collection; the criteria used to evaluate input data; and for higher risk level systems transparency is required for principal factors that led to a decision such as descriptions of decision trees or the scoring or weights of certain factors.

items.title: Pre-market guidance for machine learning-enabled medical devices (Canada)
items.justification: Transparency is a key requirement in this document which serves as a guideline for new or amended Class II-IV medical device licence applications in Canada. This document provides guidelines for measures to undertake throughout the lifecycle of such a medical device. Transparency is a throughline in the product lifecycle. This document states that transparency and explainability involve robust and detailed device labelling (including instructions for use) and providing detailed device design change performance and limitation information. Labelling requirements for transparency and explainability can be found at pages 23-25.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Transparency section of the guidelines provides a detailed breakdown of the kind of information that should be included in the labelling and instructions information associated with each relevant AI system. The list includes information such as: indications for use intended use and contraindications; instructions for the user related to using interpreting and performing monitoring of the system and its outputs; device design information such as how the system works and detailed information about the training and test datasets; device change information such as software updates and their impacts on device performance; device performance information such as performance testing results; and device limitation information.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: These guidelines describe the detailed information that ought to be labelled and disclosed for AI-powered medical devices (see pages 23-25 specifically) and as such this document concern discusses the assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs. The use of AI-powered devices for medical purposes is a high-risk context and these guidelines provide robust and detailed transparency and explainability requirements for the manufacturers of such devices.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: While this document does not provide for an individual right of action to a meaningful explanation it sets out detailed and robust explainability requirements throughout in order to ensure the safety of AI-powered medical devices. For example the Device Description section at pages 10-11 provide a list of the detailed information related to an AI-powered medical device that manufacturers ought to provide for users which explains the ML methods training algorithms and architecture used; the data used to develop or train the ML system; a description of the ML system output intended users clinical degree of autonomy; an explanation of how the ML system works amongst other salient information.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The Chilean AI policy addresses AI literacy mainly in Axis Nº1 – Enabling Factors Section 1.1 Talent Development (pp. 14-15). It promotes skills for understanding using and critically analyzing AI across schools higher education and the workforce and explicitly includes a new measure to strengthen citizen education and training on the ethical use of AI its risks and benefits promoting critical thinking and digital literacy for public officials and the general public. AI literacy is further addressed in Section 3.7 Children and Adolescents (p. 23) which highlights digital literacy in AI and critical thinking from an early age.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The policy includes explicit provisions related to curriculum reforms across primary secondary and tertiary education. In Axis Nº1 – Enabling Factors Section 1.1 Talent Development (pp. 14-15) it proposes incorporating AI skills into the school system strengthening curricular bases and generating learning resources for early education. The same section recommends integrating AI and ethics as transversal content in higher education including universities technical training centers and professional institutes confirming curriculum-oriented reforms at all levels.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The policy includes specific measures to establish and strengthen AI-related programs within the formal education system. In Axis Nº1 – Enabling Factors Section 1.1 Talent Development (pp. 14-15) it promotes the development of AI programs in Technical Training Centers (CFTs) Professional Institutes (IPs) and Higher Education Institutions as well as the strengthening of undergraduate and postgraduate pathways in AI. It also supports creating resources and structured programs to build AI capabilities across formal education.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The policy includes measures related to teacher training and educational resources for AI education. In Axis Nº1 – Enabling Factors Section 1.1 Talent Development (pp. 14-15) it proposes generating resources for learning AI in educational contexts and strengthening curricular bases to incorporate AI skills. It also promotes developing capacities within the educational community which includes training educators to implement and teach AI responsibly and ethically.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The Chilean AI Policy addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and digital violence in Section 3.10 “Safe Digital Ecosystem”. It proposes studying their impact and implementing measures to prevent and counter them including their effects on mental health (p. 25). It calls for interdisciplinary research with emphasis on vulnerable groups such as children adolescents and women and for digital education and literacy to promote the responsible use of AI and reduce harm in online environments. Section 3.7 addresses AI systems involving children and adolescents mandating the protection of their data and privacy. It requires preventing discrimination bias and abuse while guaranteeing their physical emotional and mental well-being (p.23)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Yes. In Section 3.10 “Safe Digital Ecosystem” the policy includes measures aimed at preventing harmful uses of AI. It proposes:Studying the impact of disinformation and digital violence and implementing measures to prevent and combat them.Promoting responsible use of AI in digital environments.Digital literacy measures to reduce online harm.While it does not explicitly ban AI tools from generating or amplifying harmful content it clearly sets prevention-oriented objectives (p.25).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Yes Section 3.10 “Safe Digital Ecosystem” includes measures to prevent AI-facilitated gender-based harassment and violence such as interdisciplinary research on digital violence with special focus on women and digital literacy measures to combat online violence. Additionally other sections of the Policy contain gender-focused provisions including broader commitments to prevent gender-based violence and protect women and girls in digital and technological contexts reinforcing this objective beyond Section 3.10 (Section 3.4)

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Bill (Chile)
items.justification: While the bill does not explicitly use the terms redress or remedy it addresses Access to Redress and Remedy in different sections. Title II grants individuals the right to pursue legal action to defend their consumer rights when harmed by an AI system (pp. 18 and 32). Title V requires operators to act when an AI system is linked to a serious incident including notification and corrective measures (pp. 37–38 Art. 13). Article 28 allows affected individuals to file a joint civil lawsuit to stop harmful acts and seek compensation (pp. 46–47).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The bill clearly excludes defence and security AI systems from its scope. Article 2 paragraph (a) states that the law “shall not apply to AI systems developed and used for national defence purposes.” It further establishes that the Ministry of National Defence will issue a confidential resolution listing the exempted systems (p. 27 Art. 2).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The bill reinforces judicial mechanisms for seeking remedy for harms caused by AI systems. Title VI establishes a civil liability regime enabling individuals or groups to demand cessation compensation and preventive measures (p. 51 Arts. 28–29). Additionally affected persons may challenge administrative decisions before the Courts of Appeals and the Supreme Court (p. 50 Art. 27). These provisions create enforceable judicial pathways for redress in AI-related harms.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The bill creates state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms through the competent Agency responsible for overseeing AI systems. Title IV (Administrative Procedure) establishes procedures for filing complaints investigations evidence submission and sanctions handled directly by the regulator (pp. 48–50 Arts. 26–27). These mechanisms operate outside the courts allowing individuals to raise AI-related grievances through an administrative process.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The Chilean National AI Policy (2024) addresses Children's Rights under its Governance and Ethics axis section 3.7. Children and Adolescents (NNA) (pp. 23-24). It recognises AI's profound impact on children and adolescents (NNA) in education entertainment and social media. The policy commits to promoting the responsible use of AI oriented towards exercising their rights. This includes developing regulations to protect their data and privacy prevent discrimination and abuse and guarantee their physical emotional and mental well-being. It also advocates for digital literacy and critical thinking from an early age ensuring their participation in shaping a safe AI environment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes a specific provision directly related to the protection of children's personal data and privacy. Under Axis 3.7: Children and Adolescents (NNA) the policy's key objective is to: 'Promote the responsible use of AI considering the perspectives of NNAs and oriented towards the exercise of their rights' (p. 23). To achieve this the policy explicitly recommends to advance in 'recommendations and regulations for the development and implementation of AI systems that directly or indirectly involve NNAs so that their data and privacy are protected...' This statement serves as a direct objective and recommendation making the protection of children's data and privacy a specific goal within the national AI policy.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes a specific provision to prevent AI systems from being used to harm children. Under Axis 3.7: Children and Adolescents (NNA) the policy's objective is to ensure the responsible use of AI oriented towards their rights. It explicitly calls for regulations and recommendations to: 'prevent discrimination biases and abuses' and to 'guarantee their physical emotional and mental well-being.' While there is no explicit mention to targeted advertising and inappropriate content this broad directive implicitly encompasses protecting children from exploitation manipulation and harm including them by demanding that AI systems be designed and implemented to prevent such negative outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes a specific objective that assigns this responsibility. It explicitly proposes to 'Advance in recommendations and regulations for the development and implementation of AI systems that directly or indirectly involve NNAs...' This clause directly targets developers and deployers mandating that systems must be designed to protect data prevent harm and guarantee the physical emotional and mental well-being of children which inherently requires safety and age-appropriate design yet the policy does not explicitly mention age-appropriate requirements.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The Chilean AI policy addresses cultural and linguistic diversity by embedding it in its ethical foundations and governance measures. Principle 1(e) explicitly requires AI systems to promote cultural diversity and avoid discriminatory outcomes while Section 3.5 advances inclusion by encouraging participation of diverse social groups and the use of bias-mitigation tools. Additionally Section 3.9 promotes AI capacities for preserving Chile’s material and immaterial cultural heritage fostering open databases and interdisciplinary research (p. 24). Together these elements ensure that AI development supports Chile’s cultural and linguistic plurality.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: While the main policy text refers broadly to cultural diversity (Principle 1(e)) inclusion (Section 3.5) and cultural heritage (Section 3.9) the Action Plan explicitly includes a concrete measure: 'the creation of open databases for training models in Chilean Spanish and in dialects of native peoples of the national territory will be promoted and financed' (p. 39 in the translated version of the Action Plan). This provision directly promotes the development of AI systems that are representative of a wide range of cultures and languages within Chile and Latin America.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The document contains provisions that help prevent AI systems from perpetuating cultural stereotypes or erasing linguistic diversity. Principle 1(e) requires that AI be developed in ways that promote cultural diversity and avoid discriminatory effects directly addressing risks of cultural stereotyping. Section 3.5 Inclusion and Non-Discrimination further mandates the use of bias and non-discrimination assessment tools throughout the AI lifecycle which helps prevent systems from privileging dominant cultures.
