Section 3.9 Culture and Cultural Heritage promotes AI capacities that preserve and enhance cultural heritage countering cultural erasure.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The update of the AI policy addresses Environmental Impact of AI in the Axis N°3: Governance and Ethics specifically under the new Section 3.3 “Environment and Climate Crisis” (p. 20 in translated version). It highlights AI’s dual role—both as a tool for environmental protection and as an energy-intensive technology. The policy promotes AI applications for monitoring and reducing environmental harm supports AI research for sustainability and urges the use of non-conventional renewable energies in the development of infrastructure for AI to ensure a socio-ecological development of AI.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: Yes. In Section 3.3 “Environment and Climate Crisis” (p. 20) the policy’s main focus is on developing and using AI to combat climate change promoting tools for environmental monitoring and sustainability. It also encourages renewable and low-resource energy use in AI infrastructure and mechanisms to prevent environmental impacts from AI operations. However it does not mention e-waste management; its focus is primarily on the resource and energy consumption of AI systems during operation rather than their hardware lifecycle or disposal.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: Yes. In Section 3.3 “Environment and Climate Crisis” (p. 20) the policy promotes renewable and low-resource energy use in AI infrastructure and mechanisms to prevent environmental impacts. Additionally both the Implementation Plan and the National Data Centers Plan explicitly mention energy efficiency measures to reduce the environmental footprint of data centers including improving sustainability in their operation and reducing their carbon footprint and water consumption.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: Chile's National AI Policy includes non-discrimination as one of the fundamental ethical guidelines within the first principle ‘Ethical and responsible use of AI centered on people’ which highlights the guideline ‘Diversity Non-Discrimination and Equality’ (pp. 11-12 in translated version). In its ethics and governance section it explicitly addresses these issues in several of its policy objectives including references to non-discrimination and bias reduction in ‘3.5. Inclusion and Non-Discrimination’ (pp. 21-22) and ‘3.7. Children and Adolescents (NNA)’ (p. 23). These include promoting good practices in IA development and integrating bias assessment tools throughout the AI lifecycle.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Although the policy document does not explicitly mention the concept of fairness it establishes principles and measures aimed at promoting fair and equitable outcomes in AI systems. Under Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI centered on people (pp. 11) it commits to diversity non-discrimination and equality requiring AI systems to avoid biases and discriminatory effects. Likewise Axis 3.5: Inclusion and Non-Discrimination (pp. 21–22) proposes actions such as using bias assessment tools and promoting the participation of underrepresented groups in AI development ensuring more equitable and responsible outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document includes explicit measures to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases and discrimination. Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI centred on people (pp. 11–12) requires AI systems to promote diversity non-discrimination and equality avoiding biased or discriminatory outcomes. Additionally Axis 3.5: Inclusion and Non-Discrimination (pp. 21–22) establishes actions to foster inclusion apply bias and non-discrimination assessment tools and ensure diverse participation in AI research and development directly addressing risks of discrimination by gender race ethnicity ability age or other characteristics.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document includes provisions assigning responsibilities to developers and deployers to identify and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI centered on people (pp. 11-12) establishes requirements for accountability transparency and robustness ensuring responsible system design. In particular Axis 3.5: Inclusion and Non-Discrimination (pp. 21–22)  calls for the use of bias and non-discrimination assessment tools across the AI system lifecycle promoting practices that proactively detect and mitigate biases from data collection to deployment.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: In the Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (2024 Update) Gender Equality is addressed primarily in the Section 3.4 “Gender Equality”  (pp. 20-21 in translated version) located under Axis N°3: Governance and Ethics. The policy proposes promoting women’s participation and equity in AI research development and industry areas to reach OCDE level supported by gender-focused indicators and monitoring systems inclusive labor policies and measures to prevent automation-related gender disparities. It is also addressed in PRINCIPLE 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI centred on people specifically in point e on Diversity Non-Discrimination and Equality (p. 12) and Section 3.5 “Inclusion and Non-Discrimination” (p. 22).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Yes the Chilean AI Policy includes specific provisions to prevent AI systems from perpetuating gender discrimination and bias. Measures include promoting bias and non-discrimination assessment tools throughout the AI lifecycle ensuring diverse social groups contribute to AI training data and research and encouraging the participation and equal development of underrepresented groups including women. These steps aim to mitigate biases in data and development teams ensuring AI advances equality and inclusion (see 3.5. Inclusion and Non-Discrimination p. 22 in translated version).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: Yes the Chilean AI Policy includes provisions to increase women’s representation in the AI workforce (p. 9 and pp. 20-21 in translated version). It promotes the participation of women in AI research and development aiming to reach OECD averages and ensures gender equity in AI implementation to prevent bias. The policy establishes mainly affirmative actions to address underrepresentation encouraging diverse and balanced development teams. These measures focus on creating equal opportunities for women in AI fostering inclusive and ethical practices and integrating gender perspectives throughout AI system design development and deployment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Bill (Chile)
items.justification: Chile´s AI bill addresses Human Oversight primarily as a general principle (Art. 4(a) pp. 31) and a mandatory rule for high-risk AI systems (Art. 8(f) pp. 35-36). It mandates that high-risk systems be designed for supervision by technically qualified persons to prevent/minimise risks to health safety and fundamental rights. This is embedded within a risk-based regulatory framework where oversight is a key compliance requirement linked to accountability.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Yes. The bill clearly excludes defence and security AI systems from its scope. Article 2 paragraph (a) states that the law “shall not apply to AI systems developed and used for national defence purposes.” It further establishes that the Ministry of National Defence will issue a confidential resolution listing the exempted systems (p. 27 Art. 2).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: Yes the AI bill includes specific provisions to promote meaningful human control ensuring AI assists rather than replaces human judgment particularly in critical areas. It establishes human intervention and supervision as a core principle (Art. 4(a) p.31) and mandates human oversight mechanisms for high-risk AI systems requiring they be designed for monitoring by technically qualified persons to prevent risks to health safety and fundamental rights (Art. 8(f) pp.35-36). Furthermore it explicitly prohibits unacceptable-risk systems that manipulate behavior or allow certain real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces (Art. 6 pp.33-34) thereby safeguarding human judgment in contexts with broad systemic implications.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Yes the bill includes specific provisions to prevent full automation in sensitive sectors through its risk-based prohibitions and mandatory human oversight rules. It explicitly bans AI systems of unacceptable risk including those for subliminal manipulation or exploiting vulnerabilities (Art. 6 pp.33-34) which directly applies to sensitive contexts. For permitted high-risk AI systems—which would include sensitive applications in law enforcement or medicine—the law mandates human oversight mechanisms requiring that they be designed to be monitored by technically qualified natural persons to minimize risks to health safety and fundamental rights (Art. 8(f) pp.35-36) thereby ensuring necessary human intervention and ethical judgment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes specific provisions that assign obligations to ensure oversight and accountability. Article 8(f) (pp. 35-36) mandates that operators of high-risk AI systems must ensure these systems are designed for supervision by technically qualified natural persons. Furthermore Article 4(g) (p. 32) establishes the general principle of accountability requiring that those who design develop operate or deploy AI systems ensure their proper functioning throughout the lifecycle. This framework implicitly assigns responsibility to operators to designate qualified individuals for oversight and intervention to comply with these legal obligations.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The policy does not directly address impact assessments but it does touch on related issues in section 3: Governance and ethics specifically in section 3.1 “Regulation and institutional framework” (p. 18-19) and section 3.5 (pp. 21-22) as it establishes the promotion of regulatory and ethical tools to ensure that AI systems respect fundamental rights transparency and accountability. Although it does not specify “AI impact assessments” as such it emphasises the assessment of social environmental and ethical effects as part of responsible AI governance. Where impact assessments are explicitly mentioned is in the policy implementation plan where “bias and non-discrimination tools” are translated into algorithmic impact assessments.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Yes. Section 3.1 (“Regulation and Institutional Framework” pp. 18–19) defines as one objective the development of ethical transparency and regulatory tools to ensure AI respects fundamental rights. Axis No. 3 (Governance and Ethics) aims to protect people from the social economic and environmental impacts of AI (p. 18). The AI Policy Action Plan (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c0LRa31x4-tylFuwOvimUc3CqPy4gxOy/view?usp=drive_link) also includes Initiative No. 145 which proposes ex-ante algorithmic risk assessment tools mainly for State use (p. 34). However these measures remain largely declarative and do not establish mandatory or systematic pre-deployment impact assessments.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Law No 21431 - Amends the labor code regulating the contract of workers of digital platforms (Chile)
items.justification: The document addresses AI labour protections primarily through transparency and non-discrimination rules. On pages 6-7 Article 152 (quinquies B C D E F G and H) mandates platform transparency employees´ right to information prohibits discrimination via automated decision-making mechanisms establishes requirements for worker training and protective equipment legal compensation and collective rights of digital platform workers. The Labour Directorate shall oversee compliance and define fines (p. 7-8 Art. 152 quinquies I).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Labor Directorate

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes specific provisions to protect workers from AI-driven discrimination but only for workers associated with digital platforms. It explicitly prohibits discrimination through automated decision-making mechanisms (Article 152 quinquies E p. 7) mandating platforms to implement safeguards against discriminatory practices in work assignment bonus/incentive offerings and remuneration calculation. These protections apply to both dependent and independent digital platform workers (as defined in Article 152 quater Q pp. 1-2) covering those subject to algorithmic management regardless of their formal contract status and include protections against retaliatory termination (Article 152 quinquies B pp. 5-6).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: The document sets transparency requirements for algorithmic management but only for digital platform workers. It requires platform companies upon official request to provide access to algorithmic programming and explanations of automated decisions (Article 152 quinquies D pp. 6–7). Workers also have rights to access and portability of personal data including performance evaluations (Article 152 quinquies D p. 6). Employment contracts must explain how user ratings affect workers and ensure transparent objective criteria for work assignment (Article 152 quater S p. 2) creating obligations to explain how AI systems monitor performance and affect work conditions.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document explicitly reinforces workers’ rights to organise and collectively bargain but only for a specific category of workers. Article 152 quinquies H (pp. 7-8) grants all digital service platform workers—both dependent and independent—the right to form trade unions without prior authorisation and to enjoy all related rights under the Labour Code. Crucially it specifies that unions representing these workers including those composed solely of independent workers have the right to engage in collective bargaining with digital platform companies. This provision directly strengthens collective rights in the platform-based gig economy sector shaped by algorithmic management.

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The document addresses Labour Protections mainly under Axis N°3: Governance and Ethics specifically Section 3.6 “Impacts on Work” (p. 36). This section explains how AI and automation are transforming jobs and tasks creating risks of job displacement. It proposes labour foresight retraining and reskilling pathways and the updating of labour legislation to protect workers’ rights in the context of AI-driven technological change. It also emphasises regulating human–machine interaction merely creating good practice guidelines for the ethical use of AI and preventing rights violations due to automation with potential updates to labour legislation. More specific measures are included in the action plan of the same policy.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems

Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Guide for the adoption of the recommendations from the Council for Transparency on transparency algorithms (Chile)
items.justification: The document addresses public disclosure through proactive algorithmic transparency obligations for government Automated or Semi-Automated Decision Systems (SDAs). Section V mandates that SDAs affecting fundamental rights or access to public services must be publicly disclosed on agencies’ active transparency websites under a new item titled “Algorithmic Transparency” (pp. 21–23). It specifies what must be published: (a) the SDAs in use (b) the services or procedures where they apply and (c) their specifications including purpose and data categories (Sections V.2–V.4 pp. 22–27).Earlier Section II.1 clarifies that SDA-related information qualifies as public information under transparency law subject to disclosure unless lawful secrecy
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: The document recommends creating a public listing of government SDAs through proactive publication but it does not establish a single centralized registry nor cover all AI systems. Section V requires agencies to publish information on SDAs that affect fundamental rights or access to services (p. 21) including the name/identifier of the system its purpose general operation data categories used and the responsible agency (Sections V.2–V.4 pp. 22–27). However internal systems and SDAs without public impact are excluded and publication occurs on each agency’s active transparency website not a unified government-wide registry

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The document recommend disclosure of key information about high-impact SDAs but not all elements listed. Section V mandates proactive publication of SDAs that affect fundamental rights or access to services (p. 21). Within Section V.4.3 agencies must disclose the purpose of the system its rationale general operation and categories of data used including information on training validation and testing data (pp. 27–29). However the framework does not require formal impact assessments nor mandate publication of their results. Thus it covers data use and rationale but not impact assessment outcomes.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The document provides clear guidance on what SDA-related information should be disclosed and what may be lawfully protected. Section IV.3 details how requests for access to SDA information must be assessed under the grounds for secrecy or confidentiality in Article 21 of the Transparency Law including national security cybersecurity personal data protection and intellectual property (pp. 16–17). Section V.5 further instructs agencies to apply the Divisibility Principle allowing partial disclosure when full publication would infringe protected interests (p. 30). Together these sections establish a clear disclosure–protection framework.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: The guide explicitly recommends providing a clear accessible non-technical description of how SDAs operate and how they affect individuals. Section IV.1 establishes the principle of plain language requiring information on SDAs to be concise intelligible and free of unnecessary technical jargon and suggests formats such as plain text Q&A visuals and model cards (p. 14-20). Additionally Section V.4.3 requires publishing general explanations of the SDA’s purpose operation and data categories aimed at informing the public about their potential impact (pp. 27–29)

items.title: Public Procurement Directive No. 44 on Recommendations for the Acquisition of Projects That Include Data Science and Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Chile)
items.justification: The guideline regulates the public procurement of AI by establishing a structured process ensuring ethical transparent and secure acquisitions. It details procurement phases—from problem identification solution proposals to contract management—and includes measures for transparency data protection bias mitigation and algorithmic auditing. Sections 4–5 (pp. 4–19) outline project design market research ethical evaluation and contract management for AI systems. It mandates clauses on data protection impact assessments transparency explainable AI algorithmic auditing and bias analysis. These measures ensure accountability prevent discrimination and promote responsible AI use across public bodies.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: Yes the guideline introduces AI-specific procurement recommendations that extend beyond traditional IT acquisition by including ethical social and technical considerations. Sections 4–5 (pp. 4–19) cover fairness transparency explainability bias analysis and algorithmic auditing—ethical and social aspects—while also detailing technical measures such as model validation data protection impact assessments bias assessments and cybersecurity.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The guideline explicitly recommends that vendors provide evidence of testing for bias fairness and safety in AI systems. Section 4 (in particular in pp. 12–13) requires suppliers to present documentation on model validation algorithmic auditing and bias analysis before procurement approval. It also stresses fairness and explainability as key evaluation criteria to ensure responsible and safe AI implementation in public projects.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: Yes the guideline recommends transparency from vendors about data sources algorithms and model functioning to avoid “black box” systems. Section 4 (in particular pp. 17–18) requires suppliers to disclose information on model design source code training data and explainability through Explainable AI (XAI) principles.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The National AI Policy addresses Public Sector Skills Development mainly under Axis 1: Enabling Factors – Talent Development and Axis 3: Governance and Ethics. It introduces a new objective to promote education and training programs on the ethical use of AI for public officials strengthening permanent capacity-building within public administration (Axis 1.1 Talent Development p.14-15 of translated to English document). Additionally Axis 2 highlights training and incentives to accelerate State modernization through AI (Axis 2.2 Adoption p.18). Axis 3 further reinforces skills development by promoting training for public officials on ethical AI use and the development of tools and guidelines for AI use in the State (Axis 3.1 p.19).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The policy includes measures to upskill and reskill public servants in AI but it does not define a single unified government-wide strategy nor does it explicitly include the judiciary. In Axis Nº1 Section 1.1 Talent Development a new objective promotes education and training on the ethical use of AI for public officials building foundational understanding of AI and its risks. Axis Nº2 Section 2.2 Adoption supports capacity building to modernize the State through AI. Axis Nº3 Section 3.1 Governance reinforces training and guidelines for ethical AI use in the public sector but without a comprehensive cross-government skills strategy.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The Chilean National AI Policy (2024 Update) integrates reskilling and upskilling as central to its talent development strategy under Axis 1 Talent Development (1.1). It commits to 'Promote the formation of skills for the use development understanding and critical analysis of AI for workers in Chile' (p.6) specifically with the goal of 'Enhance programs and training instruments to update and retrain (upskilling and reskilling) the country's workers' (p. 15). Within Axis 3 point 3.6 'Impacts on Work' the framework proposes to prospect and anticipate changes in the labor market. The goal is to reduce gaps in specific sectors and address the need for retraining and training (upskilling/reskilling)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Chilean National AI Policy (2024 Update) includes an explicit objective to “enhance programs and training instruments to update and retrain (upskilling and reskilling) the country’s workers” (Axis 1 p. 15) and additional measures under Impacts on Work (p. 10) including the National Labor Foresight Strategy and mechanisms to help people plan retraining routes. This shows a clear commitment to reskilling and upskilling. However while the policy recognises the need for these initiatives it does not specify that they will be government-funded or subsidised nor does it detail financial mechanisms incentives or dedicated public funding streams. Those operational elements appear only in the Action Plan not in the policy itself.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Law 21719 on protection and processing of personal data (Chile)
items.justification: The law addresses Safety and Security in the AI context through data-protection duties applicable to automated and AI-driven processing. Article 14 and its sub-articles (pp.12–17) set out obligations of data controllers including duties of secrecy or confidentiality information and transparency protection by design and by default (Art. 14 quater) the duty to adopt security measures ensuring confidentiality integrity availability and resilience (Art. 14 quinquies) and the obligation to report security breaches (Art. 14 sexies). AI-related risks are further covered through rules on automated decisions and profiling and required data protection impact assessments for high-risk automated processing (Art. 15 ter p. 18)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Personal Data Protection Agency

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The law does not define AI-specific fallback or emergency protocols but it partially addresses safeguards against system failure through general security and risk-management obligations applicable to AI systems. Article 14 quinquies (pp.14–15) requires measures ensuring system resilience prevention of loss or unauthorized access and the ability to restore availability and access to data after physical or technical incidents which functions as a fallback mechanism. Article 14 sexies (p.15) mandates reporting and management of security breaches and Article 15 ter (pp.17–18) requires impact assessments for high-risk automated processing to identify and mitigate risks.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The law does not require AI-specific pre-deployment testing or validation but it partially addresses lifecycle robustness through general obligations. Article 14 quater (p.14) requires protection by design and by default implying safeguards before and during processing. Article 14 quinquies (pp.14–15) mandates verification evaluation and regular assessment of technical and organisational measures. Additionally Article 15 ter (pp.17–18) requires data protection impact assessments prior to starting high-risk processing including automated decision-making and profiling. These provisions support robustness and documentation but do not mandate explicit AI testing or validation procedures

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Chilean National Policy on Artificial Intelligence (UPDATE 2024)
items.justification: The document addresses Transparency and Explainability in Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI centred on people (pp. 11-12 in translated version) requiring AI systems to ensure traceability and explainability so users understand their interactions results and limitations. Axis 3: Governance and Ethics (p. 18-19) further promotes ethical and transparency requirements in regulation and public procurement as well as the development and agreement on minimum requirements on transparency accountability personal data protection among others to safeguard the responsible development and use of AI.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Technology Knowledge and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly promotes clarity on how AI systems operate under Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI (pp. 11–12). It requires traceability transparency and explainability meaning users must be informed when interacting with AI understand how predictions or results are obtained and know each system’s purpose capabilities and limitations. These measures aim to strengthen public trust and accountability. Additionally Axis 3: Governance and Ethics (p. 18-19) reinforces this through ethical and transparency requirements in regulation and public procurement ensuring openness in AI decision-making and responsible system deployment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The document does not explicitly assign obligations to entities to provide explanations in specific contexts such as hiring or loan applications. However Principle 1: Ethical and responsible use of AI (pp. 11-12) establishes that all AI systems must ensure traceability and explainability informing users how results are produced and their capabilities and limitations. Moreover Axis 3: Governance and Ethics (p. 18-25) promotes ethical and transparency requirements in regulation and public procurement indirectly encouraging accountability and responsible disclosure in high-stakes AI uses -something that is addressed in the Action Plan and in the draft law on artificial intelligence.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Opinions of the State Council on Deepening the Implementation of the “Artificial Intelligence+” Initiative (China)
items.justification: The document mandates comprehensive integration of AI into formal education under the subsection 'AI+ People's Livelihoods and Well-Being': 'Introduce more productive learning approaches' (Subsection (4) point 2 page 5). It calls for: Integrating AI into 'all elements and processes of education and teaching'; Innovating 'new human-computer coordination teaching models' (e.g. smart learning partners); Promoting 'more flexible and resource-rich self-directed learning'.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The document comprehensively addresses curriculum reform across all academic levels. Subsection (12) Strengthen talent cadre construction mandates efforts to 'promote AI education at all academic levels' and 'improve the structure of academic majors' (p.9). Subsection (4) point 2 calls to integrate AI into 'all elements and processes of education and teaching' and to promote a shift in education focus from knowledge transmission to 'capability improvement' (p.5).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The framework calls for establishing programs and platforms necessary for AI education. Subsection (10) optimize the application development environment directs laying out and constructing 'a number of national AI application pilot bases' and 'build common platforms for industry applications' (p.8). Subsection (12) strengthens talent cadre construction by promoting industry-education integration and intensifying high-level talent development indicating the structural establishment of AI-focused programs (p.9).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses training for educators but does not detail resource allocation (e.g. specific grants or dedicated funding lines) for teacher training itself. Subsection (12) Strengthen talent cadre construction states the need to 'strengthen faculty development' (p.9). Subsection (4) point 2 calls for developing 'new human-computer coordination teaching models such as smart learning partners and virtual teachers' which requires training educators (p.3). Financial support is generally committed to 'AI fields' in subsection (13) but is not specifically to education (p.9).

items.title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (China)
items.justification: The document addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence primarily under Information Content Risks and through comprehensive countermeasures. Specifically it notes the risk of Al-generated content being used to fabricate and spread disinformation to mislead the public and threaten social stability and public security (3.2.2 (a); p.44). It also notes the risk of AI in faciilitating traditional illegal or criminal activities including those related to violence (3.2.2 (b) p.44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: It directly identifies the risk of AI systems' Output of illegal and harmful information (e.g. crimes pornography extremism disinformation) that can threaten social stability and public security (3.2.2 (a) p.44). It also recommends service providers to set up safety guardrails to identify intercept and mitigate risks in inputs and outputs preventing illegal content generation and prompt injection attacks. (3.1.2 (b) p.42).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The document requires content moderation through the establishment of safety guardrails to prevent illegal content generation combined with requiring providers to formulate rules for information content interaction and retain the right to terminate misuse services (4.2.2 p.52). It also mentions that input and output filtering should be set up to prevent malicious and illegal content generation and ensure AI system compliance (4.2.4 p.52). Transparency is ensured by promoting traceable management of AI-generated content requiring that all AI-generated content be labeled so that it is identifiable traceable and trustworthy and obligating service providers to maintain operational logs for at least six months (5.6 pp.57-58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: It supports establishing a mechanism for handling public complaints and reports on AI risks and hazards to form an effective public scrutiny atmosphere (5.13 p.61). However the document does not explicitly establish or recommend a formal legal right for victims to demand the immediate platform-wide takedown of harmful content.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Framework identifies the risk that can result in discriminatory content regarding... gender (3.1.1 b p.40). It also recommends deploying deepfake detection tools in scenarios such as government information disclosure and judicial evidence collection (3.2.2 b p.44). However it does not mandate the specific high-impact technical or legal protections that are typically sought against severe targeted gender-based violence.

items.title: Personal Information Protection Law of the People’s Republic of China
items.justification: The PIPL creates comprehensive legal pathways for redress against harms especially those resulting from Automated Decision-Making (AI systems). It grants individuals the right to require handlers to explain the matter and the right to refuse decisions made solely through automation that have a 'major influence' on their rights (article 24 p.7). Critically it provides for judicial redress (the right to sue) (e.g. article 50 pp.12-13 and 70 p.19) and introduces strict liability requiring handlers to bear compensation unless they can prove they are not at fault (article 69 p.19).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Cybersecurity Administration of China (CAC)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Individual Right to Sue: An individual whose request to exercise their rights (including challenging an automated decision) is rejected by a handler 'may file a lawsuit with a People's Court according to the law' (article 50 p.11-12). Group/Public Interest Litigation: People's Procuratorates statutorily designated consumer organizations and organizations designated by the State cybersecurity and informatization department may file a lawsuit with a People's Court according to the law where a handler's violation 'infring[es] on the rights and benefits of many individuals' (article 70 p.19). Compensation and Burden of Proof: Handlers 'shall bear compensation' for harm unless they can prove they are not at fault (article 69 pp.18-19).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: State Regulator Role: The State cybersecurity and informatization department and relevant departments (state regulators) have the duty to 'Accepting and handling personal information protection-related complaints and reports' (article 61 p.16); Public Right to Complain: the law states that 'any organization or individual has the right to file a complaint or report about unlawful personal information handling activities with departments fulfilling personal information protection duties and responsibilities'. The departments must process these promptly and notify the complainant of the outcome  (article 65 pp.17-18).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The PIPL places direct binding duties on companies (Personal Information Handlers) to create and use an internal grievance mechanism: 1. Handlers 'shall establish convenient mechanisms to accept and handle applications from individuals to exercise their rights' (article 50 pp.12-13). 2. Right to Explanation (AI-Specific Grievance): When 'automated decision-making produces decisions with a major influence on the rights and interests of the individual' the individual has the right to require personal information handlers to explain the matter' and they have the right to 'refuse that personal informationhandlers make decisions solely through automated decision-making methods' (article 24 p.7).

items.title: Basic Safety Requirements for Generative Artificial Intelligence Services (China)
items.justification: The document addresses children's rights in AI through multiple provisions. It requires services suitable for minors to enable parental controls for anti-addiction measures restrict paid services beyond minors' legal capacity and prioritize content beneficial to children's well-being (Section 7a)3) page 7). Services unsuitable for minors must implement preventive technical or management measures (Section 7a)4) page 7).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Section 7a)3) (page 7) obligates service providers to: allow guardians to set anti-addiction measures for minors; prohibit paid services inconsistent with minors' legal capacity; actively display content beneficial to children's physical and mental health. Section 7a)4) (page 7) requires technical/management measures preventing minors from using unsuitable services.

items.title: Special Action Plan for Green and Low-Carbon Development of Data Centers (China)
items.justification: The document addresses the environmental impact indicator by setting specific targets for data centers such as increasing renewable energy use and lowering Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) (section I p.1). It outlines key tasks to achieve these goals including optimizing layouts (section II (3) p.2) improving energy and water efficiency (section II (2) p.2) promoting the use of renewable energy (section II (4) p.3) and encouraging resource recycling and reuse (section II (5) p.3). It also mentions the application of 'artificial intelligence energy-saving technologies' to optimize operations (Section II (6) p.4).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) the National Energy Administration (NEA) and the National Data Administration (NDA)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The Special Action Plan for Green and Low-carbon Development of Data Centers includes measures aimed at reducing resource-intensive computing infrastructure associated with AI development. It sets energy-efficiency targets for data centers (e.g. PUE reduction) and promotes consolidation of inefficient facilities transformation of “old small and scattered” data centers and stricter energy and water efficiency requirements for new projects (Section II (2)–(3) pp.2–3). The plan also encourages recycling and reuse of data center equipment and improved resource efficiency (Section II (5) p.3). These measures aim to reduce excessive energy consumption and resource use in computing infrastructure that supports AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: The document directly and comprehensively addresses this topic. The entire plan is dedicated to promoting green and low-carbon development for data centers. It sets clear goals for improving energy efficiency by aiming to lower the average Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) to below 1.5 by the end of 2025 and to 1.25 for newly built large and extra-large data centers (p.1).

items.title: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions (China)
items.justification: The document addresses fairness and non-discrimination by requiring service providers to follow the principles of 'fairness and justice'. It specifically prohibits algorithmic recommendation service providers from using algorithms to engage in 'unreasonably differentiated treatment in trading conditions such as trading prices' and other such unlawful activities based on consumer characteristics (article 21 p.4). It mandates algorithms to uphold the principle of fairness and justice (article 4 p.2). The framework also mandates that providers protect the lawful rights and interests of various groups (article 10 p.3).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The framework promotes fair outcomes by explicitly prohibiting service providers from using algorithms to 'commit acts of extending unreasonably differentiated treatment in trading conditions such as trading prices' (article 21 p.4) based on consumer characteristics. It states that providers should follow the principles of 'fairness and justice' (article 4 p.2) and may not enter unlawful or harmful information as keywords into user interests or make them into user tags to use them as a basis for recommending information content (article 10 p.3).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this by prohibiting the use of algorithms for certain manipulative and discriminatory practices such as 'over-recommend' or 'manipulate topic lists or search result rankings' to influence online public opinion (article 14). It also specifically requires providers to 'not enter unlawful or harmful information as keywords into user interests or make them into user tags' (article 10).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework assigns obligations to providers to 'establish and complete management systems and technical measures for algorithmic mechanism examination and verification [and] technology ethics review' (article 7). It also mandates that providers 'regularly examine verify assess and check algorithmic mechanisms models data and application outcomes' (article 8). This demonstrates a commitment to monitoring and mitigation of potential biases.

items.title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (China)
items.justification: The framework addresses fairness and non-discrimination by stressing bias and discrimination as the inherent safety risks of AI technology. It emphasizes that the risk may lead to discriminatory outcomes including content regarding ethnic nationality religion and gender (3.1.1 b). It advises developers to avoid improper annotation of training data enhance model architectures expand diversity of training data etc. to mitigate bias (4.1.1 b).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document asks AI developers to enhance 'inherent safety features such as reliability fairness...' (6.1.1 p.62) and improve the fairness of AI applications (6.3.8 p.68). It also classifies discriminatory content generated by AI targeting ethnicity nationality gender and religion as an inherent risk (3.1.1 c p.40).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document suggests that the developers should enhance model architectures expand the scale and diversity of training data and introduce human supervision mechanisms to mitigate bias and discrimination (4.1.1.b p.49). It suggests that training data should be strictly selected to filter biased data (4.1.2.b p.50) and recommends evaluating potential biases by strengthening random checks of training data content and quality and designing reliable alignment algorithms (6.1.2 p.62).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document outlines a series of guidelines for the model developers to mitigate discrimination including diversifying training data and enhancing model architecture (4.1.1.b p.49). It also suggests that developers and deployers enhance safety throughout the full life-cycle including deploying techniques like adversarial testing to reduce potential algorithmic bias (5.3 p.56).

items.title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (China)
items.justification: The 'AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0' addresses gender equality by identifying gender discrimination as a risk to be prevented. The document states that during the research development design and training of models and algorithms biases may be unintentionally introduced which could lead to discriminatory outcomes. The framework specifically lists 'gender' as a factor for which AI could produce discriminatory content or outputs (3.1.1.(b) p.40).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The document identifies 'Bias and discrimination' as an inherent safety risk of models and algorithms (3.1.1.(b) p.40). As a countermeasure under 'Ethical risks' the document recommends using methods like training data filtering value alignment and output verification to 'effectively prevent discrimination based on ethnicity belief nationality religion gender and other factors' (3.1.1.(b) p.40). This demonstrates a recognition of the issue and a proposed method for mitigation. However the document does not include specific detailed measures objectives or recommendations that are solely dedicated to gender-related discrimination.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The document states that 'all relevant parties including model and algorithm developers service providers and users assume their respective responsibilities for Al safety' (1.3 p.37). It recommends that developers to introduce human supervision mechanisms to mitigate bias and discrimination (4.1.1.(b) p.49) . These are broad responsibilities to prevent harm and while they apply to discrimination they are not specific measurements to ensure gender equality.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: The Opinions on Regulating and Strengthening the Applications of Artificial Intelligence in the Judicial Fields
items.justification: The framework emphasizes human oversight and determination by clearly defining AI as a strictly supportive tool in adjudication. It affirms that AI must not replace judges under any circumstances with all judicial decisions authority and accountability remaining solely with human adjudicators. AI outputs are limited to supplementary references to assist decision-making rather than determine outcomes (p. 3). At the same time the framework reinforces user autonomy by granting individuals the right to choose whether to use AI-assisted tools and to terminate their interaction with such systems at any point thereby ensuring that both institutional and individual control over decision-making is preserved.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Technology Ethics Management Service Measures (Trial) (Draft for public comments) (China)
items.justification: A Next Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Plan impact assessment through provisions on risk assessment evaluation of AI’s economic social and security impacts and the establishment of monitoring testing and certification mechanisms. It includes dynamic evaluation systems early warning mechanisms and lifecycle supervision of AI systems. (p. 26 (4) Establish an AI security supervision and evaluation system).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Science and Technology Structural Reform and Innovation System Construction Leading Small Group

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions (China)
items.justification: This document addresses the indicator by explicitly requiring algorithm-recommended service providers who provide workers with job scheduling services to protect workers' lawful rights and interests in obtaining labour remuneration and to improve algorithms on platform order distribution. It also includes provisions aimed at protecting the rights of workers subject to algorithmic scheduling (article 20 p.4).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems

Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Notice on Widely Carrying out General Education for Professional Technical Personnel on Artificial Intelligence Continued Education (China)
items.justification: The document mandates promoting AI education across a professional cohort including civil servants. It focuses on advancing the AI literacy and innovation ability of professional technical personnel (section 1 page 1) by emphasizing the basic principles algorithms ethics and law of AI (see section 2 (3) p.2 learning content). The goal is to cultivate a professional workforce adapted to the digital transformation and to prevent risks posed by AI (section 1 page 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Human Resources and Social Security departments

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The strategy is designed for all professional technical personnel (including civil servants) (second paragraph) and explicitly focuses on raising AI literacy covering AI concepts basic principles algorithms and risk prevention as core content (section 2 pp.1-2). However this document does not explicitly include the judiciary (which is covered under Framework 2).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The core purpose is 'continued education'. It explicitly focuses on integrating cutting-edge technology development and aims to build an 'intelligent personalized and whole-domain lifelong autonomous learning system' (section 3 (5) p.3).

items.title: Opinions on Regulating and Strengthening the Judicial Application of Artificial Intelligence (China)
items.justification: The document mandates strengthening the skills of judicial personnel to handle AI. The final section VI. Comprehensive Supports stresses the need to enhance 'publicity and training' and encourage judicial personnel (cadres) to 'fully participate' in AI applications (Section 18 p.4).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Supreme Peoples Court (SPC)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes a specific strategy for the Judiciary by mandating that People's courts 'enhance publicity and training' and encourage judicial personnel to 'fully participate' in AI applications (point 18 p.4). This builds foundational understanding and literacy. It also emphasizes that AI application must adhere to the Principle of Security and Legality ensuring AI products are 'free from discrimination and prejudice' (points 3 4 p.2) and that 'all links of AI systems... would accept examination' (point 6 p.3) covering both applications and risks.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The document mandates the creation of specialized expert bodies but not general champion roles. It requires the establishment of Judicial AI Ethics Council (point 20 p.5) and expert teams to conduct ethical reviews compliance reviews and security assessments. This creates dedicated expert guidance mechanisms. However the framework does not mandate the assignment of general individual 'AI champion' roles like Chief AI Officers across the entire court system.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The framework contains clear long-term goals that necessitate continuous development. The Overall Objectives (Section ii p.2) set deadlines for building an AI application system by 2025 and a complete theoretical system by 2030. The document states AI is leading a new round of scientific and technological revolution (Section I p.2) and calls for courts to 'further promot[e] breakthroughs' (point 18 p.4) confirming the requirement for ongoing training and research to keep pace with rapid technological change.

items.title: Opinions of the State Council on Deepening the Implementation of the “Artificial Intelligence+” Initiative (China)
items.justification: The document directly addresses the indicator under Section (4) 'AI+ People's Livelihoods and Well-Being'. Point 1 (p.5) states the government will 'Vigorously support AI skills training to stimulate the vitality of AI-based innovation entrepreneurship and reemployment'.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The document clearly commits the government to establishing and funding these programs. Point (4)-1 p.5 states the goal to 'Vigorously support AI skills training to stimulate the vitality of AI-based innovation entrepreneurship and reemployment'. Point (12) p.9 'Strengthen talent cadre construction' mandates efforts to promote 'AI education at all academic levels and promote general education throughout society'. Furthermore Point (13) p.9 explicitly commits to 'Intensify financial and government fiscal support for AI fields' which enables funding for these skills programs.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses incentives primarily for high-level AI talents and overall AI fields but not explicitly for general workers participating in reskilling. Point (13) p.9 commits to developing mechanisms to fully leverage the role of policies on 'government funding and procurement'. Separately Point (12) p.9 mentions incentivizing high-level talent by refining evaluation systems and supporting mechanisms like 'equity and stock options to attract retain and utilize talent' in enterprises. It does not however detail specific financial support for workers (e.g. paid leave or grants for the general workforce) covering only partial aspects of this thematic area.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The document strongly encourages but does not appear to mandate specific investment percentages or funding requirements for companies. It pushes all industries to 'increase the formation of reusable expert knowledge' and focuses on ' enhancing the AI literacy and skills of all personnel' point (2)-2 p.3. Furthermore Point (4)-1 p.5 urges guiding 'innovation resources toward areas with high job creation potential to mitigate employment impacts'. However these are expressed as encouragement priorities and goals rather than mandatory legal requirements for investment by private firms.

items.title: AI Safety Governance Framework 2.0 (China)
items.justification: The document addresses AI safety and security by: 1. Classifying risks into Inherent (e.g. poor robustness unreliable output) application (e.g. cyber system risks abuse for cyberattacks) and derivative (e.g. loss of control disrupting social norms) (chapter 3 starting p.39); 2. Mandating technical measures to ensure robustness (e.g. adversarial training 4.1.1.(c) p.49) and controllability (e.g. explicit labeling 4.2.2.(c) p.52); 3. Establishing fault-tolerance measures such as decision verification circuit breakers and one-click control to mitigate harm from system failure (4.2.3 p.52).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The framework addresses the need for quality benchmarks by focusing on the core principles of accuracy and reliability: 1. Accuracy/Reliability Mandate: one goal of the framework is to create 'a safe reliable equitable and transparent AI ecosystem' (section 1 p.35). The framework aims to eliminate unreliable output by expanding training data diversity to enhance the models' generalization capabilities and the reliability of outputs (4.1.1 pp.49-50). 2. It mandates establishing an AI safety assessment system. Model evaluations within this system must specifically focus on the accuracy of generated content and the system's resilience to interference (5.8 pp.58-59).

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly mandates technical safeguards and human intervention protocols for system failure: 1. It requires establishing mechanisms such as circuit breakers and one-click control to enable rapid intervention and loss prevention in extreme situations (4.2.3 c p.52). 2. It mandates the establishment of mechanisms for decision verification fault tolerance and error correction to address algorithmic flaws and occasional randomness(4.2.3 b p.52). 3. It recommends improving redundancy design and disaster recovery mechanisms to ensure systems remain operational during abnormal conditions or attacks (4.2.1 e p.52).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The framework requires comprehensive risk assessments and specific technical testing before deployment: 1. For AI applications that strongly perceive the real world (e.g. intelligent assisted driving) it mandates that perception systems undergo testing in extreme environments before being put into use (4.2.3 d p.53). 2. It requires developers to conduct adversarial training on models to reduce susceptibility to prompt injection attacks and enhance robustness (4.1.1 c p.49). 3. Developers must generate detailed test reports and regularly conduct safety assessment tests. They must also clearly explain the internal structure reasoning logic and accurately reflect the process by which AI systems produce outcomes. (6.1.11 p.64)

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The framework dedicates multiple sections to defining and countering threats from malicious entities: 1. It explicitly addresses the risk of external adversarial attack and mandates developers conduct adversarial training on models to enhance resistance (4.1.1 c p.49). 2. It prioritizes supply chain security for chips software and tools. It asks model files framework tools third-party libraries and other components required for large model services to be obtained from valid sources (5.4 pp.56-57). 3. It requires establishing a protection mechanism to prevent models from being interfered and tampered with during operation (4.2.2 a p.52).

items.title: Internet Information Service Algorithmic Recommendation Management Provisions (China)
items.justification: The document addresses transparency in algorithmic recommendation systems through several provisions. Article 4 establishes “openness and transparency” as guiding principles for algorithmic services. Article 7 requires providers to formulate and disclose norms related to algorithmic recommendation services and implement management and review mechanisms. Article 12 encourages providers to improve the transparency and understandability of recommendation processes such as search ranking and push notifications. Additionally Article 25 requires authorities to publish filing information for registered algorithmic services enhancing public transparency.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The document fully addresses this. Article 16 (p.4) states that providers must 'notify users in a clear manner about the situation of the algorithmic recommendation services they provide and publicize the basic principles purposes and motives [and] main operational mechanisms'. This is a direct promotion of clarity and transparency to build public trust.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Article 17 (p.4) states that where an algorithm has a 'major influence on users’ rights and interests' the provider must 'give an explanation' and 'bear related liability according to the law'. Article 2 (p.1) also mentioned that 'dispatching and decision-making–type' of algorithm recommendation system is included. The document however does not specifically mention high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Article 17 (p.4) establishes the right for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision.
