thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy requires from designers to implementers to commit to minimising biases in algorithms and databases that could negatively influence automated decisions conducting continuous audits and tests to identify and correct any potential biases in AI systems and promoting diversity and inclusion at all stages of the AI system lifecycle. These obligations are established in the Equity and Non-discrimination section (p.32). The Reference Framework for Costa Rica (p.42) further requires the analysis of training data and algorithms to identify and mitigate potential biases that could result in discrimination.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The ENIA 2024-2027 addresses gender equality in AI across multiple provisions. At p. 24 the strategy defines a gender approach establishing gender equality as a substantive consideration in AI development and deployment. At p.34 gender is designated as a cross-cutting principle governing the entire strategy meaning all axes and action lines are expected to reflect gender equality considerations. At p.55 the strategy recommends that AI training programmes be accessible and inclusive explicitly ensuring that people of all genders acquire the necessary AI skills directly addressing gender representation in the AI workforce. The ENIA is a non-binding strategy; its provisions constitute recommendations rather than enforceable obligations.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Recommendation: One of the most effective measures is conducting gender audits for algorithms to identify and mitigate discriminatory biases. These audits must be systematic and applied during both the development and usage stages of AI ensuring that data models are representative and fair (p.24).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Recommendation: It is essential to work in coordination with the Ministry of Women’s Affairs the National Institute for Women (INAMU) and civil society organizations advocating for women’s rights ensuring that a gender perspective is integrated throughout all phases of the AI system lifecycle (p.24). Also it is recommended to conduct gender audits for algorithms to identify and mitigate discriminatory biases (p.24).

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: Recommendation: The Strategy indicates that it is vital to promote the active participation of women in AI development governance and decision-making processes because currently women account for only 22% of professionals in the AI field worldwide limiting the diversity of perspectives in the development of these technologies (p.24). However stops short of defining specific initiatives or programmes.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The Strategy defines this principle as maintaining ultimate human control over systems that use AI ensuring that ethical and legal responsibility can always be clearly attributed to individuals or legal entities at any stage of these systems’ lifecycle (p.31). It mentions examples for the healthcare and judicial sectors (p.31). It also says that height risk IA applications will have mandatory human oversight mechanisms (p.42).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The strategy addresses meaningful human control over AI systems across multiple sections. The Transparency and Explainability guiding principle (p.31) states that humans must retain control over decisions that significantly affect people's lives and well-being and provides sector-specific examples including that any AI-assisted diagnosis must be reviewed and approved by a medical professional before being communicated to the patient and that judicial decisions must remain under human determination. The Accountability principle (p.33) further requires that critical decisions particularly those with significant consequences for human rights and environmental well-being remain under the supervision of competent human oversight.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy does not elaborate specific measures in sensitive sectors but it presents an example that shows that sensitive sectors require a special treatment. It says that any diagnosis in healthcare that is assisted by AI must be reviewed and approved by a medical professional before it is communicated to the patient (p.31).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The Accountability guiding principle of the Strategy states that actors involved in the lifecycle of AI systems must implement robust oversight mechanisms including impact assessments particularly for decisions with significant consequences for human rights and environmental well-being (p.33). The Costa Rica Reference Framework further specifies that an impact assessment must be conducted as a mitigation measure before implementing any AI solution identified as high-risk (p.42).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Accountability guiding principle states that actors involved in the lifecycle of AI systems must implement robust oversight mechanisms including impact assessments particularly for decisions with significant consequences for human rights and environmental well-being (p.33). The Costa Rica Reference Framework further establishes that an impact assessment must be conducted as a mitigation measure before implementing any AI solution identified as high-risk (p.42). As a non-binding strategy these provisions constitute recommendations rather than legally enforceable obligations.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Accountability guiding principle states that actors involved in the lifecycle of AI systems which encompasses developers and users must implement oversight mechanisms including impact assessments for decisions with significant consequences for human rights and environmental well-being (p.33). The Reference Framework additionally requires impact assessments before implementing high-risk AI solutions (p.42). However as a non-binding strategy these provisions are recommendations rather than enforceable obligations and they do not specify the scope or methodology of required assessments.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The ENIA 2024-2027 addresses this indicator narrowly. At p.32 the strategy requires that any automated decision affecting citizens in the governmental sphere be accompanied by a clear and accessible explanation of how the decision was made including the data and algorithms used. This provision applies exclusively to the public sector. The ENIA does not establish a public registry or inventory of government AI systems nor does it require proactive disclosure of high-risk system information or impact assessment results.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: Costa Rica's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (ENIA) launched by MICITT in October 2024 explicitly prioritises AI capacity building for public officials. The Training and Education Enabling Mechanism (p.55) establishes that continuous training programmes are essential to keep public officials updated on AI advancements. Axis 5 (p.68) further sets equipping public officials with tools to understand and apply AI in their fields as a strategic objective. Both provisions directly address public sector skills development.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: Although the Strategy does not have a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants in IA it has 'Axis 5: Talent Training and Capacity Building' which includes as one objective to equip public officials with the necessary tools to understandand apply AI in their respective fields.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy says that continuous training is important to keep public officials updated on technological advancements. This includes workshops online courses certifications and professional development programs addressing technical ethical and legal aspects of AI (p.55).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The Strategy establishes continuous training for workers across all productive sectors as a cross-cutting principle recognising the need to equip the workforce with AI-related competencies (p.35). It further states that educational efforts must be directed toward AI training to ensure the workforce is prepared for future challenges (p.57). The new productive and labour model identified in the Strategy calls for policies facilitating the acquisition of skills and competencies related to AI across the labour market (p.61). As a non-binding strategy these provisions constitute recommendations rather than legally enforceable obligations.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: To guarantee safety and cybersecurity mechanisms must be implemented to allow for supervision intervention and if necessary the safe deactivation of systems. AI security and cybersecurity also entail the creation of resilient systems this includes adopting security-by-design practices implementing robust access controls encrypting data and others (p.33-34). The Cybersecurity Directorate of the Ministry must focus on mitigating cyber risks and act as a comprehensive response center (p.43). This office will be strengthened to: Development of Forensic Capabilities Incident Response in Various Contexts Efficient Response to AI Incidents Training and Multidisciplinary Collaboration and others (p.44-46).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications (and The Cybersecurity Directorate which is part of the Ministry)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy has a Reference Framework for Costa Rica (p.41-42) that identifies four levels of risk based on the AI Act of the European Union namely: Unacceptable Risk High Risk Medium Risk and Low Risk. For each identified risk level the Strategy proposes mitigation measures. One of them is Cybersecurity defined as the need to assess the system’s vulnerability to cyberattacks and its capacity to withstand security threats.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The Incident Response Center of the Cybersecurity Directorate of the Ministry will be strengthened to ensure preparedness for responding to AI-related incidents such as failures in autonomous decision-making or adverse manipulations of algorithms. This will involve coordinating with various institutions to ensure the rapid and effective containment of threats as well as providing technical guidance on how to restore systems affected by AI incidents minimizing the impact on public services (p.45).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: To guarantee safety and cybersecurity mechanisms must be implemented to allow for supervision intervention and if necessary the safe deactivation of systems. AI security and cybersecurity also entail the creation of resilient systems this includes adopting security-by-design practices implementing robust access controls encrypting data and others (p.33-34). The Cybersecurity Directorate of the Ministry must focus on mitigating cyber risks and act as a comprehensive response center (p.43). This office will be strengthened to implement several key activities such as: development of forensic capabilities incident response in various contexts and several more (p.44-46).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2027 (Costa Rica)
items.justification: The framework requests entities developing and implementing AI to provide comprehensible context-appropriate information that explains the capabilities and limitations of AI crucial to enable users to understand how and when IA impacts them (p.31). It further states that any automated decision in the public sector should be accompanied by a clear and accessible explanation of how the decision was made. And for the private sector they must inform customers when AI is used and provide options for users to opt out of being affected by these systems (p.32). And it also contains mitigation measures (p.42) such as periodic reviews by ethical and technical committees and mechanisms for correction and continuous improvement.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Science Innovation Technology and Telecommunications

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy states that it is essential to provide clear details about data sources and the processes leading to automated decisions so individuals can understand and if necessary challenge these outcomes. This commitment to transparency is also vital to strengthen accountability and trust (p.31-32). And that any automated decision in the public sector should be accompanied by a clear and accessible explanation of how the decision was made. And for the private sector companies must inform customers when AI is used in their services and provide options for users to opt out of being affected by these systems (p.32).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The ENIA therefore partially addresses this sub-question the guiding principle (p.31) establishes that individuals have the right to know when they are interacting with an AI system & the right to opt-out of being affected by it. However the term 'right' isn't used in relation to receiving explanations of AI decisions it applies specifically to the interaction with the system itself. Furthermore the obligation to accompany automated decisions with a clear & accessible explanation of how the decision was made applies exclusively to the public sector (p.32); no equivalent obligation exists for private sector actors. In sum but falls short of guaranteeing a universal individual right to understand the key factors behind an AI decision.

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 takes a concrete and targeted approach to AI literacy within the formal education system promoting measures to develop learners' understanding use evaluation and creation of AI while implicitly integrating ethical dimensions. These measures focus on the gradual integration of AI into curricula early awareness-raising among young people and training in technical and critical skills: Page 13 (section on “Training and skills development”); Pages 17-19 (sections on “Establishing specialised training programmes” and “Raising awareness and inspiring younger generations”): There are plans to introduce “basic AI concepts into school curricula with practical activities such as coding or robotics” (p. 18).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The National AI Agency (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: Partially the SNIA 2030 emphasizes the integration of AI into school curricula mainly at the secondary and higher education levels with explicit measures and reforms. However it does not explicitly address primary education (no mention of AI modules or curriculum reforms at the primary level). In fact no provision measure objective or recommendation mentions the integration of AI or curriculum reform at the primary education level (cycles 1 and 2). The approach remains focused on secondary and higher education to develop technical skills and prepare talent (pages 17 19 67).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The SNIA includes several specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations related to the creation of educational institutions or programmes. The creation of institutions or structures dedicated to AI training (Page 67 (Phase 2 Investment 3). The creation of the City of Innovation (AI HUB): Pages 57 & 66 dedicated to innovation and collaboration between start-ups researchers and companies with training/research aspects. For the creation or implementation of formal educational programmes through partnerships (Page 17_Investment Pillar): ‘Establish specialised training programmes’ and ‘Collaborate with universities [...] to design specialised curricula’ (in fields such as data science machine learning NLP computer vision).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The SNIA contains specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations related to teacher training and the resources needed to teach AI. Teacher training and capacity building: Pages 41-42 (Pillar 2: Inclusion section on Academia Research and Training). Continuing and specialised training programmes: Page 17 (Pillar 1: Investment Strengthening Local Skills): Establishment of specialised and continuing training programmes with partnerships to design appropriate curricula. Page 68 (Phase 3 Investment 4): Expansion and transformation into a regional centre of excellence with advanced modules and international collaborations to strengthen the capacities of instructors (including teachers).

items.title: Circular No. 0320: Maintaining the teaching of ICT in the National Education system in Côte d'Ivoire
items.justification: The gradual introduction of Information and Communication Technologies for Education (ICTE) from pre-primary and primary school onwards is a programme launched by the Ministry of National Education and Literacy (MENA) for the 2025-2026 school year. It began at the start of the 2025-2026 school year (early September 2025) with digital technology being integrated as a subject or teaching tool from pre-primary (nursery) and primary school onwards. This includes the introduction of ICT (basic computer skills digital tools digital literacy) as recommended by the National Education and Literacy Council (EGENA). The Ministry's circular and the associated programme set the foundations for a digital culture (simple coding use of digital tools).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: The SNIA 2030 addresses cultural and linguistic diversity in the context of AI in an integrated and positive way considering AI as a tool for preserving enhancing and promoting multicultural heritage. This approach is grounded in the principles of inclusion equity and ethics in order to avoid bias and adapt AI to local realities. Pages 3 and 4 (Section I. Introduction and Context): AI is seen as a lever for inclusive transformation. Page 11 (Section II. Vision Mission and Objectives): The vision explicitly includes promoting AI to enhance cultural and linguistic diversity. Page 37 includes inclusion as a core Developing multilingual tools is also one of the core strategic recommendations on page 40.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 establishes an ethical framework to prevent cultural and linguistic bias in the development of AI tools emphasising that ‘AI must respect the cultural and linguistic diversity of Côte d'Ivoire to avoid marginalising communities and perpetuating stereotypes’ (SNIA p. 14). This general provision is rooted in the adoption of the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI which emphasises non-discrimination and the promotion of cultural identities (SNIA p. 16). Key principles include non-discrimination language preservation (the 60+ local languages must be integrated to prevent their disappearance) and cultural equity.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 considers fairness and non-discrimination to be cross-cutting and mandatory principles in the development and use of AI. Equity and non-discrimination are integrated as fundamental principles (p. 13) concrete sectoral objectives (pp. 36–49) and operational governance commitments (pp. 49–54 58) with tools such as audits SafeAI certification and independent collaboration to prevent bias and discrimination.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The SNIA explicitly addresses the promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems by combating disproportionate bias. Guiding principles (p. 13): ‘Inclusion and social equity’ and ‘reducing inequalities’ to prevent AI from disproportionately affecting vulnerable groups. Inclusion pillar (pp. 36-49): ‘equitable access’ objective and solutions tailored to women young people rural communities and people with disabilities. Governance pillar (pp. 52-54): obligation to ‘identify and correct algorithmic biases’ ‘rigorous testing for algorithmic fairness’ enhanced audits for high-risk systems diversity of training data. The SafeAI Label (appendix): mandatory criteria on  detection/correction of biases and disproportionate impacts.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 contains explicit provisions against perpetuating or amplifying social prejudices and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics. Guiding Principles (p. 13): The principle of ‘Inclusion and Social Equity’ explicitly prohibits any discrimination based on gender age ethnicity or other protected characteristics. Governance Pillar (pp. 52-54):  Obligation to ‘identify and correct algorithmic biases’ that may perpetuate social prejudices.  The SafeAI label must be proof that the system does not amplify discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or disability.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 explicitly imposes this obligation on AI developers and deployers. Governance Pillar (p. 52): ‘Require rigorous testing to identify and correct biases in AI systems’ + ‘protect against algorithmic biases’. SafeAI label (technical appendix criteria 3 & 4): Proactive obligation to assess bias at each stage of the lifecycle (design training data training testing deployment post-deployment monitoring).  For high-risk systems (p. 53): enhanced audits are mandatory covering the entire life cycle with continuous documentation. Enforceable via ANIA: refusal of SafeAI label (and therefore funding/public procurement) in case of non-compliance.

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 addresses the issue of gender equality in the context of AI in a cross-cutting and integrated manner mainly through the ‘Inclusion’ pillar and social equity objectives. Analysis of SNIA (keywords: SNIA and gender equality) shows that it does not devote a chapter exclusively to gender but integrates gender equality as a fundamental principle to avoid bias and promote inclusive AI specifically targeting women (and young people) as priority groups for access to AI-related skills innovation and economic opportunities (page 42 section on the Inclusion pillar). It explicitly plans to ‘actively include women and young people in technology initiatives and AI training programmes’.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations related to preventing the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias. These elements are addressed in a cross-cutting and integrated manner mainly in the Inclusion and Ethical Governance pillars without constituting a separate chapter dedicated to gender discrimination. It adopts a general principle of ‘inclusive and non-discriminatory AI’ and explicitly incorporates the need to prevent gender bias in AI systems  Pages 40–41 (Ethical Governance pillar). Specific programmes to empower women and reduce inequalities Page 47 (support and empowerment measures).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 assigns responsibilities to AI developers and users under the Ethical Governance pillar. On p.41 it refers to “regular ethical audits” and accountability mechanisms to ensure compliance with principles of fairness and non-discrimination which implicitly include gender equality. Under the Inclusion pillar (p.42) and support measures (p.47) it calls for developing specific programmes to empower women. However the strategy does not appear to establish explicit binding gender-specific obligations or enforcement mechanisms directed at AI entities.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures and objectives aimed at increasing the representation of women in the AI workforce although these elements remain rather general and cross-cutting rather than quantified or ultra-detailed. The central pillar of Inclusion explicitly emphasises inclusive and equitable AI with a particular focus on women young people and vulnerable populations. Guiding principles and promotion of social inclusion: Actively encourage women in AI-related initiatives through incentive policies awareness campaigns and retraining/training opportunities. These elements indirectly aim to increase female representation in the sector (training jobs entrepreneurship in AI).

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 addresses the issue of human oversight and human in the loop/meaningful human control in a relatively clear and explicit manner but remains at the level of principles and future commitments rather than detailed operational implementation. The approach focuses on protecting fundamental rights preventing fully automated decisions in sensitive areas and ensuring meaningful human control when AI systems have a significant impact on individuals. These can be found in the Guiding Principles (Section II – Vision Mission and Principles – around p. 13): Principle No. 1: Priority to humans) and Pillar 1 – Investment (Section IV around p. 32).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The SNIA 2030 promotes meaningful human control over AI through explicit objectives and guiding principles. It affirms that humans must remain at the centre of AI development and that AI should complement rather than replace human capabilities (p. 13 “Humanity first”). This human-centred approach is reinforced under the Investment pillar which emphasises ethical inclusive and responsible AI transparency bias reduction and respect for individual freedoms particularly in areas with broad socio-economic impact (pp. 34–35).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 addresses the development of AI skills in the public sector in a prioritised and structured manner mainly through its ‘Investment’ pillar (including infrastructure and human talent) and phase 1 of implementation (6 months after launch). The aim is to modernise public administration through AI (simplification of procedures e-services) filling the skills gaps among public servants to ensure an effective and inclusive digital transformation. ‘Investment’ pillar (talent and skills). To this end there are plans to map AI skills in order to identify the needs of the public sector (administrative staff) and develop appropriate training programmes.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The SNIA 2030 includes a government-wide commitment to upskilling public servants under its “Investment” pillar (talent and infrastructure) and Phase 1 implementation measures. It plans AI skills mapping to identify gaps within public administration and the development of targeted training programmes to modernise governance and e-services. However it does not explicitly mention members of the judiciary or establish a detailed cross-branch training mechanism covering both civil servants and judges.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA2030 takes a cross-cutting and proactive approach to safety and security. It does so through four guiding principles: Page 13 (Section II. Guiding Principles) to guide the overall strategy emphasising risk prevention and the reliability of AI systems. Concrete safety and security measures:  Page 33 (Investment pillar section on innovation and infrastructure): Implementation of the SafeAI certification process.  Page 37 (Inclusion pillar section on sectoral applications): Use of AI for risk management and public safety. Page 52 (Governance pillar section on ethical safeguards): Definition of safeguards accompanying the adoption of AI including algorithmic transparency regular audits and the protection of citizens' rights.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Partially because SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations aimed at ensuring the reliable and accurate functioning of AI systems but it does not define explicit performance thresholds or measurable quantifiable quality criteria. It has Guiding Principles (Pages 13–14): Statement of principles of ‘safety’ ‘reliability’ and ‘risk assessment’ (ethical data-related and sovereignty-related) without quantitative thresholds. It emphasises the implementation of regular algorithmic audits SafeAI certification algorithmic transparency (Pages 56–59) and a SafeAI certification process explicitly mentioned as a tool to ensure the safety and quality of deployed systems without key criteria.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 partially addresses this criterion by referring to audits (P33 and 52) certifications  guarantees regarding algorithmic transparency (P52) pilot projects and validation practices aimed at improving the reliability and safety of AI to ensure their reliability throughout their lifecycle (P56-59). However it does not explicitly establish mandatory requirements for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation throughout the AI system's entire lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Partially because SNIA 2030 does refer to cybersecurity standards and audits (P55-59) as guiding principles (P13) with cross-cutting objectives with the Safe AI Label (P33) but it does not introduce explicit and binding technical security requirements specifically designed to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or malicious interference.

items.title: Côte d'Ivoire's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (SNIA) for 2030
items.justification: SNIA 2030 addresses transparency and explainability as essential pillars of ethical and responsible AI governance. These concepts are addressed in a cross-cutting manner primarily in the guiding principles Pillar 1 (Investment in the ecosystem and regulatory/ethical framework (pages 13-14) and Pillar 3 (Ethical and effective governance (pages 49-54)) with an emphasis on the need to build public trust and reduce the risks associated with opaque (‘black box’) systems. The approach is forward-looking declarative and sets out principles future obligations (audits national standards) and commitments for high-risk systems without going into the technical details of immediate implementation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Agency/Agence National de lIA (ANIA)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations concerning the promotion of clarity regarding the functioning of AI systems including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic in order to foster public trust. References: Page 32 (section on transparency and explainability) Page 32 (same section) (Accountability Mechanisms) and Pages 32–33 (Governance and Oversight Mechanisms section). These provisions are directly aimed at enhancing transparency (purpose data sources decision-making logic) and building public trust particularly in areas with a high societal impact.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations concerning the obligation for entities developing and using AI to provide relevant explanations of their systems' results particularly in high-stakes contexts such as job applications or loan applications. Key elements and specific references: Page 32 (section on transparency and explainability) Pages 32–33: Reinforcement of these obligations through:  regular algorithmic audits. These measures are in line with the principles of ethical governance and accountability (algorithmic transparency protection of citizens' rights) and explicitly aim to make the results of AI systems understandable in situations that are sensitive for individuals.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: SNIA 2030 includes specific provisions measures objectives and recommendations concerning the establishment of individuals' right to receive an explanation of a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome. Key elements and specific references: Pages 32-33 (section on transparency explainability and ethical governance). These provisions are consistent with the principles of accountability fairness and protection of citizens' rights with a requirement for clear and accessible explanations to build trust and enable effective recourse.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
