thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: National Recovery and Resilience Plan (2021-2026) (Croatia)
items.justification: Although the framework does not explicitly refer to AI it has been in practice applied to AI-related upskilling. The framework establishes the voucher system for adult education as a financial support instrument of the Croatian Employment Service enabling (un)employed persons to acquire green digital and other in-demand skills aligned with the Croatian Qualifications Framework (measure C4.1.R3.). Participants choose the training program and the voucher value is paid directly to the provider (p. 935). The system supports AI upskilling as several AI-specific courses are available in the voucher course database (https://web.archive.org/web/20260108203555/https://vauceri.hzz.hr/katalog-vjestina/popis-vjestina-i-programa/).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Governing Board

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: Although the framework does not explicitly refer to AI it has been in practice applied to AI-related upskilling. The framework establishes the voucher system for adult education as a financial support instrument of the Croatian Employment Service enabling (un)employed persons to acquire digital skills aligned with the Croatian Qualifications Framework (measure C4.1.R3.) including AI related skills. Participants choose the training program and the voucher value is paid directly to the training provider (p. 935). Several AI-specific courses are available in the voucher course database (https://web.archive.org/web/20260108203555/https://vauceri.hzz.hr/katalog-vjestina/popis-vjestina-i-programa/).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Although the framework does not explicitly refer to AI it has been in practice applied to AI-related upskilling. The framework establishes the voucher system for adult education as a financial support instrument of the Croatian Employment Service enabling (un)employed persons to acquire digital skills including AI related skills. Participants may freely choose a training program and accredited provider with the voucher value paid directly to the training provider. If the program cost exceeds the voucher amount the difference is covered either by the participant or their employer. AI courses in the voucher course database: https://web.archive.org/web/20260108203555/https://vauceri.hzz.hr/katalog-vjestina/popis-vjestina-i-programa/

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic's National AI Strategy has a dedicated pillar on talent and education with concrete AI-literacy actions: integrating age-appropriate AI modules in schools (p 49) training public-school teachers and university faculty (p 49-50) and creating secondary/vocational AI courses (p 50) to build critical thinking and STEM skills. It adds certification programs targeting 10000 students new degrees scholarships and a women-in-AI training track (p 50-52).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy  mandates curriculum changes at all levels: it adds AI concepts to the national school curriculum through age-appropriate modules (p 49). It creates secondary and vocational AI courses (p 51). And it expands tertiary curricula via new programs: a BSc in Data Science and a Master’s in AI (p 51).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy expands tertiary curricula via new programs: a BSc in Data Science and a Master’s in AI (p 51).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National AI Strategy includes a dedicated pillar for talent and education which outlines specific AI literacy initiatives. These initiatives involve training public school teachers and university faculty (p 49-50).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic's National AI Strategy (ENIA) acknowledges AI-driven threats to democracy specifically citing fake news and election hacking (p. 18). To counter these the strategy aims to implement policies that enhance online content integrity focusing on hate speech disinformation false information and identity falsification while clearly defining intermediary responsibilities (p. 39). Furthermore the strategy addresses AI-enabled violence by proposing both a domestic ban and a regional treaty to prohibit autonomous weapons (p. 40).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National AI Strategy tackles AI-facilitated misinformation and violence through two main approaches. Firstly it establishes a regulatory framework for online content to prevent AI-enabled creation amplification and spread of infringing content (p. 38). This framework targets and enables removal of hate speech disinformation and identity falsification and defines intermediary responsibilities (p. 39). Secondly the strategy addresses AI-enabled violence by committing to prohibit AI as a weapon and advocating for a regional treaty to ban autonomous weapons (p. 40).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National AI Strategy mandates that online intermediaries adhere to a regulatory framework (p. 38). This framework outlines clear policies for identifying and removing illicit content such as hate speech disinformation and identity fraud. It also defines the roles responsibilities and repercussions for non-compliance thereby imposing significant content-moderation duties on these platforms (p. 39). However the strategy does not explicitly require platforms or AI developers to disclose how their systems manage harmful content nor does it assign specific moderation obligations to developers.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy addresses user redress by updating Law 172-13 to enhance user control over personal data including rights to access modify limit or erase data along with clear notice and consent requirements (pp. 36-37). The strategy commits to an Ethical AI Code that will inform when AI is used for profiling decision-making or during interactions. This code will establish mechanisms of supervision compensation and avenues of recourse allowing regulators and courts to request system information (p. 38). It plans to implement quality monitoring incorporating transparency criteria and citizen feedback to improve complaint handling and facilitate corrective actions in AI (p. 42).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Dominican Republics National AI Strategy establishes a General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development through Objective 111 to coordinate implement and monitor the National AI Strategy and proper AI use nationwide It outlines roles for inter-agency coherence and follow-up on responsible AI use but authority timelines and enforcement tools depend on the forthcoming General Law on Innovation and Digital Development and related decrees (page 37)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy proposes non-judicial avenues for redress overseen by the state. While it does not establish a dedicated AI ombudsman or consumer tribunal it mandates OGTIC to develop an Ethical AI Code. This code is intended to include mechanisms of supervision compensation and avenues of recourse for harms caused by AI (p. 36 38). Additionally the strategy incorporates service-quality monitoring citizen feedback and ratings transparency criteria and integration into the Observatory of Public Service Quality and the Citizen Satisfaction Index (p. 42 44 72). However the strategy falls short of designating or empowering a specific body to resolve AI-related grievances.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National AI Strategy partially addresses cultural and linguistic diversity by adopting inclusion and diversity as guiding principles (page 52) promoting multilingualism in regional interoperability standards (page 65) referencing Dominican diaspora communities (page 53) and signaling participation in regional AI ethics forums (page 64). However it sets no concrete measures such as targets budgets localization requirements or minority-language datasets so recognition remains high-level and non-operational.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy only partially promotes the development of AI systems representative of diverse cultures and languages: it sets inclusion/diversity as principles (page 43) references multilingualism in regional interoperability (page 65) and notes diaspora considerations (page 53). It recommends ethics cooperation and regional standards (pages 63-65) but lacks concrete measures such as minority-language datasets localization/translation requirements for public AI services measurable targets budgets or procurement criteria. Until such specifics are adopted it provides high-level guidance rather than operational or enforceable provisions.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy prioritizes the environment as a key mission. It proposes initiatives to promote sustainability such as creating ecological open environmental datasets for research through HUB #YoSoyFuturoRD. This initiative will allocate essential financial resources to projects tackling high-impact environmental challenges (p54). Furthermore the strategy advocates for the development of regional data repositories (p56) to house climate and environmental data which will be used to inform policies on adaptation and resilience (p65).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National AI Strategy partially addresses fairness and non-discrimination by adopting human-rights and inclusion principles (pages 37and 39) committing to update personal-data rules (page 37) creating an ethical AI code with transparency and redress (page 39) and setting pre-deployment review via a regulatory sandbox (page38). However it sets no concrete measures such as legally defined fairness metrics mandatory bias/impact assessments or protected-group monitoring and reporting so recognition remains high-level and non-operational.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy sets an action plan to update Personal Data Protection Law No. 172-13 and add privacy/rights safeguards (pages 38 68) ; develop ethical AI codes nationally with notice transparency supervision and redress (page 69) ; establish a National Regulatory Sandbox Committee for pre-deployment review (page 69) ; create a framework to detect and remove infringing online content like hate speech disinformation identity falsification (page 40) ; and require clear transparent procurement evaluation with certified AI vendors (Objective 2.1.7) . However it does not set explicit anti-bias testing fairness metrics or protected-group reporting requirements.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy sets an action plan to: update Personal Data Protection Law No. 172-13 to strengthen user control transparency minimization and sensitive-data safeguards (page 37); develop a national ethical AI code with notice transparency supervision and redress (page 39); adopt online-content integrity rules addressing hate speech misinformation and identity falsification (page 39-40). However it does not mandate anti-bias testing define fairness metrics or set protections tied to specific protected characteristics.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy addresses gender equality by creating a women’s AI talent training program under objective 4.2.5 and the action plan led by the Ministry of Women; committing to detect and mitigate bias and algorithmic discrimination; aligning AI ethics with UNESCO guidance; requiring transparency and remedies when AI profiles or makes decisions about people; and expanding inclusive education and workforce upskilling to increase women’s participation in the AI ecosystem.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy includes a dedicated women’s AI talent training program (objective 4.2.5) that offers courses workshops and mentorship from fundamentals to specialized areas engages women AI experts as role models and explicitly aims to expand women’s representation and roles in AI development research and application. This initiative is formalized in the Action Plan 4.2.5.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic addresses AI public procurement in several sections. On p.42 (Objective 2.1.4) it promotes using AI and e-procurement in procurement processes to prevent fraud and enhance transparency. On p.43 (Objective 2.1.7) it proposes transforming procurement into a catalyst for the AI ecosystem by including AI criteria in contracting establishing certified vendor lists and requiring special approval processes. On p.72 it provides for a resolution to include AI systems in procurement and contracting regulations.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: General Directorate of Innovation and Digital Development

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National AI Strategy directly includes clear transparent guidelines for evaluating AI solutions a special approval process before acquiring AI systems and a registry of certified vendors meeting technical and ethical standards (p 4344).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National AI Strategy directly a registry of certified vendors meeting technical and ethical standards. The certification process covers both AI systems and the agents delivering them ensuring compliance with principles of safety privacy and responsibility while mandating transparency and data privacy notices for all parties involved (p 4344).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National AI Strategy directly tackles public-sector skills gaps. Under the Smart Government pillar it commits the State to revitalize the development of capacities competencies and technical knowledge within government so it can become an anticipatory innovative administration (p 35). It establishes a training track to prepare public servants to plan design and use AI in public-service delivery through a programme of master’s degrees courses and diplomas that form functional specialists in applying AI to public services (p 44).

It creates a national training track of master’s degrees courses and diplomas to develop functional specialists in applying AI to public services (p 44). These specialists are expected to understand the full lifecycle of AI-enabled public services from design through evaluation to ensure appropriate deployment and societal benefit. Also it establishes a Center of Excellence for AI in Public Administration with a multidisciplinary team that supports institutions in identifying AI opportunities designing tailored solutions and delivering ongoing training on responsible and ethical AI use (p 44).

thematicElements.justification: Although the Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy does not explicitly mention AI champions it proposes establishing a Center of Excellence for AI in Public Administration described as a multidisciplinary team of AI experts dedicated to research training advisory support and the development of AI related projects in the public sector which implies the creation of roles that can guide and foster AI innovation (p. 72).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the Dominican Republic
items.justification: The Dominican Republic’s National Artificial Intelligence Strategy addresses safety and security through several key concepts and actions. It highlights the role of cybersecurity as essential for national protection and assigns the National Cybersecurity Center to deploy AI systems to detect and respond to cyber threats (page 61). It prohibits the development and use of autonomous weapons promoting a regional treaty against them (page 40). The Strategy also emphasizes protecting sensitive data and ensuring integrity of online content to combat disinformation and hate speech (pages 38–40).

The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The Dominican Republic's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy emphasizes a strong commitment to the security of AI systems and data. The strategy mandates the use of AI to enhance national cybersecurity particularly by supporting the National Cybersecurity Center in developing intelligent systems for early threat detection and response. It also focuses on creating regulatory frameworks to promote cybersecurity and privacy standards in AI applications (page 61). These measures are integrated with broader data protection and ethical governance initiatives (pages 37-39) demonstrating a clear national dedication to safeguarding AI systems from adversarial interference.

items.justification: The document addresses AI literacy through structured education and talent development measures. On p.5 (1.1 Development of Human Talent) it mandates integrating AI into curricula from basic to higher education creating AI university programs with ethics components and establishing certification programs on ethical AI use. Under AXIS 1 (p.9) it sets measurable targets including a 30% increase in STEM graduates with AI training. Page 4 (G. Awareness and Education) also promotes digital skills for informed AI use.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: On p.5 (Section 1.1 “Development of Human Talent”) the document explicitly mandates integrating AI content into curricula “from basic education to higher education” which covers primary secondary and tertiary levels. This constitutes a direct curriculum reform measure. The strategy also links this reform to measurable indicators under AXIS 1 (p.9) including increasing the percentage of STEM graduates with AI-related training by 30% reinforcing its operational character.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: On p.5 (Section 1.1 “Development of Human Talent”) the document encourages the creation of university-level AI programs including third- and fourth-level degrees that incorporate ethics and responsibility components. It also promotes certification programs in the ethical and responsible use of AI. Under AXIS 1 (p.9) measurable indicators track AI-related STEM graduation rates confirming the establishment and expansion of formal AI education programs within the higher education system.

thematicElements.justification: The document promotes AI curriculum integration and the development of university programs (p.5 Section 1.1 “Development of Human Talent”) as well as certification and specialization initiatives. However it does not explicitly establish dedicated teacher training programs pedagogical resources or capacity-building measures specifically for educators. While institutional responsibilities are outlined (pp.16–17) concrete provisions targeting teacher upskilling or instructional support for AI education are not clearly specified.

And Principle H promotes the development and use of AI systems that support the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and encourages ongoing evaluation of their impacts.

items.title: Legislative Framework for Artificial Intelligence (Egypt)
items.justification: The study addresses (Access to Redress and Remedy) through provisions on civil and criminal liability (pp. 31–32). It assigns responsibility to AI developers owners and users for harms resulting from AI systems and affirms victims’ rights to compensation p.32. The framework emphasizes compliance transparency and risk assessment requiring companies to document AI operations and report incidents. It also provides for administrative and criminal sanctions for violations ensuring accountability. However while it establishes foundational principles for redress it lacks detailed procedural mechanisms for individuals to file complaints or seek remedies directly for AI-related harms.

thematicElements.justification: While it discusses civil and criminal liability (pp. 31–32) and recognizes the right to compensation (??? ???????) for damages resulting from AI use it does not outline procedural pathways such as how victims can file lawsuits appeal automated decisions or access courts or tribunals. The focus is mainly on defining responsibilities of developers owners and users and ensuring regulatory compliance and sanctions.Thus the framework provides conceptual recognition of liability and remedy but no judicial or institutional mechanism is proposed to operationalize individual access to justice for AI-related harms.

thematicElements.justification: The document directly addresses this. It states that 'special considerations must be taken to protect vulnerable and marginalized groups such as children PWDs and those with lower economic or educational level' including 'checking potential data bias' and 'preferring development team diversity' (Page 3 Section 3). It also emphasizes that data for government AI projects must be 'diverse enough to cover all potential use cases... to minimize bias' citing examples like 'different ethnicities genders age groups and medical conditions' in healthcare solutions (Page 7 Section 14g).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document mandates a 'systematic risk management approach' including 'risks specific to Al systems such as... bias' (P5 S7). Developers of AI system are encouraged to examine and address the cultural impact of AI systems (P6 S9). For data it requires 'corrections of distortions like invisibility of minorities' (P6 S11) and regular monitoring for 'data drift' (P6 S12). Government projects require impact assessments for 'data diverse enough... to minimize bias' (P7 S 14g).

items.title: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023 v1.0)
items.justification: The document strongly emphasizes Human Oversight and Determination. It explicitly states that 'Ultimate responsibility and accountability for the behavior and outcomes of an Al system must always lie with natural or legal persons' clarifying that AI systems should not have legal personality (Page 4 Section 10). Furthermore it guarantees 'Final human determination is always in place' meaning humans are always in charge of decisions able to modify stop or retire AI systems (Page 4 Section 11). This ensures AI remains a tool under human control particularly in critical areas.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The charter strongly promotes human control. It states 'Ultimate responsibility... must always lie with natural or legal persons' (Page 4 Section 10) and 'Final human determination is always in place... humans are in charge of making decisions and are able to modify stop or retire the Al system' (Page 4 Section 11).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The charter includes such provisions. It states 'Final human determination is always in place. This means that ultimately humans are in charge of making decisions and are able to modify stop or retire the Al system if necessary' (Page 4 Section 11). This applies broadly to all AI systems implicitly covering sensitive sectors.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The document states 'Ultimate responsibility and accountability for the behavior and outcomes of an Al system must always lie with natural or legal persons. Al systems should not be given legal personality themselves' (Page 4 Section 10). It further emphasizes 'Final human determination is always in place. This means that ultimately humans are in charge of making decisions and are able to modify stop or retire the Al system if necessary' (Page 4 Section 11). These provisions clearly assign obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals for oversight intervention and accountability.

items.title: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023 v1.0)
items.justification: The document emphasizes thorough impact assessments for government AI projects to ensure maximum benefit and adherence to responsible AI development. This is detailed in 'Implementation Guidelines' (page 7 section 14). These assessments should evaluate problem suitability for AI data readiness process engineering financial social and environmental impacts and data diversity to minimize bias. Projects are approved only if benefits outweigh costs.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Charter places strong emphasis on fostering a proactive risk management culture for AI systems. The Implementation Guidelines (p7-s14) explicitly require that all government AI projects undergo a comprehensive impact assessment before deployment. This assessment must evaluate financial social and environmental impacts along with data diversity to minimize bias ensuring that the benefits outweigh the costs prior to approval. Furthermore (p5-s2) recommends that every AI project be preceded by a pilot or proof of concept to test technical viability and meet defined success criteria before large-scale implementation reinforcing the importance of pre-deployment evaluation. (p6-s9) encourages AI developers to assess the cultural impact

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: (p.7 s.14) mandates that all government AI projects undergo a comprehensive impact assessment before deployment evaluating financial social and environmental impacts and ensuring data diversity to reduce bias and mitigate risks to individuals and society. Furthermore (p.5 s.7) requires developers to implement a systematic risk management approach addressing AI-specific risks including privacy digital security safety and bias reinforcing a proactive framework for responsible and ethical AI development and deployment.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Egypt National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (Second Edition) (2025-2030)
items.justification: Egypt’s AI strategy emphasizes broad capacity building across sectors. It calls for developing responsible AI training for government industry and the public and supporting AI education and research (P.48). The strategy recommends to establish pilot programs to train official data managers in technology use and data-quality control (P.58). Specialized AI training is also recommended for energy-sector workers (P.71) alongside workshops and programs for government employees and youth at Creativa Innovation Hubs (P.20).

Strengthening data governance requires data-literacy and quality-management training for managers data professionals and analysts to enable effective use of governance frameworks (P.57). A national talent drive (P.51) provides targeted training for advanced AI development. Data governance programs (P.57) reskill managers and professionals to use data effectively. Sectoral initiatives (P.71) upskill energy workers and teacher training (P.81) modernizes AI education delivery. The AI Certification System (P.85) formalizes continuous upskilling and professional growth.

items.title: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023 v1.0)
items.justification: The Charter prioritizes safety and security by mandating 'robust secure and safe' AI systems throughout their lifecycle (P5p1) ensuring proper function even under misuse. It introduces certification for 'safety transparency robustness and reliability' (P4s8). Additional measures are required for 'sensitive or mission-critical AI applications' to ensure data protection and harm avoidance (P5s3). 'final human determination is always in place' for 'security and safety' empowering humans to modify or stop AI systems (P4s11). A systematic risk management approach is advocated covering 'digital security safety' (P5s7). Data use necessitates pre-authorization anonymization encryption and adherence to security standards(p6s11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The charter calls for certification mechanisms to ensure 'reliability' of AI systems (Page 4 point 8). It also states AI systems should be 'robust secure and safe' and function 'appropriately' (Page 5 point 1). Developers must strive for 'quality and accuracy' (Page 6 point 8) and government AI projects require data of 'sufficient volume and quality' (Page 7 point 14b) with proper testing to ensure quality (Page 6 point 13).

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The document includes such provisions. It states that 'documented policies and processes should be in place to quickly respond to and resolve any adverse outcomes caused by the unauthorized use of AI systems' (Page 3 point 5). Furthermore 'final human determination is always in place' allowing humans to 'modify stop or retire the AI system if necessary' (Page 4 point 11). For 'sensitive or mission-critical AI applications' additional measures are required to ensure data protection and 'avoidance of any harm' (Page 5 point 3).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: AI projects should be preceded by a 'pilot or proof of concept (PoC) to ensure the technical viability' (Page 5 point 2). Thorough 'testing' is mentioned as part of the AI system lifecycle (Page 3 point 7). Government AI projects require a 'thorough impact assessment' (Page 7 point 14) and 'proper testing' to ensure quality and accuracy before introduction (Page 6 point 13).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this. It states that AI systems should be 'secure... throughout their entire lifecycle' (Page 5 point 1) protecting against 'foreseeable use misuse reward hacking or other adverse conditions.' A systematic risk management approach is required to include 'digital security' (Page 5 point 7) in the development lifecycle. Furthermore data used in AI systems must be protected; 'personally identifiable data must be anonymized and/or encrypted' and adhere to security standards (Page 6 point 11).

items.title: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023 v1.0)
items.justification: The document addresses a fundamental right for end-users is knowing when they are interacting with an AI system not a human as seen with automated call centers (P3S2). Developers are obligated to 'always strive to provide transparent and explainable Al solutions' acknowledging potential tradeoffs between accuracy and explainability (P6S8). In cases of doubt simpler more explainable models are preferred without compromising minimum quality (p7s15)

Developers are also urged to 'always strive to provide transparent and explainable Al solutions' (Page 6 Section 8) and government projects should use 'open source and white box/non-proprietary technologies to ensure transparency' (Page 7 Section 15).

thematicElements.justification: The document includes such obligations. items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Action Plan 2024–2026 (Estonia)
items.justification: The plan explicitly identifies the limited number of Estonian language users as a weakness that 'hinders the initiation of larger KT projects'. The strategic objective is to 'ensure the future-proofing of Estonian language technology' positioning the development of the language as a core function of AI strategy. page 31 32
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this topic extensively in its dedicated 'Language technology' section (pages 31-35) which outlines several key initiatives:Goal: The strategic goal is to ensure the 'future-proofing of Estonian language technology'. The plan aims to develop a foundation model for AI that 'takes into account the Estonian language and culture'.Data and Models: A key activity is the creation of a 'high-quality Estonian language data package' containing 15 billion words for training and evaluating large language models. This is a crucial step to ensure that AI systems are representative of the language.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The plan sets a goal to create a 'high-quality Estonian language data package' containing 15 billion words for training and evaluating large language models. A key objective is to develop a foundation model that 'takes into account the Estonian language and culture'. The document assigns responsibility for these activities to specific entities including the Estonian Centre for International Cooperation (ECI) the State Information System Authority (RIA) the Ministry of Education and Research (MER) page 33

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
