thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Code of Relations between the Public and the Administration (France)
items.justification: The document addresses this in Book III Title I Chapter II (Dissemination of administrative documents). Specifically Article L. 312-1-3 mandates that administrations must publish online the 'rules defining the main algorithmic processing used in the performance of their missions when they form the basis of individual decisions.' This article establishes an affirmative obligation for public bodies (with more than 50 employees as per Article D. 312-1-4) to disclose the logic underlying their algorithmic systems subject only to protected secrets (like national defense).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article L. 312-1-3 states that the obligation to publish algorithmic rules is 'Subject to the secrets protected pursuant to point 2 of Article L. 311-5'. Article L. 311-5 explicitly lists information not communicable due to protected interests including 'The secrecy of national defence' and 'National security public safety'. Therefore algorithmic systems used for defense and security purposes are explicitly excluded from the transparency requirements of this framework.

body.name: Commission for Access to Administrative Documents

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: Article L. 312-1-3 mandates that administrations 'publish online the rules defining the principal algorithmic treatments used in the accomplishment of their missions'. While this creates a form of public inventory identifying the 'agency responsible' and the systems ('principal treatments') it is limited in scope. It applies only to 'principal' treatments that 'found individual decisions' (lorsqu'ils fondent des décisions individuelles) rather than 'all AI systems used by the government'.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: Article L. 312-1-3 explicitly defines the boundary between public disclosure and protected information. It states that the obligation to publish is 'Subject to secrets protected in application of 2° of Article L. 311-5' (Sous réserve des secrets protégés en application du 2° de l'article L. 311-5). By referencing Article L. 311-5 the document provides clear guidelines on what must be protected (e.g. national defense state security private life) versus what is subject to the disclosure rule.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

items.title: Public procurement of innovative solutions: Practical guide (France)
items.justification: 'Practical Guide' is designed to assist public buyers in acquiring 'innovative solutions' a category that encompasses Artificial Intelligence (AI). It addresses the procurement of such technologies by outlining specific procedures for sourcing in Fact Sheet 4 (pages 30-36) defining functional specifications rather than technical ones to allow for AI solutions in Fact Sheet 4 (pages 24-29) and managing Intellectual Property (IP) rights (critical for AI software) in Fact Sheet 10 (pages 52-55). It provides operational 'Fact Sheets' on how to use legal levers within the Public Procurement Code specifically detailing the innovation partnership in Fact Sheet 13 (pages 65-71) to de-risk the purchase of emerging technologies like AI.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The guide establishes a framework for purchasing 'innovative solutions' which explicitly includes AI (e.g. AI kiosks data analysis) (Page 103 Annexes). It goes beyond traditional IT by requiring the integration of 'sustainable development objectives in their economic social and environmental dimensions' into the definition of needs (Page 24 Fact Sheet 4). It promotes 'socially and environmentally responsible purchasing' (SPASER) and links procurement to public policies like inclusion and ecology (Pages 9-10 Fact Sheet 1). However these are general guidelines for all innovative solutions not a standalone set of guidelines exclusively specific to AI (Page 6 Introduction; Page 13 Fact Sheet 2).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly identifies 'strengthening the industrial and technological sovereignty of France and Europe' as a key lever of public procurement (Page 5 Introduction). It lists 'supporting European and French supply chains' as a public policy objective that government buyers are required to achieve (Page 25 Fact Sheet 4). It also references a Senate report advocating support for innovative companies to encourage products with 'French or European technological expertise' specifically as a matter of sovereignty (Page 8 Fact Sheet 1).

items.title: Master plan for lifelong professional development for civil servants for the period 2024-2027 (France)
items.justification: The document addresses public-sector skills development through its 2024-2027 Master Plan which is structured into six strategic axes. It mandates the professionalisation of civil servants through interministerial training pathways. Key areas include training 100% of staff in Republican values and secularism (Axis I) the ecological transition (Axis II) and digital sovereignty specifically focusing on security and AI (Axis III). Pages 7 and 8 detail the induction of first-time managers and the modernisation of Human Resources practices. Axis VI (page 9) focuses on cross-cutting skills like public procurement finance and European issues.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Directorate General for Public Administration and the Civil Service (DGAFP) Mentor interministerial training platform Interministerial Digital Directorate (DINUM)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The Master Plan establishes a government-wide ('interministerial') strategy for 'State public servants' (Axis III) explicitly covering AI 'security and regulatory challenges' (Project 5.1) foundational 'AI culture and principles' (Project 8.1) and applications involving the 'design and deployment of systems based on AI' (Project 8.2). However the document specifies its scope as the 'civil service' and 'public officials' under the Ministry of Transformation and Public Function. It does not explicitly mention or target members of the judiciary (magistrates) who typically possess a distinct status separate from the general civil service in France.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly establishes a framework for ongoing professional development to keep pace with AI. The entire document is a 'Master plan for lifelong professional development policy'. Project 8.1 and Project 8.2 specifically mandate 'Annual monitoring of the progress' in the number of staff trained in AI awareness and AI integration from 2026 and 2027 onwards. Additionally Project 5.1 establishes awareness training on AI security challenges 'in 2025 and during the period of the 3rd master plan'. This multi-year approach with annual tracking confirms the requirement for continuous rather than one-off development.

items.title: AI in the service of justice: Strategy and operational solutions (France)
items.justification: The strategy prioritizes 'supporting professionals' to ensure they master new tools (p. 48). It mandates the creation of a 'Digital Justice Campus' (Campus du numérique Justice) to pool resources across the four justice schools and foster a 'shared digital culture' (p. 5 48).Key measures include:Awareness: Launching MOOCs on AI fundamentals and 'AI Justice Café' webinars to discuss ethical and technical challenges (p. 48 85).Continuous Training: Integrating AI into initial curricula and offering lifelong learning modules including 'serious games' and VR simulations for realistic professional scenarios (p. 48 86).Timeline: A 'gradual skills development' phase is specifically scheduled for 2026 (p. 8) following initial awareness.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: AI Observatory (Observatoire de lIA) AI Program Management (Direction de programme IA)Strategic Committee (Comit stratgique)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The framework addresses this requirement specifically for the judiciary and Ministry of Justice personnel but it is not a government-wide strategy. It focuses exclusively on the Justice sector (p. 3). Within this scope Axis 3 establishes a 'Digital Justice Campus' to centralize upskilling (p. 5 48). The document details a 'Roadmap' where Phase 2 (2026-2027) is dedicated to the 'Generalization of acculturation and training actions for all agents of the ministry' (p. 8-9). These measures explicitly cover building a foundational understanding of AI its operational applications and 'ethical risks' (e.g. bias security) through MOOCs webinars and initial training curricula for magistrates and clerks (p. 46 48).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this by creating a robust governance structure. It establishes a 'Direction de programme IA' (AI Program Management) attached to the General Secretariat comprising multidisciplinary experts (technical legal ethical) to provide centralized guidance and operational support (Page 9). Additionally the roadmap explicitly mandates the deployment of 'Ambassadeurs de la transformation numérique' (Digital Ambassadors) in jurisdictions during Phase 2 (2026). These champions are tasked with fostering a culture of responsible innovation and supporting peer adoption locally. The strategy also creates an 'Observatoire de l'IA' to oversee ethical compliance and ensure the strategy aligns with professional values.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this by establishing the 'Digital Justice Campus' (Axis 3) which is explicitly tasked with providing 'continuing training' (formation continue) to ensure staff can 'master new tools' and 'stay up-to-date' with technological developments (p. 48). It specifically mentions the need to adapt training content to the 'rapid evolution' of digital skills (p. 49). Furthermore the implementation roadmap designates Phase 3 (from 2028) for 'consolidation and continuous acculturation' ensuring that professional development is an ongoing process rather than a one-off event (p. 8).

items.title: Labour Code: Article L6321-1 (France)
items.justification: Article L6321-1 explicitly mandates that the employer 'ensures the adaptation of employees to their workstation' and 'watches over the maintenance of their ability to hold a job' specifically regarding the 'evolution of... technologies' ('l'évolution... des technologies'). This statutory text creates a direct legal obligation for companies to invest in training to adapt their workforce to technological changes. Since AI is a major technological evolution this provision inherently compels employers to provide upskilling for AI adoption. This interpretation is formally supported by the CCI Paris Ile-de-France (August 2025) which issued guidance stating this article imposes a direct duty to integrate AI training actions into skills plans.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Coordinator for AI

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Code establishes the Compte Personnel de Formation (CPF) (Personal Training Account) a universal government-regulated subsidy mechanism funded by mandatory employer contributions and the State. Article L6323-1 grants every worker a credit in Euros to fund eligible training. Additionally Article L6323-17-1 establishes the Projet de transition professionnelle (Project of professional transition) subsidising long-term reskilling for changing professions. Furthermore the CCI Paris Ile-de-France formally issued guidance stating that Article L. 6321-1 imposes a direct duty on employers to 'integrate AI training actions' into skills development plans to maintain employability treating failure to do so as a legal risk.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Article L6323-17-5 ensures the maintenance of remuneration for workers taking leave for a 'Projet de transition professionnelle' (Project of professional transition). Furthermore Article L6321-2 mandates that training required by the employer to adapt to the workstation must be paid as actual working time ('temps de travail effectif') ensuring financial security during upskilling.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: Article L6321-1 establishes the core binding requirement: the employer 'ensures the adaptation of employees to their workstation' and 'watches over the maintenance of their ability to hold a job' specifically regarding 'technological evolution.' This legally obliges companies to invest in training to prevent displacement due to technology.

items.title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (Third Phase) (France)
items.justification: The strategy addresses upskilling through a €360M investment in 9 'IA Clusters' to train 100000 people annually by 2030 including 20000 in continuing education [p. 17]. It leverages the 'Skills and Future Professions' (CMA) plan to generalise AI training across all qualification levels [p. 17]. Sector-specific measures include a €119M initiative to train 500000 healthcare professionals over five years [p. 32] and mandatory AI training for civil servants to support the deployment of sovereign tools like 'Albert' [p. 24 28]. Additionally 'AI Cafés' aim to raise awareness for 2 million citizens by 2027 [p. 26].

thematicElements.justification: The strategy explicitly includes provisions for government-funded upskilling programs. It allocates €360 million to 'AI Clusters' with a target of training 100000 people annually by 2030 specifically including 20000 places for continuing education to support workforce adaptation. Additionally it commits €119 million to train 500000 healthcare professionals (medical paramedical and social staff) over five years to integrate AI into their practice. The document also mentions the 'Skills and Future Professions' initiative to generalize AI training across the territory.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The government specifically allocates funds to cover the cost of upskilling workforce segments. It commits €119 million to 'train 500000 [healthcare] professionals over five years' including medical and paramedical staff. The strategy also funds the AI Clusters to provide 20000 places for continuing education annually. For the public sector it provides 'training sessions' for agents to use new tools like 'Albert' at no cost to the employee.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.
