thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: National Digital Economy Master Plan 2024 - 2034 (Gambia)
items.justification: The document includes AI as part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5). Plan explicitly calls on the government to introduce ICT education in primary and secondary schools (50). The 'Digital Literacy Curriculum in Schools' initiative proposes 'introducing digital literacy as part of the school curriculum to ensure that students acquire essential digital skills from an early age' covering 'coding application development internet safety basic computer skills.' (54).  Investment in 'the Gambian higher education system to further increase the number and quality of software development courses nationwide' (51). It also mentions investment into universities for digital connectivity (19).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MoCDE) and the Gambia ICT Agency (GICTA)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The plan calls for the government to 'introduce ICT education in primary and secondary schools' stating that 'ICT education should be designed to provide students with a basic understanding of digital technologies and how they work' with 'practical components that enable students to develop their digital skills through hands-on experience' (50). The 'Digital Literacy Curriculum in Schools' initiative proposes 'introducing digital literacy as part of the school curriculum to ensure that students acquire essential digital skills from an early age' (54). There are no equivalent proposals for tertiary education and the curriculum provisions don't mention AI specifically; however AI is part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The most directly relevant provision is the proposed 'National Artificial Intelligence Research Center' which would 'serve as a hub for research development and innovation in the field of artificial intelligence' and 'bring together experts researchers and industry professionals to collaborate on cutting-edge AI projects and applications' (42). Other programs such as Emerging Technologies Training Data Science Bootcamps Coding Bootcamp and 'École 42' (52-58) will offer AI-related courses to anyone including the youth but it is not clear whether it will be embedded into the formal education system.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The plan addresses teacher training for general digital skills through the 'Digital Skills for Teachers' program (53) and addresses educational resources through provisions for hardware investment training centers mobile labs e-learning platforms and community technology centers (51–52). These create an infrastructure within which AI education could eventually be delivered. However the plan does not include provisions for training teachers specifically in AI education — no AI pedagogy programs no AI teaching resources no AI curriculum materials for educators. The teacher training that exists prepares educators to use digital tools in their teaching not to teach AI as a subject.

items.title: The Gambia's National Child and Vulnerable Groups Online Protection Policy
items.justification: The policy aims to comprehensively address the wide spectrum of online risks and harms experienced by children women persons with disabilities and older persons in The Gambia (11)' including risks from the use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies (2). These risks or harms include AI tools being used to create spread and amplify sexual abuse material cyberbullying pornography disinformation and misinformation hate speech and content that promotes self-harm and violence (2). The policy also acknowledges the spread of technology-facilitated violence as a new form of gender-based violence (9).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Cybersecurity Coordination Directorate (dedicated section)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Policy Action 3.1 requires legal and regulatory review to address risks in the digital environment 'including risks and harms from the use of AI technologies' (14). The review must assess whether the frameworks address 'the prohibition of all forms of violence exploitation and abuse against children and vulnerable groups in the digital environment' (14). AI-specific risks are identified as AI tools being used to create  spread and amplify sexual abuse material cyberbullying pornography disinformation and misinformation hate speech and content that promotes self-harm and violence (2). However this only indirectly prevents AI tools form being used this way as it is not a direct prohibition of the usage itself.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Provisions for Digital Service Providers (Internet Service Providers Content Developers Global System for Mobile Communication) to develop codes of conduct protocols and/or guidelines including requirements for: 'blocking access to illegal and harmful websites and content online ensuring that the entire process is transparent'; 'notice and takedown of illegal and harmful content online' (Content Developers only); 'ensuring the responsible and ethical use of AI for automated systems such as automated content moderation abuse detection / content filtering and blocking.' (pillar 5 p. 15-16). AI developers are only covered if they fall under 'content developers' and limited transparency requirements.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: Includes general provisions relating to protection and seeking redress for online harms - not  specific to misinformation or tech-facilitated violence. PA 5.3 (Content Developers): 'mechanisms for users to report illegal and harmful content and activities.' PA 5.1 5.2 5.3 for Digital Service Providers: Blocking/content removal processes must be 'transparent with review and appeals mechanisms' (15-16) PA 4.1: 'strengthening institutional systems with tools and guidelines to investigate and prosecute online offences.' PA 3.1 assessing whether legal frameworks address the 'facilitation of investigation prosecution and sentencing of online offences' and 'provision of effective response recovery and rehabilitation.' (14)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The policy recognizes 'online and technology-facilitated violence as a new form of gender-based violence' (9) and that in Africa 'up to 90% of women have experienced or witnessed online and technology-facilitated violence' (2). The policy then identifies a number of AI facilitated risks and harms including that 'AI can also be used to tailor harassment to individuals' vulnerabilities and interests making them more damaging and harmful' (2). Other provisions discussed above include preventing AI tools from facilitating harm online in general which by extension would include gender-based harassment and violence on the basis that women are included as a vulnerable group (policy includes dedicated section on Online Protection of  Women 9)

items.title: The Gambia's National Child and Vulnerable Groups Online Protection Policy
items.justification: The purpose of the policy is to 'implement a comprehensive online protection framework in The Gambia that upholds the rights and well-being of all children' (pg. 12). It recognizes that there are a wide spectrum of online risks and harms for children which are exacerbated by AI (pg. 2). The policy specifically recognizes the following AI risks for children: child sexual abuse material (pg. 2-3); disinformation and misinformation (pg. 2-4); AI enabling sextortion through deepfakes (pg. 2 4); radicalization through targeted content (p.24); cyberbullying (pg. 25); targeted advertising exploiting vulnerabilities (pg. 3) ; perpetuating biases in access to services (pg. 3); chatbots encouraging harmful behaviors (pg. 26).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Cybersecurity Coordination Directorate (dedicated section)

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Policy Action (PA) 3.1 (p. 14) mandates reviewing legal frameworks to ensure: '1) the prohibition of all forms of violence exploitation and abuse against children...in digital environments; (2) higher levels of protection for the collection and processing of children's... data' 3)  obligations of digital service providers in ensuring the online safety of children. PA 5.3 (p. 16) requires content developers to implement: '(2) developing and implementing safety-by-design and privacy-by-design features in their products and services prioritizing the best interests of children'.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Policy Actions 5 (p. 15-17) requires digital service providers to develop codes of conduct protocols and/or guidelines  on the protection of children including '(1) maintaining a secure network to protect...children from online risks and harms; (2) reporting illegal and harmful content and activities online; (3) blocking access to illegal and harmful websites and content online...(6) ensuring the responsible and ethical use of AI for automated systems such as content filtering and blocking.' The policy recognizes that 'AI-driven algorithms can analyze online behavior based on the data collected to deliver targeted advertising often exploiting the vulnerabilities of children' (p. 3).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Policy Action 5.3 (p. 16-17) explicitly assigns obligations to content developers requiring:'(1) developing age-appropriate...content products and services; (2) developing and implementing safety-by-design and privacy-by-design features in their products and services prioritizing the best interests of children...'(8) ensuring the responsible and ethical use of AI for automated systems such as automated content moderation abuse detection and age verification'.

items.title: National Data Policy 2025: The Gambia (Draft)
items.justification: The Data Policy Guiding Principles include principles on 'Fairness and Inclusiveness': 'Fostering an inclusive data ecosystem that equitably distributes benefits addresses structural inequalities and amplifies the voices of marginalised groups affected by data and digital technologies. Another principle is aimed at 'ensuring data is collected processed and used ... without discrimination.' (p. 16). Layer 5 – Innovation & Emerging Technologies - of the National Data Management Framework embedded in the Policy provides: 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency: Development of principles tools and oversight mechanisms to ensure fairness explainability and inclusivity in automated decision-making systems.' (p. 28)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Policy as a whole is aimed at 'safeguarding citizen rights and safety and ethics in AI and emerging technologies' (p. 3). The Data Policy Guiding Principles provides that 'data is ...processed ...fairly and without discrimination.' 'This principle does not specifically mention certain groups but does guard against discrimination in general. The next principle-  Fairness and Inclusiveness-  calls for a 'data ecosystem' that 'addresses structural inequalities and amplifies the voices of marginalised groups.' (pg. 15). The Policy also includes the National Data Management Framework which calls for 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency: Development of principles tools and oversight mechanisms to ensure fairness...' (p. 29)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: One of the Data Policy Guiding Principles - 'Fairness and Inclusiveness' - calls for a 'data ecosystem' that 'addresses structural inequalities and amplifies the voices of marginalised groups.' (pg. 16).  The Data Policy Guiding Principle on 'Integrity and justice' provides that 'data is ...processed ...fairly and without discrimination....' The Policy does however not address bias.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: National Digital Economy Master Plan 2024 - 2034 (Gambia)
items.justification: The document includes AI as part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5). Under Pillar 6 of the plan on Digital Literacy and Skills it notes that 'The government can provide training programs for public sector workers to improve their digital skills and increase efficiency in their work...this can include training in... artificial intelligence tools.' (50). Relevant additional projects in digital skills development include: The Smart City Planning Training project targeting urban planners and local authorities (56) and Digital Skills for Law Enforcement (58). Other additional projects and flagship projects under Pillar 6 while not specifically mentioning the public sector seem to be open to both the public and private sector.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MoCDE) and the Gambia ICT Agency (GICTA)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The plan is very broad and just provides that 'The government can provide training programs for public sector workers to improve their digital skills and increase efficiency in their work...this can include training in... artificial intelligence tools' (50) and then introduces some general flagship and additional projects for digital skills. Projects seem to be more geared to applications of AI (and other rdigital technologies) rather than its risks and ethical considerations).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The plan proposes dedicated digital leadership roles within government but these are framed around digital transformation broadly — not AI specifically. It proposes assigning aChief Digital Officers (CDO) to every ministry to 'oversee IT investments processes and policies' with agreed minimum qualifications and adequate payroll to attract and sustain competencies (24). It proposes mandatory Chief Information Security Officers (CISO) and Data Protection Officers (DPO) in all ministries (60) with a networking platform and competency development model. And it proposes an AI Ethics Council (74) in partnership with global experts to 'guide the ethical development and deployment of artificial intelligence technologies' and formulate policies.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The plan states that 'digital literacy and skills are constantly evolving and it is essential to develop a culture of lifelong learning to ensure that individuals and organizations are equipped to keep pace with these changes' (51). The 'Virtual Government Training Programs' (28) are framed as providing 'continuous learning' and enhancing the efficiency of government officials. The cross-cutting themes section identifies the need for the public sector to 'be prepared to leverage new and emerging technologies' and calls for 'clear policy legal and regulatory frameworks to empower public servants to adopt and implement automation and other technologies' (78).

items.title: National Digital Economy Master Plan 2024 - 2034 (Gambia)
items.justification: The document includes AI as part of the digital economy's foundational framing (5). Pillar 6 is dedicated to Digital literacy and skills and various programs mention AI and/or emerging technologies specifically while others will also be applicable. Emerging Technologies Training (56): 'introduce participants to cutting-edge technologies such as AI....to develop expertise in these technologies preparing individuals for future job opportunities in emerging fields. Data Science Bootcamps: training participants in 'data analysis machine learning and predictive modeling' (58). Digital Skills Training Centers: serve as hubs for delivering comprehensive digital skills training to individuals of all ages including on emerging technologies (52).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy (MoCDE) and the Gambia ICT Agency (GICTA)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The plan contains extensive provisions for skills development programs that encompass both upskilling (enhancing existing competencies) and reskilling (training for new roles) for the digital economy which includes AI (51-58) to be developed by the government. It seems as if the key programs are to be funded by the government while the government will work with partners locally and globally to mobilize the needed resources for additional projects but due to not being explicitly stated whether they are government funded or subsidized partially is more appropriate.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The 'Digital Skills Scholarships' initiative will would 'provide financial support to deserving individuals especially from underserved communities to pursue digital skills training and certifications' and aims to 'ensure that talented individuals are not hindered by financial barriers and can contribute to the digital economy effectively and sustainably' (53). However aside from that scholarship there are no explicit incentives outlined for workers to participate in these programs.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: National Data Policy 2025: The Gambia (Draft)
items.justification: The Gambia National Data Management Framework forms part of the Policy and Layer 5 (Innovation & Emerging Technologies) specifically provides for 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency: Development of principles tools and oversight mechanisms to ensure fairness explainability and inclusivity in automated decision-making systems' and 'Artificial intelligence governance: Establishment of regulatory and policy frameworks for responsible AI development and deployment including algorithmic accountability and risk management.' (p. 28). Additionally one of the overarching data policy guiding principles is to 'Promote a trustworthy and secure data ecosystem that is ethical by design transparent and accountable to data subjects.' (p.16).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The policy includes 'Ethical AI and algorithmic transparency' as a management domain (p 28) and mentions establishing regulatory and policy frameworks including for algorithmic accountability (p 29). Includes transparency in guiding principles: 'ethical by design transparent and accountable to data subjects '(p. 16). However the Policy lacks specific provisions: No requirement to disclose why an AI system is being used;  No mandate to reveal what data sources feed AI systems;  No concrete requirements for explaining how AI arrives at decisions; No requirements for public registers or documentation of AI systems notice requirements when AI is being used or user rights to receive explanations.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection
items.justification: The document addresses access to redress and remedy in the AI context mainly through rules on automated decision-making and profiling. Article 19 provides procedural safeguards by allowing individuals to contest decisions based solely on automated processing express their views and request human involvement. While Article 19 does not establish a full right to remedy or compensation Articles 52 61 and 62 complement it by addressing remedies and liability outlining mechanisms for redress accountability and enforcement in cases of violations arising from automated data processing.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 2 clause 2 states: This Law shall not apply to the processing of data for the purposes of national security (including economic security) defence intelligence and counter-intelligence activities;

body.name: Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection establishes judicial and administrative appeal mechanisms that may apply to AI-related harms but only indirectly. Article 22 (“Right to appeal”) allows data subjects to challenge decisions of the Personal Data Protection Service before a court including in cases involving Article 19 on automated decision-making. However this appeal is directed against an administrative decision not against an AI system AI deployer or harm caused by AI as such. Articles 52 61 and 62 further provide general remedies and liability for unlawful data processing which may encompass AI-driven automated processing but the law does not establish AI-specific judicial mechanisms or objectives for redress.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection establishes state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms through the Personal Data Protection Service (PDPS) (Article 49). Data subjects may submit complaints concerning unlawful personal data processing including automated decision-making under Article 19. Article 52 further empowers the PDPS to examine violations issue binding instructions require corrective measures and apply administrative sanctions. While these mechanisms may be used in cases involving AI-driven automated processing they are limited to data protection infringements and do not constitute a dedicated redress framework for AI systems AI deployers or harm caused by AI as such.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Law of Georgia on Personal Data Protection does not explicitly include requirements or incentives for companies or developers to create their own grievance or complaint-handling mechanisms related to harms caused by AI systems.However it contains indirect obligations that functionally require organizations to ensure individuals can exercise their rights — which includes responding to complaints. see article 17 clause C

items.title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
items.justification: The document lists detailed steps to mitigate the bias factors (see article 9 clause 4)
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: National Bank of Georgia

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document defines bias as an inclination or prejudice in the data and/or algorithm that systematically gives an unfair advantage to an individual or a group and listes detailed steps to promote fair outcomes (see article 9 clause 4)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document does not explicitly recommend specific measures to prevent the amplification of existing social biases. However it addresses stereotypical biases and provides detailed steps to mitigate them thereby encompassing this topic as well (see article 9 clause 4)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: Article 9 clause 4 provides detailed steps to mitigate bias throughout AI lifecycle.

items.title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
items.justification: While the document doesn't use terms like 'human-in-the-loop' it mandates human control across the model lifecycle: Article 6 allows replacing model parameters based on expert judgment if validation is unsatisfactory. It requires monitoring 'overrides' made by experts to identify model limitations; (Articles 5-8 11) A qualified person independent of development must approve a model's launch. For regulatory models NBG's human assessment determines approval; The second line of defense must consist of staff with the expertise to critically analyze mathematical logic and assumptions. Transparency: Transparency requirements ensure humans can interpret 'black box' outcomes and explain the logic to customers.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: National Bank of Georgia

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document very generally states that ongoing monitoring of models should include the analysis of overrides made by expert judgment with appropriate documentation. It also mentions human judgment through requirements for expert validation ongoing human monitoring bias checks and explainability. And does not go into details (see articles 6 7 9 9.5).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document does not explicitly address preventing full automation in sensitive sectors. However it limits full automation within the financial sector by requiring human expert validation ongoing human monitoring and bias checks for all AI/ML models (Art. 6 7 9).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The document does not explicitly use the phrase 'responsible individuals for AI oversight' but it establishes a rigorous accountability framework through Articles 3 4 6 7 and 9. It mandates that entities define specific roles and responsibilities across three independent lines of defense to oversee and manage model risks. Article 6 allow for 'expert judgment' to intervene and override model results when they are unsatisfactory. Furthermore Article 9 stipulates that the entity remains the 'responsible person' for the model even when outsourced. For regulatory models Article 11 specifically requires submitting a 'list of people who are responsible for the model' to the National Bank.

items.title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
items.justification: In accordance with the Regulation on Data-driven Statistical AI and Machine Learning Model Risk Management issued by the National Bank of Georgia financial institutions must follow specific standards for model integrity: Impact Assessment: Under Article 5 Clause 10 development tests must evaluate how specific assumptions influence results and identify conditions where a model's effectiveness may decrease. Risk Management: Per Article 1 Clause 4 users must maintain a risk management system proportionate to the model's complexity and its potential impact on the institution's material risks. This framework ensures that AI and statistical tools are both transparent and aligned with a bank's/firm's overall risk profile.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: National Bank of Georgia

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: While the law includes provisions for proactive risk management it falls short of explicitly promoting a broad organizational culture regarding societal or environmental impacts. Instead it focuses on technical and material risk. Article 5 Clause 10 mandates that development testing - an essential step before deployment - must evaluate the impact of assumptions on results and identify when effectiveness decreases. While this establishes a rigorous legal requirement for impact assessment within a risk management framework the scope remains primarily focused on the model user’s material risks (Article 1 Clause 4) rather than broader ethical or environmental promotion.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly states the need to include impact assessment as an essential component of model development testing prior to deployment (article 6 clause 2) as well as to ensure its monitoring by users after deployment (article 6 clause 5b). Article 4 assigns responsibilities to the first line (developers/users) for development testing and risk management. Article 6 states that the second line of defense is responsible for internal validation and staff performing this validation must have knowledge skills and expertise proportional to the model’s complexity to ensure rigorous assessment of model risks.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
items.justification: the document addresses safety and security mainly through its model-risk management framework. It mandates that all AI ML and statistical models used by supervised entities must undergo rigorous internal validation testing and monitoring to prevent losses from incorrect model design data use or implementation. The regulation requires data quality controls (completeness accuracy timeliness audit trace) and establishes a “three lines of defense” structure—development independent validation and internal audit—to ensure transparency accountability and reliability. These provisions collectively safeguard the integrity stability and secure operation of models within financial institutions. (Article 5. Model building and testing)
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: National Bank of Georgia

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document includes explicit provisions related to establishing performance thresholds and quality benchmarks for AI systems. In particular it requires model testing and monitoring to include process verification and benchmarking (Article 6 Clause 5(b)). In addition internal policies and procedures must define the target accuracy of models and the permissible level of error alongside validation testing and procedures for reviewing and responding to unacceptable errors (Article 3 Paragraph 2). Together these provisions ensure that AI systems are evaluated against predefined performance standards to operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The document includes safeguards and fallback procedures to address AI system failure or unexpected behavior. Article 8 Clause 3 establishes an emergency safeguard by requiring the restriction or suspension of a model when there are significant changes in model risk or breaches of risk appetite. Additionally Article 6 Paragraph 5(b)(ii) provides a human-in-the-loop fallback allowing expert judgment to replace validation results or parameters when validation is unsatisfactory and alternative data or models are unavailable. Together these provisions function as mitigation and emergency protocols to limit potential harm.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes comprehensive requirements for pre-deployment testing validation and documentation to ensure technical robustness across the AI system lifecycle. Article 5 mandates documented model objectives methodology assumptions data quality standards and extensive testing (including accuracy checks sensitivity analysis scenario testing and transparency assessments) prior to deployment. Article 6 further requires independent internal validation covering model inputs calculations and outputs supported by documented conceptual soundness reviews robustness testing and risk-based validation intensity. Together these provisions ensure technical robustness before deployment and throughout ongoing model use.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Decree No. 151/04 of the Governor of the National Bank of Georgia On Approval of the Regulation about Data-driven Statistical Al and Machine Learning Model Risk Management
items.justification: Article 5 clause 10 (page 4) states that the model should be transparent and allow for explanation and interpretation. To ensure transparency the model’s logic technical content and potential biases must be examined during the validation process. The requirement for transparency becomes even more significant when the model’s decisions directly affect consumers and the decision-making
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: National Bank of Georgia

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The decree states that the model should be transparent and should allow for explanation and interpretation. In order to ensure transparency the logic and technical content of the model and existence of the bias should be checked during the model validation process. Also the user of the model should contribute to the education and awareness of consumers about the decision made by using machine learning and artificial intelligence. Moreover there is the need to describe data sources as well as the model development process and assumptions. See articles 5 9 and 11.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: There is no differentiation between high-stakes and low-stakes systems. The decree generally states that the model user should increase the transparency of the decision made by employing the model. In order to ensure transparency the model developer should if necessary be able to explain to the customer the logic of the model decision. See article 9

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Article 9 states: In order to ensure transparency the model user should if necessary be able to explain to the customer the logic of the model decision.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
items.justification: AI literacy is framed as a societal competence: under “AI skills for all” the update aims that “every citizen” is well informed about AI’s opportunities and challenges to “demystify” AI and strengthen digital skills for everyday dealings with AI (Society “AI skills for all” p.25). It operationalises this via the free online course “Elements of AI” for the full breadth of the population including those without prior knowledge (p.25). It also commits to adapting education and training curricula across school vocational and higher education plus continuing training at companies (p.11)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The German Federal Government

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy states: 'Education and training curricula are being adapted' mentioning school vocational and higher education (p. 11). For the Tertiary level it funds the 'implementation of AI in the curriculum content' (p. 26) and development of AI-related degree programs via the 'AI in Higher Education' initiative. The Strategy does not distinguish between primary and secondary school but it mentioned the STEM Action Plan (p. 12) to promote AI literacy and the integration of AI-specific modules which is for primary and secondary school (https://stip.oecd.org/stip/interactive-dashboards/policy-initiatives/2025%2Fdata%2FpolicyInitiatives%2F99998575). The Strategy also includes vocational training via the INVITE platform (p. 26).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy includes clear measures to establish AI programs within formal education. Centrally it funds the establishment of 100 new AI professorships for AI teaching (p. 10). Through the 'AI in Higher Education' program it finances the development of AI-related degree programs and the 'implementation of AI in curriculum content' (p. 12 27). The Strategy strengthens AI provision mainly in higher education: it is “of vital importance” to secure specialists “through university courses” (p.10). It will foster innovation in higher education “such as the AI-supported development of university courses” (p.11). It will also support international students through dedicated DAAD AI programs (p. 10).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The National AI Strategy madates the integration of AI into the curricula for future academic staff (p. 11 26). It expands the 'AI trainer programme' and funds 'train-the-trainer' initiatives to create a network of qualified educators (p. 17). For resources it develops an 'AI-supported online portal' for vocational training and uses the STEM Action Plan to provide AI-related learning clusters for schools (p. 11).

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Strategy of the German Federal Government (2020 Update)
items.justification: The National Strategy explicitly links preventing discrimination and bias to the inclusion of 'social diversity' within development teams going beyond just gender (p. 24: Security robustness and sustainability of AI). In the cultural sector the Strategy funds AI projects for the 'preservation development accessibility networking and communication of cultural programmes' (p.30). It also emphasises developing AI skills to verify media content specifically to ensure diversity of opinion (p.30). The strategy also aims to establish 'AI made in Europe' as a trademark rooted in 'common European rules and values (p. 2: Summary p.13).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The German Federal Government

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy does not explicitly mention preventing cultural stereotypes or erasure of linguistic diversity. However it does include a general prevention objective: under “Safety robustness and sustainability of AI” it states that AI use must ensure effective protection against discrimination manipulation and misuse and argues that reflecting societal diversity in developer teams helps prevent bias and discrimination “from the very outset” (p. 24).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Law on increasing energy efficiency in Germany (Energy Efficiency Act - EnEfG)
items.justification: The EnEfG law implements the EU Energy Efficiency Directive (EED) at a national level and regulates the environmental footprint of data centres where AI workloads run. It mandates that data centers with a load of =300 kW meet strict performance metrics such as a Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) of =1.2 (Section 11) for new facilities and an Energy Reuse Factor (ERF) of 20% by 2028 (Section 11(2)). By requiring 100% renewable energy use by 2027 and annual reporting to the Energy Efficiency Register (Section 11(5)) the EnEfG ensures that AI growth aligns with national climate goals. For reporting data center operators must submit annual energy and water usage data to the Energy Efficiency Register (RZReg) (Section 13).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the scope of the EnEfG through Section 21. This section stipulates that the mandatory energy reduction targets for public bodies and the requirement to implement management systems do not apply to the field of National Defense. These exemptions ensure that the Act's stringent technical standards such as waste heat reuse or renewable energy quotas  do not jeopardise the operational readiness or security-critical infrastructure of the Bundeswehr. While the defense sector is encouraged to contribute to sustainability through separate strategies it remains legally exempt from the EnEfG.

body.name: The Federal Office for Economic Affairs and Export Control (BAFA)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: Section 11 establishes binding Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and waste heat reuse (ERF) targets for data centers effectively preventing 'excessive energy consumption' at the hardware level. It also mandates 100% renewable energy by 2027 for these facilities. However it lacks specific provisions for e-waste management which is handled under the ElektroG and does not regulate 'resource-intensive' software practices or algorithmic efficiency directly. The Act focuses on the efficiency of the 'where' AI is trained rather than the 'how' of its development.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
thematicElements.justification: Section 13 requires data center operators to report detailed energy metrics to a national register. Section 15 obliges these operators to inform their customers including AI developers of the specific energy consumption related to their service use. This provides developers with the necessary data to assess their environmental impact. However the EnEfG does not directly legally obligate software developers to report on their AI models; that specific requirement is handled by the EU AI Act which mandates energy reporting for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: The Energy Efficiency Act (EnEfG) explicitly promotes these efforts through binding technical mandates in Section 11. It establishes a strict PUE target of = 1.2 for new data centers effectively mandating advanced cooling technologies. It also dictates a transition to 100% renewable energy by 2027 (Section 11.5) and enforces waste heat reuse (ERF) of up to 20% by 2028. Regarding water Section 13 and Annex 3 require operators to report total water consumption and efficiency indicators to a national register. While water efficiency targets are currently focused on transparency rather than binding limits the Act creates a comprehensive legal baseline for reducing the environmental footprint of the infrastructure powering AI.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
