thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Law No. 4961/2022: Emerging information and communication technologies strengthening digital governance and other provisions (Greece)
items.justification: The law requires public disclosure of government AI systems through mandatory transparency rules. Article 6 obliges public bodies to provide accessible information on system purpose parameters data categories and decision logic. Article 8 requires each body to maintain and update a public register of AI systems. Article 5 mandates an algorithmic impact assessment before deployment. These provisions ensure public disclosure of algorithmic systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4(2) of the Law 4961/2022 explicitly excludes the Ministries of National Defense and Citizen Protection their supervised bodies and the National Intelligence Service (NIS) from the scope of application of this framework (p. 4). This provision clearly indicates that defence and security sectors are not covered by the obligations and safeguards outlined in the document.

body.name: Coordinating Committee on AI National Strategy Supervisory Committee for the development of AI AI Observatory

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: Article 8 of Law 4961/2022 establishes a mandatory public registry of all AI systems used by government bodies. Each body must record and update information on every system including its intended purpose operating parameters capabilities technical characteristics data categories safety measures and the responsible authority. Articles 4 5 and 6 further require transparency regarding how systems function and the logic behind decisions.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: Articles 5 and 6 require public disclosure of key information about government AI systems including their intended purpose operating parameters capabilities categories of data processed and the rationale for their use. Article 5 also mandates an algorithmic impact assessment before deployment which must be considered in public information duties. However the law does not require disclosure of training data or detailed model documentation.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: Article 6 requires public disclosure of key information about government AI systems but limits it by safeguarding military commercial and industrial secrets. Article 4 clarifies that all transparency duties apply without prejudice to GDPR and privacy protections. The law therefore sets explicit boundaries between what must be disclosed and what must remain protected for security and privacy reasons.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: Article 6 requires public bodies to provide clear accessible and easily understandable information about how an AI system works including its purpose parameters data categories and decision logic. The law explicitly states that this information must be offered “in an understandable and easily accessible form” including formats suitable for persons with disabilities ensuring non-technical public explanations.

items.title: Law No. 4961/2022: Emerging information and communication technologies strengthening digital governance and other provisions (Greece)
items.justification: The law regulates AI related public procurement in Article 7 requiring every tender for designing or developing an AI system to include conditions ensuring: contractor obligations to provide system parameters (Art. 6(b-c)) allow study of the system’s operating mode ensure legal framework compatibility and deliver the system so the public body can improve or audit it (p. 4-5).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4(2) of the Law 4961/2022 explicitly excludes the Ministries of National Defense and Citizen Protection their supervised bodies and the National Intelligence Service (NIS) from the scope of application of this framework (p. 4). This provision clearly indicates that defence and security sectors are not covered by the obligations and safeguards outlined in the document.

body.name: Coordinating Committee on AI National Strategy Supervisory Committee for the development of AI AI Observatory

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The law contains AI specific procurement obligations that exceed traditional IT procurement. Article 7 requires every AI related tender to include conditions ensuring transparency of system parameters (Art. 6(b-c)) access for auditing and improvement and compliance with safeguards on human dignity privacy non-discrimination equality and accessibility(p. 4-5). These provisions embed ethical social and technical considerations into AI procurement.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The law requires contractors to ensure that AI systems comply with safeguards related to human dignity privacy non-discrimination equality and accessibility and to take appropriate measures during design development and operation to meet these obligations (Article 7 p. 5). However it does not explicitly require vendors to demonstrate that systems have undergone formal testing for bias fairness or safety nor does it specify testing methodologies. Thus the requirement is only indirectly addressed.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: The law mandates transparency from vendors regarding AI systems. Article 6 and 7 require contractors to provide system parameters capabilities and operating modes to the public body enabling auditing and preventing “black-box” use (p. 4-5). These provisions establish a clear mandate for vendor transparency on data models and decision parameters.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: The Greek National Digital Decade Strategic Roadmap
items.justification: The document addresses Public Sector Skills Development through targeted training measures. Measure 1A06M provides reskilling and upskilling programmes for General Government employees local authorities and healthcare staff (p.110-111). Measure 1A03M supports capacity building through the training of 120.000 teachers in digital skills (p.108). ?he Cybersecurity Skills Academy delivers specialised training for public officials including in the curricula AI cyber forensics and malware analysis (p.98). As for the measures that do not explicitly reference AI they operate national Law 4961/2022 that establishes the framework for AI and emerging ICTs in the public sector upon which the Roadmap’s skills-related measures build (p.6-7).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Transformation Executive Network ELSTAT EKT SEPE National Coalition for Digital Skills and Jobs

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document partially addresses the establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants. Measure 1A06M provides large-scale reskilling and upskilling programmes for General Government employees local authorities and healthcare staff focusing on new digital technologies and innovative systems (p.110-111). The Cybersecurity Skills Academy further strengthens the link to AI by offering specialised training for public officials with curricula that explicitly include AI alongside cyber forensics and malware analysis (p. 98). In addition Law 4961/2022 establishes the national framework for artificial intelligence and emerging ICTs in the public sector within which these skills measures operate (p.6-7).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: A Blueprint for Greece's AI Transformation
items.justification: The Blueprint for Greece’s AI Transformation emphasizes rapid reskilling and upskilling to prepare the workforce for AI adoption. It calls for training programs targeting technical non-technical employees and technology leaders promoting continuous learning and AI literacy. Universities should reduce bureaucratic barriers to offer accessible reskilling opportunities (p. 76). Generative AI is proposed to personalize training delivery while vocational AI programs and certification schemes aim to build a skilled adaptable workforce (p. 77).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Supervisory Authority

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Blueprint for Greece’s AI Transformation includes recommendations for lifelong learning professional training and vocational education to support workforce adaptation to AI-related labor market changes (p. 76-77). However while these measures emphasize public coordination and broad access to training the document does not explicitly define concrete government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs for workers nor does it specify dedicated funding mechanisms or implementation frameworks. Therefore the framework addresses the objective at a strategic level but does not fully substantiate government financing or subsidy of such programs.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The Blueprint for Greece’s AI Transformation recommends financial incentives and state support for reskilling initiatives. It proposes subsidized access to AI education platforms for specific groups (p. 18) and incentives for companies to upskill employees through certified lifelong learning programs that meet quality standards (p. 40 74 76). These measures aim to make continuous training accessible and financially viable fostering workforce adaptation to the AI economy.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The Blueprint for Greece’s AI Transformation encourages but does not mandate company investment in employee training. It recommends incentives for firms to provide AI-related lifelong learning and upskilling programs (p. 41 74 76) and emphasizes collaboration between industry and academia to align training with evolving job demands. While it highlights the private sector’s role in mitigating automation risks through workforce development it stops short of imposing formal requirements on companies to invest in such training.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: Hungary Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025–2030)
items.justification: The Strategy addresses AI literacy within the formal education sector in Section 5.3 “Oktatás kompetenciafejlesztés” (pp. 51 101–104). It includes curriculum development and teacher training in public education (p.104) data literacy programs in schools (p.101) the introduction of sector-specific AI modules in higher education (p.55). Launching a high school 'AI lab' program where students can develop simple AI applications (p. 56) and the expansion of AI capacities in universities (p.84). These measures focus exclusively on strengthening AI-related knowledge and competences in secondary (including vocational) and tertiary education.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: Section 5.3 “Oktatás kompetenciafejlesztés” (pp.51 101–104) promotes integrating MI content through curriculum and content development and teacher training (p.104). It specifies sector-specific MI modules in higher education (p.55) and expansion of university AI capacities (p.84). However it does not mandate detailed or binding curriculum reforms at primary or secondary level focusing mainly on strategic integration and tertiary education development.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: Section 5.3 “Oktatás kompetenciafejlesztés” (pp.51 101–104) supports expanding AI-related programs within formal education including sector-specific MI modules in higher education (p.55) and development of adatspecialista and developer training. Page 84 highlights strengthening domestic university MI training capacities. Section 2.1 (pp.12–13) also references institutional structures (e.g. MILAB) supporting AI education and research within the formal system.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: Section 5.3 “Oktatás kompetenciafejlesztés” (pp.51 101–104) includes dedicated measures for teacher training. Page 104 specifies “Pedagógus képzési továbbképzési programok” to integrate AI content and methodology into teacher education and continuous training. It also calls for curriculum and content development and incorporation of existing training materials supporting resources for AI education across the formal system.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: Hungary Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025–2030)
items.justification: The framework addresses linguistic and cultural diversity by explicitly prioritising the development of language technologies tailored to the Hungarian language (pp. 26 44). It recognises that without such efforts smaller or less globally dominant languages risk marginalisation in the digital and AI-driven landscape. By supporting the creation of Hungarian-language corpora open-access tools and AI-based language processing systems the framework aims to ensure that Hungarian remains functional and competitive in digital environments. It further links this to cultural preservation framing language technology as essential to maintaining national identity.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: National Education Policy 2020
items.justification: The National Education Policy 2020 promotes AI literacy by integrating AI into formal education across all levels. It mandates the introduction of contemporary subjects such as Artificial Intelligence within curricula to develop relevant skills early on (p. 15). It further emphasises expanding research capacity in AI and machine learning to build national expertise (p. 45). Additionally it recognises that emerging technologies will transform both what and how students learn calling for continued educational and technological research (p. 56).

thematicElements.justification: The document includes curriculum reforms through the introduction of contemporary subjects such as Artificial Intelligence and other interdisciplinary areas “at relevant stages” to develop key skills among students “at all levels” (p. 15). It further recognises that emerging technologies including AI will transform both what and how students learn requiring ongoing adaptation of educational content and methods (p. 56). These provisions indicate a systemic approach to curriculum reform across the education system though without explicitly detailing each level.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes the integration of Artificial Intelligence into education by introducing it as a contemporary subject at relevant stages (p. 15) and emphasises the expansion of research capabilities in AI and related fields (p. 45). It also highlights the growing role of AI in shaping educational content and methods (p. 56). However it does not explicitly provide for the establishment of dedicated institutions or formal programs specifically offering AI-related courses.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document recognises the role of “tech-savvy teachers” and the transformative impact of AI and related technologies on education noting that these developments will require extensive research on both technological and educational fronts (p. 56). It also promotes integrating AI into curricula to develop student skills (p. 15). However it does not explicitly provide for structured teacher training programs or dedicated resources specifically for AI education.

items.title: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021
items.justification: The IT rules establish rights to redress through grievance mechanisms and oversight bodies including intermediary-level grievance systems (Rule 3(2)(a)) and Grievance Appellate Committees (Rule 3A) with user rights to challenge decisions (Rule 4(8)). These apply to platforms using AI and algorithmic tools (Rule 4(4)). Importantly an official government advisory (https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=1975445&reg=3&lang=2#:~:text=Given%20the%20significant%20challenges%20posedmeasures%20t) serving as interpretative material explicitly links AI harms to redress stating that individuals affected by deepfakes should file FIRs and avail remedies under the IT rules reinforcing access to redress for AI-related harms.

body.name: Grievance Appellate Committees

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The IT rules establish formal redress mechanisms through intermediary-level grievance systems (Rule 3(2)(a)) and Grievance Appellate Committees (Rule 3A) with user rights to challenge platform decisions (Rule 4(8)). These apply to platforms relying on AI and algorithmic systems (Rule 4(4)). Importantly an official government advisory—serving as interpretative material—reinforces judicial recourse by explicitly encouraging individuals affected by deepfakes to file FIRs and seek remedies under the IT rules thereby linking AI-related harms to formal legal and judicial mechanisms.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The IT rules establish state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms through mandated grievance redressal systems (Rule 3(2)(a)) and Grievance Appellate Committees (Rule 3A) which review user complaints against intermediary decisions (Rule 4(8)). These apply to platforms using AI and algorithmic tools (Rule 4(4)). An official government advisory further reinforces their use by directing users affected by deepfakes to seek remedies under the IT rules confirming their role in handling AI-related grievances.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The IT rules require intermediaries—including platforms relying on AI and algorithmic systems (Rule 4(4))—to establish accessible grievance redressal mechanisms (Rule 3(2)(a)) and provide users the right to challenge decisions (Rule 4(8)). These obligations effectively mandate companies to implement complaint mechanisms for harms arising from content moderation and automated systems. Additionally an official government advisory reinforces this by directing users affected by deepfakes to avail remedies under the IT rules linking AI-related harms to these mandated grievance mechanisms.

It also imposes restrictions on tracking and behavioral monitoring of children. As such the law accounts for children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems. However the Act does not specifically regulate AI systems or automated decision-making involving children.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 restricts harmful data practices affecting children (Sec. 9 p.8). It prohibits processing likely to cause detrimental effects on a child’s well-being (Sec. 9(2)) and bans tracking behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children (Sec. 9(3)). These provisions indirectly limit AI-driven profiling and ad targeting. However the Act does not explicitly regulate AI-generated inappropriate content or broader AI-based manipulation of children.

It positions AI-driven language technologies as a key mechanism to ensure inclusion and accessibility for speakers of these languages. This is operationalised through the development of machine translation systems multilingual datasets and speech technologies across diverse Indian language groups alongside an emphasis on large-scale multilingual data for training AI models (Section 3).

This is operationalised through measures such as multilingual datasets machine translation systems and speech technologies alongside an emphasis on large-scale multilingual data for training AI models (Section 3) ensuring responsiveness to diverse linguistic and cultural groups.

This extends to AI-driven moderation systems. Additionally a government advisory clarifies that deepfakes fall under the IT rules and highlights their disproportionate harm to women reinforcing the framework’s role in addressing AI-enabled gender discrimination and bias.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The IT rules assign obligations to intermediaries to exercise due diligence and prevent the hosting or dissemination of content that is insulting or harassing on the basis of gender (Section 3(1)(b)(ii)) including where algorithmic or automated systems are used for editorial control. This places responsibility on entities using AI-driven moderation tools to prevent gender-discriminatory outcomes. The government advisory on deepfakes further reinforces these responsibilities by highlighting harms to women under the IT rules.

items.title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (India)
items.justification: The framework addresses the indicator by explicitly promoting the use of impact assessments across multiple dimensions including fairness privacy harm and labour market effects. It calls on developers to “identify the in-built biases and assess their impact” to mitigate discriminatory outcomes (p. 85) recommends the use of “Data Privacy Impact Assessment Tools” to manage privacy risks (p. 87) and proposes “damage impact assessment at every stage of development of an AI model” within a negligence-based framework (p. 88). It also extends impact assessment to broader societal consequences advocating continuous monitoring of AI’s effects on employment and suggesting the creation of taskforce to track labour market changes (p. 92).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Data Protection Board

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework promotes proactive risk management by recommending impact assessments across multiple dimensions including fairness privacy harm and labour market effects. It calls on developers to “identify the in-built biases and assess their impact” (p. 85) use data privacy impact assessments (p. 87) and conduct “damage impact assessment at every stage of development” (p. 88). It further supports continuous evaluation of broader societal impacts including employment effects (p. 92) indicating a lifecycle approach that includes pre-deployment considerations.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The framework assigns clear responsibilities to developers to conduct impact assessments across multiple dimensions. It calls on developers to “identify the in-built biases and assess their impact” (p. 85) recommends the use of Data Privacy Impact Assessment Tools (p. 87) and proposes “damage impact assessment at every stage of development of an AI model” (p. 88). It further extends this to broader societal risks including labour market impacts advocating continuous monitoring (p. 92) thereby establishing a comprehensive lifecycle-based obligation to assess and mitigate risks.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Indian Standard: Information Technology = Artificial Intelligence - Management System Standard (IS/ISO/IEC 42001:2023)
items.justification: The framework explicitly addresses AI security and safety by recognising that “safety and robustness” are essential for building trust particularly in high-risk applications (p. 8). It identifies concrete security risks including adversarial attacks data manipulation and model vulnerabilities across the AI lifecycle (pp. 23–24). The document further establishes a Principle of Safety and Reliability requiring safeguards risk minimisation and continuous monitoring to ensure systems perform as intended and protect stakeholders from harm (p. 41).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The framework establishes a Principle of Safety and Reliability requiring AI systems to “perform in an acceptable manner reliably according to the desired goals” and to be monitored throughout their lifecycle (p. 41). It also highlights risks to robustness and accuracy arising from adversarial attacks and system vulnerabilities (pp. 23–24). However it does not define explicit performance thresholds or quantitative quality benchmarks instead providing high-level guidance on reliability and acceptable system behaviour.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The framework includes a Principle of Safety and Reliability requiring “sufficient safeguards” to ensure the safety of stakeholders and to minimise risks arising from unintended or unexpected harm (p. 41). It also calls for continuous monitoring of AI systems across their lifecycle to ensure reliable performance. In addition it highlights vulnerabilities such as adversarial attacks and system manipulation (pp. 23–24) reinforcing the need for protective measures and risk mitigation in case of system failure or unexpected behaviour.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The framework recommends that AI systems be monitored through their lifecycle to ensure they perform reliably and safely as intended (p. 41) and it identifies technical vulnerabilities such as adversarial attacks data manipulation and model weaknesses that can undermine robustness (pp. 23–24). These points support the need for testing and validation. However the document does not explicitly require pre-deployment testing formal validation procedures or specific documentation obligations.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The framework explicitly identifies security risks in AI systems including adversarial attacks data manipulation and model vulnerabilities across the machine learning lifecycle (pp. 23–24). It also emphasises safety robustness and the need for safeguards and continuous monitoring to ensure reliable system performance (p. 41). However these are framed as high-level principles and risk awareness rather than binding or specific security obligations imposed on entities to protect systems against cyberattacks or adversarial interference.

items.title: National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (India)

It emphasizes the need for “explainability” rather than full technical disclosure ensuring that AI decisions are understandable to users especially in high-impact contexts. The document also promotes research in Explainable AI (XAI) to develop systems that allow users to understand trust and effectively manage AI outputs thereby strengthening transparency and accountability.

items.title: AI National Strategy 2020-2045 (Stranas KA) (Indonesia)
items.justification: Chapter 4 (p.49-59) focuses on building human resources and strengthening AI literacy across the country. It highlights several strategic issues such as the shortage of skilled professionals in AI and data science the limited alignment between education and industry needs and the lack of public awareness about AI technologies. It stresses that Indonesia’s education system-both formal and non-formal—must be reoriented to produce competent AI practitioners and a workforce that is ready to adapt to AI-driven transformation. To address these challenges the strategy proposes initiatives including integrating AI data science and machine learning into school and university curricula; offering training workshops and vocational programmes.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

This phenomenon increases the potential for information manipulation which can undermine integrity). It also includes steps of safeguard measures depending on the risk (page 12-13 table 1).
