The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document includes measures that directly address the prevention of AI-enabled gender-based harassment and violence particularly through its explicit focus on restricting the creation and dissemination of harmful deepfakes. By recognizing that the vast majority of sexually explicit deepfakes disproportionately target women and girls the framework highlights the gendered nature of this abuse and the serious psychological social and professional harm it causes. Its provisions aim to limit the misuse of AI tools—such as “nudify” applications—that enable perpetrators to generate non-consensual explicit content thereby contributing to the prevention of AI-facilitated gender-based harassment and violence.

items.title: Law of the Republic of Indonesia No. 27 of 2022 on Personal Data Protection
items.justification: Yes data subjects have the right to file complaints with the Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA) if they believe their personal data has been processed unlawfully or their rights have been violated (Art 56-57 p. 15-16). These articles establish a formal administrative mechanism for redress requiring the authority to follow up and resolve complaints. Art. 58 guarantees individuals the right to compensation for material or immaterial losses resulting from violations of their data protection rights allowing them to pursue remedies through civil proceedings. The law also provides for administrative sanctions (Art. 57): warnings temporary suspension and deletion of personal data and criminal sanctions (Art. 67-73) for severe breach.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA or Otoritas Perlindungan Data Pribadi)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Indonesia’s Personal Data Protection Law does not regulate AI systems as such but adopts a technology-neutral approach to personal data processing. Accordingly AI-based activities such as profiling or automated decision-making fall within the law’s scope only insofar as they involve the processing of personal data. The PDP Law provides administrative and judicial avenues for redress in such cases: Articles 56–57 set out administrative remedies Article 58 grants data subjects the right to compensation for material or immaterial losses through civil claims against data controllers or processors and Articles 67–73 provide criminal sanctions for serious violations.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: There are state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms that allow individuals to raise grievances related to the processing of personal data which can include AI systems handling such data. Art. 56–57 establish the PDPA as an independent supervisory and enforcement body. Data subjects can file complaints directly with the PDPA if their personal data rights are violated. The PDPA is empowered to investigate complaints issue warnings impose administrative sanctions and recommend corrective actions without requiring the individual to go through a judicial process. This mechanism functions as a state-based non-judicial complaint channel similar to an ombuds or regulatory body providing an accessible avenue for redress outside courts.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: It requires companies and data controllers including those deploying AI systems that process personal data to provide accessible transparent and responsive grievance or complaint mechanisms for individuals harmed by their data processing activities. Art.56 mandates internal complaint channels at the company level while Art.56-57 (p.15-16) allow unresolved complaints to be escalated to the Personal Data Protection Authority (PDPA) which can investigate and enforce corrective measures. This establishes a two-tiered grievance system internal mechanisms complemented by a state-based oversight and enforcement channel-ensuring individuals have meaningful avenues to seek redress for AI-related or general data processing harms.

items.title: Regulation of the Government of the Republic of Indonesia Number 17 of 2025 on Governance of the Organization of Electronic Systems in Child Protection
items.justification: Art. 7 (p.4) protecting children’s personal data by obtaining parental or guardian consent and conducting a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment. They must design child-accessible products services and features with high privacy settings by default and provide complete accurate and non-misleading information to users.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document contains clear and specific provisions to protect children’s personal data and privacy when interacting with AI or digital systems. Art. 7 (p.4) requires electronic system organizers to obtain parental consent conduct personal data protection impact assessments and configure products or services with high privacy settings by default for child users. Art. 10 (p.6) Electronic System Organizers may provide the option to set the level of privacy a in accordance with the Assessment of the Impact of Personal Data Protection.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The Regulation includes several specific provisions and measures aimed at preventing the use of AI and digital systems to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising and inappropriate content. Article 7 prohibits covert or non-transparent techniques profiling and the collection of precise geolocation data from children while Article 9 requires parental or guardian consent before children can access digital products and mandates data deletion if consent is denied. Article 10 ensures high privacy settings by default and their maintenance during updates and Article 11 requires transparent accurate and easy-to-understand information to avoid misleading children.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The Regulation assigns obligations to Electronic System Organizers that promote child safety and age-appropriate design. Art. 7 requires safeguards aligned with child protection principles. Art. 9 mandates parental consent and data deletion if consent is denied. Art. 10 requires high privacy-by-default settings including during updates. Art. 11 mandates clear and accessible information and Art. 12 supports digital education and empowerment. However the Regulation does not explicitly impose AI-specific design obligations on AI developers or deployers as a distinct category; obligations apply broadly to electronic system providers.

items.title: Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Informatics Number 9 of 2023 concerning Artificial Intelligence Ethics (Indonesia)
items.justification: The “humanity” principle (Art.6B.2) aligns with the definition of human oversight because it places clear emphasis on keeping humans in control of AI systems especially in contexts that affect human rights dignity and social values. The circular explicitly instructs that AI must not act as the final decision-maker in matters concerning humanity thereby ensuring that human actors retain the authority to monitor supervise control review and intervene in AI operations. By embedding the humanity principle in its ethical framework the circular mandates that human decision-making must stay central preventing fully autonomous or unchecked AI operations and thereby fulfilling the fundamental objectives of human oversight.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Circular Letter promotes human control over AI by stating that AI must function as a support for human activities and must not act as a policy maker or final decision maker in matters concerning humanity (Article 6: Contents of the Circular – Implementation and Responsibilities). It further emphasizes supervision by the government organizers and users reinforcing human monitoring and oversight of AI systems. However the document does not establish concrete operational measures enforceable safeguards or detailed procedures for human intervention review or override in high-risk or critical decision-making contexts.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Circular Letter assigns general responsibilities to business actors and public and private electronic system providers in the implementation of artificial intelligence including ensuring accountability supervision and protection of the public (Article 6: Contents of the Circular: c) Implementation and Responsibilities). It emphasizes government organizer and user supervision and requires entities to implement internal ethics and data policies for AI use. However the document does not explicitly require entities to designate specific responsible individuals or roles with defined authority to oversee intervene in or be ultimately accountable for AI system decisions.

items.title: AI National Strategy 2020-2045 (Stranas KA) (Indonesia)
items.justification: It addresses reskilling and upskilling initiatives in the context of AI primarily under its Talent / Human Resources development pillar. In Chapter 4.1 (p.49-50) the document emphasises the need to upgrade existing workforce capabilities and develop new talent so that Indonesia can keep pace with AI-driven change in industries and society. It proposes initiatives such as expanding non-formal and vocational education (e.g. training workshops certification programmes) alongside formal education thereby enabling workers already in the labour market to reskill (learn new AI-related skills) or upskill (enhance their current skills) so they remain relevant (p.51-52)

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

Victims may also request removal of harmful content from websites and sue the individuals who distributed it.p. 9 (§38): Individuals have the right to request correction or deletion of fake data held in databases.No section (§§1–53) creates rights to redress against platforms.

items.title: 2023 Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics Policy Principles Document (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses Human Oversight in Part Four under the section 'Human Involvement.' It explores the need for human participation in AI decision-making outlining both its advantages and challenges. The policy details different levels of oversight such as human-in-the-loop (where a person is part of the decision) and human-on-the-loop (where a person supervises or can veto a decision). It highlights benefits like improved accountability and legitimacy but also notes challenges like 'automation bias'. Ultimately Part Five recommends that the required level of human involvement be determined based on the context and the specific risks of the AI application.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It establishes 'The Human at the Center' as a core ethical principle in Part Six ensuring AI remains a tool to assist humans . Part Four details specific measures for 'Human Involvement' outlining models like human-in-the-loop (a person makes the final decision) and human-on-the-loop (a person can supervise or veto the AI) .Part Five recommends applying stronger human control in critical high-stakes contexts stating that the greater the risk of the decision the stronger the justification for significant human involvement .

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Part Five states that the justification for 'significant human involvement' is strongest where the potential for harm to fundamental rights is greatest. It explicitly uses medicine as a key example noting that human involvement is particularly high when it comes to irreversible decisions. Rather than a blanket ban the policy advocates for a risk-based approach ensuring that human judgment is required in critical fields where automation alone is insufficient to address ethical concerns.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The principle of 'Accountability' in Part Six explicitly states that 'Developers operators or users' are responsible for the AI's proper functioning and for upholding the other ethical principles. This is intended to establish a 'responsible party' for the artificial intelligence system.This is complemented by the 'Human Involvement' measures discussed in Part Four which detail models like human-on-the-loop. This model gives a designated human the authority to oversee supervise and intervene in the decisions made by the system ensuring there is a person who can ultimately be held accountable .

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The document presents Human Oversight as a core principle for respecting human rights and a key risk mitigation strategy.It specifies that AI outputs should be treated as support for human decision-making not as the final determination. For risk management it recommends integrating human involvement throughout the AI lifecycle (ex ante real-time or ex post). For high-risk systems the guide explicitly recommends implementing human control and an 'off switch'.These concepts are primarily discussed in the principles of 'Responsible Use' (Chapter 2) and the risk mitigation strategies (Appendix D).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It frames AI as a tool to assist humans not replace their judgment. Appendix C explicitly advises that AI outputs should be treated as 'supporting human decision-making and not as the sole source for receiving information or as a final decision'.As a primary risk mitigation strategy Appendix D lists 'Human Involvement' and 'ensuring appropriate human oversight throughout the entire lifecycle of the AI system'. For systems classified as 'High Risk' the guide specifically recommends implementing 'Human control and 'off switch'' to maintain ultimate human authority.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document's risk-based framework effectively prevents full automation in sensitive sectors by mandating human intervention as risk levels increase.Appendix D addresses scenarios like 'Risk of Health or Safety Harm' and 'Exceptional Risks' that could harm fundamental rights which apply to sectors like medicine and law enforcement. For these high-risk systems the guide requires escalating human oversight culminating in mandatory 'Human control and 'off switch''.Furthermore Appendix C instructs users to treat AI outputs as 'supporting human decision-making' not as the final decision itself ensuring that human judgment remains necessary in critical applications

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly mandates the designation of responsible individuals through its proposed governance structure.Chapter 3 outlines a framework that assigns obligations to two key roles to ensure oversight and accountability:The AI Governance Officer is the designated individual responsible at the organizational level for establishing policy operating the risk management framework and managing AI incidents.Business Implementation Officers are accountable for specific AI systems leading their implementation and managing their associated risks directly.Detailed responsibilities for these roles are specified in Appendix A and Appendix B establishing clear lines of accountability for system decisions.

items.title: 2023 Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics Policy Principles Document (Israel)
items.justification: The document discusses impact assessments primarily as tools for transparency and risk management. In Section 5.3 (Explainability) it suggests requiring AI users to publish an Algorithm Impact Statement (AIS) drawing a parallel to Regulatory Impact Assessments (RIA) used in other fields. This statement would disclose the system's development operation and expected impact.Furthermore Section 5.1 (Discrimination) recommends conducting risk assessments to evaluate concerns about discrimination and potential harm. The text also notes international precedents such as the EU's 'prior assessment' for high-risk systems and the Council of Europe's draft convention regarding risk assessment duties.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Government Knowledge and Coordination Center for AI Regulation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly promotes this via Recommendation 7 proposing a 'uniform risk management tool' for development and use.Section 6.1.2(c) states regulation should be the product of a 'risk management process'. Section 5.1(b) suggests 'Conducting Preliminary... Checks' before use to assess impacts like discrimination. Section 5.3 discusses requiring an 'Algorithm Impact Statement' (AIS) to disclose expected impacts. Ethical Principle (a) lists 'sustainable development' and 'social welfare' as core objectives.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The document recommends these measures. Recommendation 7 explicitly proposes a 'uniform risk management tool' to help developers and users assess risks .Section 5.3 suggests requiring users to publish an Algorithm Impact Statement (AIS) to disclose the system's expected impact .Section 5.1(b) discusses requiring 'preliminary and periodic checks' before use to identify risks like discrimination .Finally Ethical Principle (f) (Accountability) states developers and users must demonstrate responsibility including through 'accepted risk management concepts'.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: the document addresses this particularly in Section 5.3 (Explainability). It highlights proposals to require users to 'publish an algorithm impact statement (AIS)' for 'public review' . The text notes that broadening explainability to the general public allows for 'broad public discourse' and supervision.Additionally Recommendation 7 proposes making information and tools accessible to the public to assist in assessing risks. Ethical Principle (d) further advocates for making information about the system's decisions accessible to affected parties.

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses Impact Assessments through its Risk Management Methodology detailed in Appendix D. This iterative process functions as an impact assessment via:Analysis & Assessment (Stage 1): Users must map benefits and risks explicitly evaluating the 'magnitude of impact' and scope of affected parties (e.g. vulnerable populations).Triage (Stage 3): A decision-making phase to determine if the system should proceed based on the assessment.Mitigation: Section 3.1 mandates an 'impact mitigation plan' for high-risk systems.Rights Assessment: Appendix D Part 3 requires examining systems for significant harm to fundamental rights.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Section 2 promotes a culture where responsible use is 'embedded' organization-wide. Appendix D mandates an impact evaluation starting at 'system characterization' (Stage 1)—before deployment. This explicitly covers:Societal/Ethical: Assessing 'social risks' (e.g. bias privacy)  'human rights'  and consulting ethics experts.Environmental: Identifying 'Risk of Environmental Harm' and opportunities for 'sustainable development'.The 'Triage' stage (Stage 3) requires evaluating these factors before approving implementation

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: he guide assigns obligations to organizational users specifically the Business Implementation Officer to 'operate the risk management process'. This functions as an impact assessment requiring the identification of risks to 'individuals from vulnerable populations' and 'the public at large'. It explicitly mandates formulating a 'risk mitigation plan' and assessing the 'magnitude of risk impact'. Additionally the AI Governance Officer is obligated to establish responsible use policies. Regarding developers users are instructed to 'obtain relevant information from the system vendor' to inform this assessment.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: the document includes specific recommendations related to this goal. Section 3.1 proposes that organization management 'make accessible periodic reports of the organization's activities' in the field. Appendix A (Section 3.4) recommends 'Publishing on the organizational website information about AI systems... according to... the risk management process'. Furthermore Appendix D (Stage 4) outlines 'Transparency to the Public' as a required action mandating ongoing disclosure regarding system operations data types capabilities and limitations to the general public or affected communities  to provide information that enables addressing 'negative outcomes'.

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses Public Disclosure of Government Algorithmic Systems mainly through its transparency obligations. Chapter 3 requires organizations to “create public engagement processes” and publish periodic reports (p.6 sec. 3.1). The AI Governance Officer must publish information about AI systems on the organization’s website (p.9 sec. 3.4). In Appendix D transparency is detailed as part of system implementation including disclosure of system use data types capabilities limitations and incident reporting (pp.18–19 “Transparency to the Public”).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: Appendix A instructs the AI Governance Officer to publish on the organizational website information about AI systems in use (p. 9 sec. 3.4).It further states that AI systems will be published in the “AI Watch” system a centralized registry created by the National Digital Agency to provide a full situation picture of AI use across government bodies (p. 9 fn. 7)

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The document requires disclosure of key information about high-risk AI systems.Appendix A mandates public transparency about AI systems including information on system operation capabilities limitations and data types used (sec. 3.4).Appendix D expands this by requiring disclosure of risk levels risk-management processes and AI incident information and it describes transparency obligations during implementation and monitoring (“Transparency to the Public”)

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The document provides explicit guidance on what may be disclosed and what must be protected.Appendix C prohibits entering or exposing protected information including personally identifiable information sensitive data information restricted under the Freedom of Information Law trade secrets privileged material and classified information ( sec. 2.1.2).Transparency obligations (Appendix D) apply only “according to policy” and are bounded by these protections.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: The document requires clear accessible public explanations of AI systems.Appendix D mandates ongoing transparency about “system operation generally and accessibly to the public (including its capabilities and limitations)” and about situations of direct interaction with AI (pp. 18–19 “Transparency to the Public”).Chapter 2 also frames transparency as providing substantial understandable information to the public including system logic and limitations (p. 5 “Transparency and explainability”)

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses Public Procurement of AI mainly through guidance on acquiring and approving AI tools. Appendix A §1.3 sets a dedicated policy for procuring off-the-shelf AI tools requiring coordination with cyber privacy and accounting units and compliance with IT Directive 16.12.1.2 and cloud-procurement rules. It also discusses examining vendor information as part of risk assessment (Appendix D Stage 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The document includes AI-specific procurement guidelines that extend beyond traditional IT procurement by requiring ethical social technical and risk-based considerations. Appendix A §1.3 establishes procurement policies for AI tools including restrictions on tools from non-democratic countries privacy protection cyber-security coordination and bias-related data governance. Appendix D Stage 1 requires ethical social and legal risk assessment before procurement.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The document requires public bodies to examine vendor evidence on risks which implicitly includes bias fairness and safety testing but it does not explicitly mandate vendors to prove compliance as a standalone requirement.Appendix D Stage 1 (Identification) requires obtaining “relevant information from the system vendor” on risks including biases data issues safety and legal harms. Appendix D Stage 1 (Examination & Consultation) requires assessing discrimination privacy and safety risks and consulting experts accordingly.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns responsibilities that require transparency from vendors including data sources model logic and risks—measures aimed at preventing “black box” systems.Appendix D Stage 1 (Identification) requires obtaining “relevant information from the system vendor” about system risks and characteristics.Appendix D Stage 1 (Examination) requires assessing data quality representativeness and model-related risks (bias opacity).Appendix A §1.2 requires data governance ensuring traceability and explainability.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: The document does not explicitly prioritize local development but it does include procurement conditions that support AI sovereignty by restricting or discouraging reliance on foreign high-risk providers.Appendix C §2.1.1 instructs public bodies not to use AI applications developed in non-democratic countries implicitly favoring trusted typically local or allied providers.Appendix A §1.3 promotes procuring AI services through government cloud environments (Nimbus) which prioritizes vetted government-approved vendors.

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The guide positions skills development as essential for responsible AI. The National Digital Agency offers training via 'HaDigitalit' and an expert center (Sec. 1.4). The AI Governance Officer is responsible for 'Leading Organizational Learning Processes' (Appendix A) involving learning plans workshops and training to deepen risk understanding. End Users must maintain 'Literacy' by taking courses to understand tool limitations (Appendix C). Finally 'Awareness Raising' and 'knowledge transfer' are key risk mitigation strategies (Appendix D).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this partially. It recommends that public organizations establish 'Organizational Learning Processes' including training and workshops to deepen understanding of AI risks and benefits among employees. It identifies the National Digital Agency's 'HaDigitalit' school as a central resource for public sector training and emphasizes 'literacy' as a core principle for end users. However it frames these as organizational governance responsibilities (Appendix A) rather than a centralized government-wide strategy and it does not explicitly mention the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: the document establishes specific roles to champion responsible AI. It defines the AI Governance Officer to 'establish and operate organizational policy' and lead 'organizational learning processes' to deepen knowledge. It also designates Business Implementation Officers to lead specific AI projects and manage risks. Additionally the National Digital Agency acts as a central expert body offering an 'expert center' and support services. The guide explicitly recommends 'business-organizational means' to 'strengthen a responsible use culture' and provide 'professional supervision'.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: the document includes specific provisions for ongoing training. Appendix A (Sec. 2.2) tasks the AI Governance Officer with 'Leading Organizational Learning Processes' by establishing a plan that includes 'internal and external training and workshops' to deepen knowledge among users. Appendix C (Literacy) explicitly recommends that end users 'participate in courses and read articles on the subject regularly' to understand the technology noting that it is 'new and dynamic'. Furthermore Appendix D (Sec. 5.C) lists 'Awareness Raising' through training and workshops for users and decision-makers as a recommended risk mitigation measure.

items.title: National Program for Artificial Intelligence (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses reskilling and upskilling in Section 10.3 “Preparation for the Changes Expected in the Labor Market” (pp. 78–79). It outlines measures such as training schemes to develop AI skills a dedicated career-change track for “professions at risk” and programs for retraining vulnerable workers. The section explains that AI will redefine jobs and require new professional capabilities necessitating updated training and workforce policies to equip workers for emerging AI-driven roles.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Funding for security and defense is stated in page 5 as an issue to be treated separately. Yet AI in general is treated as a national security issue.

body.name: central directorate (These later was defined as National AI Headquarters) and the Telem Forum for R&D and different governmental offices according to topic - Labor Education and Ministry of Innovation The Ministry of Innovation is generally in charge of implementing and overseeing the AI plans in Israel but as specific tasks are under the purview of specific offices - they are each assigned the responsibility for implementation in their area Telem Forum is a bit unique in that aspect as it is an expert forum with expertise and national R&D

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The document includes provisions for government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs.Section 10.3 outlines state-led measures such as training schemes for developing AI skills a career-change track for “professions at risk” and retraining programs for vulnerable workers (pp. 78–79).These initiatives are explicitly presented as part of the government’s responsibility to prepare the labor market for AI-driven change indicating public funding and support.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: 2023 Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics Policy Principles Document (Israel)
items.justification: The document addresses Safety and Security by requiring AI systems to be reliable robust secure and safe across their entire lifecycle. It highlights risks from technical failures vulnerabilities manipulation misuse by malicious actors and the added safety risks created when physical products integrate AI that can learn or change after deployment. It also stresses risk-management duties documentation and information-sharing between actors.Key locations: Section “Reliability Robustness Security and Safety”
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Government Knowledge and Coordination Center for AI Regulation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document does not set explicit numerical performance thresholds but it does require that AI systems meet quality benchmarks such as being “reliable robust secure and safe” and operate properly under expected use misuse and hazardous conditions. It also recommends applying professional risk-management standards across the AI system’s lifecycle which functions as a form of performance/quality requirement.See “Reliability Robustness Security and Safety”

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The document does not mandate explicit pre-deployment testing or validation but it does recommend lifecycle-wide quality controls that implicitly require such processes. It calls for:Risk-management measures throughout the AI lifecycleRetrospective examination and testingDocumentation enabling review of system design and performance.These function as de facto pre-deployment validation requirements even if not labeled as such.Relevant section: “Reliability Robustness Security and Safety”

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The document includes clear security-related obligations for AI systems. It requires AI to be “reliable robust secure and safe” and explicitly warns of risks from cyberattacks manipulation and exploitation of vulnerabilities. It calls for risk-management measures to reduce “information security risks” across the AI lifecycle and notes threats from malicious actors who may exploit system weaknesses.Relevant section: “Reliability Robustness Security and Safety”

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)
items.justification: The document treats Safety and Security as core principles for responsible AI use. In Chapter 2 “System security and safety” (p. 5–6) it requires AI systems to remain reliable secure and non-hazardous in both planned and unplanned scenarios and to include mechanisms for handling risk situations.Appendix D (Risk Classification p. 17–18) details information-security risks model-manipulation attacks data leakage and safety harms. Mitigation tools appear in Appendix D pp. 19–22.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document includes guidance that functions as performance thresholds and quality benchmarks even if not labeled as such.Appendix D requires assessing accuracy reliability magnitude of impacts and likelihood of errors when evaluating risks (Risk Classification).It also recommends RAG/CAG guardrails temperature control sampling checks Red Team testing and human oversight to maintain reliable system performance (Risk Mitigation Measures).These operate as de facto quality benchmarks ensuring dependable AI behavior.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The document contains explicit safeguards and emergency protocols for AI failures.Appendix A requires crisis management and AI incident handling (Section 3.3) including immediate reporting and structured incident response.Appendix D mandates fallback procedures such as human oversight Red Team testing real-time monitoring and adjustments when risks materialize (Risk Mitigation & Stage 4 Implementation).These ensure harm is mitigated when systems behave unexpectedly.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The document requires pre-deployment testing validation and documentation.Appendix D mandates a full pre-deployment risk management process including identification examination consultation and comprehensive documentation before approval (Stage 1 & Stage 2).It also requires testing with dummy data Red Teaming and validating outputs through sampling (Risk Mitigation Measures).These steps ensure technical robustness throughout the lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The document includes clear security obligations to protect AI systems from cyberattacks and adversarial manipulation.It identifies information-security risks including attacks on AI models model-deception attacks vulnerabilities unauthorized access and data leakage (Appendix D – Risk Classification).It recommends Red Teaming controlled attacks guardrails privacy-enhancing technologies secure data governance and monitoring as protection measures (Appendix D – Risk Mitigation Measures).

items.title: 2023 Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics Policy Principles Document (Israel)
items.justification: As detailed in the Executive Summary and Part Six the policy addresses the 'black box' problem where an AI's decision-making process is opaque. It proposes that people should be informed when interacting with or being affected by AI systems. Furthermore it recommends providing explanations for an AI's decisions or actions especially considering the impact on individuals and technological limitations. This principle aims to protect human dignity enable accountability and build public trust in AI technologies.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Government Knowledge and Coordination Center for AI Regulation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Its core proposal is adopting 'Transparency and Explainability' as an ethical principle calling for users to be informed about AI activity and its decisions. This is supported by a recommended 'duty of disclosure' to ensure people know they are interacting with AI .The document explicitly states that a key objective of these policies is to increase public trust. It also references a proposed 'algorithm impact statement (AIS)' to publicly detail an AI's purpose and logic . These recommendations are found in the Executive Summary Part Five and Part Six

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The principle of 'Accountability' in Part Six states that 'Developers operators or users of artificial intelligence will demonstrate responsibility' for upholding the other ethical principles in their activities.This directly links to the principle of 'Transparency and Explainability' which calls for providing an explanation for an AI's decisions taking into account the extent of its influence and consequences.Part Five explicitly recommends applying this requirement in high-stakes contexts noting there is a 'stronger justification to demand an explanation for a system that determines whether a person can receive a loan or be accepted for a job'.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The proposed ethical principle of 'Transparency and Explainability' in Part Six calls for informing 'those who come into contact with or are affected by its activity' and providing them with an explanation for a decision or action.More explicitly Part Five discusses potential legal tools and measures including the option to establish 'a right for the data subject to receive the explanation'. This right is considered particularly relevant in cases where an individual has 'been denied an essential service as a result of the system's decision'

items.title: Guide for Risk Management and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools in the Public Sector (Israel)

Recommends Disclosure components in products (p.21

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Section 2 (p.5) - Principle #3 explicitly requires 'substantial information that clarifies the system's operation including its capabilities and limitations' information about 'data sources and the logic underlying the system.'Appendix A Section 3.4 (p.9) - Mandates AI Governance Officers to 'publish on the organizational website information about AI systems in use' promoting public transparency.Appendix D Stage 4 (p.16) - Details public transparency requirements including: 'types of information serving the system system operation generally and accessibly to the public (including its capabilities and limitations).'Appendix D (p.14 p.21) - Recommends technical measures like RAG/CAG and Reasoning to enable tracing decision-making

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
