items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The law mandates AI literacy and training across education and professional sectors. Art. 24(e)-p.15 provides “pathways for literacy and training in the use of artificial intelligence systems”. Art. 24(g)-p.15 strengthens STEM skills “within school curricula” to guide students toward AI disciplines. Art. 24(i)-p.15 requires universities AFAM institutions and ITS Academies to deliver technical understanding and informed use of AI including interpreting AI outputs.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The law mandates inclusion of AI-related skills in education at all levels. Art. 24(g) enhances STEM skills “within school curricula” to orient students toward AI fields covering primary and secondary. Art. 24(i) requires universities AFAM institutions and ITS Academies to provide AI technical understanding and interpretation of AI outputs covering tertiary.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The law requires creation and delivery of AI training programmes across formal education. Art. 24(e) mandates “pathways for literacy and training in the use of artificial intelligence systems”. Art. 24(i) establishes AI training in university AFAM and ITS Academy courses for technical AI understanding and interpretation of outputs.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The law addresses children’s rights mainly through data privacy and age-based access rules. Article 4 (p.2-3) requires parental consent for minors under 14 to use AI systems and process related personal data; minors aged 14–18 may consent directly if information on risks is accessible and understandable.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly exclude the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security field so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The document includes specific provisions regarding the protection of children's personal data and privacy when interacting with AI systems: Art. 4 section 4 addresses this issue directly establishing two key aspects: 1. Minors under fourteen years of age accessing AI technologies and the subsequent processing of their personal data requires the consent of the person exercising parental responsibility . 2. A minor aged fourteen to under eighteen can provide their own consent for personal data processing related to AI use provided that information and communications regarding data risks are easily accessible and comprehensible. These rules are established in compliance with relevant EU data protection regulation.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses: 1. Exploitation/Manipulation (via Data): Art. 4 section 4 requires the consent of the person exercising parental responsibility for minors under 14 old to access AI technologies and for the resulting personal data processing. Minors aged fourteen to under eighteen can consent themselves but the information regarding data risks must be easily accessible and comprehensible Inappropriate Content: Art. 26 section 1 letter c introduces criminal penalties for the illegal dissemination of content generated or altered with AI which is deceptive and causes unjust harm and speedy procedures are contemplated for illegalities perpetrated due to age.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The document includes general obligations regarding safety and harm prevention that apply to all users and specific requirements regarding the age-appropriateness of data interaction for minors.AI systems must be developed and applied respecting the principles of security and the prevention of harm (prevenzione del danno) (Art. 3 sections 1 3). This is an obligation applicable to all developers and deployers. While it covers safety and age-appropriate information dissemination regarding data the document does not assign a direct broad obligation to developers/deployers to design systems explicitly to be 'beneficial for children' across all potential applications.

items.title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
items.justification: The Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026 warns about stereotyping and cultural homogenization due to reliance on generative AI systems built elsewhere highlighting threats to linguistic and cultural diversity (pp. 11–12 Risks of the strategy). In order to maintain Italy's unique cultural character and democratic ideals it emphasizes the necessity of developing AI in accordance with national and constitutional norms. According to the plan generative technologies with an Italian context should be promoted cultural diversity should be respected and reliance on outside models should be avoided.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Foundation for AI

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024-2026 addresses the risk of cultural homogenization and emphasizes the importance of developing AI in accordance with Italy's national and constitutional principles rather than relying entirely on foreign models (pp. 11-12 Risks of the Strategy). It also encourages the development of Large Multilingual Models (LMMs) based on Italian and multilingual languages reflecting national/regional languages and settings (p. 19 R.3 Design of Italian LMMs). However it does not completely elaborate general measurements for a large range of worldwide cultures and languages.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
items.justification: The Strategy explicitly frames environmental sustainability as a cross-cutting priority for AI. It links competitiveness to socially responsible AI highlighting risks of energy consumption privacy and ecological impacts (pp. 4–6 8–10). Strategy for Research Action R.3 calls for 'environmental sustainability' by seeking innovative techniques to 'reduce the size of models' and their energy footprint (p. 19) also Action R.4 suggests interdisciplinary research projects focused on 'landscape protection sea or environmental protection' and the 'optimization of environmental and energy resources (p. 19).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Department for Digital Transformation - Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) - FAIR Foundation

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: Article 3 establishes “non-discrimination” and “gender equality” as guiding principles for the development and use of AI alongside transparency explainability and human oversight. Article 7(2) prohibits AI in healthcare from conditioning access to services on discriminatory criteria. Article 11(3) guarantees that AI in the workplace respects workers’ inviolable rights “without discrimination based on sex age ethnic origin religion sexual orientation.” Articles 14–15 confirm AI is supportive not substitutive safeguarding rights in public administration and justice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly removes AI-related actions pertaining to intelligence defense and national security from the purview of the law. The framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The law specifically states that 'non-discrimination' and 'gender equality' are important principles (Art. 3) that AI systems must offer transparency explainability and human oversight and that healthcare AI cannot restrict access to services based on discriminatory criteria (Art. 7). It ensures that AI respects workers' inviolable rights without discrimination (Art. 11). These principles collectively establish a clear legal requirement to prevent AI from spreading gender bias and discrimination.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The law requires human oversight and intervention in AI systems particularly in sensitive areas (Arts. 5-7 pp. 12-16) necessitates the designation of accountable personnel in charge of AI use and consequences (Art. 7 p. 15). Citizens have the right to human review and appeal of AI-based decisions (Article 9 pp. 18-19). Besides it restricts complete automation in vital areas such as justice healthcare and law enforcement (Arts. 6-7 pages. 13-15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly exclude the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security field so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The law mandates that AI systems must remain tools assisting human judgment rather than replacing it. Article 3 affirms respect for human autonomy and oversight while Articles 5–6 specify that AI must support not substitute decision-making in critical areas. Oversight and intervention mechanisms are required to ensure accountability and preserve meaningful human control (pp. 12–14).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Articles 6–7 explicitly prohibit full automation in sensitive areas such as law enforcement justice and healthcare. AI can be used to support activities like prevention or diagnosis but final decisions must rest with qualified professionals. This ensures ethical judgment and human intervention remain mandatory in critical domains (pp. 13–15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The law requires that entities deploying AI designate individuals responsible for oversight and accountability. Article 7 obliges organizations to appoint accountable persons who can intervene in and assume liability for AI-driven decisions guaranteeing clear human responsibility throughout the system lifecycle (p. 15).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: Art. 14 (p.9) requires public administrations to ensure citizens’ “knowledge of the functioning” of AI systems and the “traceability” of their use. It also mandates technical organisational and training measures to guarantee responsible use. These provisions establish transparency duties regarding how government AI operates ensuring that individuals are informed when administrative processes rely on AI tools.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The law sets broad principles: Art. 4 (p.3) requires clear simple information to users while ensuring protection of personal data and privacy. Art. 14 mandates transparency but also respects autonomy and legal responsibilities. However it does not define detailed criteria distinguishing publicly disclosable information from security-sensitive content.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: Art. 14 (p.9) requires public administrations to ensure citizens’ “knowledge of the functioning” of AI systems and the “traceability” of their use. Art. 4 (p.3) requires communications to be in “clear and simple language” ensuring understandable explanations of how AI affects individuals. Art. 7 similarly gives users a right to be informed of AI use in health.

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The law addresses AI procurement in Art. 5(d) (p. 4) requiring public e-procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions that ensure national data-center localisation disaster-recovery and business-continuity capabilities and high standards of security and transparency in training and development. It also mandates compliance with competition non-discrimination and proportionality principles in awarding AI contracts.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: Art. 5(d) instructs public e-procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions ensuring data localisation security disaster-recovery and transparency in training and development (p.4). These criteria introduce AI-specific ethical/technical considerations beyond traditional IT procurement but the law does not create full procurement guidelines or procedures.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: Art. 5(d) requires AI models to ensure “high standards of transparency in training and development methods” (p.4). This establishes a transparency expectation but does not require vendors to disclose training data model architecture or avoid black-box systems.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: Art. 5(d) directs procurement platforms to prioritise AI solutions where strategic data are processed in national data centres with disaster-recovery and continuity also located in Italy (p.4). This creates a sovereign procurement preference supporting national infrastructure and local AI providers.

items.title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
items.justification: The Strategy sets multiple actions to develop AI skills in the public sector. PA.1 (p.22) promotes awareness methodological guidance and understanding of AI risks. PA.3 (p.23) requires training staff in advanced AI-related technologies. PA.6 (pp.24–25) creates AI-focused upskilling programmes and postgraduate training within the National School of Administration and other PA training schools. The overview (p.21) highlights the need to build AI-specific competencies across the public administration.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) and National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: PA.1 (p. 22) establishes a government-wide approach to build AI awareness competencies and understanding of risks across the public administration. PA.6 (pp. 24–25) introduces national upskilling programmes and postgraduate AI training through the National School of Administration and PA training schools confirming a coordinated government-wide reskilling effort.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The implementation section creates coordination and governance structures and assigns responsibilities across PA bodies (p.21) and PA.1 (p. 22) promotes internal competence centers for AI guidance. However the Strategy does not establish specific “AI champion” roles such as Chief AI Officers or permanent expert teams in each department.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: PA.6 (pp.24–25) establishes continuous upskilling programmes and advanced training for civil servants to maintain AI-related competencies over time. PA.1 (p.22) also emphasizes ongoing awareness and capacity-building activities to keep pace with evolving AI risks tools and methodologies.

items.title: Italian Law on Artificial Intelligence Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025 — Provisions and delegations to the Government in matters of Artificial Intelligence
items.justification: The only indirect reference is in Article 15 which requires judicial authorities to understand AI systems used in justice but it does not mandate or outline training programs. There are no sections establishing AI-related training for public administration personnel
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: While still requiring adherence to constitutional rights Article 6 expressly excludes the framework of this law from developments in intelligence defense and national security fields so the framework is only applicable to civil applications but it is not applicable to the defense or security domains.

body.name: Future AI Research Foundation (Fondazione FAIR)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The law designates AgID and ACN as national authorities with supervisory and guidance roles on AI (Art. 20) and establishes the AI Observatory on Labour (Art. 12). These bodies act as institutional hubs supporting responsible AI governance. However the law does not create AI champions inside ministries or assign roles specifically responsible for fostering AI innovation within individual agencies.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Italian Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2024–2026
items.justification: The Strategy explicitly prioritises AI-related reskilling and upskilling. It states “no worker can be left behind” and “roll out a robust programme of incentives for reskilling and upskilling initiatives” (pp. 29). Action F.5 provides “training and professional development courses on AI to retrain and update workers’ skills” (pp. 33-34). Supply-chain academies offer structured reskilling  (p. 33). PA.6 mandates postgraduate AI training for public administration employees  (p. 24).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Department for Digital Transformation - Agency for Digital Italy (AgID) - FAIR Foundation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy explicitly commits to government-supported reskilling and upskilling. It states Italy will “roll out a robust programme of incentives for reskilling and upskilling” to retrain workers (p.30). Action F.5 mandates “training and professional development courses on AI to retrain and update workers’ skills” (p.33). Supply-chain academies funded via FSC support worker reskilling (p.34). FSC funds are the Development and Cohesion Fund an Italian national financial instrument that finances interventions to reduce economic social and territorial imbalances between different areas of the country. Originally known as FAS (Fund for Underutilised Areas) it works in conjunction with European Structural Funds to promote sustainable growth.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: Data Protection Act 2020 (Jamaica)
items.justification: Section 12 (“Rights in relation to automated decision-taking”) of Jamaica’s Data Protection Act (p. 22 approved in 2020 according https://oic.gov.jm/page/data-protection-act) establishes that individuals have the right not to be subject to decisions that significantly affect them when these are based solely on automated processing and it also entitles data subjects to request that such decisions be reconsidered or remade with human involvement
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Part V Exemption to Data Protection Standards or to Disclosure to Data Subject Requirements (p. 48) covers this. Section 33 (p. 48) deals with National Security. Section 33 (1) talks to exemptions for the purpose of national security.

body.name: Information Commissioner

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It includes limited safeguards related to automated decision-making and human accountability in section 12 (p 22). There it mentions explicitly human supervision of decisions related to “the individual’s performance at work creditworthiness reliability or conduct” so it covers critical areas. However it does not refer to “meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Data Protection Act 2020 (Jamaica)
items.justification: Section 6(2)(d) of the Data Protection Act 2020 (pg. 14) requires data controllers to inform data subjects of the logic involved in automated decision-making processes directly addressing explainability requirements. Section 12 (pg. 22) further reinforces transparency by entitling individuals to request reconsideration of automated decisions that significantly affect them ensuring data controllers must be accountable for the reasoning behind such decisions. Together these provisions establish a transparency and explainability framework applicable to automated processing in Jamaica.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Part V Exemption to Data Protection Standards  or to Disclosure to Data Subject Requirements (pg. 48) covers this. Section 33 (pg.48) deals with National Security. Section 33 (1) talks to exemptions for the purpose of national security.

body.name: Information Commissioner

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Section 6(2)(d) of the DPA 2020 (pg. 14) requires data controllers to inform individuals of the purpose and logic of automated decision-making upon request. Section 12 (pg. 22) further entitles individuals to request reconsideration of automated decisions significantly affecting them. However coverage is partial because transparency obligations are reactive rather than proactive require payment of a fee and don't explicitly address data sources or mandate public disclosure of how AI systems operate. The DPA doesn't require systematic publication of information about AI system design or functioning.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Section 12 of the DPA 2020 (pg. 22) entitles individuals to know when decisions significantly affecting them are based solely on automated processing and to request reconsideration with human involvement. Section 6(2)(d) (pg. 14) further requires data controllers to inform individuals of the logic involved in automated decision-making upon request. However coverage is partial because the DPA doesn't explicitly require organisations to provide detailed explanations of the specific factors or weightings that led to a particular outcome falling short of a full right to explanation as understood in AI governance standards.

items.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI at the primary and secondary education level (Japan)
items.justification: The Guidelines from the Ministry of Education Culture Sports Science and Technology (MEXT) stress that children should learn to use tools like generative AI [p.3]. They also define teachers’ roles: to use generative AI effectively in schools teachers must attain core AI literacy understanding how it works and its characteristics to build a foundation for appropriate classroom use [p.7]. In addition students should gain a scientific understanding of generative AI its operation societal effects and related laws systems and etiquette and learn to apply it to identify and solve problems [p.9].
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines outline the importance for children to master technologies such as generative AI as tools [p. 3] and the role of teachers stating that to effectively utilize generative AI in schools teachers are required to acquire a certain level of AI literacy such as understanding the mechanisms and characteristics of generative AI as this will also help to create the foundation for appropriate use in educational activities [p.7]. However there are no specific notes regarding curriculum reforms and it does not apply to the tertiary level.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines define the role of teachers: to effectively utilize generative AI in schools teachers are required to acquire a certain level of AI literacy understanding the mechanisms and characteristics of generative AI which helps build the foundation for appropriate use in educational activities [p.7]. They also state that the principles should be used as reference materials for teacher-training courses and for addressing issues when using generative AI as teaching content [p.19]. Boards of education are also expected to publicize and share precedents teaching materials and know-how and to leverage external resources such as teacher-training universities and service providers [p.21].

items.title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
items.justification: The White Paper treats AI-facilitated misinformation as a critical safety and governance concern. It highlights how generative AI can produce fake images videos and audio that enable fraud and undermine trust [p.16] and how such AI generated misinformation (especially during disasters and accidents) can become life-threatening [p.19]. It also warns of AI’s role in election interference and democratic disruption [p.19]. To counter this it urges legal measures for faster deletion of illegal content platform transparency literacy campaigns and public-private development of detection technologies [pp.20–21] linking misinformation control to preventing harm and maintaining public safety.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The White Paper includes measures to prevent AI from generating or spreading misinformation but does not mention hate speech harassment or violence explicitly. It notes safeguards against producing illegal or dangerous content such as weapons or terrorism-related material though “the model still struggles with malicious uses such as prompt injection” [p.19]. It further calls for government and platform action to speed up deletion of illegal AI-generated content and enhance transparency [p.20]. While these provisions address misinformation risks they do not extend to preventing hate speech or AI-enabled harassment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The White Paper urges “institutional arrangements” to speed deletion of illegal AI-generated content and to make platform operational status transparent [p.20]. It distinguishes appropriate governance for developers versus providers/users [p.17] and recommends minimum legal obligations on safety and transparency for high-risk AI cases [p.18]. It also promotes labeling/source attribution of AI-generated content to boost transparency of information [p.19].

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI at the primary and secondary education level (Japan)
items.justification: The guidelines adopt a human-centered rule: AI use must not violate fundamental human rights; humans make final decisions and bear responsibility [§2 Basic Concept – Human-centered principle p.7]. Student use must follow age restrictions and as needed parents’ understanding/consent [Key points for utilization p.19; Checklist p.25]. Students are instructed not to input personal information [p.19] and teachers check outputs for bias [p.19]. Transparency is required: cite AI use and inform parents of its purpose/nature [p.20]. Educators consider students’ developmental stage [Checklist p.25].
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines protect children’s data and privacy by teaching students not to enter personal information into AI tools [p.19] and ensuring educational information security [pp.21 22]. According to the Guidelines the use of Generative AI must also respect age limits and potentially require teacher supervision and/or parents’ prior understanding [p.19].

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: While the guidelines place some obligations on deployers (schools/boards) to ensure safe and age-appropriate use [p.19] and gives recommendations for handling personal data of the students [p.21] they do not assign any design duties to developers.

items.title: Governance Guidelines for Implementation of AI Principles Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
items.justification: The Guidelines recommend to AI system developers to take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of the team when developing AI systems to ensure that the diversities found in Japan are also well recognized in the discussion [p.26; 69-71].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines recommend that AI system developers take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems to ensure that the diversities found in Japan are also well recognized in the discussion [p.26; 69-71]. This also includes specific recommendations for AI developers such as using specific data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a highly diverse team when screening for diversity and sensitivity in AI outputs [pp. 70-72].

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines recommend that AI system developers take cultural differences into account and increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems to ensure that the AI outputs will entrench/impair any unfair discrimination based on certain social attributes [pp.71-72]. To be more specific AI developers are requested to use data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a diverse team screen outputs of the AI for diversity and sensitivity [pp. 70-72].

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines do recommend that AI system developers increase the diversity of their team when developing AI systems [p.71]. Specifically AI developers are requested to use data sets that avoid unfair discrimination and utilizing a diverse team screen outputs of the AI for diversity and sensitivity [pp. 70-72]. Furthermore the Guidelines stipulate that AI systems intended for provision to other countries and regions should be designed with due consideration for local regulations customs and cultural factors ensuring appropriate functionality and adaptability across contexts.

items.title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
items.justification: The Guidelines emphasizes that the development and expansion of more advanced AI is a significant impact on the environment due to the large amounts of electricity required [p.27]. Evaluation point 11 of the Procurement Check Sheet (Appendix 3) [p.62 of the PDF] explicitly states providing or using a generative AI system that considers environmental impact; for example by using models trained on hardware featuring energy-efficient semiconductors. It lists Documentation that clarifies superior environmental performance in terms of power consumption etc. as examples for supporting this goal.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines only specifically address measures and best practices for reducing power-consumption by using energy-efficient technology (see Evaluation Viewpoint 11) but nothing related to e-waste.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
thematicElements.justification: Under 'Developing and providing environmentally conscious generative AI systems' the guidelines recommend supporting measures like documentation that clarifies superior environmental performance in terms of power consumption etc. see Evaluation point 11 of the Procurement Check Sheet (Appendix 3) [p.62 of the PDF].

thematicElements.text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
items.justification: The Guidelines promote fairness by promoting the elimination of harmful bias/discrimination tied to protected traits and respecting human rights and cultural diversity [pp. 16 23].They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17].

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines state that during the development provision or use of an AI system or service it is important that each AI business actor makes efforts to eliminate unfair and harmful bias and discrimination against any specific individuals or groups based on race gender national origin age political opinion religion and so forth [p.16]. Based on the fact that biases which that results in unreasonable disadvantage to specific individuals or groups which cannot be rationally explained cannot be completely eliminated from the process of training data the Guidelines suggest to make sure AI models are trained with properly represented data sets and check AI systems assume no bias [p.28].

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: They require bias controls across the lifecycle of AI systems (data models/algorithms prompts and external services) to prevent unfair outcomes [p.23]. They also call for timely human intervention to mitigate automation bias and correct unfair results [p.17]. These obligations are explicitly extended to AI Developers Providers and AI Business users [p.23].

items.title: New Female Digital Talent Development Plan (Japan)
items.justification: The plan links gender equality to AI by noting how AI is reshaping daily life and work making AI skills essential for workers [pp. 2 4] and emphasizing women’s acquisition of AI/cloud skills to raise productivity and deliver services [p.4]. It also notes AI tools’ rapid spread and the need for women to keep skills updated [pp. 2 4]; and pairing this with measures that promote women’s economic independence and career advancement via digital upskilling pathways and targets for women’s leadership (30% executives by 2030) [p.3].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Economy Trade and Industry (METI) Gender Equality Bureau Cabinet Office (translated as Headquarters for Promoting Gender Equality)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: The plan explicitly promotes increasing women’s participation in the AI and digital workforce.
