It expands education-training benefits to include courses on “digital skills including AI” [p.6] encourages companies to update women’s AI/cloud skills [p.2] and links these initiatives to the national goal of 30% women in leadership positions by around 2030 [p.3].

items.title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
items.justification: The guidelines emphasize the necessity of having timely human intervention rather than letting AI make decisions alone and also advocate for implementing measures to protect human judgement from AI influence [pp.1517].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: While the guidelines emphasize the necessity of having controllability and timely human intervention rather than letting AI make decisions alone advocate for implementing measures to protect human judgement from AI influence [pp.1517] and state the importance of AI being a tool to the human [p.11] they do not specifically refer to any critical areas but more so do so in a general manner.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: While the guidelines emphasize the need for timely human interventions rather than letting AI make the decisions alone [p.17] they do not highlight any specific sensitive sectors.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines state that when developing providing or using an AI system or service it is important that each AI business actor executes its accountability to stakeholders within reasonable extent [p.19] and recommend to appoint someone as the person responsible for executing its accountability in each AI business actor [p.20]. However they do not assign any specific obligations for oversight and intervention.

items.title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
items.justification: The White Paper states that “the basis of Japan’s strategy is to continuously assess and reduce risks” [p.18]. It calls for ongoing updates in response to technological and business changes and close cooperation between government and industry to promote risk reduction [p.18]. To address serious risks the government should consider reviewing existing laws and regulations [p.19] and promote preventive measures [p.20]. It also emphasizes Sharing advanced use-cases of AI and quantitative and qualitative impacts in public and private sectors [p.9] and developing internationally consistent safety evaluation and red-teaming methods including checking tools and test implementation methods [pp.20–21].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The White Paper promotes a proactive approach to AI risk management by requiring businesses to “voluntarily and continuously assess and reduce risks” and to “update measures in response to changes in technology and business” [p.18]. It also calls for cooperation between government and industry and emphasizes internationally consistent evaluation methods and testing for AI safety [pp.20-21]. Moreover in areas where AI malfunctions or systemic risks could have significant consequences - such as the negative impact of AI on elections - the government is asked to review existing laws and encourage preventive measures [p.19-20]. However it does not explicitly require pre-deployment evaluation of societal ethical or environmental impacts.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The White Paper instructs businesses to “voluntarily and continuously assess and reduce risks” associated with AI and to regularly update these measures as technology and business environments evolve [p.18] and emphasizes collaboration between government and industry to ensure effective risk mitigation and highlights the need for consistent evaluation methods and testing including red-teaming to enhance AI safety [pp.20-21]. While these provisions certainly promote ongoing assessment and mitigation they stop short of assigning any kind of specific obligations to developers or users to conduct comprehensive impact assessments covering risks to individuals or society it is again more of an abstract assessment than formal obligation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
items.justification: These Guidelines are intended for gov. staff involved in procurement and use of GenAI [p. 6] and are organized around evaluation viewpoints (EV) that function as a practical checklist. Within this framework the they suggest optional requirements such as enabling reasonable disclosure or information-sharing by planners or providers to ensure that relevant prompts or system parameters are not concealed (EV8 having technical measures or documentation in place that allow end users to distinguish AI-generated outputs from human-generated information (EV13) and emphasize the need for management and oversight mechanisms that allow the system’s overview origins and operations to be verified through logs and technical specifications (EV21).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: While the Guidelines note the importance of having managements in place to ensure that the overview origins and operations of the system model and data can be verified from logs and technical specifications etc. (Evaluation Viewpoint 21) they do not suggest the establishment of a public registry/inventory meaning that those logs are just for internal assessment and verifiability.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines suggest as an optional requirement to be able to provide disclosure or share information to the planner to a reasonable extent in order to make sure that parts of the prompts or parameters entered into generative AI systems are not concealed. (Evaluation Viewpoint 8) and having technology or documentation in place to that provides mechanisms for end users to distinguish outputs by generative AI systems from information output by humans (Evaluation Viewpoint 13).

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines suggest to be able to provide disclosure or share information to the planner to a reasonable extent in order to make sure that parts of the prompts or parameters entered into generative AI systems are not concealed (Evaluation Viewpoint 8). The 'reasonable extent' note most likely contains privacy and safety considerations but there is no clear outlining of such.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines recommend having technology or documentation in place that provides mechanisms for end users to distinguish outputs by generative AI systems from information output by humans (Evaluation Viewpoint 13). This is due to concerns about the manipulation of information and public opinion through the dissemination of misinformation and deepfakes generated by AI [p.26]. However there are no specific provisions regarding a clear and accessible explanation on any specifics regarding how AI system works nor the terminology used in doing so.

items.title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
items.justification: The Guidelines emphasize the need for all individuals involved in the procurement of generative AI within each ministry or agency  understanding both the benefits and risks of generative AI and measures for mitigating the risks associated with generative AI [p.10]. It also notes the importance of Identifying and disseminating best practices for the procurement [p.17] checks on procurements [p. 19] and comply with laws regulations and guidelines related to government information systems when procuring generative AI [p.29]. They also recommend utilizing a 'Procurement Check Sheet' to organize the requirements for procuring generative AI systems [pp.36 39].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p. 6].

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes AI-specific procurement through detailed AI-tailored requirements set out in the 'Procurement Check Sheet' and 'Contract Check Sheet'  [pp.36–39]. They require procurement specifications to address points unique to Gen AI including AI governance of suppliers appropriate input/output and data handling prevention of false or harmful outputs protection of personal data transparency and explainability security and safeguards for public-use cases (e.g. disclosure). Procurement requirements are structured as mandatory “Basic Requirements” and optional requirements and are complemented by contract-level provisions on quality assurance embedding responsible AI considerations directly into procurement practice.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: The Guideline for Japanese Governments’ Procurements and Utilizations of Generative AI for the sake of Evolution and Innovation of Public Administration
items.justification: The Guideline addresses Public Sector Skills Development by requiring systematic training and literacy-building for government staff. It mandates education on responding to information-security incidents and risk cases specific to generative AI systems (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and requires role-tailored training to ensure appropriate literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics for personnel involved in development and operation of generative AI (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 further highlights education reskilling and stakeholder support as central components of ensuring AI literacy within the public sector [p.31].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The guideline does not apply to government information systems handling confidential information related to national security the maintenance of public safety and order as well as information that may potentially become confidential [p.6].

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The Guideline mandates several training-related measures but does not form a unified government-wide upskilling strategy nor does it include the judiciary. The Chief AI Officer must conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff [p.19] and provide sessions on input data and hallucinations [p.34]. It requires education on information-security incidents and generative-AI-specific risk cases (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and role-specific literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 highlights AI literacy education reskilling and stakeholder support [p.31].

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The Guideline assigns a dedicated role within each ministry or agency the Chief AI Officer (CAIO) to act as the central authority for AI governance. The CAIO is mandated to promote generative AI utilization monitor systems ensure risk management handle risk cases and conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff [p.19]. The CAIO also formulates and revises internal rules disseminates the guideline and delivers training sessions on issues such as input data and hallucinations [pp. 33 34]. These responsibilities position the CAIO as an AI champion providing expert guidance and supporting responsible AI innovation across government.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document includes multiple provisions that support ongoing professional development and continued training. It requires the Chief AI Officer to conduct trainings to enhance AI literacy among government staff and provide updated guidance on issues such as input data and hallucinations [p.19 p.34]. It mandates education and training on responding to information-security incidents and risk cases specific to generative AI (Evaluation Viewpoint 4) and role-tailored training ensuring literacy technical knowledge risk awareness and ethics (Evaluation Viewpoint 5). Guiding Principle 8 further emphasizes education literacy and reskilling [p.31] reinforcing the need for continuous skill development.

items.title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
items.justification: The Guidelines note that AI use can be viewed as a solution to some social challenges such as decreasing labor caused by a declining birthrate and aging population [p. 2]. Consequently the Guidelines prognose that work tasks will vastly change due to AI and advocates to take the necessary steps to ensure that the persons engaged in AI in each AI business actor acquire AI literacy [pp. 21 23] to discuss actively about education and reskilling to promote new ways of working [p. 21 23] and provide educational opportunities so that various people can acquire a deeper understanding of benefits of AI [p. 21].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: While the guidelines advocate to take the necessary steps to ensure that the persons engaged in AI in each AI business actor acquire AI literacy [pp. 21 23] to discuss actively about education and reskilling to promote new ways of working [p. 21 23] and provide educational opportunities so that various people can acquire a deeper understanding of benefits of AI [p. 21] they do not include any specific establishments of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs but instead keep it vague and open-ended how these 'necessary steps' should look.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: Among the Common Guiding Principles for AI Business actors involved in advanced AI systems [p. 24] the Guidelines outlines the importance to provide support for the improvement of literacy [p. 25] and to support digital literacy initiatives [p. 32]. Each AI business actor is expected to provide the persons engaged in AI in the AI business actor with the necessary education to gain the knowledge literacy and ethical views to correctly understand and use AI in a socially correct manner [p. 21]. However all of these are just recommendations not actual requirements and they are not intended to mitigate job displacement caused by automation but  rather remedy decreasing labor caused by a declining birthrate and aging population [p. 2].

items.title: AI White Paper 2024 New Strategies in Stage II Toward the world's most AI-friendly country (Japan)
items.justification: The white paper highlights AI safety and security as central to Japan’s balanced governance approach. It promotes voluntary risk assessment and reduction complemented by minimal regulatory measures for high-risk systems [p.18]. To strengthen safety infrastructure it proposes enhancing the role of the AI Safety Institute (AISI) in evaluation red-teaming and international collaboration [pp.20-21]. Further emphasis is placed on research into AI vulnerabilities and the creation of a secure data environment that fosters responsible innovation [p.21].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Safety Institute (AISI)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document recommends ensuring AI safety and reliability through evaluation methods with international consistency and the activities of the AI Safety Institute (AISI) including “checking tools and red-teaming test implementation methods” [p.21]. However it does not specify concrete performance thresholds or quantitative quality benchmarks for AI systems. The focus is seemingly more on establishing frameworks and procedures for ongoing assessment rather than defining fixed operational standards.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: While the document notes the importance of addressing systemic risks in critical sectors such as finance medicine and transport where AI malfunctions could have severe impacts [p.16] and recommends that the government review existing laws and regulations in such areas [p.19] t does not explicitly mention safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols as concrete mechanisms to mitigate harm from AI failure aside from the safeguard of clearly indicating whether content has been AI-generated or not [p.19] but this is more a measure against misinformation than failure or unexpected AI behaviour.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The document refers to the need for AI safety evaluation methods and recommends that the AI Safety Institute (AISI) conduct “investigations standards etc. necessary for AI safety assessment including checking tools and red-teaming test implementation methods” [p.21].  However there is no explicit requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation throughout the entire AI system lifecycle. The focus remains on general safety assurance and ongoing evaluation.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly identifies risks of malicious attacks such as data poisoning and cyberattacks as major AI-related threats [p.16] and recommends actions to counter them. It calls for R&D on exploitation of AI vulnerabilities and on technologies to defend against attacks embedding vulnerabilities in AI [p.21]. It also urges cooperation between public and private sectors to strengthen cybersecurity expertise and international collaboration through the AI Safety Institute (AISI) [p.21] thereby introducing clear security-oriented obligations and measures.

items.title: AI Guidelines for Business Ver. 1.1 (Japan)
items.justification: The guidelines outline the importance that each AI business actor provides stakeholders with information to the reasonable extent necessary In order to ensure verifiability relating to decisions made by AI [pp.18 23]. They also recommend to establish a situation that allows the origin of data and decisions made during the development provision or use of the AI system or service to be traced forward and backward to the extent that is reasonable and technically possible [p.19] and improving explainability and interpretability for relevant stakeholders [pp.19 23].
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines state that when developing providing or using an AI system or service based on the social context when the AI system or service is used it is important that each AI business actor provides all stakeholders with information to the reasonable extent necessary and technically possible while ensuring the verifiability of the AI system or service [p.18]. To that end they recommend that in order to ensure verifiability relating to decisions made by AI record or store logs of AI training processes inference processes rationales of decisions made by AI and the like (for example input/output generated when developing and using the AI system or service) to the extent possible based on the data amount or contents [pp.18 23].

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: While the Guidelines provide some specific measures and objectives to entities developing and using AI (AI Developer AI Provider and AI Business User [p.23]) such as ensuring verifiability and improving traceability via  Documentation of system architectures and the like or  Providing relevant stakeholders with information [pp. 18 19 23] these recommendations are meant as general guidance for Businesses involved in AI but are not specifically highlighted for any high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
items.justification: The Strategy addresses AI Literacy in pages 15 to 17 (First Objective: Building Capacities and Developing Jordanian Skills). Mainly in subsections on Raising Awareness Education and Digital Literacy. and the Integration of AI topics into school university and vocational curricula (p. 17).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The First Strategic Objective – Building Capacities and Developing Jordanian Skills (pages 15–17) explicitly calls for integrating AI concepts and digital literacy into school university and vocational curricula promoting early exposure to AI education and alignment with future labour-market needs.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy mentions on page 15 'Initiative to develop specialization in artificial intelligence at universities' and the 'Elaboration of professional and technical training programs in the field of artificial intelligence'. It also encourages AI-related programs in universities and technical institutes and partnerships with academia (page 17) .

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
items.justification: The Code of Ethics explicitly integrates access to redress and remedy under Section 5 (Responsibility and Accountability p. 19). It requires all parties developing or operating AI systems to provide affected individuals with simple accessible and prompt complaint mechanisms (point 2) and to address and correct any negative effects or harms caused by AI systems including serious material or moral damage (point 4). These provisions align with non-judicial redress and remedial accountability principles.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Page 19 (Section 5 points 2 & 4) calls on entities developing or operating AI systems to provide accessible uncomplicated complaint channels for affected individuals and to address and correct harms caused by AI.

items.title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
items.justification: In the Inclusiveness and Justice section on page 14 the Code emphasizes on 'ensuring the fairness of artificial intelligence techniques and not to be biased discriminated or targeted against any group or component of society''.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Inclusiveness and Justice section on page 14 explicitly states that it is 'Ensuring respect protection and promotion of diversity inclusiveness and impartiality in all stages of development [...] where bias is the favoritism that results from AI systems due to the use of incomplete erroneous or biased data sets or that results from individuals who design and/or train artificial intelligence systems by creating algorithms that reflect intended cognitive biases or factual biases resulting from social intolerance or institutional discrimination. Bias can enter through: building the system collecting data or preparing a set of data governed by certain features or analyzing or treating it in a discriminatory manner.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Section Inclusiveness and Justice on page 14 explicitly states 'Working on ensuring the fairness of artificial intelligence techniques and not to be biased discriminated or targeted against any group or component of society'. While the section about Risks on page 29 states against 'Marginalization of some groups and bias towards certain groups at the expense of others or the marketing of some negative extremist and violent ideas'.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: Not entirely but partially since the Code states on page 31 that it is 'Encouraging developers and researchers in the field of artificial intelligence to determine the benefits and risks of dealing with developed systems through the available means as a prototype work that shows how this Code of ethics was used for guidance and the principles contained therein are applied'. It indirectly (or rather broadly) implies it.

items.title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
items.justification: The National AI Code of Ethics addresses Gender Equality only in a limited and indirect manner. On page 9 the document states that AI systems should ensure inclusiveness and impartiality by avoiding bias linked to specific data categories explicitly including gender alongside race and religion. However the framework does not contain gender-specific objectives measures or implementation mechanisms. As such Gender Equality is acknowledged at the level of bias prevention rather than addressed as a standalone or substantive policy area.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: In the Code of Ethics the Legal Reference explicitly lists fairness and impartiality in AI decision-making 'by focusing on data related to color race religion or gender' alongside transparency and privacy protection. (page 9) Under Inclusiveness and Justice the Code requires AI to be inclusive fair transparent and impartial across all stages of development and use. (page 14) Hence the Code ethically expects prevention of gender bias/discrimination thought it frames these as principles rather than audited sanctionable duties.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
items.justification: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) addresses it in the Humanity and Society section on page 13 emphasizing that AI must respect human dignity role and status in society by “not forcing humans to submit to artificial intelligence decisions without granting AI the right of human intervention.” This principle underscores that humans retain ultimate control and decision-making authority over AI systems ensuring accountability and preventing full automation of judgment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) explicitly promotes meaningful human control. On page 13 it calls for preserving “human dignity role and status… without forcing humans to submit to AI decisions.” On page 28 it cautions against “believing that AI is superior to humans… and relying on it to make decisions absolutely without interpreting outputs in proportion to the circumstances and general context.” However the document does not define critical areas establish mandatory human-in-the-loop requirements or provide procedural safeguards or enforcement mechanisms. Human control is articulated normatively rather than operationalized through concrete measures.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: AI Regulatory Framework for the banking sector (2025) (Jordan)
items.justification: The AI Regulatory Framework for the Jordanian Banking Sector (CBJ 2024) mandates banks to conduct AI-specific impact assessments prior to system deployment (Sec. 2.4 & 6.1–6.2). Institutions must evaluate ethical operational and cybersecurity risks document decision-making logic and maintain a centralised AI-incident log. These assessments feed into the CBJ’s supervisory reviews through FinCERT and compliance audits ensuring that AI applications undergo structured risk evaluation human oversight and accountability throughout their lifecycle to prevent harm and ensure transparency.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework promotes risk management and risk assessment (p.6 21) and limiting potential risks (p.5). 'An organization is required to conduct periodic impact assessments of artificial intelligence techniques in proportion to the level of risk arranged for each application to assess privacy risks the likelihood of bias or any deviation from the objectives of intended use' (p.13).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The framework mandates institutions to conduct periodic impact assessments of AI (p. 13): 'in proportion to the level of risk arranged for each application to assess privacy risks the likelihood of bias or any deviation from the objectives of intended use. High-risk artificial intelligence applications should be subject to the reviews of AAC-Kra and Mu-kr to ensure that they are carried out in a responsible and consistent manner'.  Furthermore AI systems should comply with all regulations guidelines frameworks and circulars applying to the sector as well as the data protection law (p.14). However risks for individuals and the society to be mitigated are not listed.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
items.justification: The framework addresses the indicator by explicitly recognising the risk that AI adoption may “lead to the loss of traditional jobs” and proposing mitigation measures such as workforce retraining and rehabilitation (p. 31). It further establishes the principle that AI systems should act as “a complement to the existing workforce not a replacement for it” (p. 7) thereby directly framing AI deployment in relation to labour protection. By acknowledging displacement risks and outlining concrete measures to address them the strategy goes beyond a purely economic focus and aligns with the indicator’s inclusion of protection against job loss due to automation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) and National Council for Entrepreneurship

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems

Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Jordan Artificial Intelligence Policy 2020
items.justification: The framework addresses the indicator by explicitly identifying public procurement as a key mechanism for AI adoption stating that “government’s procurement mechanisms are the main drivers to adopt smart solutions in the public sector” and calling for a review of procurement legislation to facilitate this (p. 6). It further outlines concrete priorities for shaping this process including the promotion of open-source solutions and the empowerment of Jordanian entrepreneurs and start-ups as suppliers of AI systems (p. 6).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Ministerial Committee for AI (the Committee)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
items.justification: The Jordan AI Strategy (2023–2027) prioritizes capacity building under its First Objective (pp. 15–18) outlining initiatives to train civil servants through awareness programs technical and professional AI training and the establishment of professional standards. It also highlights education and digital literacy development across levels. Additionally the Third Axis: Data and Skills (p. 29) emphasizes training public sector cadres to enhance performance and innovation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy sets a government-wide framework for upskilling public servants through awareness workshops technical training and education reform (pp. 15–18 29) but does not include the judiciary. It builds foundational understanding of AI’s applications and risks for civil service only not judges or courts.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
items.justification: In the Strategy page 18 (Capacity Building and Upgrading Skills and Competencies) and page 30 (Risk Management). The first explicitly highlights a focus on specialized training programs for graduates and workers to build AI-relevant technical skills (p. 18). While the Risk management requires “modernization and rehabilitation projects to pave the way for employees to change their work area” (p. 30).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) and the National Council for Entrepreneurship

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The  Risk Management (pages 30–31) emphasize preparing the workforce for AI-driven market changes through reskilling and rehabilitation programs and modernization projects to help employees shift work areas. However the Strategy does not specify government funding or subsidies for these programs.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Jordan's Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan 2023 - 2027
items.justification: The Jordan Artificial Intelligence Strategy and Implementation Plan (2023–2027) addresses AI safety and security mainly under Objective Four: Ensuring a legislative and regulatory environment that supports the safe deployment of AI (page 21) and Risk Management (page 30 & 31). It mandates continuous review of laws to manage risks protect privacy and strengthen public trust. It promotes adherence to the National AI Code of Ethics includes cybersecurity measures and requires safeguards to prevent misuse and ensure reliable explainable and safe AI applications.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Economy and Entrepreneurship (MoDEE) National Council for Entrepreneurship and a Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Cybersecurity is recognized as a priority sector (pages 22 & 23) and referenced in Risk Management (pages 30–31) which calls for preventing data breaches ensuring privacy and updating cybercrime and cybersecurity laws. However these are broad policy aims not direct obligations for AI developers or operators.

items.title: The National Artificial Intelligence Code of Ethics (Jordan)
items.justification: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) explicitly addresses Transparency and Explainability across several sections. Page 9 lists Transparency among the key legal references guiding the Code. A full section on Transparency appears on page 18 detailing requirements for clarity explainability and disclosure in AI systems. On page 24 the principles for virtual environments emphasize responsibility transparency and integrity. On page 27 under Ethics of Scientific Research it mandates structural transparency in data flow and results.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) partially addresses this provision. Page 18 (Transparency section) promotes clarity on AI system purpose data sources and explainability requiring disclosure of how systems function and the rationale behind their outcomes to foster trust. However while it emphasizes transparency and user understanding it does not detail mechanisms for continuous disclosure or the full decision-making logic of AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The Jordan National AI Code of Ethics (2022) (p. 13) states that humans must not be forced to submit to AI decisions without the right to intervene aligning with the spirit of human oversight and contestability. Combined with the Transparency principle (p. 18) it implies a right to question AI outcomes. Yet it does not explicitly grant or operationalize an individual right to receive detailed explanations or the reasoning behind decisions.

items.title: Conceptual Framework for the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the System of Secondary Technical and Vocational and Post-Secondary Education for 2025–2029
items.justification: The Concept treats AI literacy as a foundational competence for both learners and teachers. For learners AI literacy is embedded in formal curricula through Digital Literacy and Informatics covering AI concepts ethics data protection and algorithmic thinking (Chapter 1.2) and conceptualised as a basic skill comparable to reading and writing under Priority 1: Educational Content (Chapter 3.1) including extracurricular programmes and partnerships. Teacher AI literacy is addressed through the development of AI competencies aligned with UNESCO frameworks (Chapter 1.4) and a structured professional development model (Chapter 3.3). Learners’ AI literacy proficiency is formally monitored within the evaluation framework (Chapter 4.3).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: JSC Taldau designated as the body responsible for coordinating monitoring and evaluation of the Concept (Chapter 42) Ybyray Altynsarin National Academy of Education responsible for methodological support development of the Open Methodological Complex AI ethics guidance and implementation of Priority 5 (Chapters 32 and 35) JSC National Centre for Professional Development rleu (NCPC rleu) responsible for teacher professional development and AI competency training (Chapters 14 and 33)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The framework includes explicit curriculum reforms across multiple education levels. It mandates the integration of AI-related content into formal curricula through Digital Literacy (introduced from grade 1) and Informatics (Chapter 1.2). For secondary education it details staged age-appropriate AI learning and expansion of subject content (Chapter 1.2; Chapter 3.1 – Priority 1: Educational Content). For tertiary-level pathways it addresses technical and vocational and post-secondary education granting institutions autonomy to embed AI within general basic and professional modules aligned with labour-market needs (Chapter 1.2). These reforms are operationalised through an implementation mechanism and monitored (Chapters 3 and 4).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The framework mandates inclusion and expansion of AI content in formal curricula (e.g. Digital Literacy and Informatics) and the planned introduction of AI modules ensuring structured AI learning pathways (Chapter 1.2; Chapter 3.1). It further establishes institutional mechanisms and programmes to support AI education including the creation of AI Labs within the national education infrastructure to pilot AI tools and develop teaching resources (Chapter 3.4 – Research and Innovation). In addition it outlines formal teacher training and certification programmes (Chapter 3.3).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The framework addresses teachers’ AI competencies and training needs (Chapter 1.4 – Digital Competencies of Teachers) and establishes a structured professional development pathway aligned with international standards (Chapter 3.3 – Priority 3: Professional Development of Teachers) including staged training (Acquire–Deepen–Create) certification and continuous learning. It also provides methodological resources through the development of an Open Methodological Complex offering lesson scenarios practical assignments ethical guidance and AI-safe materials (Chapter 3.2 – Priority 2: Methodological Support for Teachers).

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law explicitly addresses the risks of AI-facilitated misinformation and manipulation through synthetic content. Article 1(4) defines “synthetic results of AI systems” as images videos audio text or combinations that imitate people or events that did not occur. Article 17(3) prohibits the creation and use of AI systems that:- Use manipulative methods to distort individual behavior to cause or threaten harm.  - Classify individuals based on behavior or traits for discriminatory purposes. - Generate or distribute content prohibited by Kazakh law. These clauses directly regulate the creation and spread of deceptive AI-generated content and behaviors linked to misinformation and social manipulation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) only indirectly addresses prevention. Article 17(3) prohibits AI systems that:- Exploit emotional vulnerability to cause harm;- Conduct profiling that could result in discrimination;- Create or distribute synthetic outputs (e.g. text video audio) if their content is prohibited under Kazakhstan law. Article 21(2)–(3) requires synthetic AI results to be marked and accompanied by warnings with responsibility placed on owners/holders.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) contains limited but relevant provisions. Article 17(3)(1) prohibits AI systems that use manipulative methods to distort behaviour or force individuals to make decisions that may cause harm or create a threat of harm which is directly relevant to tech-facilitated violence. Article 18(2) requires owners or holders to take immediate measures including suspension or termination when such risks are identified. Article 7(2) provides procedural safeguards through transparency and objection rights and Articles 8(2) and 24 establish accountability and compensation for harm under existing law.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law addresses redress and remedy indirectly. Article 24 provides that harm caused by AI systems shall be compensated in accordance with the Civil Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan establishing a general pathway for redress.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” affirms users’ rights to object to automated processing and request explanations (Articles 7 and 16) and states that AI system owners are legally responsible for harms caused by their systems. Article 24 provides that harm caused by AI systems shall be compensated in accordance with the Civil Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan enabling individuals or groups to seek judicial redress.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Conceptual Framework for the Implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the System of Secondary Technical and Vocational and Post-Secondary Education for 2025–2029
items.justification: The framework embeds children’s rights as a core condition for the use of AI in education. The Mission statement requires AI to be used in the best interests of the learner prioritising the rights of the child and the role of the teacher (Introduction). Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of protecting the rights of the child and pedagogical responsibility requiring human oversight in significant decisions safeguarding dignity and safety and guaranteeing the right to appeal. The same chapter mandates privacy and personal data protection and prohibits discrimination ensuring inclusiveness for learners with special educational needs. Chapter 2.2 reinforces children’s autonomy via academic integrity.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: JSC Taldau designated as the body responsible for coordinating monitoring and evaluation of the Concept (Chapter 42) Ybyray Altynsarin National Academy of Education responsible for methodological support development of the Open Methodological Complex AI ethics guidance and implementation of Priority 5 (Chapters 32 and 35) JSC National Centre for Professional Development rleu (NCPC rleu) responsible for teacher professional development and AI competency training (Chapters 14 and 33)

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: While the measures are not child-exclusive in technical detail they are clearly applied to children as the primary rights-holders in educational AI systems. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of legality and personal data protection requiring lawful processing data minimisation limited retention and appropriate security measures for educational data. It also links AI use to enhanced safeguards and human oversight in education contexts. These protections are reinforced by transparency and accountability requirements including clear rules for AI use and oversight (Chapter 2.1) and by monitoring compliance with ethical norms within the Monitoring and Evaluation framework (Chapter 4.2-4.3).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The document includes general safeguards aimed at preventing harm to children from AI but it does not explicitly address all risks such as targeted advertising or commercial exploitation. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) establishes the principle of protecting the rights of the child and pedagogical responsibility requiring human oversight safeguarding learners’ dignity and safety and prohibiting discriminatory or harmful AI use. Chapter 2.2 (Pedagogical Principles) further limits inappropriate use by requiring age-appropriate application academic integrity and ensuring AI does not replace independent thinking. Transparency and mandatory labelling of AI-generated content also reduce risks of manipulation (Chapter 2.1).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: The framework  assigns certain obligations to deployers but it does not comprehensively regulate AI developers in a child-specific design sense. Chapter 2.1 (Ethical and Legal Principles) requires AI systems used in education to comply with fairness non-discrimination transparency data protection and human oversight explicitly linked to protecting the rights of the child. Chapter 2.2 (Pedagogical Principles) mandates age-appropriate use of AI and prohibits replacing learners’ independent thinking placing responsibility on those deploying AI in schools. Also Chapter 2.3 (Technological and Administrative Principles) introduces a risk-based approach and requires that only AI systems listed in a trusted registry may be used in schools.

items.title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence for 2024-2029 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 592 of 24 July 2024)
items.justification: The Concept actively promotes cultural and linguistic diversity by prioritizing AI tools that strengthen the Kazakh language. In Section 5 Chapter 2 Direction 4 (Scientific Research and AI Technologies) it mandates the development of the Kazakh Large Language Model (KazLLM) and expansion of Kazakh-language tokens and semantic units. It also supports the multilingual AI translator Tilmas covering Kazakh Russian English Turkish Tatar and Uzbek and the creation of Kazakh text-to-speech technologies ensuring AI systems function across languages and cultural contexts.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry (MDDIAI) Sectoral Council on AI Development and the Committee for AI and Innovation Development within the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The Concept contains explicit measures promoting AI systems that support cultural and linguistic diversity. In Section 5 Chapter 2 Direction 4 (Scientific Research and AI Technologies) it mandates the creation of the Kazakh Large Language Model (KazLLM) to expand AI capabilities in the national language including increasing Kazakh-language tokens and semantic units. It also supports the multilingual AI translator Tilmas (Kazakh Russian English Turkish Tatar Uzbek) and development of Kazakh text-to-speech technologies ensuring AI tools are responsive to diverse languages and cultural contexts.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (September 2025) includes limited but explicit references to environmental impact. Article 8.3 states that the creation and operation of AI systems must account for energy efficiency and aim to reduce negative environmental impact. Article 18.1–2 outlines AI risk management obligations (that could include environmental risks based on Article 8.3) requiring system owners to regularly assess and update risk mitigation measures across the AI lifecycle. While these provisions are general they reflect an emerging legal acknowledgment that AI development must consider sustainability and ecological safety.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (September 2025) addresses environmental concerns but does so only in general terms: Article 8.3 requires that during the development and operation of AI systems actors must ensure energy efficiency and minimize environmental harm. However the law does not explicitly mention the prevention of excessive energy consumption e-waste or regulation of resource-intensive AI models.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The draft AI law embeds fairness and non-discrimination as core legal principles. Article 6 (Fairness and Equality) requires that AI systems respect human dignity and rights and prohibits discrimination based on race nationality language religion beliefs or other status. Article 17(3) bans the creation or use of AI systems that classify individuals based on biometric data (e.g. to infer race religion political views) for discriminatory purposes.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (2025) promotes fairness by prohibiting discrimination based on language nationality race religion and other traits (Article 6). Article 4 establishes fairness and equality as a core principle of AI regulation. It also bans AI systems that classify individuals by biometric data for discriminatory purposes as well as systems exploiting vulnerabilities related to age disability or social status (Article 17(3)). Article 10(2) and Article 20 require the use and audit of high-quality lawful and representative datasets indirectly addressing bias risks in AI outputs.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Article 17(3) expressly prohibits AI systems that classify individuals using biometric data to infer race political views religious affiliation or similar characteristics for discriminatory purposes as well as systems exploiting vulnerabilities linked to age disability or social status. Article 6 (Fairness and Equality) mandates that AI systems be created and operated in a manner that excludes discrimination. Article 10(2) requires the use of high-quality and representative datasets while Article 20 mandates audits assessing data quality and lawfulness helping reduce bias embedded in training data.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: Article 6 requires AI systems to respect citizens' rights ensure fairness and equality and prohibit discrimination based on sex and other characteristics. Article 4 lists “fairness and equality” as a core principle of state AI regulation. These provisions establish explicit protections against gender-based bias in AI design and deployment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Article 6 of the Draft Law requires that AI systems be developed and used with respect for fairness equality and the rights of citizens explicitly prohibiting discrimination based on sex and other attributes. This directly supports the prevention of gender bias in AI tools and systems.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law assigns general obligations to all entities developing and using AI systems to ensure fairness and equality and to prevent discrimination including on the basis of sex (Article 6). However it does not contain gender-specific responsibilities or enforcement mechanisms uniquely targeting gender equality outcomes.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) strongly emphasizes human oversight. Article 9 states that AI must preserve human autonomy and free will placing human life and rights as the highest value. Article 17 introduces restrictions on fully autonomous AI systems especially those that may manipulate or exploit users without human awareness. Article 21 requires labeling of AI-generated content and prohibits automated decision-making that significantly affects individual rights without compliance with data protection rules. Collectively these provisions ensure that human actors remain in control and informed of AI decisions
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) promotes meaningful human control by prioritizing human autonomy rights and free will in Article 9. Article 17 introduces a classification of AI system autonomy and restricts fully autonomous systems that act without user awareness or outside legal frameworks. These provisions ensure that AI serves human interests and does not override human judgment.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Article 17 of the Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) classifies AI systems based on their level of autonomy and prohibits the use of fully autonomous systems that make decisions without human awareness or legal basis. While this indirectly covers sensitive sectors the law does not explicitly mention specific domains like law enforcement or medicine.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) does not mandate naming specific individuals but it does assign accountability to system owners and operators. Article 17 outlines restrictions on AI autonomy requiring developers and owners to ensure systems do not operate unlawfully. Article 22 (machine-readable forms) also emphasizes formalized control mechanisms. While not detailing individual responsibility the law partially addresses oversight and accountability by assigning duties to legal entities managing AI systems.

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law addresses impact assessments through a risk-based approach. Article 17 defines categories of AI systems by degree of risk (low medium high) and autonomy. Article 18 establishes a formal risk management process requiring owners/operators to identify analyze and mitigate both intended and unintended risks throughout the AI system’s lifecycle. This includes annual risk updates and mandatory suspension if prohibited risks are detected. Article 15(2)(3) requires documentation of the system depending on its level of impact on safety rights and public order. Article 20 mandates audits including evaluating data quality and illegal functionalities. These provisions functionally amount to a mandatory impact assessment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes provisions that encourage proactive risk management but does not fully address societal ethical and environmental impacts in all aspects. Article 17 categorizes AI systems by risk levels (low medium high) and Article 18 mandates a risk assessment for all systems particularly high-risk AI. This implies evaluation of safety reliability and societal risks before deployment. However the law does not explicitly require evaluations of ethical or environmental impacts as part of the risk assessment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) requires AI system owners and operators to assess risks but it does not explicitly mandate comprehensive Impact Assessments. Article 17 classifies AI systems by their risk level (low medium high) and requires the identification and management of risks associated with their use but it focuses primarily on technical and safety risks.  Article 18 mandates the risk assessment for both intended and unintended uses of AI systems requiring owners to take action to mitigate any foreseeable risks. However the law does not explicitly mention conducting comprehensive impact assessments.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) provides some transparency and accountability measures but does not explicitly grant the public the right to access the findings of impact assessments. Article 7 ensures that users are informed about automated decision-making including the ability to seek explanations of AI system outcomes which promotes transparency and accountability. Article 21 requires that AI-generated content (e.g. synthetic outputs) be labeled and Article 18 ensures that high-risk systems are documented for compliance with transparency and safety standards.

items.title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence for 2024-2029 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 592 of 24 July 2024)
items.justification: The Concept addresses AI-related reskilling and upskilling in Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital. It mandates implementing reskilling and upskilling programs mentorship for AI instructors and allocating 15% of Tech Orda vouchers for AI training (Direction 3 item 1). It also provides for integration of AI modules into higher and vocational education and creation of regional competence centers to train 25000 specialists (Direction 3 items 1-4). Workforce forecasting is revised to align training with AI-driven labour needs (Direction 3 item 3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry (MDDIAI) Sectoral Council on AI Development and the Committee for AI and Innovation Development within the Ministry of Digital Development Innovation and Aerospace Industry

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The AI Concept 2024–2029 includes explicit measures for government-supported reskilling and upskilling in response to AI-driven labour market demands. In Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital it mandates: Reskilling and upskilling programs funded through national initiatives; Allocation of 15% of Tech Orda vouchers specifically for AI training (Direction 3 item 1); Creation of regional competence centers to train specialists (Direction 3 items 1-4); Integration of AI modules into education to develop workforce skills.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The AI Concept 2024–2029 includes financial support elements but they apply to specific groups rather than all workers. In Section 5 Chapter 2 (Approaches) Direction 3: Human Capital the Concept directs that 15% of Tech Orda vouchers be allocated to AI training in private schools - this is a government subsidy supporting reskilling. 'The Tech Orda program provides government-funded grants of up to 600000 KZT for citizens aged 18–45 to study at private IT schools.' (Direction 3: Human Capital).  It also mandates the creation of competence centers and public AI courses but the document does not specify direct financial incentives for individual workers beyond these voucher-based supports.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” includes detailed provisions to ensure the safety and security of AI systems.  Article 10 requires AI operators to implement protective measures against unauthorized access system misuse and data breaches. Article 17(3) prohibits the use of AI systems that can lead to mass violation of human rights such as covert surveillance emotion detection or social profiling without consent.
