Article 18 requires AI system owners to conduct risk assessments document their systems and ensure the reliability of high-risk AI applications. The law mandates immediate suspension of AI systems if they pose foreseeable harm and outlines criteria for classifying systems as critical infrastructure.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) requires developers and owners of AI systems to ensure accuracy reliability and safety especially for high-risk systems (Article 18). It mandates documentation of system functionality and risk levels and obliges operators to prevent malfunctions and unauthorized access (Article 10). However the law does not define specific quantitative performance thresholds or technical benchmarks such as accuracy percentages or error tolerances which would qualify as explicit quality standards.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes explicit safeguards and emergency measures to mitigate harm from AI system failure or unexpected behavior. Article 11(1)–(3) requires AI systems to be created and operated safely exclude misuse and obliges owners and holders to conduct risk management to eliminate potential threats. Article 18(1) establishes continuous risk management throughout the AI system lifecycle including identification of foreseeable risks and predictable misuse. Crucially Article 18(2) requires immediate measures including suspension or full termination of an AI system where risks related to prohibited harmful functionalities under Article 17(3) are identified.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes documentation and assessment obligations that directly support technical robustness across the AI lifecycle. Article 15(2)(3) requires owners and holders to maintain documentation on AI systems proportionate to their impact on safety rights and public order. Article 18(1) establishes continuous risk management throughout the lifecycle including identification and assessment of foreseeable risks and predictable misuse. Article 20 requires audits of AI systems including assessment of data quality and the absence of prohibited functionalities. Together these provisions address lifecycle robustness.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) includes explicit security obligations for AI system operators. Article 10 requires developers and users to implement measures preventing unauthorized access data breaches and illegal storage or processing of personal data. Article 18 mandates the management of foreseeable risks including technical and operational threats that may lead to harm.

items.title: Dossier on the Draft Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025)
items.justification: The Draft Law embeds “transparency and explainability”  among the foundational principles of state regulation in the AI domain (Article 4). Article 7 mandates that users receive full information on the operational characteristics and limitations of AI systems and grants individuals subject to automated decisions the right to be informed to object and to seek protection. Article 21 requires that  -Users be informed when goods or services are produced using AI systems. Synthetic results (e.g. AI-generated content) must be labeled in machine-readable form. Article 22 adds that legal information must be encoded to support automated recognition.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Article 4 establishes transparency and explainability as a fundamental principle of AI regulation. Article 7 requires that users be informed about the operational characteristics and limitations of AI systems. Article 16(4-5) entitles users to receive explanations regarding AI-generated outcomes affecting their rights and to request information about the data on which decisions were based. Article 21 mandates disclosure when goods or services are produced using AI systems and requires clear labeling of synthetic AI-generated content and Article 22 ensures that machine-readable formats support transparency of legally significant data.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) assigns obligations to AI providers to inform users about the functioning and consequences of AI systems (Article 7). However it does not explicitly require context-specific explanations nor does it define what constitutes a “meaningful explanation.”

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Article 7 of the Draft Law “On Artificial Intelligence” (September 2025) grants individuals the right to be informed about the consequences of AI-based decisions affecting them and to seek protection of their rights. However it does not fully articulate a right to receive a detailed explanation of the decision-making process or the key factors that influenced the outcome.

items.title: Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025-2030
items.justification: The Strategy addresses AI literacy through its pillar on Talent Development [p.76] where it sets key objectives such as; Integrating AI and data science into school circular at all levels [4.1 P.76] where it lists flagship projects for the implementation of the objective. These include; Development of an AI awareness and foundational skills awareness for schools Roll out of AI awareness and foundational skills curricula in schools and Development and implementation of a Training program for AI trainers program across different [schooling] levels.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The objectives under the Talent Development pillar call for this. The flagship projects under objective 4.1. [Pg.76] require the state to roll out AI awareness and foundational skills curricular in schools Develop an AI awareness and foundational skills awareness for schools Roll out the AI awareness and foundational skills curricula in schools and Develop and implement common courses on AI in tertiary education.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: One of the flagship projects under objective 4.1. [4.1.3] requires the government to Develop and implement a Training program for AI trainers program across different levels.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: Data Protection Act No.24 of 2019 (Kenya)
items.justification: Sections 57–66 of Kenya’s Data Protection Act establish enforcement and redress mechanisms. They empower the Data Commissioner to investigate complaints issue enforcement and penalty notices and compel compliance with the Act. Individuals may lodge complaints regarding unlawful or unfair processing including automated processing by AI systems. The Commissioner may order cessation correction or compensation for violations. Offences and sanctions ensure accountability providing individuals with effective remedies for data misuse arising from automated or AI-driven processing.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Section 51(2) of the Act states that the processing of personal data is exempt from the provisions of the Act if it is necessary for national security or public interest.

body.name: Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems

items.title: Concept: Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028
items.justification: The Concept promotes AI literacy primarily through education and capacity-building initiatives. Chapter 2 §5 “Artificial Intelligence” (p.7) outlines measures to introduce AI training programs in higher education institutions covering AI machine learning neural networks and big data. In particular training of the following specialties: Data Scientist Data Engineer AI Architect DataArchitect AI Project Manager. The document also establishes a National Council for AI Development tasked with popularising AI and involving schoolchildren and students in the process of AI learning and teaching AI technologies (p.7). The Action Plan (Task No.12) operationalises these commitments through concrete measures related to AI education.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Concept includes curriculum-related measures but coverage is uneven across education levels. It provides explicit provisions for higher education calling for the introduction of training programmes in universities in areas such as artificial intelligence machine learning neural networks and big data (§5 “Artificial Intelligence”). At earlier levels the document refers more generally to the development of digital skills through a digital education platform and training initiatives for the population including students (pp. 12–13) but does not explicitly mention AI-specific curriculum reforms at primary or secondary levels.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly provides for the establishment of AI-related programs within formal higher education institutions. It calls for the introduction of training programs in universities in fields such as AI machine and deep learning neural networks and big data and specifies new AI-related specialties including Data Scientist Data Engineer AI Architect and AI Project Manager (§5 Artificial Intelligence p.18). While it focuses mainly on tertiary education references to education at the school level relate primarily to digital education systems and general digital literacy rather than to AI-specific learning content (pp.13–14).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: It provides for a unified register of teachers and educators which includes information on their professional development and digital competence (p.13–14) and aims to improve teachers’ digital skills through digital education platforms. However while it highlights digital and data literacy training it does not yet specify structured AI-specific teacher training programs or dedicated teaching resources for AI education (§5 Artificial Intelligence).

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2024) ensures Access to Redress and Remedy in AI through several provisions. Article 84 grants individuals the right to object to automated decision-making and to appeal such processing to a regulator or court. Articles 67 119 162 and 170 establish complaint and dispute mechanisms for digital services while Article 90 designates the State Agency for Personal Data Protection as the complaint-handling authority. Articles 194–196 outline developer and operator liability for AI-related harm.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2024) includes provisions reinforcing judicial mechanisms for remedy in cases involving AI systems. Article 84 grants individuals the right to appeal automated decision-making including AI-based processing before a regulator or court. Articles 67 119 162 and 170 further establish judicial and administrative review procedures for digital rights violations. These collectively ensure access to judicial remedy for harms caused by AI or automated systems.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code  includes provisions for state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms. Articles 90 119 162 170 and 190 establish the role of sectoral regulators (e.g. in personal data telecom and the national digital ecosystem) to handle complaints and disputes including those involving AI systems. These regulators act as non-judicial bodies empowered to investigate issue binding decisions and ensure redress for digital and AI-related grievances.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Articles 119 and 196 require digital service providers and users of high-risk AI systems to ensure mechanisms for handling complaints halting harmful AI use and informing affected individuals. These obligations function as grievance and redress mechanisms at the company or developer level ensuring accountability and protection for individuals harmed by AI systems.

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code addresses children’s rights in the digital environment including AI systems through Article 81 “Peculiarities of processing children’s personal data.” (p.56). It establishes safeguards for lawful processing of children’s data requiring that it be in the child’s interest and subject to protection of fundamental rights and freedoms. Processing is only permitted under specific legal grounds or with consent of a legal representative while children aged 14+ may give consent themselves. It also mandates child-accessible language for consent requests and obliges controllers to prevent unlawful processing.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code (Art. 81) includes explicit provisions on the protection of children’s personal data and privacy. It restricts processing of children’s data to specific lawful grounds (e.g. vital interests healthcare justice public health security research) and requires parental or guardian consent when no other legal basis exists. It also mandates clear accessible language for children’s consent and obliges data controllers to prevent unlawful processing directly safeguarding children in digital/AI-related environments.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code (Art. 81) provides safeguards for the processing of children’s personal data requiring that it be in the child’s interest with special protections and parental/guardian consent where necessary. These measures indirectly prevent potential misuse of AI systems to exploit or manipulate children’s data. However the Code does not explicitly address risks such as targeted advertising algorithmic manipulation or exposure to inappropriate content. Thus it covers protection of data but not the full scope of AI-related harms.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Art. 81 assigns obligations to all data controllers (“owners of records”) to ensure children’s personal data is processed only under strict conditions with safeguards to protect rights and freedoms and with parental consent where required. It also requires information and consent requests to be presented in clear accessible language for children. However the Code does not explicitly impose obligations on AI system developers or deployers to ensure systems are safe age-appropriate or beneficial for children.

The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code establish foundational fairness and non-discrimination principles that apply across all digital technologies including AI systems. Article 3 establishes fairness and proportionality principles and prioritizes individual interests. Article 41 guarantees non-discrimination principle in digital identification ensuring equal rights regardless of identification status. Article 113 prohibits discrimination in digital services based on gender race language disability ethnicity religion or other status. Article 176 promotes equal competition among telecom operators.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code includes provisions that indirectly promote fairness in AI outcomes. Article 124(4)(4) mandates methods for checking data samples for bias while Article 191–193 require AI systems to ensure accuracy explainability and minimize risks to protected goods (life rights equality). It also guarantees equal and non-discriminatory access to digital services (Article 5). However it lacks explicit fairness metrics or auditing mechanisms for AI.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Code contains multiple provisions (Articles 71–72 83–84 113(6)) that explicitly prohibit discriminatory data processing based on different grounds and provide redress mechanisms thereby helping prevent AI systems from amplifying societal bias.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: National Strategy of the Kyrgyz Republic to achieve Gender Equality by 2030
items.justification: The National Gender Equality Strategy 2030 of Kyrgyzstan explicitly links gender equality with AI (section 5.7. pp. 40-41) which mandates training-of-trainers on new academic standards and subjects including artificial intelligence cybersecurity and neural networks alongside the development of training modules and video lessons. This aims to strengthen women’s participation in STEM and reduce gender gaps in emerging technologies.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Labor Social Security and Migration of the Kyrgyz Republic

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: It promotes women’s participation in STEM and AI-related fields. Section 5.7 (pp. 40–41) mandates training modules and video lessons on AI cybersecurity and related subjects for students at KSTU and OshTU targeting increased access for girls and women. Earlier sections also highlight the need to reduce gender gaps in education and technology sectors (pp. 15 section 1.4. - p. 28) and to boost women’s representation in the technology field workforce.

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code addresses Human Oversight and Determination through explicit provisions: Article 57(2) grants the right to human oversight of automated decisions; Article 122(1) mandates that health-related decisions be made only by humans. And Chapter 23: Artificial Intelligence Systems: Article 191(4) introduces the principle of effective human control requiring human oversight in AI use; Article 192(3) assigns responsibility to AI owners for preventing harm; Article 196(1)(3) obliges users of high-risk AI to ensure effective control of system operation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: Article 191(4) establishes the principle of effective human control (??????? ????????????????) requiring that AI use remains under human oversight. Article 122(1) mandates that critical areas such as health-related decisions be made only by humans ensuring human judgment in critical areas. Articles 192–196 further require risk management accountability and continuous human supervision of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifecycle.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (2025) includes explicit provisions preventing full automation in sensitive sectors. Article 122(1) states that decisions concerning an individual’s health including diagnosis can only be made by humans (principle of human decision-making). This establishes a clear prohibition of full automation in the medical field and sets a precedent for similar human oversight in other high-risk areas.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code assigns explicit obligations for human accountability in AI use. Article 192(3) requires AI owners and users to take all necessary measures to minimize risks and bear responsibility for any harm caused. Article 196(1)(3) mandates users of high-risk AI systems to ensure effective human control and designate individuals responsible for such oversight. These provisions ensure identifiable human responsibility and intervention authority over AI decisions.

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code addresses AI-related Impact Assessments through two mechanisms. Article 82 establishes requirements for impact assessments on personal data protection prior to automated decision-making or large-scale data processing including risk management and stakeholder consultation. Article 193 introduces a hazard assessment for AI systems mandating evaluation of potential risks to protected interests at design deployment and modification stages aligned with global practices.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code promotes proactive risk management by requiring AI system owners to conduct a hazard assessment before deployment as outlined in Article 193. This assessment evaluates potential risks that AI systems may pose to protected societal interests and must be performed at design implementation and modification stages following global best practices.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Article 193 of the Digital Code assigns clear obligations to AI system owners to conduct hazard assessments at key stages - during design before deployment and after significant changes. These assessments must identify and mitigate risks AI systems may pose to protected interests aligning with the principle of proactive risk management and societal protection. In the Code 'hazard' refers to the risk of harm that an AI system may cause to protected interests which include life and health rights and freedoms the environment defense capability national security and public order (Art. 193(1) Art. 192(1)). Assessments must identify and mitigate such risks and be published openly.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 193(4) of the Digital Code (2025) mandates that the results and methodology of AI system hazard assessments be published on the owner’s website in a clear and understandable form and as open data. This provision ensures public access to assessment findings enabling transparency and accountability regarding the societal impacts of AI systems.

items.title: Concept: Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028
items.justification: The Concept addresses Public Sector Skills Development in: §1 Reform of public administration §5 Artificial Intelligence and §10 Digitalization of the judiciary. It mandates digital and AI-related training including AI competence centers specialist education (AI Architect Data Scientist etc.) and public servant upskilling. The text also mentions training programs for civil servants in digital skills data management analytics and cybersecurity; introduces digital competence certification (p.4) and integrates digital skills into daily workflows. §10 adds continuous courses for judges and court staff on digital tools and AI-based systems. §5 emphasises AI research education and training programs for officials and institutions.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Council for AI Development

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The Concept for the Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic 2024–2028 includes elements of AI-related upskilling but not a full government-wide strategy. §1 “Reform of public administration” and §5 “Artificial Intelligence” promote AI competence centers and specialist training for civil servants. §10 “Digitalization of the judiciary” provides for continuous digital and AI tool training for judges and court staff. However it lacks coordinated measures on AI risks or a unified national AI skills framework.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: §5 “Artificial Intelligence” establishes national-level bodies: the National AI Council and AI Development Center (ai.gov.kg) to oversee strategy implementation conduct expert reviews and promote AI awareness through competence centers and research hubs. These bodies act as national AI champions. However the Concept does not assign dedicated AI teams or champions within individual ministries or agencies.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The Concept addresses ongoing professional development in AI. §1 “Reform of public administration” and §10 “Digitalization of the judiciary” provide for continuous digital and AI-related training of civil servants judges and court staff. §5 “Artificial Intelligence” promotes AI competence centers and specialist education.

items.title: Concept: Digital Transformation of the Kyrgyz Republic for 2024-2028
items.justification: The Concept addresses reskilling and upskilling in the context of AI through multiple sectoral initiatives. It emphasizes training medical staff in digital skills including the use of AI in healthcare and continuing professional development (§ 1. Digital health). It also calls for training and professional development in digital and AI tools for the labor market and AI competence centers and AI research support under the National AI Platform (§ 5. Artificial Intelligence). It further promotes digital education and AI training for specialists in defense and construction (§ 12. Digital development of the armed forces) and train civil servants in digital skills data management cybersecurity (p.4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Council for AI Development

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Concept mentions government-funded and donor-supported reskilling and upskilling initiatives but more details on it are mentioned in its Action Plan (https://drive.google.com/file/d/13ox2MKj5VSnk1m8vJyE0B7WtZPmWKZc_/view): it calls for training programs for specialists to work with new digital tools (clauses 132 162) and for universities to introduce AI machine learning and data science programs (p. 7) funded through the Republican budget and donor resources (clauses 132 162).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code’s Chapter 23 “Artificial Intelligence Systems” (Articles 191–197) establishes AI Safety and Security principles. Article 191 defines key principles: risk reduction openness explainability human control accuracy reliability and safety. Articles 192–196 introduce mandatory risk management danger assessment conformity declaration reliability and data-quality standards and obligations for monitoring control and suspension of unsafe systems. Article 194 adds stricter requirements for high-risk AI systems mandating characteristics that ensure openness explainability controllability accuracy reliability digital resilience and high-quality data.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Chapter 23 of the Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic (Articles 191–196) establishes principles of accuracy reliability and safety and mandates risk management danger assessment and compliance confirmation for AI systems especially high-risk ones. However while it requires adherence to these principles and maintaining data quality and system reliability it does not specify quantitative performance thresholds or detailed quality benchmarks only general obligations to ensure reliability and accuracy.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code Chapter 23 (Articles 191–196) requires AI systems to ensure resilience to random failures and malfunctions and to adopt measures preventing interruptions and preserving core functions during failures (Article 191 §2(6) principle of reliability). It also mandates risk management and suspension or termination of unsafe systems (Articles 194–196). However it does not define detailed fallback procedures or emergency protocols only general safeguards against harm.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Chapter 23 (Articles 193–195) mandates danger assessment of AI systems before use confirmation of compliance through a declaration and the creation of technical documentation maintained throughout the system’s lifecycle. These provisions imply pre-deployment evaluation and documentation to ensure robustness. However the Code does not explicitly mention testing or validation procedures or define technical standards for such assessments.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Article 64 establishes mandatory risk-management measures for digital systems including AI. It requires identifying risks such as cyber threats applying measures to reduce their likelihood and impact and conducting testing to determine appropriate security controls. It also links these obligations to national cybersecurity legislation and mandates documentation of testing results for high-risk AI systems. Article 64(4) explicitly mentions “testing of high-risk artificial intelligence systems” confirming that such AI systems must undergo risk assessment testing and the implementation of security and risk-management measures.

items.title: Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic 2025
items.justification: The Digital Code of the Kyrgyz Republic explicitly embeds Transparency and Explainability principles for AI systems. Article 191(2–3) establishes clarity predictability and openness as core principles and requires availability of technical documentation (“principle of openness”) and clarity of the basis for AI decisions and their re-verification (“principle of explainability”). Article 194(4) mandates that high-risk AI systems ensure openness explainability controllability and reliability. Article 197 requires disclosure when AI generates deepfakes or biometric classification reinforcing transparency to affected individuals.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Digital Development and Innovative Technologies

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Article 191(2) establishes the principle of clarity and predictability of AI system characteristics and requires availability of technical documentation (“principle of openness”). Article 191(3) adds the principle of explainability - clarity of the basis for AI decisions and the ability to re-verify them. Article 194(4) mandates that high-risk AI systems ensure openness explainability and reliability directly promoting understanding of AI purpose data use and logic.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Article 191(3) establishes the principle of explainability requiring clarity on how AI decisions are formed and allowing their re-verification. Article 194(4) directs the Cabinet of Ministers to set requirements for high-risk AI systems ensuring openness explainability controllability and reliability—obligating developers and users to provide understandable explanations of AI outputs especially where these impact individuals’ rights or opportunities.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The Digital Code promotes explainability and transparency (Articles 191(3) and 194(4)) by requiring AI systems to provide clarity and allow re-verification of decision bases. Moreover Article 196(2)(2) requires users of high-risk AI systems upon request to provide affected individuals with clear and accessible information enabling them to understand and verify the premises and methods used to generate results that impact their rights or interests. This provision establishes a corresponding right for individuals to receive an explanation for AI-driven decisions that affect them.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Centre Law (Latvia)
items.justification: The Artificial Intelligence Center Law establishes the creation of an artificial intelligence technology ecosystem its legal framework for cooperation between the public and private sectors and universities supporting the responsible use and development of artificial intelligence technologies. One of the Center’s goal is to enhance societal skills and equality in the field of artificial intelligence.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Centre

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.justification: The Law aims to promote the sustainability of the Latvian language the inclusion of cultural data in artificial intelligence solutions and adaptation to them.

body.name: AI Centre

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The Law aims to promote the sustainability of the Latvian language the inclusion of cultural data in artificial intelligence solutions and adaptation to them (Article 4 (7)).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The Law aims to promote the sustainability of the Latvian language the inclusion of cultural data in artificial intelligence solutions and adaptation to them (Article 4 (7)).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 2(3) states that: 'does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market put into service or used with or without modification exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' and 'does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military defence or national security purposes...' Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

body.name: AI office coordinates EU implementation (art64) European AI Board composed of one representative per Member State aims to issue guidance support consistent application and coordinate national authorities (art65 66) the national competent authorities (art70) once each country must designate at least one market surveillance authority and a notifying authority The Advisory Forum (Art 67) provides technical expertise advising the commission and council The Scientific Panel of Independent Experts (Art 68) provides support with specialized scientific and technical knowledge However neither directly participates in implementation

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related to gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Training datasets for high-risk AI must be designed to avoid biases that could lead to discriminatory outcomes related to the sex and gender as a sensitive attributes (Art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable risks of discriminatory outputs throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments covering discrimination risks before deploying high-risk systems in sensitive domains (Art. 27). Market surveillance authorities incluiding equality bodies can voluntary investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outputs (Art. 74(10)).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Risk management systems must address discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (Art. 9). Providers must implement data governance practices ensuring training datasets are examined for biases producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 10). Deployers of high-risk AI must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments covering discrimination risks before deployment (Art. 27). However these obligations are covering general non-discrimination without targgeting gender-specific.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Minimum cybersecurity requirements (Regulation of the Cabinet of Ministers) (Latvia)
items.justification: The Cabinet of Ministers' Regulation provides General outsourcing requirements specific outsourcing requirements for ICT critical infrastructure; specific outsourcing requirements for essential service providers (see 86-107)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Security Oversight Committee National Cybersecurity Center

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The Regulation states: 'When purchasing an outsourcing service the entity: 87.1. provides a description of the outsourcing service and sets out precise requirements regarding the scope and quality of the outsourcing service; 87.2. provides references to the requirements set out in the National Cybersecurity Law and these Regulations.  The Regulation applies to information systems including which integrates AI. Ethical and social considerations are not included though.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The Regulation states: 'When purchasing an outsourced service the entity: 87.4. determines the tests to be performed on the network or information system including the mandatory tests specified in the National Cybersecurity Law and these Regulations as well as the tests that the entity has determined in accordance with the cybersecurity policy and cyber risk management and ICT business continuity plan'. While the provision focuses on cybersecurity and system integrity rather than AI-specific risks it establishes a general requirement for testing outsourced digital systems that could also apply to AI systems procured by public entities. Therefore the measure provides partial evidence regarding requirements for vendor system testing.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: State Administration Modernization Plan for 2023–2027 (Latvia)
items.justification: The document lays out core competencies required for public sector employees in the context of AI and digital transformation. This includes technical skills (like basic AI literacy data management and algorithmic understanding) as well as softer skills (such as ethical reasoning transparency and decision-making in AI contexts) (p.7 1819 28).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document defines AI-related competencies for public sector roles and lays out training roadmaps (“cela kartes”) for acquiring them (p.39-42). These roadmaps serve as guidance for upskilling and reskilling covering foundational AI literacy ethical considerations and AI applications relevant to administrative tasks. Judiciary is not directly covered. There is no centrally mandated strategy or implementation unit only decentralized recommendations meaning that it does not establish a coordinated government-wide strategy.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.justification: The Artificial Intelligence Center Law establishes the creation of an artificial intelligence technology ecosystem its legal framework for cooperation between the public and private sectors and universities supporting the responsible use and development of artificial intelligence technologies. The Artificial Intelligence Center Law states that the AI Center shall promote awareness and the enhancement of artificial intelligence skills in public and private sector.

The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
