Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Lithuanian Action Plan for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies 2023-2026
items.justification: Companies and institutions face a shortage of AI specialists training or the necessary expertise (p. 20). Concrete activities and specific targets are planned. Learning program for young professionals to acquire the knowledge and practical skills needed to work with AI including participation in distance learning courses intensive courses to prepare for the real implementation of AI projects and project implementation in companies/institutions (p. 19- 20). Funding for AI summer camps/courses/internships is also aimed at AI specialists working in companies (p. 12). Program participants will also benefit from mentoring networking and practical experience. Participants remain working in AI or R&D (p. 2).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Innovation Agency connect to the Minister of Economy and Innovation

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: Measure: To create conditions for talent growth in Lithuania and attract talent from abroad and to promote networking at national and international levels through funding participation in AI summer camps/courses/internships/conferences aimed at university professors researchers and AI specialists working in companies. Participation is funded up to 100% for universities and researchers and 70-100% for companies. (p.22).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Funding is available for participation in AI summer camps/courses/internships/conferences for university professors researchers and AI specialists working in companies. Anyone wishing to participate who was not included on the list of funded activities may apply for partial funding or propose inclusion on the list (p.22). Related to the apprenticeship program designed to help young professionals acquire the necessary knowledge and skills to work with AI the program covers the salary costs of the program participants (p.21).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.justification: The Data Protection Act 2024 requires impact assessments for personal data processing likely to pose high risk to rights and freedoms including automated processing and profiling (Section 30 pp. 44–46). Assessments are mandatory for AI-related large-scale or sensitive processing with reports submitted to MACRA before processing. Section 25 also addresses automated decision-making (pp. 41–43).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Act mandates ex-ante impact assessments for high-risk automated data processing requiring evaluation of societal risks and risk mitigation before deployment (Section 30 pp. 44–46). However while ethical and societal impacts are covered environmental impacts are not explicitly addressed.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Section 30 (pp. 44–46) requires all data controllers and processors potentially including AI system developers and users to conduct impact assessments for high-risk processing explicitly to identify and mitigate risks to individuals and society before deployment.

items.title: Guidelines for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) Technology in Teaching and Learning (T&L) in Higher Education
items.justification: The document addresses AI Literacy by formally guiding students and educators on the understanding responsible use and critical application of Generative Artificial Intelligence in teaching and learning including expectations on ethical use academic integrity and appropriate integration into curriculum and assessment practices. It embeds AI literacy within formal higher education processes covering governance instructional design assessment and professional development for educators thereby ensuring learners acquire competencies to use AI tools knowledgeably and responsibly. (Introduction and Scope p 4–5 7–9; Governance and Academic Integrity p20–24; Professional Development p24–26)
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The document includes recommendations related to curriculum and teaching practices at the tertiary (higher education) level only specifically addressing the integration of Generative AI into teaching learning and assessment in higher education institutions; it does not address curriculum reforms at primary or secondary levels. (Scope and Application; Teaching and Learning Guidance p7–9 20–24).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document includes specific recommendations for teacher training and resources by requiring higher education institutions to support professional development of educators on the use of Generative AI in teaching and learning including capacity building guidance and continuous upskilling to ensure responsible and effective AI use in education. (Professional Development and Institutional Responsibilities p24–26).

items.title: National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) (Malaysia)
items.justification: The guidelines establish Environmental Impact as one of the three pillars of sustainability that AI policy-making must balance requiring that policies assess the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with AI hardware infrastructure data centers and computing resources (p70). To mitigate these risks the framework encourages Sustainable AI policies to promote the development and adoption of energy-efficient algorithms hardware and practices (p70).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines address environmental challenges by making Environmental Impact a central pillar of policy-making requiring assessment of energy consumption and carbon footprint from AI hardware infrastructure data centers and computing resources (p70) and encouraging Sustainable AI policies that promote energy-efficient algorithms hardware and and practices to mitigate environmental harm and align government initiatives with SDG & ESG Principles (p70).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
thematicElements.justification: While the document does not contain an explicit binding obligation for developers to formally 'report' on energy usage and environmental impact in a standardized regulatory manner (as the guidelines are generally voluntary [p21 p32 p81]) it includes strong objectives and requirements directed at policymakers and industrial stakeholders (including developers) to measure assess and mitigate environmental impact stemming from AI development and deployment (p70).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: 1. Prevention/Mandate: The framework requires policy-making to balance environmental concerns by assessing the energy consumption and carbon footprint associated with AI hardware infrastructure data centers and computing resources (p70).2. Assignment of Obligations: It mandates that industrial contributions align with ESG Principles explicitly requiring the collection of Environmental data on factors like annual carbon emissions and energy consumption water usage waste and pollution output (p103).3. Promotion of Efficiency: It encourages Sustainable AI policies that promote the development and adoption of energy-efficient algorithms hardware and practices to mitigate environmental harm (p70).

items.title: National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) (Malaysia)
items.justification: As a foundational principle fairness in the AIGE mandates that AI systems must be designed to avoid discrimination and bias against target users across diverse demographics requiring the use of unbiased and representative data and the implementation of regular algorithmic auditing procedures to ensure equitable treatment and outcomes (page 107).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly addresses the promotion of fair and equitable AI outcomes under Section B2.0: Responsible AI for Policy Makers specifically: Principle 1: Fairness which recommends that policymakers develop policies for unbiased data collection algorithmic decision-making and regular algorithmic audits to detect and rectify bias; and Principle 4: Inclusiveness which calls for integrating diversity and inclusivity requirements into AI policies assessing impacts on different demographic groups and addressing the needs of underrepresented communities (page 51).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly includes measures to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal bias and discrimination under Appendices – “Diversity Non-Discrimination and Fairness in the Use of AI” which requires AI developers and owners to identify and mitigate unfair bias arising from data training or programming including bias related to race ethnicity gender religion age nationality disability and other legally protected characteristics. The section further mandates vigilance in data selection assessment of disparate impacts and the implementation of controls to reduce harm to affected population groups (p134).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: 'C2.0 RESPONSIBLE PRINCIPLES FOR SECTOR PLAYERS - Ensure that AI systems are unbiased and treat allindividuals fairly regardless of their race gender ethnicityor other characteristics. This involves considering diverseperspectives during the design phase and implementingmeasures to mitigate bias in data and algorithms.' - page 74

items.title: Malaysia National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2021 - 2025 (AI-RMAP)
items.justification: Based on the document Malaysia National AI Roadmap 2021-2025 on the page 59 at the Section S4.3 - Attracting & Retaining AI Talents this document addresses Gender Equality in AI through two main areas: 1. Promotion of women's participation in AI programmes; where it establishes Women-in-AI (WAI) initiatives such as WAICamp WAI-2-Go and WAIDatathon (Horizon 1 2021-2022) directly targeting female engagement and leadership in AI development. 2. Institutional support and recognition: under Horizon 2 (2023-2024) the Women-in-AI Awards are introduced to strengthen visibility mentorship and recognition for women AI professionals reflecting a commitment to equitable representation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Human Resources

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: On page 57 of Section S4.3 the document supports this objective through the Women-in-AI program which introduces targeted sub-initiatives such as Childcare for Women-in-AI and AI-Work-From-Home demonstrating a firm strategy to increase women's representation in the AI workforce by addressing structural barriers to participation and retention.

items.title: Public Consultation Paper No. 3/2025: Automated Decision Making and Profiling Guideline (ADMP Guideline) (Malaysia)
items.justification: The document addresses the issue by proposing mandatory ADM Restrictions when AI is used to make decisions that legally or significantly affect a data subject (p. 17 Para 2.24; p. 7 Para 2.9). The proposed restrictions formalize human determination rights including the Right to Refuse a solely automated decision and the Right to Request a Human Review (p. 9 Para 2.13). To ensure meaningful oversight the Right to Human Review requires the reviewer to have the ‘authority and competence’ to go against the automated recommendation (p. 18 Para 2.25(f); p. 11 Para 2.13(c)(i)).  The Right to Information mandates transparency by requiring data controllers to provide meaningful information about the logic involved (p. 10 Para 2.13(b) 34).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the application of the core regulatory measures of the framework as the ADM Restrictions (Right to Refuse Right to Information and Right to Human Review) will not apply to personal data processed for the prevention or detection of crime investigations or the apprehension or prosecution of offenders (p. 14 Para 2.19(b)(i) (ii)).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes meaningful human control by introducing mandatory ADM Restrictions that ensure AI decisions having legal effects concerning the data subject or significantly affecting the data subject (page 7 Paragraph 2.9) are subject to human determination via the Right to Human Review (page 10 Paragraph 2.13(c)).Specific measures ensure AI remains a tool rather than a replacement for judgment by requiring that human reviewers must have actual ‘meaningful’ influence on the decision and the ‘authority and competence’ to go against the automated recommendation (page 18 Paragraph 2.25(f)) and by recommending that data controllers ensure that AI is not implemented as the only factor involved (page 18 Paragraph 2.25(e)).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The document partially addresses the prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors through the ADM Restrictions which mandate human review for decisions having a legal effect or significantly affecting the data subject (p. 7 Para 2.9) thus preventing AI from entirely replacing human judgment in critical areas like access to health services (p. 8 Example (b)). Pg 4 mentioned sensitive sectors such as finance (example a) and machine learning in healthcare (example d).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The framework mandates that the Right to Human Review (page 10 Paragraph 2.13(c)) creates an obligation for the data controller to use a reviewer who has the 'appropriate authority and capability to change the decision' (page 11 Paragraph 2.13(c)(i)).Furthermore to ensure accountability and oversight the human reviewer must have 'actual ‘meaningful’ influence on the decision' and the 'authority and competence’ to go against the automated recommendation' (page 18 Paragraph 2.25(f)) thereby making that individual responsible for intervening in and overseeing the system's output.

items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes proactive risk management under Table 2: Examples of Components for Each Responsible AI Principle which operationalises impact assessment and risk analysis across the AI lifecycle (p88).Specifically the table requires pre-deployment evaluation of societal ethical and environmental impacts through Impact Assessment components (e.g. context analysis data metrics algorithmic trade-offs fairness-aware pre- and post-processing and AI impact assessments) and Risk Analysis elements (e.g. human safety privacy loss reputational and financial risks). These provisions embed systematic consideration of potential harms and externalities before deployment thereby fostering a culture of proactive AI risk management (p88)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: For policymakers the AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) Framework requires developing relevant index measurements followed by conducting an Impact Assessment and Risk Analysis to determine the risk level for each AI system. This happens within the 'Performance Measures & Evaluation' block which is part of the planning and design phases of the AI lifecycle (page 62 pink color box). In part C for developers and suppliers of AI testing of AI is mentioned as a critical step to ensure that the developed machine-learning models are accurate reliable and effective (p. 84) and the responsible AI impact assessment tool is presented as a relevant example to evaluate risk (p. 86).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) (Malaysia)
items.justification: The document addresses labour protections in the context of AI through the principles of Fairness and Accountability requiring AI systems used in employment contexts (e.g. recruitment promotion monitoring) to prevent discrimination ensure transparency to employees respect privacy and remain auditable (pp. 25–28 67–69 133).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: The guideline addresses workplace AI fairness by stating under “Scope of AI Usage – AI in the Workplace and Fair Working Conditions” that AI used for automated/semi-automated employment decisions (including hiring and promotion plus employee monitoring) should be transparent notified to employees privacy-respecting and free from bias (p. 133) and it further strengthens anti-discrimination expectations in “Diversity Non-Discrimination and Fairness in the Use of AI” by warning against discriminatory outcomes when AI filters job candidates across protected characteristics (p. 134) —however it does not explicitly spell out protections for termination decisions nor specifically mention non-contract/gig workers under algorithmic management.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly requires transparency in workplace AI management mandating that when AI is used for employee monitoring hiring promotion or other employment decisions its use must be transparent and employees must be notified with AI actions required to be fair and free from bias. These requirements are reinforced through Accountability and Transparency which require human accountability periodic reviews explainability of AI decisions and controls to prevent or reduce harm ensuring workers can understand question and be protected from AI-driven management outcomes (p. 133-134).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Guidelines for the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Public Sector (Malaysia)
items.justification: The document address public procurement of AI by requiring responsible AI principles to be applied across the AI value chain. These principles are Data privacy and security transparency accountability fairness inclusiveness reliability and robustness and sustainability (p.44). Developers are required to conduct comprehensive testing at various stages of the development phase before launching the AI system to ensure it delivers robust and consistent results in a variety of situations and environments (p. 59).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the application of the core regulatory measures of the framework as the ADM Restrictions (Right to Refuse Right to Information and Right to Human Review) will not apply to personal data processed for the prevention or detection of crime investigations or the apprehension or prosecution of offenders (p. 14 Para 2.19(b)(i) (ii)).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The document stated that it require AI implementer to conduct testing validation risk and impact assessments and certification to demonstrate that AI systems are reliable safe and ethically deployed as part of the principles Reliability Safety and Control and Accountability (p. 70). It also states that clear responsibilities for stakeholders including developers should be established regarding periodic audits (p. 90). The document further mandates bias and fairness testing for developers (p. 129 ). However vendors are not directly mentioned.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: It mandate Transparency as a core principle (p.43). AI implementers need to provide explanations of the functions of AI systems and decision making processes to the public and stakeholders (p.129). The guidelines further AI system developers and law enforcement agencies should ensure the workings and decisions of AI tools are clear and understandable to users and stakeholders (p.131). However vendors are not mentioned nor clear guidelines on procurement.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2021-2025
items.justification: The document explicitly provides AI-specific upskilling initiatives for public sector actors including “AI awareness programs for government officials” targeting Federal and State officials as well as senior middle and junior public servants with a concrete target of training 3600 officials (p. 61) and further expanding these into “Accelerated AI programs” designed to enhance practical understanding and drive AI adoption across ministries through mechanisms such as AI performance ratings (p. 64) thereby clearly going beyond general digital literacy and constituting a structured public sector AI skills development effort aligned with the indicator.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: It notes that 'While other countries strategically focus on specific areas of AI such as national security defence cybersecurity energy and healthcare to drive their national agenda at least in the public arena it is therefore proposed that Malaysia places a strategic focus on AI in Supply Chain Management (SCM).' Based on this it can reasonably be said that the framework does indeed not try to regulate defence related issues.

body.name: AI Coordination and Implementation Unit (AI-CIU)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: Malaysia National Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2021 - 2025 (AI-RMAP)
items.justification: Strategic Initiative 4.2 highlights the necessity of reskilling and upskilling the existing workforce to mitigate job disruption or displacement caused by AI stressing that this effort must be strategic and include both workers with no prior AI exposure and those who already possess AI-related skills. To operationalise this the document proposes the development of a dedicated AI Reskilling and Upskilling System (AI-RUS) online platform which will initially focus on sectors with the highest likelihood of AI disruption and subsequently expand to all sectors supported by features such as asynchronous reskilling and upskilling modules and job-matching mechanisms for reskilled AI talents (p55).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Human Resources

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Initiative 4.2: Reskilling and Upskilling Existing Workforce: With Dedicated Reskilling System : A central measure is the development of a consolidated online platform called the AI Reskilling and Upskilling System (AI-RUS). i. AI-RUS is intended to reskill workers initially focusing on sectors facing the highest probability of AI disruption before expanding to all sectors ii. It includes modules for asynchronous reskilling job matching for reskilled AI-Talents and mentoring for continuous upskilling. iii. Targets for AI-RUS implementation include registering 500000 employees and reskilling 50000 workers and 133000 technicians and skilled labour.(p5556).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Initiative 4.2 (Reskilling and Upskilling Existing Workforce: Subsidized HRDF Programs: The roadmap explicitly targets the subsidy of reskilling programs through government-related entities. A key activity is to 'Promote AI and Data Science HRDF Programs' with a target set for '5000 HRDF reskilling programs subsidized'. The Human Resources Development Fund (HRDF) is listed as a collaborator alongside the Ministry of Human Resources (MOHR) (p55).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The framework actively recommends specific actions for employers (companies) to integrate workforce development: i. Employers are recommended to integrate reskilling and upskilling activities as part of their annual appraisals. ii. Employers are recommended to design On-Job-Training (OJT) that further supports the reskilling of mid-career workers (p55).

items.title: National Guidelines on AI Governance and Ethics (AIGE) (Malaysia)
items.justification: The document addresses Safety and Security by requiring AI systems to be reliable robust and secure with risks identified and mitigated throughout the AI lifecycle including design development testing and deployment (p. 21 25). It emphasises risk management safeguards against misuse system reliability and protection against security vulnerabilities supported by monitoring and human oversight to prevent harm from AI system failures or malicious use. (p.39)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document recommends ensuring reliability robustness testing validation and monitoring of AI systems as part of Safety and Security but it does not define explicit performance thresholds or measurable quality benchmarks under specified operating conditions. (p18–27)

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The document calls for risk management security safeguards monitoring impact assessment and mitigation of unintended harm throughout the AI lifecycle which implies the need to respond to failures or unexpected behaviour; however it does not explicitly prescribe concrete fallback procedures or emergency protocols (e.g. shutdown rollback incident response playbooks). (p18–27)

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly requires pre-deployment testing validation and ongoing monitoring to ensure technical robustness and reliability across the AI system lifecycle including design development deployment and post-deployment phases; it also emphasises documentation and traceability to support safety and security assurance. (p18–27)

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: These principles encourage developers designers technology providers and suppliers  to adopt safeguards and ensure responsible AI deployment (p.72). However the guidelines do not provide specific enforceable obligations or detailed technical measures to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference. Therefore coverage is partial rather than full.

items.title: Guidelines for the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Public Sector (Malaysia)
items.justification: The Guidelines for the Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the Public Sector explicitly addressed in the dedicated Transparency section (pp. 49-51) which requires agencies to ensure AI systems are and the data is understandable traceable and properly documented including disclosure of system purpose data usage and decision logic with human oversight to ensure AI-assisted decisions in the public sector remain reviewable and accountable.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the application of the core regulatory measures of the framework as the ADM Restrictions (Right to Refuse Right to Information and Right to Human Review) will not apply to personal data processed for the prevention or detection of crime investigations or the apprehension or prosecution of offenders (p. 14 Para 2.19(b)(i) (ii)).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Transparency is one of the guiding principle of the guidelines (p.43): which 'involves efforts to ensure that the processes and decisions of AI systems in public sector agencies can be understood by stakeholders including the public'. Public sector is meant to provide information on how decisions are made clearly and easily accessible. Guidelines also promote open data sharing 'facilitate AI explanations for user understanding and ensure clarity in AI processes to build trust' (p.45) where 'the technical system and the decisions made by the involved humans can be clearly understood' (p.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The AI systems used in public agencies should provide information on how decisions are made clearly and easily accessible (p.43). High-risk systems must follow auditing and risk assessment procedures while transparency requirement are not directly targeted.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: In this document the Right to Information (Explanation): This mandates that data controllers provide meaningful information about the logic involved in the automated decision. This requirement specifically includes describing the type of information collected or used in making the decision and what the likely impact is going to be/how it’s likely to affect the data subjects (the outcome). The Right to Human Review (Accountability/Redress): This provides the right to request a review and if requested the data controller must provide justification and/or reason on the decision made (page 10).

items.title: Public Consultation Paper No. 3/2025: Automated Decision Making and Profiling Guideline (ADMP Guideline) (Malaysia)
items.justification: The Automated Decision Making and Profiling Guideline (ADMP Guideline) which is proposed to be enforced under the Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709) mandates Transparency and Explainability (T&E) by establishing specific rights for individuals when a decision based solely on automated means legally or significantly affects them. This approach requires data controllers to provide the Right to Information (meaningful disclosure of the logic involved data used and likely impact) and the Right to Human Review which must be conducted by someone with the authority and capability to change the decision to ensure meaningful scrutiny of algorithmic outcomes (page 10 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defense and security are explicitly excluded from the application of the core regulatory measures of the framework as the ADM Restrictions (Right to Refuse Right to Information and Right to Human Review) will not apply to personal data processed for the prevention or detection of crime investigations or the apprehension or prosecution of offenders (p. 14 Para 2.19(b)(i) (ii)).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Page 10 - The Automated Decision Making and Profiling Guideline (ADMP Guideline) explicitly addresses the promotion of clarity to foster public trust by proposing the Right to Information (a transparency requirement) which mandates that data controllers provide meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decisions specifically requiring disclosure of the type of information collected or used (data sources) and the importance and potential impact of the processing (purpose and decision logic) thereby helping to address public concerns that arise when users do not know how their personal information is processed.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this issue under Section 2.8 (Risk-based approach to automated decision-making) and Section 2.9 (Proposal) of the Automated Decision Making and Profiling Guideline (ADMP Guideline) which recommend that obligations—such as providing explanations and safeguards—apply when AI-driven decisions produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect the data subject. The accompanying Explanation section further clarifies that such high-stakes contexts include automated credit refusals and e-recruitment decisions without human intervention thereby assigning responsibility to entities developing or using AI systems to ensure meaningful transparency and accountability in these scenarios (page 7).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: In this document the Right to Information (Explanation): This mandates that data controllers provide meaningful information about the logic involved in the automated decision. This requirement specifically includes describing the type of information collected or used in making the decision and what the likely impact is going to be/how it’s likely to affect the data subjects (the outcome). The Right to Human Review (Accountability/Redress): This provides the right to request a review and if requested the data controller must provide justification and/or reason on the decision made (page 10).

items.title: Guidelines on the use of AI in Higher Education (Mauritius)
items.justification: This is a formal framework for building AI literacy within tertiary institutions. On page 19 there is a recommendation to develop critical AI Literacy and competency where the main aim is to implement continuous and regular AI literacy training for stakeholders involved in higher education. On page 16 there is also a recommendation for Mauritian institutions to promote diversity and inclusion in AI literacy research and faculty development to bridge digital and knowledge divides.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: In chapter 'Teaching Learning Assessment and Research' page 18 of the guideline some mentions of updates to curricula is made. Furthermore on Pages 14 and 16 there is a recommendation to include AI literacy in all UG and PG programme across all disciplines as part of curriculum integration.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: It recommends incorporating AI literacy into undergraduate and postgraduate programmes across all disciplines and introducing AI-focused courses and modules as part of curriculum integration. However the framework does not specify the creation of new dedicated educational institutions nor does it extend these measures to primary or secondary education levels. pages 16 and 19

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: In page 16 it is mentioned 'Promote capacity building exercises for staff of the institution'

items.title: Responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in financial services (Fintech Series Guidance Notes 4)
items.justification: The guideline recognizes that bias in data not properly taken care of might result into AI decision making which might discriminate certain groups. It states that AI systems that treat consumers unfairly or violate fundamental rights including the right to non-discrimination should not be brought to market. To prevent this it requires a “fairness by design” approach embedded within AI governance and risk management systems supported by organisational culture staff training continuous monitoring auditing and transparency to detect and mitigate bias. Section 6.0;Page 10
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Page 10;section 6.0. This section clearly discusses about fairness and bias mitigation of AI systems. This section advocates for strong data governance and provides more depth to the dangers of bias with AI systems. It discusses the implementation of fairness by design methodology effective governance continuous monitoring and auditing of AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document recognises bias and discrimination as key challenges associated with AI systems page 13. It specifically references discrimination based on race gender social class and other factors particularly in the financial sector. However it does not on its own set out detailed preventive measures or mitigation requirements

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: Responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in financial services (Fintech Series Guidance Notes 4)
items.justification: The guideline specifically calls for governance through human oversight in section 5.0 in pages 8 and 9. It entails that existing human supervisory expectations should still be maintained though the development and use of AI systems. It also states that insurers that rely heavily on AI in areas that significantly influence consumer outcomes it is crucial to have sufficient expertise at the Board level to ensure that AI solutions are consistently effective and protective against consumer harm.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It provides some general recommendations related to governance but nothing specific. E.g on page 22 under section 'Accountability' there are some clauses discussing the establishment of procedures to monitor AI systems but this is not 'meaningful human control' over AI systems. On page 9 there is a specific discussion on oversight in terms of insurers that rely heavily on AI in areas that significantly influence consumer outcomes to have sufficient expertise at the Board level to ensure that AI solutions are consistently effective and protective against consumer harm. The question here is whether those oversights need to exist at the board level or more at an operational level.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Mauritius Artificial Intelligence Strategy (November 2018)
items.justification: The strategy explicitly promotes workforce reskilling and upskilling in response to AI driven transformation including recognizing the need for workers to “adjust” to new AI tools and emphasizing education training and talent development to prepare the workforce for AI adoption (pp. 16–17); the framework further identifies “skill attraction/capacity building” as a core strategic focus area and highlights that “training of domestic talent is of paramount importance” (Executive Summary p. 3; p. 17).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

It places expectations on licensees for documentation explainability and human oversight(Page 22). Furthermore on page 11 Transparency and explainability are being precisely referenced in terms of being able to meaningfully explain how decisions are made to be able to identify any potential biases in the process

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: In section 7.1page 11 the guideline recommends that financial institutions are expected to provide “clear timely and adequate information” to customers so they can understand AI-supported decisions affecting them. It is not specifically stated whether financial institutions should be providing details about purpose data sources and decision making logic. Hence this guideline partially meets the question.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: page 22 (Appendix: Principles — Transparency). This clause states 'Promote transparency in AI systems by providing clear and understandable information on how algorithms are used for decision-making purposes'. Thus the rights of individuals to receive information is addressed but not the key factors that leads towards a specific outcome.

items.title: Guidelines and Principles for the Strategic Development and Regulated Use of Artificial Intelligence at the National Electoral Institute (Mexico)
items.justification: These guidelines establish a reference framework for the development adoption validation and responsible use of AI systems at the National Electoral Institute ensuring technical feasibility and alignment with institutional principles. They include specific provisions on authorization mechanisms risk supervision data protection transparency non-discrimination equality and freedom of expression. AI use within the Institute is strictly auxiliary subject to human oversight and may not replace institutional decision-making particularly in electoral functions or the protection of political-electoral rights (Acuerdo INE/JGE175/2025). The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
