items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The law addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence through explicit prohibitions and duties. It bans AI systems that generate simulated audiovisual or textual content for fraud disinformation or digital violence unless they include authentication and visible labeling mechanisms (Art. 38.V). General duties prohibit AI from inducing harmful violent or manipulative outcomes (Art. 35.V). For children specifically AI systems that promote violence hatred discrimination or disseminate false distorted or decontextualized information are prohibited including synthetic sexually exploitative material (Art. 63 Ch. XIV)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: it prevents AI tools from creating/disseminating misinformation and enabling digital violence by banning AI systems that generate simulated audiovisual/textual content for fraud disinformation or digital violence unless they include authentication and visible labeling (Art. 38(V) Ch. X p. 33). It also covers hate/violence mainly in the child-protection chapter prohibiting AI that disseminates false/distorted/decontextualized information and content promoting violence/hatred/discrimination (Art. 63 Ch. XIV pp. 46–47). However it does not fully detail broader “harassment”/hate-speech controls for all contexts.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: It assigns transparency/traceability/audit and incident-reporting duties to developers/operators/users (e.g. periodic technical audits traceability/explainability reporting incidents and biases) (Ch. IX; Arts. 35–37; pp. 32–33). It also requires safeguards for simulated content linked to fraud/misinformation/digital violence via authentication + visible labeling (Art. 38(V) p. 33). However it does not set detailed “platform content moderation policies” as such.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: It grants protection and redress rights via: (a) liability of any public/private operator and joint liability when multiple entities are involved (Ch. XIII Arts. 52–53 p. 41); (b) a right to full reparation and access to courts/defenders/autonomous bodies and administrative complaint mechanisms (Art. 57 pp. 43–44); and (c) complaint/review/remedy mechanisms including complaints against platforms or entities operating the system with required accessible channels plus appeals and precautionary measures (Ch. XXVIII Arts. 136–138 pp. 78–79).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: It does not mention “gender-based harassment” explicitly but it targets related harms. It bans AI systems that generate simulated content for “fraud disinformation or digital violence” without authentication/visible labeling (Ch. X Art. 38(V) p. 33). It also prohibits AI that generates/disseminates child sexual exploitation material including hyperrealism “deep lies” (Ch. XIV Art. 63(V) pp. 46–47). And it embeds non-discrimination on gender as a guiding principle (“Equity”) (Defs. p. 8).

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The Federal Bill for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of AI (April 2025) establishes a comprehensive redress framework. Art. 5.XVII defines Algorithmic Harm Redress as a legal administrative or technical mechanism for affected persons to obtain restitution compensation or corrective measures against unfair or discriminatory automated decisions. Art. 56 grants affected persons the right to full reparation and access to courts public defenders autonomous bodies and administrative mechanisms. Arts. 131–138 (Ch. XXVII–XXVIII) establish complaint review and appeal procedures including precautionary measures against AI systems causing harm.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Right to Access Courts for Full Reparation: Persons affected by the development implementation or use of artificial intelligence systems shall have the right to access courts public defenders' offices autonomous bodies and administrative complaint mechanisms to demand full reparation for damages. The imposition of sanctions must guarantee the right to a hearing adequate defense and access to administrative or judicial review mechanisms. The National Council for Artificial Intelligence and the National Algorithmic Audit Platform may issue opinions alerts and technical reports that serve as evidence or technical references in the corresponding administrative civil or criminal proceedings. Arts. 56575960132133135 & 138.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Art. 7 designates existing state-based bodies as competent authorities for the law's application and surveillance including the National Human Rights Commission (CNDH) for monitoring fundamental rights compliance and the Federal Consumer Protection Agency (PROFECO) for user protection. Art. 22.VI assigns the PNAA the function of receiving and addressing citizen complaints about unjustified opaque or discriminatory automated decisions. Art. 56–57 confirm that affected persons may access non-judicial administrative and autonomous-body mechanisms for redress without being required to resort to courts.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Art. 37.VI requires developers of high-risk AI systems to establish update security and incident-reporting protocols with care channels for affected persons. Art. 37.VIII guarantees people the right to access question and appeal automated decisions that affect them. Arts. 131(iv) 133 135 establish complaint and review procedures including accessible channels through which persons may file complaints against entities operating AI systems and seek precautionary measures and remedies.

items.title: General Law on the Rights of Girls Boys and Adolescents (Mexico)
items.justification: Children and adolescents enjoy the right to universal access to Information and Communication Technologies as well as to broadcasting and telecommunications services including broadband and the Internet as established in the Political Constitution and the Federal Telecommunications and Broadcasting Law (Art. 101 BIS). The State must guarantee safe access and use of the Internet by promoting policies for the prevention protection response and punishment of cyberbullying and all forms of ICT-facilitated violence (Art. 101 BIS 3 added DOF 24-12-2024). These provisions apply to AI systems as technologies encompassed within the ICT framework (Arts. 11-12 101 BIS - 101 BIS 3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National System for the Comprehensive Protection of the Rights of Children and Adolescents

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The General Law on the Rights of Girls Boys and Adolescents it does not include specific provisions measures objectives or recommendations explicitly related to 'The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems.' However the document does contain general rights and recent provisions for online and digital protection that would apply to any technology including AI: Safe Use of Digital Technologies: The law establishes the Right of Access to Information and Communication Technologies.  Chapter 20 named: Right of Access to Information and Communication Technologies (Art. 101 BIS - 101 BIS 3)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: It does not include the terms 'Artificial Intelligence' 'AI' or 'targeted advertising' in its provisions. Therefore it does not have specific measures or objectives that name AI as a tool for exploitation or manipulation. However the law does contain broad high-level provisions aimed at preventing all forms of exploitation manipulation and harm including those that would apply to AI systems under the umbrella of 'Information and Communication Technologies' (ICTs) and media regulation: Prevention of Exploitation Manipulation and Harm via ICTs

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: there are no specific provisions measures objectives or recommendations that mention 'developers and deployers of AI' or assign them obligations related to designing AI systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children. Video Game Regulation: There are obligations for distributors marketers and lessors of video games to follow guidelines for classification and advertising. Retailers and lessors are specifically required to 'demand proof of age' for games classified as exclusively for adults. he State is obligated to 'guarantee access to and safe use of the Internet' and promote policies for the 'prevention protection care and punishment of cyberbullying and all forms of violence that cause harm to their privacy

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft law establishes non-discrimination and algorithmic justice as a guiding principle requiring AI systems to avoid direct or indirect discrimination based on ethnic origin gender sexual orientation age social status disability or any other personal condition (Art. 6.VIII). Equity is defined as an AI-specific obligation to eradicate perpetuation of inequalities (Art. 5.VII). Persons affected by discriminatory automated decisions may demand suspension of the system correction of results and compensation (Art. 44.II). The PNAA is mandated to audit datasets for structural biases and differential impact risks (Art. 22.I).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 6.VIII establishes non-discrimination and algorithmic justice as a guiding principle requiring AI systems to avoid disproportionate impacts on any group. Art. 22.I mandates the PNAA to audit training datasets identifying structural biases representativeness deficiencies and differential impact risks. Art. 22.II requires evaluation of AI models using technical metrics of fairness and parity. Art. 37.VII obliges high-risk system developers to certify that training data is representative ethical verifiable and free of structural biases. Art. 43 authorizes the RENSIA authority to conduct random audits and impose corrective measures for non-compliance.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Art. 44.II prohibits AI systems from discriminating based on ethnic origin gender age religion sexual orientation disability socioeconomic status ideology language or any other protected category. Persons affected by discriminatory automated decisions may demand suspension of the system correction of results and compensation. Art. 6.VIII requires all AI systems to be designed and implemented to avoid direct or indirect discrimination on any of these grounds. Art. 46.III obliges developers to avoid training data that reproduces unjustified or structural biases directly targeting discrimination at the source of AI development.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: Art. 46.III obliges developers to avoid training data that reproduces unjustified or structural biases. Art. 46.II requires technical and legal impact assessments before commercialization. Art. 49 mandates Algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk systems explicitly requiring analysis of differentiated risks by gender age disability and ethnicity. Art. 22.I assigns the PNAA the function of auditing datasets throughout the AI lifecycle to identify structural biases and differential impact risks. Art. 37.VII requires certification that training data is representative and free of structural biases prior to deployment.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft addresses gender equality mainly as non-discrimination inclusive governance and anti-bias controls. It defines “Equity” to prohibit discrimination by gender and sexual preferences (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and sets “Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice” as a governing principle (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires gender parity in the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 p. 22). It mandates audits of training data for representativeness and “differential impact” (Art. 22.I p. 26) and gives people the right to challenge discriminatory automated decisions (Art. 44.II p. 36). It also calls for participation of women and LGBTIQ+ in AI decision-making (Art. 103 p. 66).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: It sets anti-discrimination principles and some controls but not full mandatory bias-audit regimes for all high-risk uses. It prohibits discrimination by gender and sexual preferences under “Equity” (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and adopts “Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice” as a principle (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires audits/monitoring to identify “differential impacts” and data representativeness (Art. 22.I p. 26) and gives a right to contest discriminatory automated decisions (Art. 44.II p. 36). But it does not mandate sector-specific bias audits (e.g. hiring/credit/health) with standard metrics or explicit gender-bias testing protocols.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: It assigns broad duties to prevent discrimination but does not spell out detailed gender-specific developer/user obligations. It applies to all public/private entities handling AI (Art. 3 p. 6) and sets binding principles of Equity (no discrimination by gender/sexual preferences) (Art. 5.VII pp. 7–8) and Non-Discrimination & Algorithmic Justice (Art. 6.VIII pp. 12–13). It requires audits/controls to detect differential impacts and ensure data representativeness (Art. 22.I p. 26) and creates governance duties via the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 pp. 21–22). But it lacks explicit requirements like “use gender-diverse datasets” standardized gender-bias audits or user-side transparency duties tailored to gender equality.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: The bill supports increasing representation mainly via policy objectives not concrete programs. It calls for strengthening the AI ecosystem by promoting participation of women and LGBTIQ+ in training/R&D and decision-making (Art. 103 p. 66). It also mandates gender parity in the National AI Council (Arts. 15–16 pp. 21–22) which can influence priorities and resource allocation. But it does not establish specific initiatives such as scholarships mentorship/funding schemes hiring targets or mandatory workforce gender reporting for AI companies/institutions.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft law addresses human oversight through several provisions. Article 6(d) grants users the right to request review and appeal of automated decisions affecting their rights. Article 26 requires entities using AI for automated decisions to guarantee that those decisions are explainable and subject to human review. Article 27 establishes that individuals may request review before the OR-IA and appeal before an independent body in case of rejection. Article 38(III) additionally mandates qualified human supervision for AI systems interacting with children. These provisions collectively address accountability obligations human review of automated decisions and individual appeal rights.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: It includes extensive provisions measures and principles to promote meaningful human control and ensure AI remains a tool to assist not replace human judgment particularly in critical areas. The document establishes human control through the following points: Guiding Principle (Meaningful Human Oversight); Individual Rights and Review; Reinforced Control in Critical/Strategic Sectors; Obligation for High-Risk Systems

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Article 6(d) grants users the right to request review and appeal of automated decisions affecting their rights (p. 25). Article 27 further establishes that individuals affected by automated decisions may petition the OR-IA and in case of rejection appeal before an independent body (p. 34). However these rights are reactive mechanisms — available upon request — rather than proactive obligations requiring mandatory human oversight before or during automated decisions. The framework therefore partially addresses individual rights to human review.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft bill defines Algorithmic Impact Assessment (AIA) as the estimation of harm an AI system may cause to the population (Art. 5.VIII). High-risk AI systems — those with significant impact on human rights life health or public safety — are subject to strict design requirements and conformity assessments (Art. 5.XIII). The Risk Traffic Light System classifies all AI systems by their potential impact on fundamental rights health the environment and democratic institutions (Art. 5.XXIII). The Precaution Principle requires that innovation be guided by prior ethical social and environmental impact assessments (Art. 6.XV).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Article 6(XV) establishes the Principle of Precaution and Proportionality in Innovation mandating that technological innovation be guided by the precautionary principle avoiding implementation without prior ethical social and environmental impact assessments. Article 25 requires that all high-risk AI systems undergo evaluation by the PNAA before registration in the National Registry (RENSIA) establishing pre-deployment assessment as a mandatory requirement. Together these provisions establish a culture of proactive risk management applicable to all actors before deployment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: art. 25 establishes that AI systems classified as high-risk must undergo a PNAA evaluation before registration in the RENSIA constituting a mandatory pre-deployment impact assessment for high-risk actors. The PNAA is assigned technical functions to audit training datasets identify structural biases and differential impact risks and evaluate AI models against metrics of equity explainability and traceability (Arts. 21-22). However these obligations apply specifically to high-risk systems; comprehensive AIA obligations for all developers across risk levels could not be confirmed from the available text

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: raticle 25 establishes that AI systems classified as high-risk must undergo a PNAA evaluation before registration in the RENSIA constituting a mandatory pre-deployment impact assessment for high-risk actors. The PNAA is assigned technical functions to audit training datasets identify structural biases and differential impact risks and evaluate AI models against metrics of equity explainability and traceability (Arts. 21-22). However these obligations apply specifically to high-risk systems; comprehensive AIA obligations for all developers across risk levels could not be confirmed from the available text

items.title: Decree adding various provisions to the Federal Labor Law regarding digital platforms (Mexico)
items.justification: Article 291-J regulates assignment algorithms: 'through algorithms or similar mechanisms' must be transparent clear and known to all workers. It requires platforms to develop an 'algorithmic work management policy' explaining: consequences of complying or failing to comply with instructions (waiting times travel etc.); impact of customer ratings; incentives & penalties affecting the intensity frequency & pace of work; existence & rules of categories that positively or negatively affect task assignment; & other criteria affecting access to future tasks bonuses & sanctions with the aim of reducing information asymmetry. Article 291-P requires human oversight for decisions interrupting a worker's connection & linking.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Chapter IX Bis protects platform workers from AI-driven discrimination through multiple provisions. Article 291-J mandates that task assignment algorithms be transparent clear and known to all workers and requires platforms to publish an algorithmic management policy disclosing criteria affecting task access penalties and incentives. Article 291-P requires that decisions interrupting a worker's connection or access be subject to human review. Articles 291-I and 291-R extend full labour rights and non-discrimination protections to workers governed by algorithmic management including those previously lacking formal employment contracts.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Article 291-J requires platforms to develop and publish an algorithmic work management policy that explains: criteria governing task assignment; consequences of compliance or non-compliance with instructions; the impact of customer ratings; incentive and penalty structures affecting work intensity and frequency; and rules of any categorisation system affecting future task access or sanctions. Article 291-K further requires disclosure of how algorithmic systems interact with workers' rights and conditions directly addressing transparency in AI-driven labour management.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
thematicElements.justification: Article 291-I explicitly extends all collective labour rights recognised under the Federal Labor Law — including the rights to unionise strike and collectively bargain — to platform workers operating under algorithmic management systems. Given that task allocation performance monitoring and access to work in this sector are governed by algorithms the reinforcement of collective rights directly addresses workers' capacity to organise in response to AI-driven changes in working conditions. This fills a prior legal gap where gig workers were excluded from collective protections.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree to Reform the Articles 153-CY and 153-K of the Federal Labour Law
items.justification: This Senate bill filed November 5 2024 proposes two operative reforms to the Federal Labor Law. Article 153-C introduces a new mandatory obligation for employers to provide AI competency training to workers. Article 153-K requires the National Committee on Concertation and Productivity — convened by STPS and the Secretaría de Economía — to incorporate AI skills into its national training and productivity recommendations. Together these provisions establish a binding legal basis for employer-led AI reskilling directly addressing workforce adaptation to AI-driven transitions.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The proposed addition of fraction II to Article 153-C establishes a direct mandatory obligation for employers (patrones) to provide AI competency training to their workers specifically to ensure they can understand and apply AI tools adopted in the workplace. This constitutes a binding requirement for companies to invest in workforce development as a response to AI-driven automation directly addressing the risk of worker displacement resulting from technological transition.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft establishes a comprehensive AI safety and security framework. It defines a Risk Traffic Light System classifying AI into minimal limited high-risk and prohibited categories based on potential harm to rights health environment and democratic institutions (Art. 5.XIII 5.XXIII). High-risk systems are subject to prior algorithmic impact assessments mandatory registration periodic technical audits traceability obligations and meaningful human oversight (Arts 33.III 37).Developers must certify training data integrity and implement incident response protocols (Arts. 46 50). The PNAA is mandated to define and update technical evaluation metrics and audit standards (Art. 21)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The National Algorithmic Audit Platform (PNAA) in coordination with the National AI Council must 'define publish and periodically update the technical metrics methodologies of evaluation and international standards applicable to audits of artificial intelligence systems ensuring objective verifiable criteria in line with global best practices'. The PNAA must maintain up-to-date methodologies and tools to preserve their 'effectiveness reliability and compliance with the state of the art'. Provisions related to quality and performance standards: pg: 713182325263259 and 75

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Article 37 (VI): High-risk systems must establish 'reporting protocols incidents' and care for affected people. Article 46 (V): Developers must design mechanisms that allow for 'reversibility of the results.' Article 47 (V): Entities using AI systems must 'Report any incident failure detected bias or negative impact to the corresponding authority.' Article 50 (Incident Response Protocol): This article specifically mandates an incident response protocol; Article 58 (III): The authority may order the Correction limitation or deactivation of the system causing the damage; art.98128(IV)138(III)

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes specific provisions measures and objectives related to the requirement for pre-deployment testing validation and documentation to ensure the technical soundness (robustness) of AI systems throughout their lifecycle. Mandatory Impact AssessmentArticle 37 (I) High-risk systems must have an 'algorithmic impact assessment prior to implementation.'Developer's Duty to AssessArticle 46 (II) Developers must carry out 'technical and legal impact assessments before the commercialization or implementation of the system.'Validation by PNA.Article 22 (IV) The National Algorithmic Audit Platform (PNAA) Minimum Technical Documentation Art.86 Requires documentation on: (III) Sources nature and quality of training

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The law partially addresses cybersecurity obligations. Art. 35.II subjects all AI systems to the minimum obligation to guarantee the right to privacy personal data protection and digital security. Art. 37.VI requires high-risk systems to establish update and security protocols. Art. 38.VII prohibits AI systems that facilitate cybercrimes unauthorized data hacking or attacks against critical infrastructure. Art. 5.XIV(g) classifies such systems as prohibited AI. However no dedicated chapter establishes specific obligations to protect AI systems against adversarial interference manipulation of training data or model-level cyberattacks.

items.title: Initiative with Draft Decree by Which the Law is Issued (Federal for the Ethical Sovereign and Inclusive Development of the Artificial Intelligence) (Mexico)
items.justification: The draft law establishes explainability and algorithmic transparency as a foundational guiding principle requiring AI systems to operate under mechanisms that allow their decisions processes and criteria to be understood for accountability and oversight (Art. 6.VI). An entire chapter (Ch. XVI Arts. 83–90) is dedicated to explainability transparency and algorithmic traceability mandating differentiated explainability for different user profiles technical documentation and prohibiting black-box systems. Developers and operators of high-risk systems must ensure meaningful explanations adapted to citizens authorities and technical auditors (Art. 85).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The principle of transparency and explainability is a foundational pillar of the proposed law with an entire chapter dedicated to it. The law mandates clarity on how AI systems operate through a comprehensive set of principles rights and obligations for developers and users: Guiding Principles and Definitions; Rights of Users and Affected Persons (Public Trust); Specific Obligations for Clarity (Decision-Making Logic and Data Sources). The 'principles section' (Chapter III) Article 36 and Chapter X all contain specific provisions that promote clarity on how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic which serves to foster public trust.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: This requirement is a core tenet of the proposed law addressed through the guiding principles of Explainability and Transparency.Key Provisions and Obligations: Right to an Explanation (Chapter XI); Obligation for High-Risk and Strategic Systems (Chapter IX & XII); The Principle of Explainability (Chapter III & XVI); The entire Chapter XVI is dedicated to 'EXPLAINABILITY TRANSPARENCY AND TRACEABILITY ALGORITHMIC'

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Art. 44.IV grants every person the right to know in reasonably understandable language the reasons and criteria behind automated decisions significantly affecting them with high-risk systems required to provide explainability mechanisms tailored to specific profiles. Art. 84 recognizes the right to request and receive a reasoned explanation of the data used criteria applied and system logic leading to the decision. Art. 85.II specifies that affected individuals must receive a detailed description of the process followed data used how it was weighted and what options exist to challenge or reverse the decision (Ch. XVI).

items.title: Education System Digitalization Strategy 2022-2027
items.justification: The Education System Digitalization Strategy 2022–2027 developed by Ministry of Education Science Culture and Sport with support from UNICEF Montenegro addresses AI literacy under Strategic Goal 3: Development and Improvement of Digital Skills and Competences.Strategy recognises AI as a key driver of digital transformation and highlights the need to develop digital competences for participation in society and the labour market (page 53). Objective 3.1 focuses on strengthening the digital skills and competences of employees in educational institutions including teachers (pages 53–54). Objective 3.2 states that as AI and digitally enabled automation evolve rapidly students children need to acquire basic understanding of AI (page 54).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Ministry of Education Science Culture and Sport (now Ministry of Education Science and Innovation)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: Curriculum reform is addressed through measures on the development and revision of curricula teaching programmes and learning outcomes to integrate digital competences and the use of advanced digital technologies. This includes preparation and adoption of rulebooks curricula and educational programmes as well as alignment of curricula with digital skills requirements and teacher training for curriculum implementation. These measures are operationalised in the “Objectives 2022–2027 and Action Plan” ((pages 64–108).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy addresses AI-related education indirectly through measures aimed at strengthening digital competences. It refers to developing student's understanding of emerging technologies including AI. However the document does not explicitly provide for the establishment of dedicated educational institutions or formal programmes offering AI-specific courses within the education system. AI is therefore covered as part of broader digital skills and curriculum modernisation rather than as standalone AI programmes (pages 53–55).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document includes measures related to teacher training in digital competences and the use of advanced digital technologies including AI (pages 53-54). Also it foresees creating and accrediting training programmes for staff of educational institutions including teachers ICT coordinators managers and professional support services as well as self-guided courses available to education staff and parents (page 56 section “The activities planned in this strategy”).

items.title: National Strategy 'Digital Morocco 2030'
items.justification: The Digital Morocco 2030 strategy is structured around 2 strategic axes and 3 accelerators to which AI and its inclusive deployment are integral parts_p.9. The AI-related section highlights the need to develop Al skills p.23. The 'Inclusive Digital Use' part promotes further the inclusion of digital education as early as primary school p. 24. Additionally under the 'Digital Talent' accelerator goals have been set to achieve concrete KPIs in relation to initial training upskilling/reskilling and new alien talents. The strategy also outlines the aim to develop a repository of digital skills with stakeholders in the public and private ecosystem and ensure its monitoring p. 19.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The 'Inclusive Digital Use' section promotes further the inclusion of digital education as early as primary school p. 24. Additionally the Ministry aims to develop a repository of digital skills with stakeholders in the public and private ecosystems and ensure its monitoring as well as tailor initial training courses to the needs of the labour market p. 19. Further details on curriculum reforms for primary and secondary levels have not been explicitly specified.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: Fake news: From disinformation to access to proven and available information (Morocco)
items.justification: The Opinion of the Economic Social and Environmental Council discusses new advances in disinformation and offers recommendations to address these challenges. It emphasises that verifying the quality of information remains difficult in the digital environment where the development of sound image and video manipulation techniques (deepfakes) based on AI can create audiovisual documents that appear to be authentic (pp. 10-11). One of the recommendations highlighted is to establish a public digital platform for 'fact-checking' official information in Morocco capitalising on initiatives launched by certain institutions (The High Authority for Audiovisual Communication Maghreb Arab Press Agency (MAP) etc.) (pp. 7-8).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Royal  Decree  No.  1-09-15  of  22  Safar  1430  (February  18  2009)  promulgating  Law  No.  09-08  relating  to  the  protection  of  individuals  with  regard  to  the  processing  of  personal  data
items.justification: The law explicitly regulates “automated data processing intended to define the profile” and prohibits decisions producing legal effects from being based solely on such automated processing (Art. 12) thereby addressing profiling practices that are functionally equivalent to AI-driven decision-making and establishes multiple access to remedy mechanisms including the right to object (Art. 11) the right to understand the logic of processing (Art. 9) the right to rectification (Art. 10) and complaint procedures before the CNDP with investigative and corrective powers (Arts. 28–30).

The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Opinion of the Economic Social and Environmental Council: What are the uses and prospects for the artificial intelligence in Morocco?
items.justification: Approved by its general assembly in 2024 the Economic Social and Environmental Council published a set of recommendations to guide the development of artificial intelligence in Morocco (p.5). They recommend the sensible use of AI tools in all sectors both public and private by developing a dedicated support plan including training components (p.8)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The framework recommends the sensible use of AI tools across all sectors public and private by developing a dedicated support plan including training components (p.8). It does not specify the establishment of a government-wide strategy nor does it explicitly mention civil servants and members of the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: National Strategy 'Digital Morocco 2030'
items.justification: The 'Digital Morocco 2030' strategy is structured around 2 strategic axes and 3 accelerators to which AI and inclusivity are integral parts (p 9). Under 'Digital Talents' the strategy aims to ensure the availability and adaptability of talents to market needs with a specific focus on 'upskilling/reskilling' where the aim is to upskill/reskill 50000 trained talents in 2030. A set of measures is planned to achieve this KPI: scaling up bootcamp-type training programs tailoring the training to the needs of the labour market and developing appropriate certification programs across the Kingdom (p 19).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.justification: The strategy aims to scale up boot camp-type training programs and tailor the training to the needs of the labour market (p 19). However it does not specify how the government will fund such initiatives.

items.title: National Strategy 'Digital Morocco 2030'

Regarding AI-related goals the strategy's measures include the need to apply evaluation mechanisms to support the responsible use of AI develop AI skills build robust infrastructure for responsible operation and engage in multidisciplinary research to study its impact on society_p.23. The document stressed the remaining challenge of results explainability (p. 14) and the need to define a specific legal framework to ensure the ethical and responsible use of artificial intelligence systems (p. 31).

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Bots fake accounts and automated conduct are mechanisms of disinformation campaigns (recital 85) and as such rules are needed to combat them (recital 9). Systemic risk assessments apply to large-scale online platforms and search engines (art. 34) and explicitly include the dissemination or amplification of misleading or fraudulent content and the negative effects on gender-based violence. This includes recommendation systems and other relevant algorithmic systems (art. 34). Mitigation measures include testing and adapting algorithmic and recommendation systems; speeding up the processing of notifications of illegal hate speech and cyber violence; and labeling content generated or manipulated by AI (art.35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The act partially establishes preventative measures requiring platforms to mitigate systemic risks (amplification) arising from the dissemination of illegal content including hate speech harassment and content that poses risks to public safety (Art. 34). Regarding dissemination platforms must adapt their content moderation processes (illegal hate speech and cyberviolence) test their algorithmic systems and apply visible labels to generated or manipulated content (Art. 35). However there are no obligations for creators of AI tools with responsibility falling on intermediaries.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Intermediary service providers must publish annual transparency reports including content moderation automated means objectives accuracy indicators and error rates (Art. 15). Users must be informed when a content restriction decision is moderated by AI (Art. 17). Platforms must explain the parameters of automated recommendation systems to users. Large platforms and search engines must adapt and test their algorithmic systems to mitigate systemic risks such as illegal hate speech or cyberviolence (Art. 35) and publish risk assessments independent reports and mitigation measures (Art. 42 44). However there are no obligations for developers of AI. The measures are platform-centric.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes a set of rights for affected users: a free electronic complaint handling system (Art. 20) access to certified extrajudicial bodies including disputes over harmful content (Art.21) as well as judicial remedies; ease of notification of illegal content with the platform required to respond promptly; a statement of reasons with all information intended for affected users (Art.17); priority notification through a specialized knowledge entity (Art. 22). However there is no liability regime for the reparation of data from victims of disinformation or violence facilitated by AI. The provider must only inform about applicable means of redress for illegal products or services (Art. 32).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Large platforms and search engines should conduct specific risk assessments (Recital 83) covering the actual or foreseeable negative effects related to gender-based violence (Art. 34). Relevant measures include accelerating the processing of cyberviolence complaints (Art. 35) including the non-consensual sharing of intimate or manipulated material (Recital 87). However there are no measures to prevent use as the general provisions on systemic risks cyberviolence and illegal content are reactive.

items.title: EU GDPR
items.justification: The law provides a layered redress framework that applies in AI contexts whenever personal data is processed. Data subjects harmed by automated processing based on AI-driven profiling and decision-making hold the right to express their point of view and the right to contest the decision (art. 22); presenting complaints to supervisory authorities (art. 77) resorting to legal measures against gaps in the authorities (art. 78) and bringing proceedings directly against controllers or processors (art. 79). Organizations may be mandated to exercise the rights collectively on behalf of data subjects (art. 80). Supervisory authorities may impose administrative fines because of the violations of core provisions (art. 83).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Regulation shall not apply to the processing of personal data by Member States in the context of carrying out activities relating to the Union's common foreign and security policy (recital 16). The processing of personal data by Member States does not apply to activities related to the protection and prevention of threats to public security (Art. 2).

body.name: The law establishes the European Data Protection Board is comprised of representatives from the supervisory authority of each member states (Arts 68) acting independently (Art 69) providing guidelines recommendations and binding decisions to ensure consistence across Member States (Art 70) The Member State must to establish am independent supervisory authority responsible for monitoring and enforcing the regulation (Art 51)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: According to the law data subjects have the right to take legal action against data controllers or processors in the courts (EU members) of the controller's country or the court of their habitual residence (art. 79). The absence of supervisory authorities within three months is under the judicial remedy (art. 78) Controllers and processors responsible for damages related to processing may be required to pay compensation for material and non-material damages (art. 82).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: It is mandatory estabilish a independente supervisory authority to receive and investigate complaints in each member state from data subjects (art.51 57). The supervisory authorities must inform the progress and outcome of their complaint incluiding a judicial review (art. 77 78) and ordering controllers to comply with data subject rights imposing processing bans and sanctioning infringements (art. 58). Organizations can represent data subjects (art. 80). The European Data Protection Board coordinates the enforcement and dispute resolution mechanisms (art. 65 70).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law partially supports the rights of data subjects. Controllers are obliged to facilitate the exercise of data subjects' rights in a transparent process responding to requests promptly and free of charge (Articles 12 13 14). Data Protection Officers must be accessible to data subjects particularly regarding the processing and exercise of their rights (Articles 37 and 38). Codes of conduct may include out-of-court procedures and dispute resolution between controllers and data subjects (Art. 40). However the law stops short of mandating company-level AI-specific complaint systems.

items.title: EU Digital Services Act
items.justification: Online platform service providers must ensure the privacy security and protection of minors in their services (Art. 28) including prohibiting advertising based on profiling through the automated processing of data about children (Art. 28). Terms and conditions must be understandable to minors (Art. 14) ensuring a high level of privacy and security by default based on good practices (recitals 70 71). Large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines systematic risk assessment applies periodically evaluating potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34). Mitigation measures are determined: age verification parental control tools abuse reporting tools and support for minors (Art. 35). Voluntary standards apply (Art. 44).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Digital Services Coordinators

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act contains substantial provisions protecting the privacy and personal data of children in digital environments (Art. 28) including profiling by algorithmic systems and safeguards for data minimization (Art. 28 (23)). Systemic risk assessments and potential foreseeable negative risks to minors are mandatory for large-scale online platforms and large-scale search engines (Art. 34). However it does not impose specific measures for the protection of minors' data and the development of AI systems. There is a partial privacy-by-default recommendation for interface design (Recital 71).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Advertising based on AI systems that exploit the attention and personal data of children to generate revenue based on profiles targeting known minors (Art. 28). Trust indicators or other mechanisms may be used in relation to content harmful to vulnerable users such as minors (recital 62). There is a direct prohibition on the design of manipulative AI-based interfaces applicable to all users (Art. 25). This is relevant for very large platforms and very large search engines that intentionally or unintentionally exploit minors (Recital 81). Periodic systematic risk assessment applies including potential negative effects on minors (Art. 34) including through the design of online interfaces that encourage addictive behaviors (recital 83).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Online platforms must guarantee a high level of privacy security and protection for minors (Art. 28). Whenever an intermediary service is primarily intended for minors or used by them the service must be explained understandably as well as the restrictions (Art. 14.). Large platforms and search engines have an obligation to periodically evaluate their algorithmic systems including verifying the risks for minors (Art.34) assessing the level of understanding of how the service works (Recital 81) taking into account the best child interests when adapting their service and interface (Recital 89) incluinding age verification tools parental controls and tools for reporting abuse (art.35). Thus there is no AI developers obligation.

items.title: The Government-wide vision on generative AI of the Netherlands
items.justification: It emphasizes supporting open and public language models trained on underrepresented languages such as Frisian Papiamento and sign language to ensure accessibility and equal representation (p.13 Section 3b – Challenges and risks). It also explores participation in the Alliance for Language Technologies (ALT-EDIC) to strengthen European cooperation on linguistic technologies (p.37 Section 5c – Shaping and applying laws and regulations). It highlights opportunities for Generative AI to enhance accessibility and inclusion noting its ability to translate large volumes of text accurately (p.10–11 Sec. 3a) and adjust language levels to make government information more accessible (p.10).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Algorithms Coordination Directorate (DCA) and Government AI Validation Team (Rijks Al-validatieteam)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: For Linguistic Diversity: The document provides concrete actions such as encouraging the development of AI models for specific minority languages like Frisian and Papiamento and launching a national Dutch-language model (GPT-NL) to create local alternatives.(Pages 13-14). For Cultural Representation: It directly addresses the need for cultural representativeness by first identifying the risk of bias from developers with 'one-sided perspectives' and then recommending a solution: inclusive development methods like 'democratic AI' which involves a 'representative selection of people' in the creation process. (Page 25)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: It highlights that “training data may contain biases or one-sided perspectives that are then reproduced by the model” (Section 2.1 p. 11) acknowledging the risk of cultural stereotyping and emphasising responsible data practices to avoid such outcomes. To actively prevent the erasure of linguistic diversity the framework includes direct actions to support less-dominant languages.(Page 13). It also talks about developing Dutch GPT or more eurocentric GPTs to decrease reliance on dominant cultures.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The framework assigns some obligations related to datasets particularly for government procurement and through the broader legal framework of the AI Act. However the adaptability of all systems to various cultural and linguistic contexts is framed more as a high-level objective and recommendation rather than a direct obligation. The document acknowledges the need for representative and unbiased training data(p.26) noting that “an important risk of generative AI is the representativeness of the training data: these may contain biases or one-sided perspectives that are then reproduced by the model” (p. 11).

items.title: The Government-wide vision on generative AI of the Netherlands
items.justification: Sustainability is one of the four guiding principles ensuring that AI development supports both prosperity and climate goals. The document stresses that the development and deployment of generative AI must not negatively affect the climate or ecosystems. It also recognises substantial energy demand and climate change as key environmental risks arising from generative AI’s lifecycle (Sec. 3b p. 12).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The law focuses on the risk classification system (Art. 6) and the requirements imposed on high-risk AI systems. It requires suppliers of high-risk AI systems to establish implement document and maintain a risk (and damage) management system throughout the system's lifecycle (Art. 9). Training validation and test datasets must conform to data governance in terms of representation error-freeness completeness contextualization and the function the system will be used for handling special personal data for monitoring purposes and detecting and correcting biases. High-risk AI systems must have consistency throughout the lifecycle by requiring appropriate levels of accuracy and robustness and reducing the risk of bias (art.15).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Art. 9 and 10 require a risk-management process and relevant representative data with bias detection and mitigation; Art. 15 adds that systems must be accurate and robust limiting feedback loops where biased outputs skew future inputs. However. the Act focuses on controls and process not on guaranteeing specific outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a list of prohibited AI applications including practices related to the vulnerabilities of specific groups of people who may be marginalized or systems that infer from sensitive attributes (Art. 5). It requires that datasets for high-risk AI be examined for potential biases that could lead to discriminatory results based on geographic/contextual characteristics (Art. 10). It requires that high-risk AI systems be accompanied by instructions for use that include information about known or foreseeable biases (Art. 13). And it limits high-risk AI systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market or in service when there are biased results that influence future operations (Art. 15).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The law requires a risk management system throughout the entire lifecycle including non-discrimination through testing to verify compliance (Art. 9). It requires robust data governance including bias analysis in training validation and test datasets allowing for the identification and correction of such discrimination before data use (Art. 10). Suppliers must produce technical documentation before placing the system on the market including risk assessment performance metrics in population subgroups and bias mitigation measures (Art. 11). Implementers specifically in the public sector must conduct Impact Assessments addressing vulnerable groups or interference with the rights to equality and non-discrimination (Art. 27).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act addresses gender equality through non-discrimination and fundamental rights provisions. Training datasets for high-risk AI must be representative avoiding the discriminatory outcomes and protecting attributes explicitly related gender (Art. 10). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessments before deploying high-risk AI including gender-based discrimination (Art. 27). Equality bodies are granted market surveillance powers enabling them to investigate and sanction AI systems producing discriminatory outcomes (Art. 74).

items.justification: The Act establishes requirements to ensure human control over high-risk AI systems requiring providers to design systems that enable natural persons with a minimum level of comprehensibility to monitor outputs detect anomalies and intervene or interrupt operations when necessary (art. 14). Deployers must assign oversight to competent natural persons with authority to act (art. 26). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing and incident reporting reinforce human control (Arts. 55 73). Additional oversight provisions are set in the fundamental rights impact assessment (art. 27) and Annex (IV) 2(e) as part of technical documentation requirements (art. 11).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly frames human oversight as ensuring AI remains an instrument serving human values rather than supplanting human judgment (Recital 47). High-risk AI systems must be designed to allow a natural persons oversee their operation. Providers are obliged to build technical interfaces to facilitate the monitoring interpretation and intervention. Operators must be able to override interrupt or stop system operations (art.14). Deployers must ensure oversight is exercised by competent individuals with sufficient authority and resources (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: According to the law high-risk AI systems in law enforcement judicial processes employment healthcare and critical infrastructure must include human oversight mechanisms preventing solely automated consequential decision-making (art. 14) (Annex III). Biometric identification in public spaces is prohibited with exceptions preserving human authorization requirements (art. 5). Deployers in sensitive sectors must designate a natural person responsible for oversight and intervention (art. 26). General-purpose AI with systemic risk is also subject to oversight obligations including incident reporting (Art. 55). However the Act does not define sector-specific automation thresholds leaving this to sector-specific legislation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Deployers of high-risk AI must assign human oversight to specific natural persons with the competence authority and resources necessary to fulfill oversight functions (Art. 26). These human overseers must be capable of understanding system capabilities and limitations correctly interpreting outputs and taking corrective action when necessary (art. 14). Providers must ensure oversight mechanisms are technically embedded in system design designating persons who can exercise it (art. 14). Thus providers are obliged employ human oversight for the system design and conformity (art. 16) and deployers for operational oversight and appropriate use (art. 26).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Law establishes an assessment architecture according to the type and level of risk of the system. High-risk AI suppliers must identify analyze and mitigate risks during the design development and implementation phases within a risk management system (Arti.9) with comprehensive technical documentation (Art.15) and monitoring of operations and anomalies (Art. 26). For AI implementers in the public sector a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment applies before implementing high-risk systems listed in Annex 3 (Art.27). Compliance assessment must include self-assessment or third-party audits depending on the criticality of the system (Art. 43 47). There are ex-post assessments and post-commercialization monitoring (Art.72).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: An integrated risk management system within the development processes requiring the identification and analysis of known foreseeable and unintended risks is mandatory for high-risk systems (Art. 9). Implementers particularly in the public sector must proactively assess social and ethical impacts including effects on vulnerable groups before deployment (Art. 27). The code of practice (art. 56) ensures that general-purpose AI model providers develop extensive technical documentation and evaluation processes (art. 53-55). Voluntary codes of conduct (art. 95) encourage evaluations guided by ethics and trust environmental sustainability inclusive and diverse design of AI systems especially for vulnerable groups including gender.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The law does not use the terminology of developers and users addressing (Article 3) providers and deployers. Providers have the duty to implement risk management systems prepare technical documentation and conduct conformity assessments (Article 16). There are specific obligations when the provider and deployers are distinct entities (Article 25). Regarding deployers: certain AI system implementations require a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article 27) and they must operate AI systems according to instructions ensure human supervision and monitor and mitigate residual risks (Article 26). However there are no obligations relating to users.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes a public database where high-risk AI systems must be registered before implementation indicating the system's purpose the supplier's identity and its compliance status (Art. 71). However there are confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive information (Art. 78). Suppliers must ensure transparency for deployers and affected users regarding the system's operation and limitations (Art. 13). However there is no access to complete assessment documentation including technical compliance reports. In specific contexts such as emotional or biometric recognition individuals interacting with AI systems must be informed (Art. 50).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: The Act classifies systems for recruitment promotion termination and worker management as high-risk AI systems (Annex III(4)) (art. 6). Prohibited AI practices include bans on emotion-recognition in the workplace (art. 5). Providers must implement risk-management addressing discrimination (Art. 9) ensure representative datasets and bias-control (art. 10) and maintain technical documentation (Arts. 11). Deployers must conduct fundamental rights assessments before deployment (art. 27). Art. 26 (7-9) establishes safeguards: workers must be informed and may request explanations of AI use. However the Act does not regulate pay conditions or compensation so it mitigates risks without constituting a full labour-rights regime.

thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

items.title: Act of 25 October 2021 containing rules on the accessibility of information of public interest (Open Government Act) (Netherlands)
items.justification: The Wet open overheid (Woo) (Stb. 2021 499) does not explicitly regulate transparency of government AI or algorithmic systems but provides an implicit legal basis for public access to information through general access-to-information obligations. Art 2.1 broadly defines a “document” as any recorded information which may include documentation related to algorithmic or automated decision-making systems. Art 3.3 and 3.3a establish proactive publication duties for certain categories of information potentially covering research reports or impact assessments underlying algorithms while Art 5.1 limits refusals to narrowly defined exceptions. In practice the Woo has already been used to obtain algorithm-related information about government.

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
