thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: Generative AI: Guidance and resources for education professionals on the use of artificial intelligence in schools (New Zealand)
items.justification: NZ's Ministry of Education released an initial advisory on generative AI (Ministry of Education 2024) acknowledging AI’s growing role in education and provided high-level principles for schools emphasising student safety data privacy and the primacy of human judgement. Schools have been encouraged to update their digital technology policies to cover AI use and to approach classroom experiments with generative AI in a cautious supervised manner Page numbers are not provided due to the guidance published in a webpage format.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The advisory guidance emphasises on improving teaching and learning supporting knowledgeable and skilled teachers. It reinstates that human teachers must: remain central in students’ educationtake responsibility for students’ learning. The guidance also provides recommendations for schools and teachers on the use of AI for marking. The guidance follows and promotes a principles-based approach around 3 key principles: teacher responsibility and professional judgement; human oversight and appropriate use cases. Page numbers are not provided due to the guidance published in a webpage format.

items.title: AI resource series for educators
items.justification: Ako Aotearoa National Centre for Tertiary Teaching Excellence is a publicly funded organisation. In 2023 the centre released a 6-part beginner's series guide is meant for tertiary educators on using AI and covers many aspects of AI literacy. The series supports educators in using AI in ways that are a) culturally sustaining inclusive and grounded in Aotearoa values (Part 4); b) explore the ethical use of AI in ways that uphold cultural values learner rights and trust in education (Part 5); c) shares practical steps for AI strategy capability and leadership in Aotearoa's tertiary sector. (Part 6).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: It is not meant to be a training but rather a guide to help teachers/educators with using AI responsibly ethically. It also offers  links to research and tools practical steps real examples and reflective tools to support educators AI journey.

items.title: Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill (New Zealand)
items.justification: This Bill holds accountable those who use digital tools to violate other individuals’ agency. It does this by amending both the Crimes Act 1961 and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 to expand the definition of an 'intimate visual recording' to explicitly include images created synthesised or altered to show a person’s likeness produced without consent (Explanatory Note General Policy Statement Pg 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The bill amends the Crimes Act 1961 and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 to cover any individual or entity regardless of whether they are in the public or private sector that creates synthesises or alter to show a person’s likeness produced without consent including deepfakes. (Explanatory Note Pg 1). Its focus is on harmful conduct but does not cover hate speech and misinformation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The bill establishes that non-consensual intimate imagery is a rights infringement and the false representation of a person in intimate contexts without consent. This conduct misappropriates a person’s image for exploitative purposes causing reputational psychological and often material harm. Criminalising such acts and enabling victims to seek removal and redress aligns with a commitment to defending individuals from coercion fraud and aggression. (Pg 1).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: It frames non-consensual deepfake intimate imagery as a rights infringement with explicit recognition of the reputational psychological and material harm such acts cause forms of digital abuse. It does not use the word harassment and does not cover gender based violence. (General policy statement Pg 1).

items.title: Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill (New Zealand)
items.justification: This Bill holds accountable those who use digital tools to violate other individuals’ agency. It does this by amending both the Crimes Act 1961 and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 to expand the definition of an 'intimate visual recording' to explicitly include images created synthesised or altered to show a person’s likeness produced without consent (Pg 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The bill amends the Crimes Act 1961 and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 to cover any individual that created synthesised or altered to show a person’s likeness produced without consent including deepfakes including deepfakes. False representation of a person in intimate contexts without consent misappropriates a person’s image for exploitative purposes causing reputational psychological and often material harm. Criminalising such acts and enabling victims to seek redress and removal aligns with a commitment to defending individuals from coercion fraud and aggression (Pg 1).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (New Zealand)
items.justification: The Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service (GenAI) guidance is designed specifically for NZ’s public sector and strongly emphasises on cultural diversity particularly protection for Maori Pacific People and ethnic communities (Pg 31-33). It mandates agencies to assess the impact of GenAI systems on these groups consult with iwi Maori respect Maori data sovereignty and align approaches with Maori-Crown relationship frameworks (Pg 31-33). The document suggests agencies to evaluate the sensitivity of indigenous data foster Maori-led and community-informed GenAI applications and build confidence for culturally safe engagement (Pg 33).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The guidance recommends agencies actively involve Maori and ethnic communities in GenAI decision-making (Pg 31) build skills for culturally respectful engagement and foster diverse teams especially in governance (Pg 27). It urges agencies to validate outputs for fairness and equity (p.26-27) encourages Maori-led approaches in GenAI (Pg 31-32) and calls for careful stewardship of indigenous data to avoid bias and stereotyping (Pg 33). Agencies are instructed to ensure GenAI reflects New Zealand’s cultural diversity and to monitor for unintended harm or exclusion. The document does not specifically address linguistic diversity.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The guidance details how GenAI can perpetuate bias and discrimination noting these often reflect stereotypes and unfair treatment based on race ethnicity sex gender or other protected characteristics (Pg 26). It emphasizes that GenAI trained on existing data may reinforce these patterns risking repeated inequalities and harm (p 26). To counter this the document recommends identifying/ mitigating bias at every development stage and includes best-practice tips for reducing harm and ensuring fairer outcomes (Pg 26–27). The document does address protecting Maori data governance (Pg 38) and being aware of indigenous communities' (incl Pacific community) data to prevent perpetuating bias (Pg 33).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The document includes specific provisions encouraging public sector entities to ensure their AI systems are trained on diverse datasets and adaptable to various cultural contexts (Pg 32). It directs agencies to assess representativeness of training data with a focus on Maori Pacific Peoples and ethnic communities (pp. 31). The document encourages agencies to engage these communities in system development and governance (Pg 33). It does address limits of Gen AI in understanding nuances of languages (Pg 20) indigenous data (also includes languages Pg 38) Maori Data Governance (includes  promoting the ethical use of data to enhance wellbeing of Maori people language and culture; Pg 38).

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: This guidance draws on the OECD values-based AI Principles: inclusive growth sustainable development and well-being; human rights and democratic values. It aligns with international equivalent guidance materials while taking into account New Zealand values and interests including respecting te reo Maori (Maori language) Maori imagery tikanga and other matauranga (knowledge) and Maori data (Pg 4). It suggests businesses to preserve and take into account NZ’s diversity including by taking care of New Zealanders’ data exercising good practice engagement with impacted communities. (Pg 4-5)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The guidance highlights that businesses handling Maori data must distinguish between noa (non-sensitive) data and tapu (sacred) data where Maori have strong interests and appropriate tikanga must be respected. It suggests involving Maori in AI development and decision-making to identify what data is tapu and ensures extensive safeguards where needed. It stresses putting in place guardrails such as data accuracy ethical sourcing supporting creators’ IP cybersecurity transparency minimise bias reflecting diversity (Pg 24-25). The document also mentions the importance of respecting te reo Maori?: Maori language (Pg 5).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The guidance highlights that businesses handling Maori data must distinguish between noa (non-sensitive) data and tapu (sacred) data where Maori have strong interests and appropriate tikanga must be respected.  The guidance emphasises on how 'AI systems can enable misrepresentation misappropriation or misuse of data and matauranga Maori and other Indigenous knowledge. It also discusses the inappropriate commodification of that data disregard for indigenous protocols around that data or reinforcement of stereotypes which perpetuate inequality and harm in reference to reflecting cultural diversity (Pg 24-25). It however does not address linguistic diversity.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The guidance in the Maori data section specifically advises organisations that including Maori data in datasets highlights the need to establish appropriate guardrails and follow good practice such as data accuracy and ethical legal data collection. (Pg 24). The guidance also recommends taking into account diversity including New Zealanders data by exercising good practice engagement with impacted communities and enable equitable impact of AI where possible (See 'Why use this Guidance' Pg 5).

items.title: Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand
items.justification: This Charter demonstrates a commitment to ensuring New Zealanders have confidence in how government agencies use algorithms. This Charter is one of many ways that government is demonstrating transparency and accountability identifying and mitigating biases in AI systems to ensure that privacy ethics and human rights are safeguarded (Privacy Ethics and Human Rights Pg 3). The Charter is a commitment by government to minimise unintended bias better reflect the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi and strike the right balance between making sure access the algorithms to ensure deliver better services to New Zealanders whilst still maintaining the trust. (Pg 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Algorithm Charter commits to the following: Make sure data is fit for purpose by understanding its limitations and Identifying/ managing bias b) Deliver clear public benefit through Treaty commitments by embedding a Te Ao Maori perspective in the development and use of algorithms consistent with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi and c) Ensure that privacy ethics and human rights are safeguarded by regularly peer reviewing algorithms to assess for unintended consequences and act on this information. (Pg 3).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Algorithm Charter addresses the risk of bias in algorithmic systems but does so in general terms rather than through detailed anti-discrimination provisions. Under the Data commitment agencies are expected to ensure that data used in algorithms is fit for purpose including understanding its limitations and identifying and managing bias. Additionally the Privacy Ethics and Human Rights section calls for regular peer review of algorithms to assess unintended consequences. While these measures can help identify and mitigate discriminatory outcomes the Charter does not explicitly reference specific protected characteristics (such as race gender or religion) or establish detailed safeguards specifically targeting discrimination.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Algorithm Charter includes commitments related to identifying and managing bias but does not establish detailed lifecycle obligations. Under the Data commitment agencies are expected to ensure that data used in algorithms is fit for purpose which includes understanding data limitations and identifying and managing bias. In addition the Privacy Ethics and Human Rights section calls for regular peer review of algorithms to assess unintended consequences. While these provisions encourage monitoring and mitigation of bias the Charter does not explicitly require systematic bias assessment across the entire AI lifecycle from data collection through deployment.

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: The guidance outlines the potential legal implications of AI under the Human Rights Act 1993 which holds individuals and businesses accountable for avoiding discrimination based on sex race and other protected grounds in specified areas and for protecting civil and political rights (See Compliance and legal obligations; Pg 10). Beyond the Human Rights Act the guidance highlights a range of other legal obligations to help businesses understand their responsibilities across all areas of operation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The Guidance promotes fair and equitable AI by recommending legal compliance (Pg 9; legal compliance) championing workforce training on bias (Pg 16; Skills/Knowledge building) supporting diverse governance advocating transparency and documentation of data (Pg 21; Data Modelling) and recommending technical bias audits (Pg 25; Model Efficacy). Businesses are advised to comply with human rights/privacy laws and to regularly review AI outcomes. By combining education process transparency inclusive development and continuous improvement the guidance seeks to prevent bias in AI although it does not explicitly state that bias mitigation is intended specifically for certain groups.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Guidance suggests developers and deployers to ensure recordkeeping and documentation of AI lifecycle (Pg 13; Recordkeeping). It further recommends an AI model card detailing model purpose data sources  training methodologies performance metrics and potential biases. (Pg 26; Model Efficacy) and recommending technical bias audits (Pg 25; Model Efficacy). All the stated aspects are intended exclusively for developers and deployers to identify measure and mitigate sources of bias from data-related factors to model audits.

items.title: Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand
items.justification: This Charter demonstrates a commitment to ensuring New Zealanders have confidence in how government agencies use algorithms. This Charter is one of many ways that government is demonstrating commitment to Retain human oversight by: Nominating a point of contact for public inquiries about algorithms providing a channel for challenging or appealing of decisions informed by algorithms clearly explaining the role of humans in decisions informed by algorithms. (Human Oversight Pg 3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Charter has a special commitment towards promoting and retaining human oversight by: a) nominating a point of contact for public inquiries about algorithms b) providing a channel for challenging or appealing of decisions informed by algorithms and c) clearly explaining the role of humans in decisions informed by algorithms.( Human Oversight Pg 3).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: The Guidance dedicates a section to explain about the 'Human-in-the-loop decision-making' aspects highlighting two scenarios with one of them being if an AI system is helping to make big decisions like those about money health or the law a person should always be involved. The level of human involvement will likely depend on the risk associated with those decisions or the cost of harm of a ‘wrong’ decision. This can range from having a human consistently make the final decision (informed by an AI output) or having human oversight over particularly high-risk or low-confidence AI results. (Human-in-the-loop decision-making Pg 29).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Guidance shares 'Human-in-the-loop decision-making' aspects highlighting two scenarios with one of them being if an AI system is helping to make big decisions- a person should always be involved. The level of human involvement will likely depend on the risk associated with those decisions or the cost of harm of a ‘wrong’ decision. This can range from having a human consistently make the final decision (informed by an AI output) or having human oversight over particularly high-risk or low-confidence AI results. (Human-in-the-loop decision-making Pg 29).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: On p.29 the doc recommends that for high-stakes domains explicitly mentioning decisions about health and law a person should always be involved (“human-in-the-loop”) and contrasts this with low-risk uses where “human-out-of-the-loop” may be acceptable. However it does not set a strict rule prohibiting full automation across defined “sensitive sectors” (eg law enforcement) and instead frames human involvement as a risk-based governance recommendation rather than a categorical ban.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Guidance does not explicitly specify who holds the obligations; however it underscores that humans should ultimately remain responsible in situations where human-AI interactions influence decisions about individuals or groups (Human-in-the-loop decision-making Pg 29). It also highlights the importance of maintaining human-in-the-loop mechanisms particularly in managing feedback from AI use ( Feedback and complaints Pg 19) and ensuring that recordkeeping and oversight of gen AI within an organisation remain under human control (Recordkeeping Pg 39).

items.title: Algorithm impact assessment user guide (New Zealand)
items.justification: This Algorithm Impact Assessment User Guide forms part of the Algorithm Impact Assessment (AIA) process and documentation prepared by Stats NZ to help government agencies meet their commitments under the Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand(the Charter) (p. 4). It is designed to facilitate informed decision-making about the benefits and risks of government use of algorithms and how it affects people (pp 13 20). Adopting a responsible approach to the development and use of algorithms and AI systems is a key contributor to innovation rather than something that stifles or blocks it. The guide takes a risk-based approach intended ensure agencies can use algorithms to provide better services (p. 4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document provides reasons for the Algorithm Impact Assessment (AIA) process noting that at a societal level poorly governed algorithmic and AI systems can amplify inequality undermine democracy and threaten both privacy and security (pg 8). It discusses situations in which bias occurs and its impact on societal bias (pg 36) as well as how unfair outcomes of AI can reinforce existing societal stereotypes (pg 40). The document offers discussion prompts on ethical considerations for identifying people impacted by algorithms (pg 20). However it does not mention assessing the impact of AI on the environment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The guide does not offer obligations to developers or users however it recommends a risk-based process requiring an initial threshold assessment and if warranted a detailed AIA questionnaire and report; designed to identify assess and address risks such as bias privacy human rights impacts unfair outcomes and societal harms. It also recommends that AIA process is best completed by involving a diverse and multi-disciplinary range of inputs from people with a wide range of knowledge skills and experience (p12) including from privacy legal and security domains. (p13). The guide encourages making AIA reports or summaries accessible to the public to help them understand and scrutinize the potential impacts of algorithms and AI p. 59

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: The MBIE Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses advises New Zealand organisations to apply structured risk management and impact assessments at all stages of the AI lifecycle (pp. 11-14). It encourages businesses to identify assess and mitigate privacy and stakeholder risks using international standards and tools such as Privacy (p23) and Stakeholder Impact Assessments (p11). The guidance highlights the need for clear documentation record keeping (p 13) and ongoing monitoring to ensure transparency and accountability. It promotes a context-driven approach supporting responsible and trustworthy AI use in the private sector.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The guidance promotes a risk management approach to mitigate ethical legal operational reputational and technical risks. It recommends engaging with Maori communities to manage and understand AI's impacts especially regarding Maori data or services affecting Maori (p28). It advises collecting and processing data ethically to respect rights protect privacy and safeguard reputation (p22). It emphasizes paying special attention to potential bias in training data when model outputs and decisions directly impact individuals (p17). It recommends businesses to conduct cost-benefit analysis including any intangible or indirect costs the organisation may be interested in for example potential environmental impact while considering AI(p3 7).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The guidance recommends developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive impact assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals including Maori communities and society. It recommends businesses use structured risk management processes (p12) such as stakeholder impact assessments and risk inventories throughout the AI lifecycle to proactively spot document and address risks like bias discrimination privacy breaches (p17). The guidance also points to existing toolkits and international standards including Privacy Impact Assessments (p23) & the Stats NZ Algorithm Impact Assessment (p12) as practical resources for fulfilling these. However there are no assigned obligations to do so.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand
items.justification: This Charter demonstrates a commitment to ensuring New Zealanders have confidence in how government agencies use algorithms. This Charter is one of many ways that government is demonstrating transparency and accountability in the use of data. However it does not fully address important considerations such as Maori Data Sovereignty as these are complex and require separate consideration (Pg 3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: While the Charter commits agencies to transparency by requiring plain English documentation and public disclosure of information about the algorithms it stops short of mandating a central government-wide public registry or inventory of all AI systems. It commits signatories to take a particular focus on those algorithmsthat have a high risk of unintended consequences and/orhave a significant impact if things do go wrong particularlyfor vulnerable communities (Pg 1). The focus is on making information about individual algorithms and decision processes available rather than creating an overarching inventory or registry.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The Charter does not specify the key type of information of a high risk AI system but it instead commits signatories to take a particular focus on those algorithms that have a high risk of unintended consequences and/or have a significant impact if things do go wrong particularly for vulnerable communities (Pg 1). The Charter also recommends govt agencies to make information about the data and processes available (unless a lawful restriction prevents this) and publishing information about how data are collected secured and stored but it does not mention about making results of impact assessments public. (Pg 3).

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The Charter does require agencies to maintain transparency by making information about algorithms and underlying data available to the public “unless a lawful restriction prevents this”. (Pg 2). However it does not spell out clear operational criteria or step-by-step guidelines for distinguishing between information that must be disclosed and information that should remain confidential for security or privacy reasons. The Charter leaves it to each agency to determine what lawful restrictions apply in each case.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: Under the section 'TRANSPARENCY' agencies are required to: maintain transparency by clearly explaining how decisions are informed by algorithms and provide plain English documentation of the algorithm. (Pg3).

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (New Zealand)
items.justification: NZ Responsible AI Guidance covers the Procurement Framework which is flexible and can accommodate the fast-paced innovative nature of generative AI. This flexibility depends on following procurement best practice and incorporating adequate risk assessment and mitigation in the organisation's procurement plan. The guide mentions several domestic and international best practice guides for procuring AI. The guidance shares current NZ Government Procurement website Rules Principles and Charter in line with government policies to help guide the process on any procurement projects in general and also with regards to generative AI. (Pg 15-17).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The document partially addresses AI-specific procurement: it recommends that procurement teams conduct thorough market research on generative AI suppliers and offerings considering reputation capability pricing contract value supply chain risks and ongoing management (Pg 15-16). It encourages agencies to address every phase of the procurement cycle and align procurement with Government Procurement Rules and Principles. However while these guidelines go beyond traditional IT procurement and touch on ethical and risk considerations they remain primarily best-practice recommendations rather than enforceable requirements. (Pg 16-18).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: New Zealand’s Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with confidence
items.justification: The Strategy document identified lack of AI skills as a barrier to AI adoption after research and consultation. It cites a 2024 Datacom State of AI Index: AI Attitudes in NZ survey which identified skills shortage as a major barrier for respondents with 43% of non-users specifically citing lack of expertise as their main reason for not adopting AI (Pg 12). To address this in the public sector a few initiatives launched by the Government Chief Digital Officer include AI masterclasses for leaders and foundational courses for public servants reflecting a strong commitment to integrating AI across government operations.(Pg 12).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The document describes government-supported efforts to address AI workforce skills shortages (p.12). Budget 2025 allocates funding for tuition and training subsidies STEM education and student enrolments helping individuals transition into higher-level study or employment. It also highlights training initiatives by businesses and government including MBIE-supported mentoring programs and AI masterclasses and foundational courses for public servants aimed at strengthening AI-related skills across the workforce.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: The guidance is for private sector and is applicable to AI systems and dedicates a section to model efficacy outlining that models can be evaluated for safety issues such as prompt stereotyping encoded bias (Pg 25-26). Model safety assessment methods mentioned include penetration testing red teaming threat modelling and audits (Pg 25-26). The guidance advocates for a secure-by-design approach to ensure both physical and digital resilience protecting against attacks and supporting reliability and consistency in operations (Pg 14). By aligning with international best practices agencies are encouraged to rigorously test and secure AI systems to maintain safety & public trust throughout their lifecycle.?
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The document recommends organisations to explore opportunities to experiment safely via ‘AI sandboxes’ where AI systems can be tested in a way that is isolated from real-world operations (Pg 7). Suggests stakeholders involved through internal discussions decide what the AI system should do design how it works select the right training data as and/or testing and improving the system (Pg 17). The document also suggests to make sure AI systems work properly they should be tested often and actively monitored (Pg 25). Additionally in order for the systems to operate under conditions it suggests establishing success metrics and thresholds to evaluate the model against and monitor performance over time (Pg25).

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The guidance suggests businesses who may be using Maori data can avoid its misuse or exploitation with appropriate safeguards consultation and cultural considerations (Pg 24). It suggests a secure-by-design approach to support physical and digital resilience protecting against attack and enabling reliability and consistency in system operations (Pg 14). In the model efficacy the doc recommends developers building and developing AI models to be mindful of exactly what they want it to do. (Pg 25). While the document does address safeguards it does not include fall back procedures or emergency protocols explicitly.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The Responsible AI Guidance recommends that businesses prioritise AI model safety by conducting penetration testing ‘red teaming’ threat modelling and/or audits (pg 26). It also recommends businesses to maintain thorough recordkeeping and documentation supports accountability and helps clarify where and how decisions are made. AI-specific documentation like AI model cards is particularly useful: it allows builders and developers to maintain and communicate key information and enables users and deployers to understand details about model purpose data sources training methodologies performance metrics and potential biases (Pg 13). These measures are recommended throughout the entire AI lifecycle (pg 3 13).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The guidance dedicates a section to IT and cybersecurity recommending a secure-by-design approach to support both physical and digital resilience protect against attacks and maintain reliability and consistency in system operations. It notes that digital datasets and systems including AI can be exploited by malicious actors: attackers may seek to undermine an AI system’s integrity (by deceiving users) disrupt its availability or compromise the confidentiality of training data intellectual property or input data. Recommends steps to mitigate any security or privacy breaches In line with the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Security Framework. (Pg 14).

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for the Public Service: GenAI (New Zealand)
items.justification: The guidance specifically applies to Gen AI in the public sector discusses “GenAI security (Pp 13-15) and reliability (P 21)” emphasizing that new risks including system vulnerabilities misconfigurations and unreliable outputs can affect public sector organizations. The guidance highlights that high-quality representative data and robust ongoing testing are essential to prevent hallucinations and incorrect information (pg 19-20). It also shares examples of scenarios of security and GenAI along with certifications and guidances on securing AI systems (pg 15).
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The guidance calls for appropriate testing maintenance and ongoing governance of AI software to ensure it is secure of high quality and properly supported (Pp 13-15) b) Continuous quality assurance impact and risk assessments and validation that AI models and training data are accurate fair and effective (P12) c) monitoring system performance emphasizing the importance of reliable operation and limiting inaccurate or biased outputs. (p29). While the evidence does recommend testing etc it falls short of setting a performance threshold or benchmark against which to assess the reliability and security of the GEN AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The guidance calls to establish risk assessment frameworks and document processes for identifying and responding to GenAI failures. (Pg 11). It recommends continually assess GenAI use including intended and unintended impacts (Pg 8) and consider to go back to an earlier stage and iterate to produce trustworthy and useful results (pg 40). It also suggests orgs to examine the impact and check all GenAI results to reduce the potential for discrimination/ keep reviewing overtime to make sure biases are not developing. Refer to the AI Lifecycle and ensure rigorous evaluation at all stages of AI development and use. (Pg27)The guidance does not mention about emergency protocols or fallback procedures.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The guidance recommends maintaining data quality and using representative data to help avoid hallucinations. It also advises reliable testing for GenAI results thorough checks to reduce discrimination and ongoing review to prevent the development of bias. Agencies are encouraged to refer to the AI lifecycle ensuring rigorous evaluation at every stage of development and use (Pg 40).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The guidance sheds light on basic security measures that help achieve an acceptable level of risk. The document suggests treating Gen AI like a software system and have key guardrails in developing the strong foundations for Gen AI usage. It also shares resources for security leads (Security risks of Gen AI Pg 13).

items.title: Algorithm Charter for Aotearoa New Zealand
items.justification: The document addresses transparency and explainability through explicit commitments requiring government agencies to clearly communicate how algorithms influence decisions. Under the Transparency commitment agencies are expected to provide plain English documentation of algorithms make information about the data and processes used available and publish details on how data are collected secured and stored (p.3). The Charter also reinforces explainability through human oversight mechanisms including identifying a public point of contact for inquiries and providing channels to challenge or appeal algorithm-informed decisions (p.3). In addition the Charter emphasizes the importance of transparency in maintaining public trust.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes clarity regarding how algorithmic systems operate in order to build public trust. Under the Transparency commitment agencies are expected to provide plain English documentation of algorithms make information about the data and processes used available and publish details on how data are collected secured and stored (p.3). In addition the Charter emphasizes that transparency and accountability are essential to ensuring public confidence in the government’s use of algorithms (p.1). These measures aim to improve public understanding of the purpose data sources and functioning of algorithm-informed decisions.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The Charter promotes transparency and communication about how algorithms influence decisions but does not explicitly require detailed explanations of specific system outputs. Under the Transparency commitment agencies are encouraged to provide plain English documentation of algorithms and information about the data and processes used (p.3). In addition the Human Oversight commitment requires agencies to provide a public point of contact and channels to challenge or appeal algorithm-informed decisions (p.3). While these measures support greater understanding and accountability the Charter does not explicitly require entities to provide case-specific explanations of algorithmic outputs or target high-stakes contexts such as hiring or loan.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The Charter promotes transparency and accountability in algorithm-informed decision-making but does not explicitly establish a formal right for individuals to receive detailed explanations of specific decisions. Under the Transparency commitment agencies are encouraged to provide plain English documentation of algorithms and disclose information about the data and processes used (p.3). In addition the Human Oversight commitment requires agencies to nominate a public point of contact and provide channels to challenge or appeal decisions informed by algorithms (p.3). While these measures can help individuals seek clarification about decisions the Charter does not explicitly create a right to receive individualized explanations.

items.title: Responsible AI Guidance for Businesses: Investing with confidence (New Zealand)
items.justification: The document promotes transparency and explainability by encouraging organizations to clearly communicate when and why AI systems are used and how they influence decisions. It recommends informing users when they interact with AI or AI-generated content and providing information about how systems function including training data sources monitoring practices and performance metrics (pp.18 38). The guidance also suggests labeling AI-generated content documenting risks and mitigation measures and offering channels for feedback complaints or corrections. Additionally it emphasizes that strong governance and oversight should support transparency and explainability to demonstrate responsible and trustworthy AI use (p.9).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The guidance directs businesses to define and communicate their “why” for AI (purpose) before deployment ensuring alignment with legal and ethical standards. It further recommends that organisations disclose when AI is used explain how outputs are generated and document system design data origins and decision logic as part of the AI Transparency Checklist (Pg 27 38; Transparency Checklist). The checklist operationalises this by requiring detailed disclosure on system purpose dataset sources model performance identified risks governance measures and feedback mechanisms to promote transparency.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The guidance assigns clear responsibilities to developers and users of AI systems to provide meaningful explanations of outputs (Pg 18;  Transparency). It promotes transparency by requiring businesses to disclose when AI influences outcomes explain how and why those results occur and maintain documentation of data inputs model logic and decisions.(Pg 13; Recordkeeping). This aligns with the Privacy and Human Rights Acts to ensure fairness non-discrimination and accountability in AI deployment. (Pg 9-10 Compliance and Legal Obligations).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Law No. 2022-59 (16 December 2022) on the protection of personal data as amended by Law No. 2023-31 (4 July 2023) (Niger)
items.justification: The law allows individuals affected by AI or automated processing to seek redress. The data subject (the person impacted) must first raise the issue with the data controller (Art.107). If the issue is unresolved or causes harm the same individual may file a complaint with High Authority for the Protection of Personal Data (HAPDP) which can investigate and order correction or erasure of data (Art.15 p.12; Art.69; Art.108). Decisions based solely on automated processing can be challenged (Art.51–52). The individual may appeal to the Conseil d’État or seek judicial or urgent remedies (Arts.109–110).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: HAPDP (High Authority for the Protection of Personal Data/ Haute Autorit de Protection des Donnes caractre Personnel)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law is not AI-specific and does not create new AI-focused courts/mechanisms. However it reinforces judicial remedy for harms from automated processing (incl. AI) by guaranteeing an effective judicial remedy where rights under the law are violated and allowing urgent summary proceedings for serious/immediate violations (Art.110). It also provides an appeal route to the Council of State against HAPDP sanctions/decisions (Art.109) and allows complaints to HAPDP for harm from automated processing (Art.108).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The law creates a state-based non-judicial complaint mechanism via HAPDP. HAPDP is established as the national data protection authority (Art.2; Art.6 - 8) and its missions include receiving “claims…petitions and complaints” on personal data processing and informing complainants of follow-up (Art.15). For AI-related grievances the law expressly covers automated processing or AI (Art.51–52; Art.57) and allows complaints where a person is harmed by automated processing (Art.108).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law does not require companies or AI developers to set up a dedicated AI grievance mechanism but it does require accessible channels to handle data-subject claims or requests (which can cover AI harms involving personal data). Individuals must submit complaints or claims to the Data Controller first (Art.107). Controllers must indicate the service or person through whom the right of access is exercised in filings (Art.30) and must designate a personal data protection officer or correspondent (Art.79–80). No incentives are provided.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
items.justification: The NAIS addresses AI literacy mainly under Pillar 3: Accelerating AI Adoption and Sector Transformation (pp. 38-43) and its Guiding Principles (p. 29). It calls for increasing AI literacy among stakeholders (Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41) and empowering citizens with the knowledge and skills to engage with AI (p. 29). It mandates a comprehensive AI skills development programme including teacher training (p. 41). Across the strategy it stresses building national AI capacity urging skill development (p. 35) warning of AI literacy shortages (p. 36) and setting a goal to expand AI professionals within five years (p. 34).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The NAIS only partially addresses curriculum reform across education levels. It proposes a comprehensive AI skills development programme and teacher training to embed AI concepts into learning including curriculum reform and reskilling initiatives (Strategic Pillar 3 Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41). It also seeks to improve the public education system (p. 35) and emphasizes tertiary education through AI Centres of Excellence and the EduAI Hub (Sec. 1.1.3 p. 15). However while tertiary reforms are explicit there are no specific provisions for distinct primary or secondary curriculum reforms.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: Under Pillar 2 (Strategy 2.3.2 p.37) the NAIS calls for the creation of AI Centres of Excellence (CoEs) at local universities to develop industry-specific AI solutions train next-generation AI talent and nurture skilled professionals. It also mandates developing AI-driven training and education systems to expand diverse AI talent (Pillar 3 Strategy 3.3.1 p.41). The strategy references existing initiatives like National Centre for Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (NCAIR)  and the EduAI Hub at the University of Lagos confirming tertiary-level implementation within Nigeria’s AI ecosystem.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The NAIS explicitly includes teacher training and resource provision for AI education. It mandates a comprehensive AI skills development programme with a specific focus on teacher training (Strategic Pillar 3 Sec. 3.3.1 p. 41) to embed AI concepts into learning. This aligns with the broader goal of building a digitally competent workforce (Introduction p. 14) and improving the public education system. While resource provision is implied rather than detailed teacher tra

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
items.justification: Page 50 of the strategy identifies misinformation as one of the societal risks associated with AI systems and further provided that strategies should be developed to mitigate each risks including misinformation in page 53. But does not specifically address AI- facilitated misinformation and violence
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The strategy focuses on mitigating known AI vulnerabilities that facilitate misuse by acknowledging the risk of 'misleading models' and systems being easy to 'mislead and manipulate with variations in input' (Section 1.6.1 Page 48). The overarching AI Risk Management Framework (Objective 5.1 Page 46) is the mechanism intended to prevent or mitigate the amplification of these risks but it lacks direct provisions for hate speech harassment or violence (p.50- 52).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The strategy addresses the underlying issues that facilitate gender-based harm but lacks a specific explicit provision against the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence. Objective 4.2 (P. 45) mandates establishing a legal framework that protects human rights and fundamental freedoms. Furthermore Objective 4.1 (P. 44) mandates an AI Ethics Assessment Framework designed to address ethical implications including bias and discrimination which are the recognized root causes of such harm. These measures provide a high-level preventive foundation against gendered misuse but the strategy lacks a dedicated measure specifically targeting the harassment and violence manifestation of the harm.

items.title: Nigeria Data Protection Act
items.justification: Where the existence of automated decision-making including profiling the significance and envisaged consequences of such processing for the data subject and the right to object to and challenge such processing (section 27). Any data subject whose rights have been violated through automated processing may present a complaint with the National Commission (section 46) seek compliance and enforcement orders (sections 47 48) institute civil proceedings for damages (section 51) and invoke the right to human review of automated decisions (section 37). Data controllers and processors found in violation are subject to administrative fines (section 49).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Law does not apply to the processing of personal data carried out by one or more persons exclusively for processing by a competent authority to the extent necessary for national security(section 3).

body.name: Nigeria Data Protection Commission

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: A private right of civil action enabling any data subject harmed by unlawful data processing to institute proceedings before a Nigerian court and seek compensation (section 51). The National Commission can support a judicial review (section 50). The judicial pathway is available but remains confined to data protection violations; there is no dedicated AI judicial mechanism.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The National Commission is primarily a state-based non-judicial mechanism for AI-related grievances (section 46) empowering any data subject or their representative to lodge a complaint with the Commission regarding violations of the Act including those arising from automated processing. The Commission is obligated to investigate complaints and may issue compliance orders (section 47) and enforcement orders (section 48) requiring controllers to cease unlawful processing rectify violations and implement remedial measures.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Data controllers to inform data subjects of their right to lodge a complaint with the national commission (section 27). It covers the automated processing of data; there is no provision in terms of the developer of AI either a specific phase in the cycle of data or the AI lifecycle.

items.title: Nigeria Data Protection Act
items.justification: The law refers to the Rights of the Child Act (section 65) where a child is defined as any person under the age of 18 – they do not have the legal capacity to independently consent to the processing of their personal data (section 31). Consent for processing must be obtained from parents or legal guardians. Controllers must adopt consent verification mechanisms checking if it was given by an authorized adult (section 31). Therefore no data subject including children will be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing including profiling (section 37) with applicable and explicit exceptions. A data privacy impact assessment is also required (section 28).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: This Law does not apply to the processing of personal datacarried out by one or more persons exclusively for the purpose of processing by a competent authority to the extent necessary for national security (section 3).

body.name: Nigeria Data Protection Commission

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Act applies to all personal data processing carried out by automated means (section 2). Children below the age of 18 have no legal capacity to consent to the processing of their personal data and parental or guardian consent is mandatory; data controllers must implement verification mechanisms to confirm such consent has been obtained (section 31). Where automated decision-making including profiling is employed data subjects must be informed of its existence significance and envisaged consequences in a clear format appropriate to the class of data subjects targeted (section 27).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Data controllers targeting children through automated systems must incorporate consent verification mechanisms from adults or guardians into those systems as a condition for lawful operation (Section 31). However the law does not provide explicit provisions regarding design standards or obligations for solutions that use automated data processing before going to market or that operate on continuous processing.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
items.justification: The Strategy promotes a Nigeria-centric approach ensuring local communities provide cultural context and define safety thresholds (p.14). It commits to diversity in AI R&D under the 'Inclusivity and Shared Prosperity' principle (p.28). Art. 4.1.1 establishes a High-Level AI Ethics Expert Group (AIEEG) with diverse stakeholders to guide implementation. Furthermore Art. 4.1.2 mandates the development of National AI Ethical Principles aligned with Nigerian values specifically highlighting decoloniality humanity inclusion and solidarity.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The strategy promotes AI that reflects Nigeria’s social and cultural diversity explicitly noting that “replicating Nigeria’s social context and cultural diversity with AI tools… will drive AI accessibility across education agriculture healthcare and other sectors” (Pillar 3 p.38) and reinforcing this in Section 3.1 Drive Locally-led AI Innovation (p.38) which reiterates that locally-led solutions should mirror Nigeria’s social context. Its Vision/Guiding Principles (p.28) commit to inclusivity and representation in AI research and deployment. However while cultural diversity is well covered in principle the document does not explicitly require support for a wide range of languages nor does it set concrete enforceable measures.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The strategy contains explicit measures to prevent cultural bias its Guiding Principles call to “actively promote diversity and representation in AI research development and deployment” (p.28) and Pillar 4: Responsible & Ethical AI Development requires ethical principles addressing fairness non-discrimination and decoloniality to counter dominance of foreign or majority cultures (p.44). The strategy also flags the risk of biased non-representative systems (pp.37 - 38). However while cultural protection is explicit the document does not separately or clearly mandate measures to prevent the erasure of linguistic diversity so language inclusion remains implicit rather than explicitly required.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
items.justification: The National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS) explicitly addresses the environmental impact of AI focusing on Green AI carbon footprint and energy efficiency across multiple sections. Page 5 outlines under Pillar 1 has one of its aims as building AI infrastructure with 'reduced carbon footprint and improved energy efficiency” Pages 31 and 32 detail strategies for deploying energy-efficient AI powering clusters with clean energy (less than 50% grid reliance).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) and the AI Governance Regulatory Body (Pillar 5 Objective 512 pp 4546) However in practice the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) working through the National Centre for AI and Robotics (NCAIR) is currently coordinating activities aligned with the Strategy (see ecosystem/delivery actors on p 16 and the high-level Roadmap for Implementation on p 59)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy promotes energy efficient AI infrastructure but does not cover all the listed elements. It:targets improved energy efficiency and clean energy for AI infrastructure (1.4.2 Pillar 1 outcomes p.32). encourages powering AI clusters with clean/renewable energy (Strategy 1.1.3). However the document does not explicitly mention  (i) advanced cooling technologies or (ii) water consumption (e.g. WUE) in the context of data centres. Hence it only partially satisfies the criterion.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 (Nigeria)
