items.title: Law that typifies and punishes the creation dissemination and use of deepfakes and manipulated content
items.justification: The draft law addresses AI-facilitated misinformation by criminalising the creation and distribution of deepfakes and digitally manipulated synthetic content. The motive of the law describes risks such as reputational harm deception sexualised non-consensual content and threats to public order caused by AI-generated media. Article 4 defines deepfakes and manipulated content while Articles 5–8 establish penalties for producing sharing or using AI-generated falsified images audio or video to harm or mislead individuals.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The draft seeks to prevent the use of AI tools to produce or spread harmful synthetic media. The justification highlights risks such as deception harassment reputational damage and violence facilitated by deepfakes. Articles 5–8 criminalise creating distributing or using AI-manipulated content directly targeting the misuse of such tools for misinformation or harm.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: It offers partial protection through criminal penalties for perpetrators. Again in articles 5 to 8 it establish offenses enabling victims to pursue criminal action against individuals who produce or distribute deepfakes causing harm. However the law does not create explicit victim rights protection mechanisms or remedies against platforms nor does it outline procedures for redress beyond criminal prosecution. It will be executed throughout the criminal justice system.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The draft references risks such as sexualised non-consensual deepfakes and digital gender-based violence produced through manipulated images and videos. In articles 5 to 8 penalise the creation and distribution of such content which directly contributes to preventing AI-generated gendered harassment and abuse even though gender-specific terminology is not isolated in the articles themselves.

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: Chapter II establishes enforceable rights for persons affected by AI systems including the right to information and explanation (Arts. 5 7 8) the right to challenge AI decisions with legal/significant effects and correct underlying data (Art. 9) and the right to request human intervention or review (Art. 10). Art. 6 allows enforcement before competent administrative bodies and courts (individual or collective). Chapter V establishes liability and full reparation for AI-caused harm including objective liability for high-risk/excessive-risk systems (Arts. 27–29).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The draft partially addresses this question by recognising liability and the right to reparation without creating enforcement mechanisms specific to AI-related harms. Article 27 establishes the right to full reparation of damages caused by AI systems including strict liability for high-risk and excessive-risk systems and reversal of the burden of proof in other cases. However the draft doesn't establish specialised judicial mechanisms dedicated AI tribunals or specific procedural reforms to enforce these rights. Article 6 allows individuals to pursue rights before competent administrative bodies and courts but doesn't include specific remedy provisions.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The draft bill refers to the possibility of seeking redress before competent administrative bodies in cases of harm caused by AI systems (Art. 6) indicating the use of state-based non-judicial avenues. However it does not establish a dedicated AI ombuds regulator or complaint mechanism nor does it set out detailed procedures for handling AI-related grievances. Article 32 further provides that the Executive Branch shall designate a competent authority including functions such as the registration of high-risk AI systems but the structure mandate and complaint procedures of such authority are to be defined only after the law’s approval and regulation

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: In articles 19 & 20 the draft requires internal administrative structures & processes. Chapter VI article 30 allows codes of good practice including complaint-related procedures but it does not mandate a standardised grievance mechanism for all private deployers.

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: The Draft Law explicitly includes the right to non-discrimination and the right to the correction of discriminatory biases in AI systems (Art. 5). It also refers to transparency explainability and human oversight ensuring that AI systems operate fairly and ethically. These principles align with the UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) the MERCOSUR Declaration on Human Rights in AI (2024) and the Paraguayan Constitution which guarantees the right to equality and non-discrimination.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Although it does not addresses specific groups it partially addresses fair and equitable outcomes by requiring non-discrimination bias correction and risk mitigation measures. Article 5 establishes the right to non-discrimination and to the correction of discriminatory biases in AI systems. Articles 19(c) 20(b) & 21(c) and 24 require data management algorithmic impact assessments and transparency to prevent discriminatory or disproportionate effects.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: It includes explicit provisions to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying discrimination. Article 5 recognizes the right to non-discrimination and to the correction of discriminatory biases (direct indirect illegal or abusive). Article 12 prohibits the use of AI systems that cause discrimination based on race ethnicity gender sexual orientation age disability religion or political opinions. Articles 19(c) 20(b) & 21(c) require bias-mitigation and data-management measures but enforcement mechanisms remain undefined.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: It assigns obligations to developers and deployers to identify and mitigate bias but not to measure it systematically. Articles 19(c) 20(b) require adopting data-management measures performing tests to prevent discriminatory biases and ensuring human supervision of high-risk systems. Article 24 mandates algorithmic impact assessments to detect and mitigate discriminatory effects. However it lacks detailed or continuous bias-measurement requirements across all AI lifecycle stages so coverage is partial.

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: The draft law addresses human oversight and determination through some provisions: In 3(c) it establishes human participation in the AI lifecycle and effective supervision. In 5(d) it recognises the right to human participation and determination in AI-based decisions affecting individuals. In 7 (d) & 8 (e) concern information and explanation rights requiring disclosure of the role of AI and humans in decision-making but do not themselves impose oversight obligations. In 9–11 require human review and final human determination where AI decisions produce significant irreversible or legally relevant effects. Finally arts 20–21 impose concrete oversight documentation and override obligations only for high-risk AI systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The draft law explicitly promotes meaningful human control supervision and accountability as core principles (Art 3(c & j). It guarantees human participation and determination in AI-assisted decisions through rights to explanation challenge human intervention and final human determination particularly where decisions have significant or irreversible impacts (Arts. 5(b & d) 8(e) 9–11). For high-risk AI systems the framework mandates human oversight mechanisms enabling operators to understand system behavior detect anomalies avoid automation bias override outputs or stop system operation altogether (Arts. 20–21).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The draft includes explicit limits on full automation in sensitive sectors that are considered high-risk. For instance regulates remote biometric identification in public security to cases with prior judicial authorisation preventing autonomous operation. It require human review intervention and final human determination for decisions with significant or irreversible impacts directly limiting automation in areas such as law enforcement and health-related high-risk applications (article 16 & 17).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The draft law assigns accountability to providers and operators requiring internal structures to ensure security and traceability across the AI lifecycle (Art. 19). For high-risk systems it mandates effective human oversight enabling designated personnel to intervene override or interrupt operations (Arts. 20–21). However it lacks an explicit requirement to designate specific individuals who are ultimately accountable for the system's final decisions.

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: The draft introduces algorithmic impact assessments as a mandatory obligation for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems (art. 13 & 22). It requires developers and deployers to conduct ex-ante assessments identifying potential risks to fundamental rights safety and public interests including risks related to data quality bias discrimination and misuse (Chapter IV). These assessments must document the intended purpose data sources risk mitigation measures and residual risks and be updated through continuous monitoring during deployment. The bill also links impact assessments to transparency auditability and human oversight obligations (Arts. 17–26) establishing a preventive risk-based approach to AI governance.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: It promotes proactive risk management by requesting ex-ante algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems including the identification of risks to fundamental rights safety bias/discrimination data quality and the definition of mitigation measures with ongoing monitoring obligations (Chapter IV; Arts. 17 to 26). However the framework doesn't require assessments of environmental impacts nor does it mandate a unified societal & ethical impact methodology applicable to all AI systems. As such it addresses key elements of proactive risk management but not all dimensions referenced in the statement.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The evidence will assign binding obligations once adopted to developers providers and deployers of AI systems to conduct algorithmic Impact Assessments for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems. These assessments must identify potential risks to fundamental rights safety bias discrimination data quality and misuse define mitigation measures and be subject to monitoring and updates throughout deployment (Arts. 1718 & 22 to 26).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: It seems that public access to assessment findings is only partially addressed. The draft includes transparency and information obligations that indirectly support public accountability such as requiring documentation of risks mitigation measures and auditability for high-risk AI systems and granting affected individuals rights to information and explanation (Arts. 5 7 to 10 & 22 to 26). However it doesn't establish a general right for the public to access or request the findings of algorithmic Impact Assessments nor does it mandate publication of assessment summaries or a public AI register.

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: Although the draft framework could not be considered as thorough regarding this indicator Article 17 (c) includes among High-Risk AI those systems that could be use within the employment sector to hire recruit select filter and evaluate candidates. It also includes AI-powered systems to manage employees and access to employment. As a consequence of this classification such systems are subject to the mandatory obligations applicable to high-risk AI systems established in Articles 19 onwards.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: It does not include specific provision related to the topic; however it does classifies AI-powered systems used in employment sector to hire promote or evaluates employees as High-risk (art. 17(c)). It does include some provisions to apply to those considered high-risk AI systems though but in general not specifically.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: The draft addresses AI safety and security through a risk-based regulatory approach. It classifies AI systems into prohibited high-risk & excessive-risk categories & establishes differentiated obligations accordingly (See chapter III; Arts. 14 to 18). For high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems it requires compliance with security accuracy robustness data quality human oversight monitoring & traceability obligations as well as the adoption of mitigation measures to prevent harmful or unsafe outcomes (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26). Certain AI practices are prohibited due to unacceptable risks reinforcing preventive safety safeguards (See art. 14).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The draft bill requires accuracy robustness data quality and continuous monitoring for high-risk and excessive-risk AI systems (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26) which function as qualitative reliability requirements. However it doesn't define explicit quantitative performance thresholds or standardised quality benchmarks nor does it set measurable accuracy or reliability metrics applicable across systems.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The draft requires risk mitigation measures human oversight monitoring and traceability for high-risk & excessive-risk AI systems (Chapter IV; Arts. 19 to 26) which can function as safeguards to reduce harm. It also restricts or prohibits certain uses based on risk (Art. 14). However it doesn't mandate fallback procedures shutdown mechanisms or emergency response protocols for system failures or unexpected behaviour nor does it specify standardised incident-response processes.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The draft requires technical documentation risk classification and pre-deployment obligations for high-risk & excessive-risk AI systems including documentation of system characteristics data quality mitigation measures and ongoing monitoring (Chapter IV; Arts. 19–26). These requirements imply elements of testing and validation prior to deployment. However the framework doesn't explicitly mandate standardised pre-deployment testing protocols or validation benchmarks applicable across the AI lifecycle nor does it prescribe detailed testing methodologies.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Draft Bill 'which Regulates the Development Implementation and Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems' (Paraguay)
items.justification: The draft law addresses transparency and explainability through multiple obligations. Article 1 and 2(h&j) includes transparency and explainability as a guiding principle. Articles 5(b) 7(abei) 8(albc)–11 (pp. 12–16) grant rights to prior information clear explanations of automated decisions human review and non-discrimination. Articles 19–21 (pp. 22–24) require transparency in AI deployment disclosure of system logic documentation public consultations and publication of evaluations. Article 35 (p. 29) mandates a public database of high-risk AI systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: It includes several provisions requiring clarity about AI systems’ purpose data sources and decision-making logic. Article 7 (b) obliges providers to disclose the system’s purpose types of decisions operators involved and (c) categories of data used. Article 8 guarantees the subject`s right to require explanations of the logic (a) criteria factors and data that influenced an automated decision (c). Article 20(e) mandates information on how the model works and the criteria used to generate outputs supporting public trust.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The draft assigns some obligations to provide meaningful explanations of AI outputs. Article 5(b) grants a right to explanation for any AI decision. Article 7 requires disclosing automated decision-making system purpose human roles and data used. Article 8 impose obligation to providers to explain logic criteria and factors influencing a specific decision. Article 20(e) mandates information enabling interpretation of model results especially for high-risk systems.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The draft establishes rights to explanations. Again article 5(b) grants individuals the right to an explanation of any AI decision that affects them. Article 7 requires prior information on automated decision-making system purpose human roles and data categories involved. Article 8 mandates explanations of the logic criteria data sources and main factors influencing a specific outcome ensuring individuals can understand how the decision was reached.

items.title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
items.justification: he Law defines digital literacy as a continuous process of acquiring and developing essential digital skills for functioning in digital environments including for studying working accessing goods and services socializing and exercising citizenship (Art. 6). It further establishes digital literacy as a guiding principle for AI-based systems emphasizing the need to promote skills connected to the design development implementation and use of AI (Art. 7). Art. 13 also introduces the National Digital Talent Platform (coordinated by the SGTD) which explicitly includes the use of AI to develop student competencies under the National Basic Education Curriculum aiming to prepare students for the digital future by promoting equality and cl

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Law includes guiding principles one of which is digital literacy which highlights the need to promote the development of skills related to the design development implementation and use of AI-based systems (Article 7). This principle gives rise to a specific obligation for educational institutions which is to “implement study programs aimed at developing AI skills” in coordination with the National Authority (Article 13). The obligations apply to schools colleges and universities. According to Art. 6(f) the AI education is “promoted at all stages of a person's development” meaning it covers primary secondary and tertiary levels.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The Law includes guiding principles one of which is digital literacy which highlights the need to promote the development of skills related to the design development implementation and use of AI-based systems (Article 7). This principle gives rise to a specific obligation for educational institutions which is to “implement study programs aimed at developing AI skills” in coordination with the National Authority (Article 13). However there is no mention to the creation of institutions within the formal education system and the reference on the programs is very vague.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Law states that the Ministry of Education is responsible for 'promoting the responsible ethical transparent and inclusive use of AI for the development of student skills within the framework of the National Basic Education Curriculum with the aim of preparing students for the digital future by promoting equality and closing gaps. It also promotes the training of teaching staff in AI and digital technologies for their pedagogical use in public and private educational institutions' (Article 13).

items.title: Supreme Decree 115-2025-PCM (Peru)
items.justification: The law establishes that there are “Misuses of AI” which are prohibited in all cases. One such misuse is when an AI-based system is used to: 'Deceptively or manipulatively influence people's decision-making especially when: using subliminal or deliberately deceptive techniques or exploiting vulnerabilities with the aim of affecting a person's ability to make conscious and informed decisions; it exploits the cognitive emotional or socioeconomic vulnerabilities of specific individuals or population groups in order to substantially modify their behavior; and it misleads or manipulates information through an AI-based system to affect people's decision-making autonomy.' (Article 23)

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Yes Article 4 of the law expressly states that the provisions do not apply to the use of Artificial Intelligence-based systems for national defense and security.

One such misuse is when an AI-based system is used to: 'misleads or manipulates information through to affect people's decision-making autonomy'. Article 24 (Use of high-risk AI-based systems) then establishes that AI-based systems shall be considered “high risk” when these systems perform assessments of children and adolescents in the education sector. It should be noted that the regulation establishes specific obligations for high-risk systems.

In addition AI-based systems that are used “to analyze classify or infer sensitive data about individuals based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their racial or ethnic origin political opinions union membership religious or philosophical beliefs sexual life or sexual orientation” are prohibited (Article 23).

Since it only covers the preliminary phase but not the entire system life cycle the document is considered to only partially address this area.
