thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: AI systems used for recruitment promotion performance evaluation and termination are explicitly classified as high-risk triggering mandatory bias mitigation and non-discrimination obligations (Annex III (4)). Training datasets must be examined and corrected for biases that could produce discriminatory such as employments outcomes (art. 10). Risk management systems must identify and mitigate foreseeable discrimination risks throughout the AI lifecycle (art. 9) incluidng the human oversight obligations for AI systems used (art.14).

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Deployers must ensure sufficient transparency for individuals such as workers to understand system functioning and limitations (Art. 13) (Annex III(4)). Deployers must notify individuals such as workers subject to AI-assisted employment decisions (art. 26). Workers may request an explanation of AI-influenced employment decisions (art. 86). Technical documentation requirements ensure that performance monitoring systems are documented and auditable (art. 11 Annex IV). Deployers must monitor system performance and report anomalies affecting workers (Art. 26).

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: National Programme to Promote the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Slovenia by 2025 (NpAI)
items.justification: The National Programme addresses public procurement through Strategic Objective 4 specifically Section 6.4 (Page 35) which focuses on deploying AI reference implementations in the public sector. The document explicitly states that standard procurement procedures are often too rigid for AI and therefore promotes 'innovation public procurement' (Measure 4.2 Page 38) to foster an agile environment. To implement this the programme utilizes specific instruments detailed in Table 4 (Page 62) and Appendix 3 (Page 90) including Pre-commercial procurement (PCP) for R&D services and Public Procurement of Innovative Solutions (PPI) for deploying mature technologies.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Public Administration and the NpAI Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: Measure 4.2 (Page 38) explicitly recommends 'promoting innovation public procurement' because 'standard public procurement procedures... are often not suitable' for AI due to its complexity and the need for agile verification. It calls for using instruments like 'Public Procurement of Innovative Solutions (PPI)' that go beyond traditional 'lowest price' criteria. However while it mandates these new approaches and establishes a broader ethical framework in Strategic Objective 8 (Page 51) it does not explicitly detail a specific new set of 'procurement guidelines' or checklists within the document itself.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Objective 8 (Page 51) sets the goal of ensuring 'safety' and 'fairness' as part of a trustworthy AI framework. Specifically Measure 8.1 (Page 52) calls for 'Establishing an appropriate environment for the verification of the operation of AI systems' and developing 'certification mechanisms'. While this establishes the objective for such testing and certification to be available and likely required for public use the document does not explicitly phrase this as a direct clause requiring vendors to demonstrate this in the current procurement text.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: Strategic Objective 7 (Page 49) and Strategic Objective 8 (Page 51) explicitly list 'transparency' 'explainability' and 'traceability of decisions' as key components of the national AI strategy. Measure 8.1 (Page 52) aims to develop mechanisms to ensure these properties. Although the strategy clearly prioritizes eliminating 'black box' risks through these 'Trustworthy AI' standards it does not explicitly contain a procurement mandate compelling vendors to disclose specific data/models in the text provided.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: A core motivation of the programme is to 'accelerate the transfer of domestic knowledge... into products' (Strategic Objective 1 Page 29) and to 'initiate a spiral of supply and demand in selected key sectors of the national economy' (Introduction). Measure 4.2 (Page 41) promotes 'innovation public procurement' explicitly to allow the public sector to act as a 'first customer' thereby reducing risks for the domestic private sector and stimulating the local AI innovation ecosystem.

items.title: National Programme to Promote the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Slovenia by 2025 (NpAI)
items.justification: The framework addresses public sector skills under Strategic Objective 4 (p. 35). SO4 focuses on providing quality public services and increasing administrative efficiency with Point 4 specifically detailing 'Digital services of public administration' (p. 38). Implementation is driven by measures on p. 41. Measure 4.1 mandates professional training programmes (seminars courses) for development teams from the public sector. Measure 4.8 ensures ethical capacity by supporting education and awareness of the 'legal and ethical aspects of AI development and deployment' for public sector employees (p. 41).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Public Administration and the NpAI Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: While Strategic Objective 2 (p. 30) focuses on general workforce AI literacy and upskilling Strategic Objective 4 (p. 35) and Measures 4.1 to 4.9 (p. 41) provide a specific government-wide mandate for the public sector. Measure 4.1 explicitly targets 'professional training programmes' for public sector teams while Measure 4.8 (p. 41) focuses on the 'legal and ethical aspects of AI' for public administration employees ensuring a foundational understanding of risks. Additionally Point 4 of SO4 (p. 38) emphasizes the digital transformation of public servants through these enhanced skills. However they do not include members of the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The NpAI foresees the establishment of governance and coordination structures for AI implementation including inter-ministerial coordination key stakeholders and the creation of a National AI Observatory (SO10). These mechanisms support expert guidance and coordination but do not explicitly establish designated “AI champion” roles within each authority. Relevant references include Sections 6.10 and 7.3 on governance structure and coordination mechanisms

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The NpAI strongly emphasises lifelong learning continuous skills upgrading and adaptability to rapid technological change. It explicitly links AI deployment to continuous education and competence development across the innovation lifecycle including public administration. However it does not introduce binding obligations such as mandatory periodic recertification or annual training requirements for public servants or judiciary members. Relevant discussion appears under SO2 and the implementation plan sections

items.title: National Programme to Promote the Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Slovenia by 2025 (NpAI)
items.justification: The NpAI explicitly addresses workforce adaptation under Strategic Objective 2 (SO2): 'Education and strengthening of human resources.' It outlines measures to support 'lifelong learning' and 'reskilling' for employees to acquire AI-related skills (Measure 2.9). It aims to 'prevent the digital divide' by funding training programs for those whose jobs are threatened by automation. Specifically Measure 2.10 focuses on 'Forecasting future skills needs' to align training with market demands. The strategy also supports 'Digital Innovation Hubs' (DIHs) to act as intermediaries for SME workforce training.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Public Administration and the NpAI Steering Committee

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: Measure 2.9 ('Support for lifelong learning and career redirection') specifically aims to fund training for employees to adapt to technological changes. Measure 2.3 and 2.4 focus on integrating AI into vocational and adult education. The document explicitly mentions using EU funds (Recovery and Resilience Facility) to subsidize these 'reskilling' efforts for the workforce to prevent unemployment due to automation.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The NpAI (and the associated Recovery Plan) provides funding for the programs themselves (making them free or subsidized) effectively incentivizing participation (Measure 2.9). However it does not explicitly detail direct financial stipends or 'paid leave' mandates specifically for the workers attending AI training in the private sector beyond the general subsidization of the training costs.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The NpAI encourages and 'supports' companies to train staff (via subsidies and awareness raising) but it does not impose a mandatory legal requirement (a 'mandate') for private companies to invest their own funds or set aside specific budgets for AI retraining to mitigate displacement.  It provides for a public call to finance employee AI training programmes (Measure 2.9 pp. 71 87) targeted support for professional training of development teams in companies and the public sector (Measure 4.1 pp. 41 76) funding for management awareness programmes on the advantages and risks of AI deployment (Measure 4.2 pp. 41 77) and a broader focus on education and strengthening human resources across the economy (Strategic Objective 2 p. 30).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Safety and security is core to the Act. It establishes a risk-based framework for risk identification and mitigation (Art. 9) oversight measures (Art. 14) and robustness and accuracy requirements (Art. 15). To ensure ongoing safety the Act mandates technical documentation and record-keeping (Arts. 11–12) and in certain high risk situations a conformity assessment procedure prior to market placement (Art. 43). Post-market obligations in Arts. 72–73 require providers and deployers to monitor performance report serious incidents and take corrective action. For GPAI models posing systemic risks Arts. 55–56 impose additional safety and cybersecurity duties including model evaluation and risk mitigation following the Code of Practice.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

Recital 24 explains that this exclusion is due to Art. 4(2) of TEU which notes that national security remains the sole responsibility of Member States but that if a defense or security system is used outside this scope then it temporary would fall within the regulation.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must achieve adequate levels of accuracy robustness and cybersecurity functioning throughout their entire lifecycle including metrics stated in the instructions for use avoiding performance degradation over time and serving as benchmarks (Art. 15). Technical documentation for high-risk systems must include performance metrics and test results ensuring that the systems function for their intended purpose and without unacceptable risks (Art. 9). For GPAI with systemic risk providers must perform model evaluation using standardized protocols and tools and document it (Art. 55(1)(a)). The Code of Practice for GPAI provides a way for providers to meet those safety and performance expectations.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Systems must be interpretable enough for operators to detect anomalies and unexpected behavior in real time (Art. 14). Technical redundancy solutions including backup or fail-safe plans are mandated for systems operating in continuous learning contexts Art. Post-market monitoring must report serious-incident defined timeframes activates emergency response and response mechanisms (art. 72 73).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Providers must test high-risk AI systems throughout development using pre-determined metrics and protocols (art.9) plus an extensive technical documentation covering system design training processes and testing results (art.11) before placing them on the market. Pre-deployment conformity assessment is mandatory with third-party involvement required (Arts. 43–47). Adversarial testing before deployment is required for general-purpose AI model providers (Art. 53). Post-deployment monitoring plans must be established before launch ensuring lifecycle validation continuity (Art. 72). For GPAI with systemic risk: Perform model evaluation adversarial testing and documentation also applies for GPAI with systemic risk (Art. 55).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI must be technically robust against attempts to alter system use outputs or performance through adversarial manipulation data poisoning and model evasion attacks (Art. 15). Specially for the resilience mechanisms for systems operating in dynamic environments are required covering adversarial input scenarios (Art. 15). For general-purpose AI with systemic risk adversarial testing must be conducted to identify security vulnerabilities before deployment ensuring a level of cybersecurity for the model and infrastructure (art.55). Post-market monitoring must detect security incidents emerging operationally and report to the authorities (Art. 7273).

items.title: EU AI Act
items.justification: Articles 11 12 and 13 establish several transparency and documentation obligations for AI developers and deployers. High-risk AI systems must include clear information on their capabilities limitations and intended purpose (Art. 13) and providers must maintain comprehensive technical documentation and automatic logging to ensure traceability (Arts. 11–12). These measures enable deployers to better understand the systems and authorities to audit or investigate when necessary. There are disclosure obligations that require notification when individuals interact with AI systems particularly chatbots and emotion recognition tools (Art. 50). Also for general-purpose AI in terms of model documentation and summary of training data (Art. 53).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: High-risk AI systems must be designed to enable deployers to understand system outputs and use them incluiding the purpose performance levels known limitations and input data specifications (Art.13). Technical documentation asks a detailed description of the elements of the AI system such as disclose development methodology training data characteristics and tecniques system architecture design choices and performance testing results making decision-making logic accessible to regulators (Art.11 Annex IV). General-purpose AI providers and generate synthetic AI system content need to be published as technical documentation (Art.50 53). It is mandatory to register in the EU public database before deploying the high-risk AI (Art.49).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Providers of high-risk systems must provide deployers with technical information to help them understand the outputs and use it properly (Art. 13). For many uses and essential services like credit deployers must inform people and on request give a clear explanation of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 26 Annex III); incluiding explanation requested by affected by high-risk AI systems decision made. Employment and credit are explicitly identified as sensitive domains requiring heightened transparency (Recital 58).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The individuals must be notified by deployers when high-risk AI systems are used in decisions affecting them (art.26). Any affected person subject to a decision which is taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed with exceptions which produces legal effects or significantly affecting their health safety or fundamental rights have right to obtain from the deployer explanations about the role of the AI system decision-making procedure takeb and main element (art.86).

items.title: Law No. 5 of 2023: Data Protection Act (Somalia)
items.justification: The Act includes the 'Right Not to Be Subject to Automated Decisions' (cited as one of the rights of a data subject in the articles. 20-23). This right mandates that individuals can request human intervention and an explanation if a decision significantly affecting them is based solely on automated processing (AI/algorithms). The second point formal complaint (Remedy Mechanism): The Act through Article 35 grants the 'Right to Lodge a Complaint' with the established Data Protection Authority (DPA). The DPA is mandated to investigate and enforce compliance providing the non-judicial remedy path for individuals whose rights including the right to challenge an automated decision have been violated.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 5 (3) (Exemptions) page 8 states: ' the law does not apply to processing of personal data' when carried out by competent authorities as 'necessary for national security' or for 'the prevention and investigation of crimes by public authorities national security and the prevention and defense of a legal claim. The Data Protection Authority (DPA) is explicitly mandated to comply with directions from the President and Cabinet in the interests of 'national security public order and the defence of the Federal Republic of Somalia' (Article 6 (4)(b)).

body.name: Data Protection Authority

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The act establishes the legal foundation for seeking redress in the judicial system but lacks specific provisions to reinforce those mechanisms for complex AI harms. The act covers aspects of Judicial Remedy where individuals harmed by automated decisions can seek compensation and remedy through the formal court system (article 40 page 28). The act is not covering establishing specialized courts or judicial panels with expertise in algorithmic harm. Also not shifting the litigation procedure burdens from the individuals harmed by automated decisions to the automated decisions' deployer.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Law No. 5 of 2023: Data Protection Act (Somalia)
items.justification: The Act establishes the Right to object (Art. 22) and the Right not to be subject  to a decision based solely on automated decisions (Art. 23) including profiling when these produce legal or significant effects. Art. 22(1) allows data subjects to object to processing that causes substantial unwarranted damage or distress or violates Art. 23. Per Art. 22(2) controllers must cease processing unless public interest or legitimate grounds outweigh the damage. Additionally Art. 2 defines 'Data processing' as any collection storage or disclosure of personal data by electronic means. These provisions directly address human oversight and determination and provide a clear mechanism for redress.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Art. 5(3) the law does not apply to data processing by competent authorities for national security or the prevention investigation and prosecution of criminal offences.

items.title: Law No. 5 of 2023: Data Protection Act (Somalia)
items.justification: The act addresses AI through Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) in Article 29 (p. 24) mentioning controllers must provide a systematic description of envisaged processing and evaluate necessity and proportionality. Article 23 (p. 20) regulates automated processing and profiling. Article 30 (p. 26) mandates prior consultation with the Data Protection Authority before deployment to ensure algorithmic accountability.

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 5 (3) (Exemptions) page 8 states: ' the law does not apply to processing of personal data' when carried out by competent authorities as 'necessary for national security' or for 'the prevention and investigation of crimes by public authorities national security and the prevention and defense of a legal claim. The Data Protection Authority (DPA) is explicitly mandated to comply with directions from the President and Cabinet in the interests of 'national security public order and the defence of the Federal Republic of Somalia' (Article 6 (4)(b)).

body.name: Data Protection Authority

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The data protection act (2023) addresses several components of proactive risk management but does not explicitly cover all the specific dimensions (especially environmental impacts). Article 29 (p. 24): Mandates a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for processing activities 'likely to result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject.' This requires a systematic evaluation of risks before deployment. Article 30 (p. 26): Requires prior consultation with the Authority if a DPIA indicates high risks that cannot be mitigated forcing a proactive ethical check.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Article 29 (p. 21): Mandates that a data controller of major importance must carry out a 'data protection impact assessment' prior to any processing that is likely to result in a 'high risk to the rights and freedoms of a data subject' due to its nature scope context or purposes. Article 29(4) (p. 22): Specifies that the assessment must identify and mitigate risks by including an assessment of the 'risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects' and the 'measures envisaged to address the risks. While the Act focuses heavily on individual rights (Article 3 p. 6; Article 29 p. 21) it does not explicitly list broader 'societal' or 'environmental' impacts as mandatory components of the impact assessment beyond the constitution.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: In the background section of the Framework it emphazises that it 'addresses the need for capacity building and economic development by promoting AI education and training programmes.' (p.1). The first strategic pillar of the framework is entitled 'Talent Development / Capacity Development' and is aimed at ensuring that South Africa has a robust AI talent pool which includes 'incorporating AI into the educational curricula from basic education to tertiary levels.' (p. 9 pillar 1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.justification: In order to ensure that South Africa has a robust AI talent pool the framework calls for : 'incorporat[ing] AI into the educational curricula from basic education to tertiary levels.' (p. 9 pillar 1).

items.title: Protection of Personal Information Act (No. 4 of 2013) (South Africa)
items.justification: Chapter 3 provides conditions for the lawful processing of personal information and ‘processing' is defined as 'any operation or activity or any set of operations whether or not by automatic means concerning personal information.' (Section 1). Section 74 read with Section 73(1) provides that a person can submit a claim to the Information Regulator for non-compliance with certain provisions of the Act including Chapter 3 which will be investigated by the Regulator. A settlement may be reached according to Section 80. But if an investigation conducted by the Regulator concludes that there has been non-compliance then individuals may institute a civil action for damages in terms of Section 99.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 6(1) of the Act specifically provides that: 'This Act does not apply to the processing of personal information—a)by or on behalf of a public body—i)which involves national security including activities that are aimed at assisting in the identification of the financing of terrorist and related activities defence or public safety...'

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: South Africa’s National AI Policy Framework explicitly includes a strategic pillar called “Promotion of Cultural and Human Values' (section 6.12.) Strategic pillars of this AI Policy are the fundamental components or key areas of focus that support and drive the implementation of the policy’s goals and objectives. They serve as the core framework around which the policy is structured providing clear guidance and direction for its development (pg. 9). Related is the pillar on Fairness and Mitigating Bias (section 6.9)  which provides -'Inclusive Data Sets: Ensure AI systems are trained on diverse data sets representing all demographics.'
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: South Africa’s National AI Policy Framework explicitly includes a pillar called “Promotion of Cultural and Human Values'  (see section 6.12.). Adding that the aim is 'to align AI development with societal values.' (pg. 11).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The Framework provides that for 'Inclusive Data Sets: Ensure AI systems are trained on diverse data sets representing all demographics' as a component of the Fairness and Mitigating Bias Pillar but does not assign specific obligations or responsibilities to an entity. Pillar 9 page 11)

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: The AI Policy framework integrates guidelines for ethical AI development including to ensure that AI systems are 'designed to promote fairness while mitigating biases'(p. 1) as well as 'discrimination' [p. 12] This is emphasized in two of the strategic pillars (fundamental components/key focus areas that support and drive the implementation of the policy's goals and objectives). Pillar 5 on 'Ethical AI Guidelines Development' provides for ethical development and deployment 'addressing issues which include bias [and] fairness' (p. 10). Pillar 9 is dedicated to Fairness and Mitigation Bias to 'ensure equitable AI development.' This includes developing methods to identify and mitigate biases in AI systems and inclusive datasets (p. 11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: While the framework does not mention biased results disproportionally affecting certain groups it does promote fairness and bias mitigation to 'ensure equitable AI development' and mitigate discrimination risks (page 11 and 12).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: While the framework does not address preventing 'perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics' it does call for bias mitigation in the design of AI systems as well as ensuring that  'AI systems are trained on diverse data sets representing all demographics' (pillar 9 p. 11). It also acknowledges under the Transparency and Explainability pillar (pillar 8) that 'biases can unintentionally be amplified in AI systems due to skewed training data or inherent biases in algorithms.' (p. 10)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: At this stage it is just a framework for policy development but the ultimate policy will apply to developers and will require the development of methods to identify and mitigate biases in AI systems and ensure AI systems are trained on diverse datasets representing all demographics 9 p. 11). The policy however does not address the lifecycle of AI in this context.

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: The AI Policy framework 'emphasizes the importance of human-centered AI ensuring that AI applications augment human decision-making rather than replace it'. (p. 1). This is especially captured in Pillar 10 - pillars are fundamental components/key focus areas that support and drive the implementation of the policy's goals and objectives - on 'Human Control of Technology (Human Centered Approach in AI Systems) and requiring 'Human-in-the-Loop Systems: Ensure critical AI decisions involve human oversight (especially in Generative AI)' and developing 'frameworks for AI decision-making that prioritize human judgment.' (p. 11)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The framework does not make specific provision for  'critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications' but does provide that human control has to be maintained over AI systems (pillar 10 p.11) and that 'AI applications [should] augment human decision-making rather than replace it.' (p. 1)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: While the document does not specifically mention 'public sector skills development' it applies to both the private and public sectors. items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

It has two components: 1) Cybersecurity Measures: Implement robust cybersecurity protocols to safeguard AI systems; 2) Risk Management: Develop frameworks to identify and mitigate risks associated with AI. (p. 10)

The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: South Africa National Artificial Intelligence Policy Framework
items.justification: The AI Policy framework is aimed at establishing robust data governance frameworks that sets standards for AI transparency and explainability (p. 1). This is emphasized in a strategic pillar for Transparency and Explainability (Pillar 8): 'Explainable AI: Promote the development of AI systems that provide clear understandable outputs (The ability to understand and interpret how AI systems arrive at their decisions or conclusions)' which includes principles of trust and acceptance accountability and bias detection and mitigation and insight and improvement; ' Transparency: The clear and open operation of AI systems ensuring that their processes decision making criteria and outcomes are understandable and accessible...' (p.11).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Pillar 8 on Transparency and Explainability promotes 'the clear and open operation of AI systems ensuring that their processes decision making criteria and outcomes are understandable and accessible to users and stakeholders including insights into model functionality data usage decision logic and potential impacts' to build public trust in AI. (p10-11)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The framework does not reference any high-stakes contexts but does require that AI systems are developed that provide clear understandable outputs and that 'Explainability enables developers and organizations to be accountable for the actions and outcomes of AI systems.' (Pillar 8 p.10).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The framework does not explicity establish a right but does note that Explainable AI builds trust and acceptance: 'Users and stakeholders are more likely to trust and accept AI systems if they can understand how decisions are made' and provides for ''Public Awareness Campaigns: Educate the public on AI technologies and their implications.' (Pillar 8 p. 10-11).

items.title: Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust (South Korea)
items.justification: Article 3(4) requires that national and local governments create policies that help all people “adapt stably” to social economic cultural and daily-life changes brought about by AI implicitly requiring public AI education. Article 13(2)(6) authorizes the government to conduct education and awareness-raising projects to improve public understanding of safe AI development safe use and proper usage practices. Article 29(4) requires polices for the promotion of education and public campaigns for a secure and trustworthy AI society. Article 26(3) assigns the Korea AI Promotion Association to conduct “education and promotion of the development and use of safe and reliable AI” making AI literacy an explicit national goal.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4(2) states that “This Act shall not apply to AI developed and used solely for national defense or national security purposes as prescribed by Presidential Decree.” This means that while the Act applies horizontally across all civilian sectors including industry economy and government it carves out an exception for military and security-related AI systems.

items.justification: The core discussion regarding deepfakes is found in Article 31 (Obligation to Secure Transparency) page 20. Paragraph 3 specifically targets outputs that are 'virtually indistinguishable from reality.' Providers must clearly notify or label such content so users are not deceived. The law balances this by allowing 'flexible' labeling for artistic or creative works to avoid ruining the viewer's experience provided the user is still made aware. While the Basic AI Act sets high-level rules the specific technical methods for how to label these deepfakes (e.g. visible watermarks vs. metadata) are detailed in Article 22 of the Enforcement Decree (which is not available in English).

items.title: FRAMEWORK ACT ON INTELLIGENT INFORMATIZATION
items.justification: The Act meets the minimum threshold as it explicitly covers AI through its definition of “intelligent information technology” including technologies that perform learning reasoning and decision making (Art. 2(4)(a)). Article 63(1) requires rapid and fair remedial measures for user complaints and damage as well as systems for compensation and protection of rights. These apply to “intelligent information services” thereby covering AI enabled systems. Article 19(3) further provides avenues for petitions and mediation. While no AI specific procedural rights are set the Act establishes a general framework for complaints remedies and dispute resolution applicable to AI satisfying the indicator at a baseline level.

items.title: Guidelines for the protection of children's and adolescents' privacy
items.justification: The guidelines explicitly regulate AI-enabled services including conversational systems such as AI speakers chatbots and similar devices noting that they do not unfairly collect children’s personal information and that inappropriate content is not provided to children (p. 40). It also suggests limiting profiling-based services and requirements to implement protective measures where automated processing may negatively affect children (p. 41) and restrict the use of behavioral data for personalized advertising targeting children under 14 noting the need for prior consent and in many cases complete avoidance (p. 35) and discourage the use of manipulative “nudge” techniques that could exploit children’s decision-making (p. 36–37).

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

Article 1 (p. 1) frames the Act around protecting “human rights and dignity” and Article 3(2) (p. 4) requires providing “meaningful explanations” to affected persons. Article 27(1) (p. 17) establishes ethical principles such as safety reliability and accessibility yet omits fairness or equity. It mentions safety and risk-management obligations in Articles 32–34 (pp. 20–21) and the impact-assessment requirement in Article 35(1) (p. 22) but it does not mention bias and non-discrimination. Chapter 2 Article 6 (5): 'Measures for establishing a foundation of trust ensuring the fairness transparency accountability ..

However this obligation applies only to the ten categories of high-impact AI specifically defined in Article 2 (p. 2).

This exemption is explicitly stated in Article 4(2) (p. 4) of the Act which specifies that the Act does not apply to such AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act promotes meaningful human control over AI through several provisions: Article 34 (p. 21) requires human management and supervision of high-impact AI systems; Article 31 (p. 20) mandates transparency and Article 32 (p. 20) requires safety measures to allow human evaluation and intervention; Article 35 obliges impact assessments for high-impact AI ensuring risks are identified and addressed.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The Act addresses the prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors by designating certain high-impact AI applications under Article 2 (p. 2) where decisions significantly affect human life safety or fundamental rights. These sectors include energy supply drinking water management healthcare operations medical devices nuclear facilities biometric analysis employment and loan screening transportation systems public administration decisions and student evaluations as well as other areas prescribed by Presidential Decree. In these critical domains Article 34 (p. 21) requires human supervision risk management transparency and accountability.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Act establishes the assignment of responsibility in Article 36 (p. 22) which requires AI business operators domestic and foreign to designate a domestic representative if their operations affect the Korean market. This article also implies that a responsible individual within the organization must oversee high-impact AI systems intervene when necessary and be accountable for AI-generated decisions ensuring compliance with transparency safety and risk management obligations and reinforcing human oversight in sensitive or high-risk areas.

items.title: Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust (South Korea)
items.justification: The Act addresses impact assessments primarily through Article 35 (Impact Assessment of High-Impact AI). This provision requires business operators who develop or use designated high-impact AI systems to conduct AI impact assessments to evaluate potential risks including those related to safety reliability and social or ethical implications.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 4 (Scope of Application) states that the Act shall not apply to AI developed and used solely for national defense or national security purposes. That means that the defense and national security uses of AI are functionally outside the scope of the Basic Act excluding them also from the impact assessment provisions in Article 35.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment

Article 35(1) (page 21) covers mandatory pre-deployment impact assessment (fundamental rights). Article 32(1) (page 20) addresses risk identification assessment and mitigation across the lifecycle. Article 34(1) (page 21)  covers the risk management plan for high-impact AI. However environmental impact assessment is not included.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Act explicitly requires developers and users of high-impact AI systems to conduct comprehensive impact assessments under Article 35. These assessments must identify potential risks to individuals society and public interests and require operators to implement appropriate mitigation measures before deployment.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

Article 2(7) defines an “AI business operator” to include government agencies engaged in business related to the AI industry (p. 3). Accordingly Articles 30 and 31 require transparency and disclosure when AI systems are used including informing users when they interact with AI and clearly labeling AI-generated content (pp. 19–20). In addition where government systems qualify as high-impact AI Articles 33–35 require prior review and impact assessment to ensure safety rights protection and accountability (pp. 20–22).

Article 6 requires that the Basic Plan include measures for “training professional talent” and establishing a foundation for developing and utilizing AI. Article 21 mandates that the Minister of Science and ICT “train and support AI and AI technology expert talents” to advance AI technology and the AI industry and allows the government to recruit and support overseas AI experts. Together these provisions form the legal basis for Korea’s AI-related reskilling upskilling and talent-development policies.
