As noted in a previous question the key measures include AI literacy programs targeting girls underrepresented groups and rural populations (Annex 1; Action 1.2.11; p. 8) national literacy and gender parity targets (Annex 2; Target 2.1; p. 26) and women-centric scholarships for AI and data science (Annex 2; Target 2.11 p. 26). While these initiatives enhance access and skills they fall short of mandating direct hiring or representation measures within the AI industry itself.

items.title: Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) No. 9 of 2022 (Sri Lanka)
items.justification: The Act addresses human oversight primarily through ex post review and appeal mechanisms. Section 18 (pp. 11–12) grants data subjects the right to request a review of decisions based solely on automated processing implying human intervention. Section 19 (pp. 12–13) establishes a right to appeal such decisions to the Authority which can investigate and determine their lawfulness with further appeal to courts. Schedule V (pp. 58–59) requires transparency about automated decision-making. Additionally Section 33 (pp. 29–31) empowers the Authority to regulate automated decision-making and ensure compliance.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Data Protection Authority of Sri Lanka

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Act supports elements of meaningful human control through ex post human review mechanisms. Section 18 (pp. 11–12) allows data subjects to request review of decisions made solely by automated processing implying human intervention. Section 19 (pp. 12–13) provides appeal mechanisms to an Authority and courts. Transparency obligations (Schedule V pp. 58–59) further support oversight.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Act assigns accountability to entities (controllers/processors) and requires oversight roles such as the designation of a Data Protection Officer (Schedule V pp. 58–59 reference to contact details where applicable). It also mandates controllers to comply with obligations (Section 4 p. 3) and enables regulatory oversight by the Authority (Section 33 pp. 29–31). However it does not specifically require designated individuals to oversee or intervene in AI system decisions nor explicitly link accountability to AI-specific decision-making processes.

items.title: Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) No. 9 of 2022 (Sri Lanka)
items.justification: The Act addresses impact assessments through a privacy-centric framework applicable to AI systems that process personal data. Section 24(1) requires controllers to conduct Personal Data Protection Impact Assessments prior to high-risk processing including profiling and systematic monitoring. These assessments must identify risks of harm to data subjects and specify mitigation measures and safeguards and must be updated where there are changes in technology or methodology (Sections 24(2) and 24(4) p. 18). Section 25 obliges controllers to mitigate identified risks before processing and where risks remain to consult the Authority which is empowered to require additional safeguards or the cessation of processing.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Data Protection Authority of Sri Lanka

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Section 24(1) requires controllers to conduct personal data protection impact assessments prior to high-risk processing including profiling systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas or telecommunication networks or other processing determined by rules based on scope and risk (p. 17). Subsection (2) requires these assessments to identify mitigation measures and safeguards. Section 25 further obliges controllers to mitigate identified risks before processing and where risks remain to consult the Authority which may require processing to cease (pp. 18–19). However these provisions are limited to risks to data subjects’ rights and do not require the assessment of broader societal ethical or environmental impacts of AI systems.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Section 24(1) partially addresses this by assigning obligations to controllers to conduct Personal Data Protection Impact Assessments prior to high-risk processing including profiling and systematic monitoring or other processing determined by rules based on scope and risk (p. 17). These assessments must identify risks of harm and specify mitigation measures and safeguards (Section 24(2) p. 18) and controllers are required to mitigate identified risks before processing with regulatory consultation where risks remain (Section 25 pp. 18–19). However these provisions are limited to risks to data subjects’ rights and don’t require comprehensive impact assessments identifying and mitigating potential risks to individuals and society.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
items.justification: Initiative 2.2 of Annex 1 underscores that when developing the AI Playbook for the public sector to drive government AI adoption it must include “procurement guidelines that favour open-source and open-standards technology while also limiting vendor lock-in” (p. 16). Additionally the finance pillar of the operational model of the National Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) is responsible for “managing contracts and procurement processes to support AI project implementation” (Appendix B10 p. 84).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The document partially addresses AI-specific procurement beyond traditional IT procurement. Initiative 2.2 of Annex 1 requires the public sector AI Playbook to include procurement guidelines that favour open-source and open-standards technologies and limit vendor lock-in reflecting AI-specific technical and strategic considerations (p. 16). In addition responsibility for managing AI-related procurement is assigned to the NCAI (Appendix B10 p. 84). However the document does not specify ethical or social procurement requirements such as bias and fairness assessments transparency of data and models or accountability and monitoring obligations which are not yet detailed.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: Initiative 2.2 of Annex 1 notes that the AI Playbook for the public sector must include “procurement guidelines that favour open-source and open-standards technology while also limiting vendor lock-in” (p. 16). While this indirectly relates to reducing dependency on foreign vendors the document does not include provisions that prioritise local AI developers or outline mechanisms to promote AI sovereignty. It also lacks anti-competition safeguards or local-first procurement requirements.

items.title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
items.justification: The evidence addresses public sector skills development under Section 1.2 of Annex 1 which sets out a series of preliminary initiatives aimed at public sector training and competency development (pp. 6–7). For instance it outlines concrete actions to build AI capacity among civil servants including AI awareness courses and AI project design and management training for senior officials (Actions 1.2.1–1.2.2 p. 6). It further proposes updating the Digital Government Competency Framework (DGCF) and defining AI and data competencies for public sector roles (Actions 1.2.3–1.2.4 p. 7). The annex also includes training for the judiciary and relevant regulatory agencies on responsible AI regulation and governance (Action 1.2.6 p. 8).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: Initiative 1.2.5 of Annex 1 outlines the development of a “data and AI skills roadmap to guide the implementation of skills development initiatives for the public sector on data-driven decision-making and responsible public sector transformation through AI” (p. 7). Additionally Initiative 1.2.6 notes that training programs will be developed for the “judiciary and relevant regulatory agencies on Responsible AI Regulation and Governance leveraging existing online resources (including MOOCs)” (p. 7).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: Initiative 1.1.13 of Annex 1 recommends updating the Digital Government Competency Framework to include a “functional job profile for a Data Officer to be introduced in every government organization to oversee data collection management and sharing in compliance with the requisite laws and governance standards” (p. 6). Additionally section 2.2 of Annex 4 underscores the designation of “principal champions” within each agency who would advocate for the principles provide guidance and conduct internal audits to ensure principle alignment (p. 90).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document includes multiple provisions that support ongoing professional development and continuous training. Initiative 1.2.15 of Annex 1 proposes designing and implementing an “AI Ethics certification program for public and private sector professionals” (p. 9). Section 6.2 of Annex 4 further recommends developing “role-specific AI training modules for different levels of government officials” establishing “mentorship programs pairing AI experts with government departments” and conducting “regular AI workshops and seminars for continuous learning” (p. 98).

items.title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
items.justification: On page 54 of Annex 3 as part of the immediate setup and functions of the National Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) capacity building and talent development are identified as a key pillar outlining efforts to “establish AI learning pathways” with a focus on up-skilling the current workforce and integrating AI modules into higher education. Initiatives 1.2.16 and 1.2.17 mention the launch of a “Data and AI Skills Development Fund” to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives alongside data- and AI-focused vocational training for professionals affected by job displacement (Annex 1 p. 9). In addition postgraduate AI programs aim to upskill existing professionals with advanced technical knowledge (Annex 7 p. 158).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: On page 9 Initiative 1.2.16 of Annex 1 outlines the launch of a “Data and AI Skills Development Fund” to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives. This is a long-term initiative to be undertaken by the NCAI the Ministry of Technology (MoT) the Ministry of Finance and industry partners. Progress will be measured based on funding allocations as well as the number of individuals and organizations benefiting from the fund. Further Initiative 1.2.17 introduces data- and AI-focused vocational training programs for professionals at risk of job displacement (p. 9). This will be measured based on the number of AI-focused vocational training programs introduced participant numbers and post-training employment rates.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Initiative 1.2.16 of Annex 1 outlines indicators measuring the amount of funding allocated as well as the number of individuals and organizations benefiting from the Data and AI Skills Development Fund to support upskilling and reskilling initiatives (p. 9). This indicates the availability of public financial support for training activities. However the document does not clearly specify the types of financial support that would be provided to workers to enable their participation in AI skills and capacity development programs.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: On page 9 Initiative 1.2.17 of Annex 1 aims to introduce a “Data and AI-focused vocational training programs for professionals at risk of job displacement”. This is a long term initiative that would be undertaken by the NCAI Ministry of Skills Development vocational training institutes and Industry partners. This will be measured based off the number of AI-focused vocational training programs conducted number of participants and post-training employment rates.

items.title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
items.justification: The trust and safety pillar of the National Center for Artificial Intelligence (NCAI) seeks to ensure the responsible development and use of AI through legal and ethical oversight (Appendix B9 p. 83). Its mandate includes developing AI governance frameworks monitoring compliance and managing risks associated with AI deployment. Safety and security are further operationalised through performance metrics with KPIs on accuracy reliability system uptime and stability (Annex 6 pp. 118–119; Annex 7 pp. 142–143). Annex 7 additionally introduces a system-specific AI development lifecycle requiring rigorous testing to ensure functionality and accuracy prior to deployment (p. 136).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Section 7.2 of Annex 11 sets a clear benchmark requiring deployed language models to “achieve a benchmark accuracy rate of 95% on standard language processing tasks within the first year post-deployment (p. 203).

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The evidence includes provisions related to safeguards and mitigation procedures in the event of AI system failure or unexpected behavior. For instance Section 5.4 of Annex 4 outlines risk-mitigation measures such as developing “redundancy systems and robust backup solutions” to address system downtime (pp. 95-96). It also requires agencies to “implement safeguards and monitoring mechanisms to detect and address emerging risks' (ibid).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Section 3.1 of Annex 7 outlines the second stage of a system-specific development lifecycle for AI which “focuses on creating the actual AI models and the accompanying software system” (p. 136). Data engineers would prepare and manage the data with AI scientists developing and training the models and finally the software engineers building the application framework. As a last step this phase would include “rigorous testing to ensure functionality and accuracy before deployment” (ibid). While this confirms a requirement for pre-deployment testing the document does not specify detailed testing protocols or stress-testing procedures.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Sri Lanka's National Strategy on AI (July 2024 - Draft Strategy for Public Consultation)
items.justification: On page 19 Action 3.4 of Annex 1 states that an AI Governance Framework must be developed in line with Sri Lanka’s AI governance approach addressing harm disclosure impact assessments transparency risk mitigation human oversight and redress mechanisms. Annex 4 further notes that government agencies are to use AI to enhance efficiency transparency and accessibility for improved public service delivery (p. 86). It emphasises that trustworthy and transparent AI is “fundamental to building public trust” and requires robust ethical standards privacy safeguards and security protocols aligned with international frameworks (p. 88). Subsection 9.2 further outlines criteria to ensure transparency in government AI decision-making (p. 102).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: On page 90 subsection 2.3 of Annex 4 states that clear AI transparency guidelines must be developed which could include “AI Fact Sheets” for each deployed system ‘detailing its purpose data sources decision-making process and potential limitations which must be made accessible to the public to foster trust and understanding’. Meanwhile subsection 5.2 emphasizes prioritizing “open-source and open standards technologies to promote interoperability” though this serves as a technical standard rather than a transparency-related provision clarifying how AI systems operate (p. 94). Additionally subsection 9.2 calls for the creation of public registries of AI systems used in government decision-making.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: On page 88 subsection 2.1 of Annex 4 outlines one of the core principles as following a human-centric approach implying that government AI systems must be designed to ‘augment human decision-making and improve efficiency while maintaining human oversight especially in critical areas’. Further subsection 9.2 states that mechanisms must be implemented “to provide citizens with explanations of AI-driven decisions affecting them” (p. 102). However there is no specific provision outlining whether citizens or government employees have the right to request specific data points an AI system used to make a decision about them.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in the State of Palestine
items.justification: The framework addresses the indicator by including a project on “artificial intelligence in culture protecting Palestinian content and natural language processing” (p. 10) thereby linking AI development to cultural context and local content preservation. It also promotes the use of Arabic language processing technologies to enhance accessibility and usability of AI systems in the local context (p. 10). In addition the strategy recognises the role of AI in fostering inclusion noting its potential to “integrate marginalized groups into initiatives that promote human development and self-improvement” (p. 7).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research the Ministry of Entrepreneurship and Empowerment

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in the State of Palestine
items.justification: While the strategy includes broad capacity-building measures across public and private sectors it also contains specific provisions targeting the public sector bringing it within the scope of the indicator. In particular the guidance media and implementation plans explicitly provide for building and developing governmental capabilities and skills in artificial intelligence and supporting exchange programs (pp. 8 11–12 18). In addition the strategy mandates raising awareness of artificial intelligence across all government agencies (p. 9) and emphasizes the necessity of digital transformation within the government sector (p. 5).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research the Ministry of Entrepreneurship and Empowerment

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Policy (Palestine)
items.justification: The framework explicitly identifies the need to “build capacity and adapt to the rapid changes in skills and requirements of the intelligence-based labor market” (p. 3) directly linking AI deployment to workforce transformation. It supports this through measures such as training and education across sectors and levels from foundational skills to lifelong learning (p. 4) and integrating AI and data competencies into the education system including training for teachers and administrators (p. 8). It further calls for reskilling and upskilling in response to labor market changes (p. 10) alongside workshops awareness programs and investment in local talent through scholarships and training (pp. 8 10).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: National AI Team

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
items.justification: The law serves as a pillar to combat manipulation disinformation or violence when it involves the processing of personal data by AI systems: profiling high-risk profiling (Art. 5) high-risk profiling carried out by private entities or any profiling by federal agencies (Art. 6); protection against manipulation and automated decisions (Art. 21); impact assessment (Art. 22); and sanctions (Art. 60). The communication from the Federal Commissioner clarifies that the law is directly applicable to data processing by AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). It states that 'the use of programs that allow the falsification of faces images or voice messages of identifiable people must be indicated.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The communication states that the use of programs that allow the falsification of faces images or voice messages of identifiable individuals must also always be clearly indicated. This is based on Article 6 of the law and appropriate measures to correct erase or destroy data that is incorrect or incomplete with respect to the purpose for which it was collected or processed. The adequacy of the measures depends on the scope of the processing and the risk that the processing entails. Article 21 mandates the provision of information in the case of automated individual decision-making. However there is no preventive measure.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
items.justification: The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. (Art. 21) The data subject may request that incorrect personal data be corrected; an individual can request that a specific data processing activity be prohibited and that the personal data be deleted or destroyed. (Art. 32) A person can view automated decisions they have the right to stop the unlawful processing of the personal data concerned redress the consequences of unlawful processing declare the processing to be unlawful. (Art. 41) While protection in the context of automated decisions is clearly stated a specific connection to redress and remedy in the context of AI is missing. However such connection can be implicitly assumed.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). According to the law article 32 regarding data processing the applicant may also request that any correction deletion or destruction prohibition of processing or disclosure to third parties marking as contested or judgment be communicated to third parties or published. In the public sector (Article 41) any person with a legitimate interest may request the responsible federal agency to remedy the consequences of illegal processing.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The law suggests that companies to have a data protection officer (Art. 10). The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). Article 21 is based exclusively on automated processing in accordance with information obligations. The FDPIC as a complaint or grievance body. (Art. 23 49).  The entity opens an investigation against a federal body or a private individual who must provide all information and documents necessary for the investigation. If the data subject has filed a complaint they must be informed of the measures taken in response and the outcome of any investigation (art. 49 4).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The data protection law applies to AI (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai).  The law suggests that companies establish internal mechanisms to handle complaints for example by appointing a data protection officer (Art. 10). Individuals have the right and companies have the duty to provide information (Art. 19). The data controller must provide the information free of charge. The Federal Council may provide exceptions particularly if the effort required is disproportionate. The information must generally be provided within 30 days (Art. 25). However there is no incentive for accessible mechanisms.

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: Guideline 1: Putting people first (p. 3) states that the use of AI should help improve people's quality of life and sustainably develop our society. Guideline 2: Regulatory conditions for the development and application of AI: AI should help ensure high-quality living standards based on the principles of sustainable development (p. 3). AI offers the potential for economic growth prosperity security and employment as well as for reducing the ecological footprint and energy consumption and this potential should be explored in the best possible way (p. 4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines defined that the AI offers the potential to reduce the ecological footprint and energy consumption and this potential should be explored by developing new business models. Regulatory conditions for digital solutions should be designed in a way that does not hinder innovation and contributes both to greater value creation and sustainable development (p. 4). AI systems must be designed to be safe robust and resilient in order to have a positive impact on people and the environment (p.5).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: Individuals groups and genders must be protected from discrimination and stigmatisation (page 3). The Confederation must ensure well-balanced high-quality data are used or that 'suitable compensatory safeguards' are put in place to counter inherent bias (page 3). The use of AI should actively create equal opportunities for people and 'encourage and facilitate their access to education goods services and technology (page 3). AI applications likely to affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an 'Equality Impact Assessment' (EIA) as a frame of reference in addition to continuous monitoring and safeguards (page 3).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The primary directive is that individuals groups and genders must be protected from discrimination and stigmatisation. The use of AI should create equal opportunities for people and encourage and facilitate their access to education goods services and technology. The Confederation must ensure that well-balanced high-quality data are used or that 'suitable compensatory safeguards' are put in place to counter inherent bias. (page 3) AI applications that are likely to affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an 'Equality Impact Assessment' (EIA) continuous monitoring and appropriate safeguards.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: AI applications that may affect fundamental rights must be accompanied by appropriate technical and organizational safeguards and controls. Therefore individuals groups and genders must be protected against discrimination and stigmatization (p. 3). Generally applicable norms include the prohibition of discrimination and the promotion of equality guaranteed by the Federal Constitution the Gender Equality Law the Law on Discrimination Based on Disability the Swiss Civil Code on the protection of personal privacy the International Covenant on Economic Social and Cultural Rights the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (p.9).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: Preservation of Human Agency: The guiding principle is to prioritize people mandating that Self-determination should be preserved and that individuals must be able to participate in life in an autonomous manner. The role of AI is to complement and enhance human activities and skills. (page 3) Non-Delegation of Responsibility: The framework strictly limits AI's authority under Guideline 4 (Accountability) which explicitly states: 'It must not be possible to delegate responsibility to machines' (page 5) Legal Mandate for Human Review: The Federal Act on Data Protection (FADP) provides the mandatory 'human-in-the-loop' mechanism: Individuals have the right to review automated decision(page 10)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines prioritize human control by establishing that 'It must not be possible to delegate responsibility to machines' (page 5) under Guideline 4: Accountability. In critical decision-making contexts the framework ensures AI remains a tool by granting individuals the right to have any automated decision that significantly affects them 'be reviewed by a natural person' (page 10)  thereby preserving human judgment.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: There are general requirements for AI developers. Civil and criminal law dictates that traffic accidents or medical errors can constitute cases of liability attributed to the use of AI-based software (p. 9). The Data Protection Act plays a key role in terms of profiling AI including health-related data. There are requirements applying to the processing of particularly sensitive personal data related to genetic and biometric data. There is a duty to provide information in the case of automated decision-making and this can be reviewed by the data subject (p. 10). However there are no longer measures for total prevention.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: In the case of an automated decision the data controller must inform the data subject about any decision based exclusively on automated processing when such a decision has legal consequences for the data subject or significantly affects him or her (p.10). So the obligation applies only in case of consequences and advance supervision for intervention.

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: The document's core purpose for mandating Impact Assessment is to achieve proactive risk management and prevent harm across multiple dimensions. The guidelines mandate proactive assessments by requiring that AI applications be designed with 'ethics by design'. This ensures safeguards are integrated from the planning stage to eliminate or mitigate risks early preventing reactive crisis management. Assessments are explicitly required where AI is likely to affect fundamental rights necessitating the upfront evaluation of potential societal harm including discrimination and bias. They demand the tracking and assessing of impact across a broad scope: individuals society the economy and the environment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: In the document it is explicitly stated that AI applications which are likely affecting fundamental rights should be accompanied by an impact assessment. (page 3) Specifically also in Guideline 5 (Safety) it says: 'By adequately tracking and assessing the impact of the use of AI the risks for individuals society the economy and the environment can be identified at an early stage and either eliminated or mitigated.' (page 5) Ethics by design is considered a inherent feature of designing and using AI. (page 3)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly mandates an assessment whenever fundamental rights are at risk. (page 3) It requires developers to integrate risk assessment and ethical considerations into the AI system's design phase making the process itself a tool for proactive risk management mentioning using the principle 'ethics by design'. (page 3)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Federal Act on Data Protection (Switzerland)
items.justification: The document addresses specifically profiling which means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person's performance at work. (Art. 5)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Regarding automated decision-making (Article 21) the data controller must inform the data subject of any decision based solely on automated processing that has significant legal consequences or adverse effects for the data subject. The data subject must upon request allow the controller to express their point of view. The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. However there are no specifications regarding adverse effects such as any type of discrimination.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Concerning automated decision-making (Article 21) the data controller must inform the data subject of any decision based solely on automated processing that has significant legal consequences or adverse effects for the data subject. The data subject must upon request allow the controller to express their point of view. The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person. This does not apply when there is a contract in place and consent for the decision to be automated.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

items.title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
items.justification: The strategy sets parameters for the Federal Administration's digital transformation using AI. It emphasizes that the administration must lead by example and use AI systems in accordance with shared principles including legal/ethical principles ensuring public interest and placing high value on trustworthiness including explainability transparency data protection accuracy. (page 3) The main goal for public disclosure is found under field of action 2 'Earning trust': The expected benefit is that internal and external stakeholders from the general public will 'gain transparency about which Al systems are used in the Federal Administration and how their use is monitored'. The use of AI systems 'must remain traceable'. (page 6)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Digital Transformation Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: The strategy's most direct objective is for the general public to 'gain transparency about which Al systems are used' (page 6) and it includes a non-prioritized goal to maintain a 'comprehensive overview' of systems. (page 10) This fulfills the need for an inventory and public access. However the document does not include an explicit measure that requires public disclosure of all specific key information for high-risk systems such as training data the rationale for use and the results of impact assessments (pages 6 10). It addresses these topics internally but lacks the specific public mandate for all listed elements.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

items.title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
items.justification: The document addresses public procurement of AI primarily by linking it to the overarching core principles for AI use. It includes an unprioritized strategic goal explicitly stating that procurement legislation and organizational principles must 'enable and promote procurement of Al systems in accordance with the principles for the use of Al systems in the Federal Administration' (Appendix page 10). The goal integrates specific requirements into the procurement process namely the core principles (page 3) which mandate that procured systems must be: trustworthy (explainability transparency data protection accuracy); governed by clearly defined responsibilities and accountability across the entire Al system's life cycle. (pages 3 10)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Digital Transformation Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The strategy requires that AI acquisition guidelines go beyond traditional IT but this is not defined (p. 3). Although acquisition legislation and organizational principles allow and promote the acquisition of AI systems in accordance with the principles for the use of AI systems in the Federal Administration this requirement was not prioritized in the current strategy and 'will be evaluated during each sub-strategy review and reprioritized if necessary' (p. 10).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty
thematicElements.justification: The strategy requires that procurement aligns with AI principles and mandates defining the approach to digital sovereignty specifically including open-source requirements  (page 11). However it is only partial because while it connects procurement and sovereignty to high-level principles it lacks explicit provisions that prioritize local AI developments as a concrete strategy to achieve that sovereignty. Also it is related to the governance of the AI system and not directly to procurement.

items.title: Strategy Use of AI systems in the Federal Administration (Switzerland)
items.justification: The document addresses public sector skills development as its dedicated field of action 1: Developing skills (page 4). The strategic objective is to ensure the Federal Administration has the necessary skills and knowledge to competently design and use AI systems (page 5). The primary goal is that employees have access to training and further education programmes on the use of AI that are appropriate to their level and role and that they are prepared for changes resulting from AI use (page 5). New skills are explicitly required in fields such as AI data science law and business management (page 4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Digital Transformation Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document includes a government-wide strategy with objectives for upskilling the public servants (Federal Administration) covering their foundational understanding of AI's use and risks. Specifically field of action number 1: Developing skills mandates access to training and further education programmes to help employees manage risks and gain skills in AI data science law and business management. However the strategy does not include specific provisions measures objectives or recommendations targeting members of the judiciary. (pages 45)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The document includes objectives and mechanisms for assigning expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI through existing roles and interdepartmental structures but it does not include specific provisions for assigning dedicated 'AI champions' or new teams strictly for that purpose. The strategy mandates interdepartmental interdisciplinary coordination structures in place to share experiences (page 5) and relies on internal and external service providers to offer support (page 5 10). It aims for strategic knowledge management (page 10) but lacks the specific provision to create new dedicated roles for this function.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The strategic goal for Field of action 1: Developing skills is that employees have 'access to training and further education programmes on the use of Al that are appropriate to their level and role' (page 5). The term 'further education' directly implies continuous upskilling. The document acknowledges the necessity of staying current by stating the Federal Administration must design its use of AI systems 'in lockstep with technological developments' (page 5). The strategy emphasizes continuous adaptation by stating it has 'no set validity period' because 'Al is developing rapidly' (page 9) and its goals can be 'reprioritised by the Federal Digital Transformation Council in order to respond to advancements in Al technologies' (page 9).

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: The document addresses specifically safety in the context of AI namely Guideline 5 discusses the safety of AI systems and that they have to be designed to be safe robust and resilient. (page 5) Importantly it does not include security.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: AI systems must be designed to be safe robust and resilient in order to have a positive impact on people and the environment. (page 5) The data policy must strike a balance between the protection of privacy and the use of data. It should work towards ensuring that data used for AI applications are of sufficient quality and are documented. (page 4)  Decision-making processesbased on AI should be designed in such a way that ensures that they are traceable for directlyand indirectly affected persons and the mode of action must also be verifiable for experts. (page 4) However no quality limits or parameters were developed.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: AI applications that may affect fundamental rights should be accompanied by an impact assessment continuous monitoring and appropriate safeguards and controls especially in the case of self-learning systems. (page 3) Thus individuals groups and genders must be protected against discrimination and stigmatization. To this end adequate technical and organizational safeguards and controls must be provided. Furthermore balanced and high-quality data should be used or appropriate compensatory safeguards should be implemented. (page 3) Appropriate safeguards should also be implemented to prevent serious misuse. (page 5) However there are no specific guidelines for cases of AI system failure or unexpected behavior.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines (Guideline 3: Transparency traceability and explainability) determine the documentation regarding data specifically data used for AI applications ensuring quality. The documentation includes the collection and use of data appropriate for its purpose with ethical standards. The data policy is related to the requirement for transparency regarding automated decisions as per the data protection law (p. 4). Although documentation exists it does not cover the entire AI lifecycle. In terms of use AI use of AI the risks for individuals society the economy and the environment can be identified at an early stage and either eliminated or mitigated. (p.5)

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

items.title: Guidelines on Artificial Intelligence for the Confederation (Switzerland)
items.justification: To ensure trustworthiness the guidelines impose core requirements for transparency traceability and explainability and confirm that the existing federal legal framework such as the Data Protection Act (FADP) fully applies to all AI applications. (page 4)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Transparency traceability explainability are basic requirements for trustworthy AI (page 4). AI-based decision-making and interaction with AI systems should be clearly recognizable (page 4). To guarantee compliance with other principles and fundamental human rights the functioning of AI its purpose should be disclosed in a responsible legally compliant manner (page 4). The data sets used for the training or development of AI should be disclosed within the framework of legal obligations in order to enable monitoring (page 4). AI decision-making processes should be designed in such a way that ensures that they are traceable for directly and indirectly affected persons and the mode of action must also be verifiable for experts (page 4).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: 'the data subject has the right to express his or her stance on the decision and may request that the decision be reviewed by a natural person.' (referring to the Federal Act on Data Protection) (page 10)

items.title: The Strategy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040
items.justification: The document Literacy in AI usage among its key objectives - section 3 subsection 2 provision #60; It also outlines establishing of AI courses and department in education institutions section 4 subsection 2 provision #84
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Council on AI

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: the document refers to insufficient curricula in schools and universities but no mention of the reform (section 4 subsection 2 provision 84). Also throughout the whole document education is listed among key sectors that has strategic importance for the use of AI. (e.g page 3). Education is one of the backbones of AI development in Tajikistan as can be inferred by looking how many times it is mentioned in the strategy therefore it can be said that there might be some decisive changes in curricula of secondary schools and universities. However the strategy does not concern primary education which prompts to indicate the strategy is partially oriented on curriculum reform mostly focusing on secondary and tertiary education

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: It mentions opening courses on AI in 7 higher education institutions section 4 subsection 2 provision 84 'Key Measures for Sector Development'. The measures include: Implementing AI-based learning management systems in general schoolscolleges lyceums institutes universities and other educational institutions; Establishing AI departments and faculties in at least 7 higher education; institutions in Tajikistan by 2026; Preparing young researchers in AI in collaboration with international organizations at the master’s and PhD levels in institutions of developed countries; Integrating an AI module into the “Information Technology” course in upper grades of general education schools.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: Shortage of qualified teaching staff in artificial intelligence is mentioned among key challenges (section4 subsection 2 provision 84) but no specific measures on preparation of or training for AI teachers  is mentioned

items.title: The Strategy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040
items.justification: The strategy explicitly includes public sector capacity-building in the context of artificial intelligence. It provides for the creation of institutional structures within government bodies and addresses personnel shortages (p. 7) while mandating training increasing AI literacy and integrating AI into public administration (p. 8). It further introduces concrete measures to improve the qualifications of civil servants and retrain personnel within government structures (pp. 16–17) particularly in relation to digital governance and AI-based systems.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Authorized state body

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: The Strategy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040
items.justification: The strategy states as one of the principles that AI should be human and human security-centered  —simple understandable and beneficial and that it also should ensure information security protection of human dignity Section 3 sub-section 2 provisions # 59-60 page 9
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

items.title: The Strategy on Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Tajikistan until 2040
items.justification: The strategy states that AI should be used based on principle of transparency. This is outline among key objectives of the strategy section 3 paragraph 2 point #60. It also contains a provision that states that AI should be simple understandable and useful - section 3 subsection 2 point #59
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).
