items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan for the Development of Thailand (2022–2027)
items.justification: In the NAIS Strategy 3: Enhancing Human Resource Capacity and Advancing AI Education aims to promote AI literacy among the public by equipping people with the knowledge understanding and skills needed to use artificial intelligence responsibly and beneficially in ways that are appropriate and aligned with their level of education and age group. (pp.147-148)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Minister of Education and Ministry of Higher Education Science Research and Innovation (p149)

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The strategy addresses education and skill training in relation to AI by strengthening core competencies from the school-age period through lifelong learning. It emphasises developing analytical thinking problem-solving creativity collaboration and technological proficiency among students which are foundational for AI literacy (p.13). It also highlights the need to strengthen domestic capabilities through AI skills and education to support the development and application of AI particularly in public services (p.88).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: This is a requirement of the strategy. AI-related undergraduate programmes are offered by public and private universities including King Mongkut’s Institute of Technology Ladkrabang Chulalongkorn University and Chiang Mai University mainly through faculties of engineering science and information science. At the basic education level the Institute for the Promotion of Teaching Science and Technology (IPST) provides AI curricula covering awareness core concepts models and integration supporting the development of AI competencies in the formal education system (pp. 231–232).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: Teachers are among the target groups for training programmes aimed at enhancing their competencies in artificial intelligence and digital technologies according to specific skill areas. (p.148)

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: AI systems should be designed developed and deployed to generate benefits for humans society and the environment throughout their lifecycle (p.17). The document requires accountability mechanisms including internal and external audits of data algorithms deployment and outcomes to identify and mitigate environmental and societal risks (p.19). Designers and developers must ensure data integrity ethical compliance and environmental protection (p.20). AI should be developed sustainably adapt to different environments and include built-in risk mitigation security recovery mechanisms and continuous testing under real-world conditions to avoid harm to human life and the environment (pp.23–33).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models
thematicElements.justification: It can be considered “partially” as although the provision is not specific and appears non-binding it states that data integrity accuracy availability personal data protection and impacts on ethics human life and the environment should be taken into account and that relevant actors should comply with these requirements. While explicit measurement mechanisms are not clearly specified they appear to be implicitly reflected in the requirement that these factors be considered.

thematicElements.text: The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: The Guideline embeds fairness and non-discrimination across the entire lifecycle of AI systems. It requires AI design and development to recognise social diversity and actively reduce exclusion and bias with the aim of maximising benefits for society particularly for disadvantaged and vulnerable groups. It also mandates that key decisions in AI research design deployment and use be demonstrably fair rather than assumed to be neutral. To achieve this the Guideline emphasises diverse research teams representative datasets and technical and procedural mechanisms to assess and verify fairness in practice (p. 13-14).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: AI should be researched designed and developed with an understanding of diverse user needs including minority and disadvantaged groups such as persons with disabilities while respecting human abilities and potential. Stakeholders who may be affected by bias or unfairness should participate in the design and development process. AI systems must also be reviewed and corrected when they produce unintended biased outcomes which may result from interactions with different groups or incorrect assumptions about users. (p.29-30)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document provides guidance to prevent artificial intelligence systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal bias and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age disability or other protected characteristics. It promotes the use of bias detection tools and encourages testing on unseen data and underrepresented populations to ensure equitable performance. The Guideline also recommends involving persons with disabilities in testing and design processes to enhance accessibility and inclusion and advises developers and service providers to provide appropriate training tools and access channels for users (p.31).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: It can be considered partially as the provision states that significant decisions related to the research design development deployment and use of artificial intelligence should be demonstrably fair. The term “demonstrably” implicitly suggests that bias must be identified and assessed and the reference to research design development and deployment reflects a lifecycle approach. However the provision does not establish clear or binding obligations for developers and deployers.

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: Under the topic of Laws Ethics and International Standards the AI Ethics guideline clearly states that artificial intelligence should be designed based on a human-centred approach with humans as the final decision-makers.(p.10)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: A human-centred (Human-Centric) approach should guide the design and deployment of artificial intelligence ensuring that humans retain the authority to make final decisions. AI systems should be designed so that their tasks and decision-making can always be transferred back to humans. They must also allow human intervention in all decision-making processes preserving human autonomy to reject AI-generated outputs. Appropriate mechanisms should be included to ensure that humans can override or interrupt the operation of the AI system whenever necessary. (pp.23-24)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: Under the topic of Laws Ethics and International Standards the AI Ethics Guideline states that public procurement should require AI developers and service providers to comply with transparency principles conduct impact assessments on how data processing affects human rights and privacy and assume responsibility for any negative consequences arising from the use of artificial intelligence (p.18).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document states that artificial intelligence should be reviewed and assessed to ensure that its research development and deployment generate benefits and promote the well-being of humans society and the environment (p. 22). It also encourages organisations to establish dedicated oversight bodies to supervise AI development and deployment provide legal ethical and human rights guidance assess potential risks and negative impacts and ensure accountability of researchers designers developers and service providers (p. 23). However it does not explicitly specify that such reviews or assessments must be conducted prior to deployment and therefore does not clearly establish a mandatory pre-deployment evaluation requirement.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: There should be support for establishing organisations and regulatory bodies overseeing the development and use of artificial intelligence. These bodies should provide guidance to AI researchers designers developers and service providers on legal ethical and human rights implications assess risks that may result in negative impacts and ensure appropriate accountability mechanisms for those involved in AI research design development and service provision. (p.18)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: There should be mechanisms to ensure accountability for AI researchers designers developers service providers users and other stakeholders throughout the system’s entire life cycle. This includes auditing datasets algorithms design methods deployment and outputs through internal and independent external reviews. Audit results should be reported risks assessed and mitigation measures implemented to prevent adverse impacts on people and the environment (p. 19). However while this creates obligations for developers and stakeholders it does not grant the public the right to access these audit findings.

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: Under the topic of Laws Ethics and International Standards the AI Ethics Guideline states that public procurement should require AI developers and service providers to comply with transparency principles conduct impact assessments on how data processing affects human rights and privacy and assume responsibility for any negative consequences arising from the use of artificial intelligence. (p.18)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: It may be considered “partially.” Although not explicitly specified in the guideline page 23 states that public procurement processes should require AI developers and service providers to comply with transparency principles including human rights and privacy impact assessments and to ensure accountability for adverse impacts. This demonstrates that human rights considerations a core component of AI ethics are integrated.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: It can be considered partially as AI developers and service providers are required to conduct human rights and privacy impact assessments of data processing in public procurement (p. 23).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: This can be considered partially as although transparency principles are required for vendors it is not explicitly stated that black-box systems should be avoided.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan for the Development of Thailand (2022–2027)
items.justification: In the NAIS Strategy 3: Enhancing Human Resource Capacity and Advancing AI Education aims to develop and strengthen AI-related capabilities among personnel in the government sector by providing training that meets national needs and enhances their ability to work effectively with artificial intelligence systems. (p.148)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Ministry of Higher Education Science Research and Innovation (Office of the Science Research and Innovation Promotion Commission) and the Digital Government Development Agency

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan for the Development of Thailand (2022–2027)
items.justification: In the NAIS Strategy 3: Enhancing Human Resource Capacity and Advancing AI Education aims to promote education and develop specialised skills at all levels of learning (Upskill / Reskill / Newskill). It requires a targeted plan for AI workforce development and encourages the public to gain knowledge of artificial intelligence cultivating AI literacy an understanding of and ability to use AI technologies effectively appropriately and responsibly in accordance with one’s level of education and age group. (p.147)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Minister of Education and Ministry of Higher Education Science Research and Innovation (p149)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: It can be considered partial as Objective 2 (p.147) aims “to improve the skills of the workforce in the industrial sector.” Page 148 provides further details on measures supporting scholarships work placements and talent mobility by offering financial aid to develop expertise in science and technology within high-capability target fields particularly at the Master’s Doctoral and Postdoctoral levels. These provisions indicate an intention to promote reskilling and upskilling through grants and educational support. However the measures are primarily focused on advanced academic training and highly skilled personnel rather than the broader workforce suggesting limited inclusiveness in comprehensive workforce-wide skill development.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Scholarships also support work placements in the private sector and promote talent mobility. (p.148)

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: Under the topic of Security and Privacy the AI Ethics guideline states that AI should be created to serve but must not be used to deceive oppose or threaten human beings. AI should be designed with risk-prevention principles to protect against attacks and other threats ensuring the security of data and systems. This includes safeguarding personal data ethics and the safety of human life and the external environment throughout the system’s entire life cycle. It should also have the capability to detect report and respond in order to avoid or mitigate negative impacts. (p.12)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Artificial intelligence should be designed and developed with the capability to implement fallback plans for system recovery from various failures including mechanisms to revoke data and services in order to ensure that users’ rights and interests are not violated and that no harm is caused to human life or the environment during recovery operations. (p.35)

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: AI models should be tested under conditions that reflect the dynamic nature of real-world environments to ensure the safety of users and the surrounding environment. They should also be continuously monitored reviewed and appropriately updated. However as pre-deployment testing is not explicitly specified this provision only partially addresses the requirement (p. 39).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The document requires AI systems to be designed developed and deployed with strong risk-prevention measures to protect system security prevent misuse and safeguard critical data personal information human life and the environment (p. 27). Systems must include capabilities to monitor detect and respond to threats resolve incidents restore normal operations after attacks and implement fallback plans including mechanisms to revoke data or services to protect users’ rights (p. 29). Researchers and developers should continuously update their skills to reduce emerging risks (p. 29). Public and private organisations must also comply with the Cybersecurity Act 2019 to ensure the cybersecurity of AI systems (p. 34).

items.title: AI Ethics Guideline (Thailand)
items.justification: Under the topic of Transparency and Explainability the AI Ethics guideline clearly states that AI should be researched designed developed provided and used in a transparent manner with explainable and predictable outcomes and with the ability to audit and review past activities. Also AI should have the capacity for traceability to monitor and detect anomalies and to diagnose system failures.(p.11)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: AI systems should transparently disclose their purposes decision-making reasons datasets capabilities limitations algorithms processes and reliability. The information should be explained in a way that affected individuals can understand considering different levels of knowledge and varied use contexts. This allows users to question how the AI works and to detect bias errors and unintended outcomes more easily. (p.25)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Stakeholders who may be affected by AI should be properly informed and have the right to request information about why AI is used on them and the impacts of such decisions. They should also be able to participate directly or indirectly in the design and development of AI throughout its life cycle. Users must be notified when they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human and made aware that decision outcomes are generated by AI. (p.26)

items.title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
items.justification: It does not create dedicated rules for deepfakes election interference or gender-based or child-focused harms. Instead it addresses these risks through its general AI governance and risk-management framework. Clause 4.2 requires organisations to assess impacts on affected stakeholders while Clause 6.1 mandates identification and mitigation of risks from foreseeable misuse. Annex C lists social psychological and reputational harm and B.5.5 explicitly refers to misinformation for political gain and deepfakes. However no sector-specific prohibitions safeguards or victim-redress mechanisms are established.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: National Digital Transformation Strategy 2024-2027 (Trinidad and Togo)
items.justification: While the NDTS 2024-2027 is a broader digital strategy it contains explicit provisions addressing AI fairness and non-discrimination. Page 69 commits to removing bias from systems to ensure they are representative of and relevant to the diverse needs of society directly addressing algorithmic fairness in AI systems. Page 59 establishes that the e-ID system must focus on preventing discriminatory practices providing a concrete non-discrimination requirement in an AI-relevant context. Together these provisions demonstrate a demonstrable and explicit link to the Fairness and Non-Discrimination indicator
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Public Administration and AI (MPAAI)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Partially covered: Commitment to bias removal and representative systems (p.69). Non-discrimination principles (p.59) Recognition of vulnerable groups (p.29 59). Ethical research framework (p.30 69).  The framework establishes aspirational goals for fair AI outcomes but defers concrete measures to future policy development (p.68: forthcoming AI strategy).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: There are broad commitments to bias removal and non-discrimination (p.59 69)  recognition of some not all vulnerable groups: gender age disability (p.29 59 75).   Human rights framework (p.26 31). The document defers detailed provisions to the forthcoming AI Policy Strategy (p.68) making current protections aspirational rather than operational.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

items.title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
items.justification: The standard establishes a dedicated AI impact assessment process through Annex B.5 requiring evaluation of effects on individuals groups and society. Annex B.5.4 (p. 31) addresses impacts on individuals/groups; Annex B.5.5 (p. 32) covers broader societal and health/safety impacts. Annex A (p.20) summarises these controls. Supporting clauses include: Clause 6 (risk-based planning) Clause 8 (operational controls) Clause 9 (performance monitoring) and Clause 10 (corrective action). Together these establish a lifecycle-wide framework for both ex-ante & ex-post AI impact assessment.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The standard doesn't explicitly require pre-deployment assessment of ethical and environmental impacts specifically making current provisions partial. Yet it promotes proactive risk management through Annex B.5 (AI impact assessment process) B.5.4 (impacts on individuals/groups) and B.5.5 (societal and health/safety impacts) alongside Clauses 6 8 and 9.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The standard explicitly assigns obligations to organisations developing & using AI to conduct structured impact assessments. Annex B.5 establishes a mandatory AI impact assessment process; B.5.4 requires assessment of impacts on individuals and groups; B.5.5 requires assessment of broader societal impacts. Clause 6 further requires organisations to identify and treat AI-related risks systematically. These are explicit obligations to conduct comprehensive impact assessments identifying and mitigating risks to individuals and society.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: National Digital Transformation Strategy 2024-2027 (Trinidad and Togo)
items.justification: Page 66 refers explicitly to ' Future-proof skills by continuously ensuring curriculum relevance by matching Emerging Technologies with growing opportunities;' (ai is defined as emerging tech) and page 77 states that: High engagement in emerging technology training equipping citizens with the skills needed to participate in and shape the future of the digital landscape. The strategy commits to reskilling and upskilling the workforce to support 'emerging technologies' including AI (p. 18). The Strategy mandates continuous reskilling of public officers to manage automated and data-driven digital systems (p. 27). It promotes lifelong learning and future-ready competencies aligned with evolving labour market needs (p. 20).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Public Administration and AI (MPAAI)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
items.justification: The Draft TTS/ISO/IEC 42001:2023 embeds safety & security throughout its AI management system architecture such as safety policy update requirements (B.2.3); assignment of roles & responsibilities (B.3.2); inclusion of diverse trustworthiness experts including safety specialists (B.4.6); assessment of societal impacts (B.5.5); AI system verification against safety requirements including acceptable error rates (Clause 6.2.4); structured risk assessments (Clause 6.2); impact assessment (Annex B.5.4); incident communication plans for safety problems (B.8.4); and safety explicitly listed as a risk source in Annex C (p.50). Lifecycle-wide monitoring & corrective a action mechanisms (Clauses 9-10) further ensure ongoing safety compliance.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: It is partially. The standard addresses reliability and accuracy through B.6.2.4 which requires organisations to document evaluation criteria based on safety requirements including acceptable error rates and B.5.5 which requires assessment of societal impacts on health and safety. However the standard doesn’t establish specific numerical performance thresholds or minimum accuracy requirements before deployment it assigns obligations to define and document such criteria organisationally rather than prescribing fixed benchmarks.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The draft standard provides organisational safeguards through operational controls (Clause 8.1) continuous monitoring (Clause 9.1) corrective-action requirements (Clause 10.1) and risk identification in Annex C. Yet it doesn't prescribe specific technical fallback mechanisms or emergency-shutdown procedures for AI system failures.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The draft promotes lifecycle robustness through impact-assessment provisions (Annex B.5.4) AI system verification requirements including documentation of evaluation criteria & acceptable error rates (Clause 6.2.4) data provenance & accuracy documentation requirements (Annex B.7.2-B.7.3) general documentation obligations (Clause 7) & monitoring obligations (Clause 9.1). However the standard doesn't impose detailed or standardised technical testing and validation procedures prior to deployment though it establishes governance & documentation obligations rather than prescribing specific technical validation protocols.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: The draft includes general security-related governance through risk-management requirements (Clause 6.1) operational controls (Clause 8.1) information-control provisions (Clause 7) and explicit identification of malicious or adversarial threats in Annex C. However it doesn't impose detailed or technical cybersecurity obligations tailored specifically to AI systems.

items.title: Information technology — Artificial intelligence — Management system (PTTS/ISO/IEC 42001:20XX) (Trinidad and Tobago)
items.justification: Transparency is identified as a core principle within the standard and is to be incorporated into the design of organisational processes information systems and control mechanisms (p. x). Clause B.5.4 specifies that AI impact assessments must take account of transparency and explainability considerations. Clause 7.2 further requires that data-management practices address transparency and explainability including how data are used to determine system outputs. Clause 9.3 lists transparency among the objectives guiding the responsible use of AI. In addition Annex C.3 highlights a lack of transparency as a key AI-related risk that organisations should assess and mitigate.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The standard contains substantive provisions on documenting AI system purpose data sources and decision-making processes (see Clause 4.2 Clause 7.5 and A.8.2 etc

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: A.8.2 and A.8.3 assign transparency and reporting obligations to organisations but without sector-specific explainability requirements for high-stakes contexts.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (Uganda)
items.justification: The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 provides several specific sections that relate to access to redress and remedy including in contexts relevant to automated processing and decision making. Section 27 Rights in relation to automated decision-taking (p. 11 - 12) gives a data subject the right to challenge a decision significantly affecting them if that decision is solely based on automated processing. It mandates notification to the data subject gives a right to require reconsideration and allows a complaint to the regulator.' to include specific wording about automated decision taking and remove non-AI specific sections about redress and remedy.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: According to Section 7 subsections 2 (ii) and (iii) personal data collected for purposes of national security or the prevention detection investigation and prosecution of offenses are exempt from the standard consent requirements. Subsection (3) further clarifies that while data subjects generally have the right to object to data collection this right does not apply to data processed under the aforementioned legal exceptions in subsection (2)

body.name: The Personal Data Protection Office

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Section 31 gives power to data subjects to lodge a complaint with the Authority; section 32 gives power to the Authority to investigate a complaint and direct a data collector data processor or data controller to remedy any breach; section 33 gives power to the data subject to apply to  Court  for compensation from the data collector data processor or data controller; & section 27  gives rights to the data subject to seek reconsideration from the data controller of decisions solely based on automated decision-taking.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (Uganda)
items.justification: In Section 27 (Rights in relation to automated decision-taking p. 11-12) a data subject may require a data controller to ensure any decision that significantly affects them is not based solely on automated processing of personal data. If a significant decision is based solely on automated processing the controller must notify the data subject as soon as reasonably practicable and the data subject may require the controller to reconsider the decision within 21 days. In response the controller must inform the data subject in writing of steps taken. Also the data subject may complain to the Personal Data Protection Office (PDPO) if unsatisfied.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: According to Section 7 subsections 2 (ii) and (iii) personal data collected for purposes of national security or the prevention detection investigation and prosecution of offenses are exempt from the standard consent requirements. Subsection (3) further clarifies that while data subjects generally have the right to object to data collection this right does not apply to data processed under the aforementioned legal exceptions in subsection (2)

body.name: The Personal Data Protection Office

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 (DPPA) does not explicitly mention  AI or the phrase “meaningful human control.”However it indirectly promotes and enforces human oversight in automated decision-making processes. Section 27 gives a data subject  a right to give a notice in writing to a data controller require that a decision which significantly affects him or her is not based solely on automated processing of personal data. Where a decision which significantly affects a data subject is based solely on automated processing the data controller shall notify the data subject as soon as reasonably practicable.And a data subject may request reconsideration of such a decision within twenty-one days.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.justification: (p.4) In cases where media outlets resort to AI-generated content in particular to illustrate cultural materials model situations and illustrate examples and theories they are recommended to: check whether the content generated by the AI system clearly and accurately reflects reality; assess in each specific case whether the use of AI-generated content is contextually appropriate and whether the use of such content will not mislead readers/viewers/listeners even if labeled and refrain from using or distributing news and news-analytical content generated by AI that contain hate speech propaganda for war or any other kind of unlawful content.

items.title: Law of Ukraine on Personal Data Protection
items.justification: Article 8 addresses automated decision-making by granting individuals the right to be protected from automated decisions that have legal consequences for them (Art. 8(13)). It also establishes avenues for redress by allowing data subjects to lodge complaints with the Commissioner or courts and to use legal remedies in case of violations of personal data protection legislation (Art. 8(8)–(9)).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 25 of the Law explicitly provides for restrictions on the application of Articles 6 7 and 8 in the interests of national security. This constitutes an explicit exclusion of defence and security domains from the core obligations of the framework.

body.name: Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights as an ombudsman responsible to receive complaints and other appeals on issues of personal data protection (p.10) allowing data subjects to lodge complaint where their data are processed unlawfully. However these rights only cover personal data and AI-related grievance are not directly targeted.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The law establishes the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights as an ombudsman responsible to receive complaints and other appeals on issues of personal data protection (p.10). However AI-related grievance are not directly targeted.

The results of AI tools should be reviewed and critically evaluated before being used or shared. It is important to understand the limitations of AI and the importance of cross-referencing to verified sources. Results generated by AI should be verified using reliable sources before being used in educational or administrative activities. (p.22)

items.justification: It is necessary to critically evaluate and adjust the results obtained from AI to ensure that they reflect and protect the interests of the client. It is imperative to conduct a final check of the results generated by the system. items.title: Advisory on responsible use of artificial intelligence by public servants (Ukraine)
items.justification: (p.2) These tips are one of the components of the roadmap for regulating artificial intelligence (hereinafter referred to as AI) in Ukraine. The text outlines a systematic approach to the implementation and responsible use of artificial intelligence in professional activities by public servants. Basically the document's aim is to improve the civil servants' skills and capacities to engage with AI responsibly and ethically.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: (p.13) Public servants can use educational series available on the Diia.Osvita platform (a government-led resource) to further study and understand the basics of cyber hygiene and digital security. - there is a reference to multiple educative materials that build up an ecosystem of AI literacy for state sector. items.title: Concept for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Ukraine
items.justification: The Concept explicitly addresses workforce reskilling and upskilling in response to AI-driven labour market transformation. It directly acknowledges the risk of job displacement due to automation (p. 3) and provides targeted workforce measures most notably the development of a roadmap for retraining individuals whose work may be automated in the next five to ten years (p. 5). In addition the framework includes provisions for advanced training and professional retraining of personnel including adult education programs in artificial intelligence and support mechanisms such as scholarships for individuals undergoing such retraining (p. 4).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Recommendations on responsible development of systems using AI technologies (Ukraine)
items.justification: (p.4)The objectives of these recommendations are:To guide AI system developers in adhering to ethical principles in the development and use of AI including risk-based security and reliability privacy and data protection fairness and justice transparency and accountability human oversight and monitoring leadership and awareness-raising and protection of intellectual property rights.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Scope limitations — contextually specific challenges in the development and use of AI systems such as industry differences data access restrictions privacy etc. that cannot be fully covered by general recommendations. These recommendations do not cover issues related to the national security and defense sector. (p.4)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: (p.14) The fifth factor is benchmark results. Comparing models using standardized tests helps to choose the most effective solution. The main metrics for evaluation include classification accuracy (Accuracy / F1-score) the balance between correct detection and avoidance of false positives (Precision / Recall) prediction execution time (Inference time) and the amount of memory required (Memory footprint). Using open platforms such as Papers with Code Hugging Face Leaderboard Chatbot Arena or MLPerf you can evaluate competing solutions based on real-world performance metrics.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: First of all it is necessary to clearly allocate responsibilities for the supervision of the AI ??system. Depending on the scale of the model’s functionality the number of people in the field and the risk issues identified during the human rights impact assessment and risk assessment it is necessary to determine: the number of people responsible for carrying out professional supervision clear areas of their responsibility depending on their expertise and profile an accountability system a crisis protocol in case of incidents. (p.27)

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: (p.46) While the evidence includes provisions for the need to test and train data sets it does not include further requirements for pre deployment testing. However it extends requirements to the quality and origin of datasets.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: (p.45) The evidence indicates that developers should pay special attention to risks from cyber attacks such as attacks through data or model poisoning creation of backdoors (hidden access) for abuse or model inversion. There are no further measures for obligations or legal responsibility for non-compliance.

items.title: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Regulation in Ukraine: Vision of the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine
items.justification: The document provides for a list of measures to be introduced within the governance and regulatory framework. One of such measures is Voluntary Labeling of AI Systems. Quote: Labeling of AI systems is the provision of clear and structured information about the design functions algorithms and other aspects of artificial intelligence systems. This process is aimed at ensuring transparency and openness regarding the way intelligent systems operate. Following the disclosure of information about the system by the developer such a system receives the appropriate labeling tags. - p.20
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defence Sector is Not Subject to Regulation. While implementing our approach during the full-scale invasion of the Russian Federation were main aware of the importance of developing innovative solutions to repel aggression and in noway intend to propose regulation of AI systems in the defence sector. This is due to both the national interests of the state and the real state of affairs in the security sector – unilateral regulation (restriction) of the use of AI in the defence sector at the level of national legislation will only put our country in a less favorable position compared to the aggressor which will not implement such regulation. - p.10

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The document provides for 'building trust' as one of key priorities of state policy in AI sphere. Quote: User trust: labeled and therefore transparent AI systems help to build trust among users. Knowledge of AI system operations and information about its capabilities and limitations allow users to make informed decisions about their interaction with the technology similar to how end users can choose their diet through food ingredient labeling. Industry Trust: in the industry transparency fosters trust between companies researchers and developers of safety policies and regulations. Open sharing of information about AI systems encourages collaboration and thedevelopment of best safety practices.- p.21

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: There are no obligations however there is the suggestion of voluntary labelling of AI systems for both public and private sector which pursues the purposes of ensuring accountability ethics and compliance as well as building trust - p.21. The document generally refers to the need to establish risk-based classification of AI systems and apply safeguards according to the risk level including explainability - p.22

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

Industry Trust: in the industry transparency fosters trust between companies researchers and developers of safety policies and regulations. items.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The Data Subject has the fundamental right to object to any decisions resulting from automated processing including profiling that adversely affect them(18). The Controller shall include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions upon request providing immediate remedy against algorithmic error or bias. Data Subjects have the right to submit complaints to the UAE Data Bureau if a violation occurs(24). The Bureau examines complaints and can impose administrative penalties against the Controller/Processor if the violation is proven serving as a formal redress action. Individuals may communicate directly with the DPO regarding their rights and submit requests and complaints related to their personal data processing.(12)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Provisions of the Decree by Law shall not apply to Personal Data held by the security and judicial authorities. Provisions also shall not apply to Government Data which often encompasses defence and security-related information. However the framework includes a caveat regarding international data transfer stating that the cross-border transfer of data requires the Data Subject's consent provided that such transfer shall not contradict the public or security interest of the State

body.name: The UAE Data Bureau (Office)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: It focuses on administrative and internal non-judicial remedies: Individuals must submit a complaint to the UAE Data Bureau if a violation occurs (Art 24 c1). The Bureau examines the complaint and imposes administrative penalties (Art 24 c2 & 3). Stakeholders can submit a written grievance to the General Director of the Bureau against any penalty or decision it issues (Art 25). It is not permissible to challenge the Bureau's decision until this grievance is submitted (Art 25). The Data Subject has the non-judicial remedy to request the Controller include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions (Art 18 c4). The Decree explicitly states its provisions shall not apply to Personal Data held by judicial authorities (Art 2).

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The UAE Data Bureau (Office) is established as the primary regulator and state-based non-judicial body responsible for: receiving complaints imposing administrative penalties if a violation is proven. and dealing with any grievances against any decision or penalty imposed by the Bureau in the first instance.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Companies (Controllers and Processors) must maintain internal grievance mechanisms for issues related to AI-driven processing (Art 11 c1b). The Data Protection Officer (DPO) is required to receive and manage complaints on personal data (Art 11 c1b). Data Subjects may directly contact the DPO about any data processing concerns including automated decisions (Art 12 c2). Controllers must provide clear accessible channels for such contact (Art 19). These internal mechanisms complement the external complaint process overseen by the UAE Data Bureau ensuring layered recourse and accountability. (Art 24 c1)

items.title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The framework explicitly addresses the protection of children in AI systems particularly under the Human-Centered AI (Principle 6) which require that AI systems capable of influencing behavior must be designed to distinguish between adults and children and implement additional safeguards for vulnerable populations such as children “when informed consent cannot be obtained or when it may not be a sufficient safeguard” (p. 35).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

items.title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
items.justification: The policy addresses the UAE's diversified culture (over 200 nationalities) as its greatest advantage for AI development (p40). This diversity provides unique 'impeccable' data sets essential for machine learning and Artificial Intelligence applications specifically citing diagnostics for diseases like Tuberculosis (p40). The document also seeks to contextualize global AI debates for young Arab countries and leverage the strong regional talent pool in MENA (p7). For Linguistic Diversity the AI Office will establish an open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic (p39). This initiative aims to boost the research sector and close the research gap in the region (p39).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: UAE AI and Blockchain Council

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The UAE's 'diversified culture with more than 200 nationalities' is deemed its 'greatest advantage'. This results in 'impeccable' data sets that can be used for responsive applications such as diagnosing diseases like Tuberculosis (TB) using Artificial Intelligence.For language the AI Office will create an 'open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic'. This aims to 'boost the research sector in the region' making knowledge culturally and linguistically accessible. The Strategy also required contextualizing debates for 'young and ambitious Arab countries'.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: It addresses prevention indirectly through ethical data and linguistic measures. The strategy focuses on a 'values-driven approach to AI' and mandates a National Governance Review of 'ethics'. This moves beyond abstract principles to 'useable guidelines'. Quality control is established via the UAI Seal of Approval recognizing 'high quality ethical AI companies' through a 'robust rigorous and comprehensive certification methodology'. The strategy leverages the UAE’s diversified culture as an asset for developing 'impeccable' data sets countering bias inherent in limited training data. To prevent linguistic erasure the AI Office will establish an 'open-access digital library of research and papers in both English and Arabic.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The document addresses fairness and non-discrimination under 'Fairness (Principle 1)'. It mandates that AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups' and must be 'provably fair' especially for 'significant and critical decisions'.To ensure this organizations must define their context-specific meaning of fairness and undertake 'Discrimination Impact Assessments'. Guidelines require mitigating and disclosing 'biases inherent in datasets' and ensuring data is 'accurate and representative of the affected population'. The framework emphasizes 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights' and requires considering whether subjects receive 'equal treatment' in the same circumstances
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The core principle of the guidelines is that the UAE 'will make AI systems fair'(3.1.1). Guidelines ensure that benefits are 'available and accessible to all'(3.1.2.1) & that AI systems respect 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights'(1.3). AI systems should be designed to achieve a 'fair and just society'(3.6.2.4). AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups in a way that could have an adverse impact'(3.1.2.1). Organizations must implement 'Discrimination Impact Assessments' (3.1.2)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: It states AI systems 'should not discriminate against people or groups in a way that could have an adverse impact'(3.1.2). Requires assessing 'demographic groups that may be adversely impacted' and ensuring data is 'representative of the affected population'(3.1.2). Under Privacy (3.8) the document explicitly lists characteristics such as 'race descent gender age language religion political opinion national origin ethnic origin social origin... or disability' as sensitive data that must be fully secured due to potential for damage injury or hardship if disclosed. Steps must be taken to 'mitigate and disclose the biases inherent in datasets' & evaluate all datasets to assess 'inclusiveness of identified demographic groups'(3.1.2)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework assigns proactive obligations to developers and operators to address bias throughout the lifecycle: Data must be 'accurate and representative of the affected population' to avoid 'non-operational bias'(3.1.2).Organizations must 'mitigate and disclose the biases inherent in datasets'(3.1.2).They are advised to use 'Discrimination Impact Assessments' & identify 'demographic groups that may be adversely impacted'(3.1.2).The goal is to ensure 'equal treatment' (3.1.2) respecting 'inclusiveness equality human benefit and rights'(1.3)& achieving a 'fair and just society'(3.6.2.4). Sensitive characteristics are protected under Privacy ensuring data is not used to 'unlawfully or unfairly discriminate' (3.8.2)

items.title: DIFC Regulation 10 – Accreditation and Certification Framework For Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems Processing Personal Data (“Framework”) (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: DIFC Regulation 10 addresses gender equality indirectly through its mandatory principle of Fairness. It requires high-risk AI systems to be certified and designed to 'treat all individuals equally and fairly regardless of race gender or other specifically subjective factors'. The framework also mandates that systems must be designed to avoid or mitigate 'unjust bias' and 'discrimination'. This creates an enforceable auditable mechanism to challenge gender-based harm from AI within the DIFC's jurisdiction.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Regulation 10 Advisory Committee

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The document provides general provisions for the assignment for obligations and responsibilities to developers of AI systems which are applied to protect gender equality.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The framework ensures human oversight in AI through explicit rights and obligations on automated processing (Art18 c.4). Under Article 18(p21) individuals may object to decisions made via automation or profiling that have legal or adverse effects (c.1). When an objection is raised the Controller must include human review(c.4) ensuring a person reassesses the outcome. For high-risk automation a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment (PDPIA) is required to evaluate risks and safeguards (Art 21 c.1) p23. Together these provisions guarantee that AI-driven decisions remain subject to meaningful human intervention.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 on Personal Data Protection explicitly excludes defence security judicial authorities and government entities from its scope (art 2 c.2). This carve-out preserves state sovereignty and public order as such data is governed by specialised security and intelligence laws. The exemption ensures national security operations aren’t constrained by data-subject rights like erasure or objection(art17 c.2 & art18c2.b). The law further allows processing and transfers tied to judicial or security procedures confirming that critical state functions operate under separate higher-level legal regimes (art 4 c3 & art 23 c. 1(ce)).

body.name: The UAE Data Bureau (Office)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 promotes meaningful human control by ensuring human judgment can override automated decisions with serious consequences. Data Subjects have the right to object to automated or profiled outcomes and Controllers must include human review upon request. For high-risk automation a Data Protection Impact Assessment is required to evaluate and mitigate risks. Transparency is ensured through information rights on automated decisions while DPO oversight strengthens accountability and safeguards against uncontrolled automation.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 ensures human intervention and ethical judgment in automated decisions with significant impact. It grants individuals the right to object to automated or profiled outcomes and requires Controllers to conduct human review when requested. For high-risk automation a Data Protection Impact Assessment must evaluate potential harms and mitigation measures. Although security and health data may fall under other laws the Decree guarantees human oversight for any automated decision that adversely affects individuals within its scope.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 assigns clear accountability for oversight and intervention in high-risk data processing. It designates the Controller and Processor as responsible entities and mandates appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO) for sensitive or automated processing. The DPO verifies compliance advises on risk evaluations and ensures timely involvement in data protection matters. Controllers must keep records of authorized access and are accountable to the UAE Data Bureau which may impose penalties for violations ensuring strong human oversight and accountability.

items.title: AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The guidelines addresses Impact Assessments (IA) through specific non-mandatory guidelines (p5 1.1). It recommends Discrimination Impact Assessments (DIAs) for fairness which should be conducted both pre-release and regularly after as an ongoing evaluation (p17 3.1.2). For Privacy preserving AI algorithmic systems require adequate Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) that must also include societal and ethical considerations (p42 3.8.2). Operators should consider internal risk assessments and human rights impact assessments (p37 3.6.2.4). The document also mandates that AI applications be assessed through critical examination of resource usage and environmental impact throughout the AI lifecycle (p.38 3.7.1).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes proactive risk management and requires ex-ante evaluation for AI systems making 'significant decisions'. Mechanisms mandated for evaluation before deployment include:Recommending formal Discrimination Impact Assessments (DIAs) (p17 3.1.2) pre-release & requiring Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) that cover societal & ethical considerations (p40 3.8.1). Developers must identify & mitigate significant inherent risks and requiring critical examination of resource usage and energy consumption(p38 3.7.1). Efforts must be made to estimate and understand sustainability and environmental impact (e.g. CO2 emissions) throughout the AI lifecycle making carbon impacts a core consideration during model development. (p38 3.7.2)

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines assign obligations to AI developers and operators to conduct risk and impact assessments before and after deployment. (3.1.2.1 p17) They recommend Discrimination Privacy and Human Rights Impact Assessments to ensure fairness data protection and ethical use. (3.1.2.1 p17) Under Accountable and Robust AI principles actors must identify and mitigate risks (3.2.1 p20) assess the impact of incorrect decisions prevent harm and perform vulnerability and safety assessments. These measures promote fairness safety and accountability in AI systems making significant decisions. (1.1 p5)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The guidelines recommend public release of audit findings for AI systems making critical decisions of civic interest to ensure accountability (p22 3.2.2.3). Under Accountable AI such systems should undergo external audits (p20 3.2.2) with results publicly released where outcomes significantly affect individuals or society (p22 3.2.2.3). The guidelines also promote transparency through responsible disclosure of data algorithms and decision factors and suggest public sector AI systems may share source code and explanations (p26 3.3.1). Documentation of impact assessments and traceability records further supports accountability.(p22 3.2.2.3)

items.justification: Under Safety the UAE places great importance on ensuring that all AI systems comply with the highest safety standards (p3 s2). The country also actively encourages modifying or removing systems that pose risks (p3 s2). Regarding security the Charter emphasizes that the development of AI must ensure peaceful coexistence with the technology (p5 s10). This peaceful coexistence is crucial to ensure technology enhances well-being without compromising human security or fundamental rights(p5 s10).Furthermore the principles of Human Oversight Governance and Accountability and Commitment to Treaties and Applicable Laws collectively enforce a robust and responsible environment that ensures safety and protects the rights of the UAE community (p5.

items.title: Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 Concerning the Protection of Personal Data (United Arab Emirates)
items.justification: The document addresses AI transparency and explainability through specific controls on 'Automated Processing' and 'Profiling'. Processing must be transparent. Data Subjects have the right to information regarding 'Decisions made based on automated processing including profiling' and the right to object to adverse decisions resulting from such processes. Crucially the Controller must include the human element in reviewing automated processing decisions upon the Data Subject's request. Furthermore automated processing involving systematic assessment or high risk requires a Personal Data Protection Impact Assessment and a Data Protection Officer.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Scope of Application (Article 2) mandates that the provisions of the Federal Decree by Law No. (45) of 2021 shall not apply to personal data held by the security and judicial authorities. This clause ensures that data processing activities handled by authorities responsible for security functions are exempted from the law's obligations.

They have the right to object to such decisions especially when legally or personally significant and to demand human review ensuring meaningful explanation of key factors behind the outcome.
