items.title: National AI Strategy (2021) (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The strategy addresses AI literacy under Pillar 2: Skills and Talent (pp. 40–47). It promotes access to AI data and digital skills via computing education in schools Skills Bootcamps and lifelong learning. It backs teacher training through the National Centre for Computing Education and calls for inclusive pathways into AI careers. The strategy emphasizes AI literacy as vital for public understanding equity and preparing the workforce for the AI-driven economy.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Office for AI

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy supports AI programmes in schools (e.g. via the National Centre for Computing Education) (Summary of key actions pp. 8–9).  It also backs tertiary provision via AI/data science Masters conversion courses across universities (pp. 22–23). However it does not set out explicit curriculum reforms across all primary/secondary/tertiary levels.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: It describes new/expanded formal education programmes: '2500 new Masters conversion courses in AI and data science…delivered across universities' (Skills & Talent pp. 22–23). It also cites '16 new AI Centres for Doctoral Training…delivering 1000 new PhDs' (From Sector Deal to AI Strategy p. 18). It further commits to support the National Centre for Computing Education so AI programmes for children are accessible (Pillar 1 Actions / Summary of key actions pp. 38–39 / pp. 8–9).

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy commits to supporting the National Centre for Computing Education (NCCE) so AI programmes for schools are accessible (Summary of key actions pp. 8–9; Pillar 1 Actions pp. 38–39). However it does not explicitly set out dedicated teacher training measures in the text.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Online Safety Act 2023 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: While the Online Safety Act 2023 framework is relevant as it regulates the algorithmic systems through which such content spreads. Section 152 (p. 158) establishes an advisory committee on disinformation and misinformation to guide OFCOM. Sections 9(5)(b) and 11(6)(b) (pp. 8 11) require providers to assess risks considering 'algorithms used by the service and how easily quickly and widely content may be disseminated.' Section 231(10) (p. 229) defines 'proactive technology' utilising 'artificial intelligence or machine learning' for content identification and moderation. Thus the Act addresses the infrastructure enabling harmful content dissemination
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the Act's scope. Schedule 1 paragraph 9(3) (p. 248) states that the provisions do not apply to services provided by the Crown which includes government departments and agencies such as the Ministry of Defence and intelligence bodies. The Act's duties apply only to commercial online services not to state-run defence or security systems.

body.name: The Office of Communications

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The Online Safety Act 2023 addresses the prevention of AI tools being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation hate speech harassment and violence. It requires providers to assess and mitigate risks arising from algorithms and other service functionalities that may amplify illegal or harmful content (s. 9(5)(b) p. 9). Providers must take proportionate measures relating to the design and operation of algorithms and features to reduce such risks (s. 10(4)(b)–(e) pp. 9–10) including the use of proactive technology. The Act mandates removal of illegal content such as terrorism threats and hate-based abuse (s. 10(2)–(3) pp. 9–10).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The Online Safety Act 2023 assigns clear obligations to platforms but not to AI developers as a distinct actor. Providers of regulated services must implement robust content moderation systems to address illegal and harmful content including duties to use proportionate systems and processes and proactive technology (ss. 9–10 pp. 8-9). The Act also requires transparency including mandatory provider transparency reports on content moderation practices (s. 77 pp. 80–81) and empowers Ofcom to require information about algorithms and systems (s. 85 pp. 87–88). However the framework does not impose standalone obligations on AI developers focusing instead on platform-level moderation and transparency.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Online Safety Act 2023 establishes protective and redress-related mechanisms for individuals targeted by misinformation and tech-facilitated violence but does not create a direct individual right to sue platforms. Providers must offer accessible reporting and complaints procedures and act on reported illegal and harmful content (ss. 17–18 pp. 15–16). Users may escalate unresolved complaints to the Office of Communications which can investigate and enforce compliance against platforms (Part 7 ss. 131–147 pp. 133–147). However it does not provide a standalone civil redress mechanism against platforms; enforcement is regulator-led not victim-initiated.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 addresses Access to Redress and Remedy in the AI context primarily through safeguards for automated decision-making. Articles 22A–22C (pp. 95–96) define significant decisions based solely on automated processing and require protections for individuals affected. These safeguards include providing information about the decision enabling individuals to make representations obtain human intervention and contest the decision ensuring meaningful avenues for redress. Further provisions on meaningful human involvement and reconsideration of decisions are set out in Article 22D and related sections (pp. 96–98) reinforcing the right to challenge and remedy AI-driven outcomes.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.

body.name: Information Commissioner

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 explicitly relies on state-based non-judicial mechanisms to handle grievances arising from automated and AI-driven decision-making. The Information Commissioner is empowered to supervise compliance receive complaints investigate controllers’ reliance on exemptions and enforce safeguards related to automated decisions (Articles 22A–22D pp. 95–99). Individuals can challenge automated decisions and seek remedies through the Commissioner making this a clear use of an existing regulatory body as a non-judicial complaint mechanism for AI-related harms.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 imposes mandatory safeguards on controllers using automated or AI-driven decision-making requiring them to enable individuals to make representations obtain human intervention and contest decisions (Articles 22C and 50C pp. 96–98). These function as internal grievance and review mechanisms within organisations. However the Act does not require companies or developers to establish standalone or formal complaints systems nor does it provide incentives such as trust marks. Therefore it addresses access to grievance mechanisms in substance but not in full scope (pp. 95–98).

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Online Safety Act 2023 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Act protects children from AI-driven harms by requiring regulated services to assess and mitigate algorithmic risks (ss. 9–13 pp. 9–15). It obliges providers to consider how algorithms automated decision-making and design features affect children’s exposure to harmful content (s. 11 (6)(b) p. 11). Services must use proportionate age-verification or estimation technologies (s. 12 (4–8) pp. 12–13) and apply safety-by-design principles. Ofcom enforces these duties ensuring AI systems used online uphold children’s safety and wellbeing.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the Act's scope. Schedule 1 paragraph 9(3) (p. 248) states that the provisions do not apply to services provided by the Crown which includes government departments and agencies such as the Ministry of Defence and intelligence bodies. The Act's duties apply only to commercial online services not to state-run defence or security systems.

body.name: The Office of Communications

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Sections 9–13 (pp. 9–15) require regulated services to assess and mitigate risks to children arising from algorithms and data-driven features indirectly protecting privacy. Section 12 (4–8) mandates proportionate age verification or estimation measures limiting children’s data use. However the Act does not establish standalone provisions on personal data or AI-specific privacy rights which remain under data protection law.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Sections 9–13 (pp. 9–15) require services to assess and mitigate risks to children from the design and operation of algorithms and functionalities. Section 11(6)(b) (p. 11) specifically includes “algorithms used by the service” as potential causes of harm. Section 12 (4–8) mandates measures to prevent children’s exposure to harmful or manipulative content including AI-driven recommendation or targeted advertising systems.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Sections 9(2) and 11(6)(b) (pp. 9 11) require service providers to assess and mitigate risks to children arising from the design of functionalities and algorithms. Section 12(4–8) (pp. 12–13) mandates age-appropriate design and proportionate measures to ensure children’s safety. These provisions assign clear obligations to developers and operators of AI-driven systems to design platforms that are safe and suitable for child users.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Act strengthens children’s privacy in AI contexts by amending UK GDPR data-protection-by-design duties to include “children’s higher protection matters” (Bill cl.81) and by requiring ICO codes of practice on AI/ADM and EdTech. It also revises ADM rules with safeguards (info challenge human intervention). DSIT’s guidance highlights a dedicated section on Children’s Data Protection and ADM safeguards.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.

body.name: The Information Commissioner (ICO)

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Act amends UK GDPR Article 25 to require data-protection-by-design that takes account of “children’s higher protection matters” for services likely to be accessed by children (Art.25(1A)–(1B)). ADM provisions add safeguards (info challenge human intervention contestation) where decisions are solely automated.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: The Act limits harmful automated decision-making via restrictions and safeguards (Arts.22B–22C) and strengthens design duties for children (Art.25(1A)–(1B)) reducing manipulation risk. However it does not directly regulate content or targeted advertising to children (addressed primarily by Online Safety law).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: Controllers must factor children’s higher protection matters into technical/organisational measures (Art.25(1A)–(1B)). Where decisions are solely automated controllers must implement safeguards (provide info enable representations human intervention contestation) and additional measures can be set by SoS regulations.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: National AI Strategy (2021) (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The diversity focus is limited to workforce representation (gender race disability) on pages 16-17 (Reflecting and protecting society section) and page 23 (conversion courses diversity statistics). Page 31 addresses algorithmic bias through representative datasets and mentions bias detection using sensitive data. The Commission on Race and Ethnic Disparities is referenced on page 51 regarding algorithmic bias concerns not cultural/linguistic preservation.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Office for AI

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses bias prevention but not cultural/linguistic diversity specifically. Page 31 states 'Poor quality datasets can also be un-representative especially when it comes to minority groups and this can propagate existing biases.' It commits to permitting data collection 'to monitor and mitigate bias in AI systems.' Page 51 acknowledges 'concerns around fairness bias and accountability.' Page 58 references CDEI's work on 'algorithmic bias.' However there are no provisions addressing cultural stereotypes linguistic diversity erasure or AI favoring dominant cultures.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The document addresses Environmental Impact minimally primarily in Section 1.1 'Building sufficient secure and sustainable AI infrastructure' (pages 7-9). Recommendation 5 (page 9) calls on government to 'mitigate the sustainability and security risks of AI infrastructure' and support companies demonstrating 'sustainability or security advancements.' Recommendation 4 (pages 8-9) references accelerating 'clean power' provisioning for AI Growth Zones.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The UK Sovereign AI and Digital Centre of Government

thematicElements.text: The prevention of resource-intensive AI development and deployment that contributes to excessive energy consumption and e-waste
thematicElements.justification: The document makes limited reference to sustainability by stating that government should “mitigate the sustainability and security risks of AI infrastructure” and support hardware that demonstrates “performance sustainability or security” improvements. However these mentions remain general and aspirational. There are no specific provisions measurable targets or concrete policy tools addressing excessive energy consumption resource-intensive AI development or e-waste management. (pp. 7-9).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers to measure and report on the energy usage and environmental impact of their AI models

The promotion of efforts to improve the energy efficiency of data centers including the use of renewable energy sources advanced cooling technologies and optimized hardware to reduce their significant carbon footprint and water consumption
thematicElements.justification: The plan partially addresses renewable energy: Recommendation 4 (page 8) specifies AI Growth Zones should be provisioned with 'clean power' and Recommendation 5 (page 9) references mitigating 'sustainability risks' and leveraging sustainability 'advancements.' This covers renewable energy sourcing at a high level. However no provisions address advanced cooling technologies optimised hardware water consumption or carbon footprint reduction targets.  Only one of the four aspects (renewable energy) is partially addressed.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Act addresses fairness and non-discrimination through Section 80 on Automated Decision-Making. Article 22B restricts significant decisions based solely on automated processing when involving special categories of personal data (e.g. race ethnicity health political opinions) under Article 9(1). Article 22C mandates safeguards including: (a) informing data subjects about automated decisions; (b) enabling representations; (c) providing human intervention; and (d) enabling individuals to contest decisions. Section 50B-50C extends similar protections for law enforcement contexts. These provisions protect against discriminatory AI outcomes by limiting automated decisions on protected characteristics and ensuring redress mechanisms.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.

body.name: Information Commissioner

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Article 22B (Page 95) restricts automated decisions based on special categories of personal data (race ethnicity religion health) under Article 9(1) preventing discriminatory processing. Article 22C (Pages 95-96) requires safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest decisions providing redress mechanisms. The Act lacks explicit requirements for: proactive bias auditing of AI systems fairness metrics or testing bias impact assessments pre-deployment monitoring for discriminatory algorithmic outcomes or mandates to ensure equitable results across demographic groups. The focus is on procedural safeguards and individual rights rather than systemic measures to promote fair AI outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Article 22B (Page 95) prohibits significant automated decisions based solely on processing of special categories of personal data under Article 9(1) which includes race ethnicity religion political opinions health and biometric data. This restricts discriminatory automated processing based on protected characteristics. Article 22C (Pages 95-96) mandates safeguards and Section 50B (Page 97) extends restrictions for sensitive processing in law enforcement contexts.However the Act does not explicitly require measures to prevent AI systems from perpetuating historical biases in training data auditing algorithms for discriminatory patterns monitoring for bias amplification or proactive detection of systemic discrimination.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Plan promotes gender equality by committing to “increase the diversity of the talent pool” in AI noting that Only 22% of people working in AI and data science are women and that the government needs to focus on increasing the representation by targeted education and initiatives (pp. 11-12).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Opportunities Unit

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: The Plan commits to “increase the diversity of the talent pool” in AI noting that only 22% of AI and data-science workers are women (pp. 11–12). It calls for expanding the representation by targeted education initiatives (p. 12).

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Act hardwires human oversight into AI decisions. Part 2 s.14 (p.14) supplementing UK GDPR Art.22 requires that when a 'qualifying significant decision' is made solely by automated processing the controller must notify the person and if asked within one month reconsider or take a new non-automated decision. For law enforcement (Part 3) ss.49–50 (pp.50–51) and ss.50A–50D (pp.52–54) enable individuals to obtain human intervention make representations and contest decisions; reconsideration must involve 'meaningful human involvement.' For intelligence services (Part 4) ss.96–97 (pp.93–94) provide similar rights.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.

body.name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: Article 22 of the UK GDPR restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect individuals and grants the right to human intervention promoting meaningful human control. However the law applies only when decisions are solely automated and significantly impactful and it does not explicitly emphasize human oversight in all AI uses or critical systemic areas. Thus while it supports human judgment in some contexts it does not fully address all elements of the statement.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Article 22 of the UK GDPR prohibits solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects unless certain conditions are met ensuring human review in high-impact scenarios. This offers protection in some sensitive sectors (e.g. public services credit or employment) but the law does not explicitly target or prohibit full automation in specific fields like law enforcement or medicine. Thus it partially addresses the prevention of full automation in critical sectors.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 assign accountability to data controllers requiring them to ensure lawful processing including for automated decision-making. Controller obligations are set out in s.6 (p.8) and the general obligations in Part 3 s.56 (p.58) while automated decision-making safeguards appear in s.14(4)–(5) (p.14). While data protection officers must be designated for law enforcement processing under ss.69–71 (pp.66–68) the law does not explicitly require the appointment of named persons to oversee or intervene in AI decisions specifically. Therefore while accountability is mandated designation of specific individuals for AI oversight is not directly stated.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: It addresses impact assessments primarily through Section 64 which mandates Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) when processing is 'likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals.' Controllers must conduct DPIAs prior to processing including a description of operations risk assessment mitigation measures and safeguards. Section 65 requires prior consultation with the Information Commissioner when a DPIA indicates high risk. These requirements apply directly to AI systems processing personal data particularly those involving automated decision-making or profiling. Court-case proving application of the law to AI: https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/R-Bridges-v-CC-South-Wales-ors-Judgment
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.

body.name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The Act promotes proactive risk management by requiring controllers to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before processing that is likely to pose a high risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms (s.64(1)). The DPIA must assess the nature of the processing risks to data subjects and the measures and safeguards planned to mitigate those risks (s.64(3)). Where the assessment indicates a high risk that cannot be adequately mitigated the controller must consult the Information Commissioner prior to processing (s.65(2)). Together these provisions require risks to be evaluated and addressed before deployment of potentially harmful data processing activities.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Act assigns obligations to data controllers to conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) where processing is likely to pose a high risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals (s.64(1)). The DPIA must include a description of the processing operations an assessment of risks to data subjects and the measures and safeguards planned to mitigate those risks (s.64(3)). Where the assessment indicates that risks remain high the controller must consult the Information Commissioner before processing begins (s.65(2)). These provisions require organizations to systematically assess and address potential harms before deploying high-risk data processing activities.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: The Data Protection Act 2018 establishes accountability mechanisms enabling individuals to hold organizations accountable for AI system impacts. Section 165 (page 155) grants data subjects the right to lodge complaints with the Commissioner regarding data protection violations. Section 167 (page 157) provides the right to apply to courts for compliance orders. Section 168 (page 159) enables compensation claims for contraventions. Section 124C (page 121) requires the Commissioner to publish impact assessments for codes of practice.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: Article 22(1) provides workers the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling which produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect them. Recital 71 explicitly references employment contexts including 'e-recruiting practices without any human intervention' and decisions evaluating 'performance at work.' Article 22(3) mandates safeguards including the right to obtain human intervention express one's point of view and contest automated decisions. Articles 13(2)(f) and 14(2)(g) require employers to provide meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decision-making and its significance and consequences.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The Act contains broad national security exemptions (e.g. Section 26) and a separate regime for intelligence services (Part 4) which allow the government to disapply many GDPR-style protections including Article 22–type rights. As a result human oversight is not legally guaranteed for individuals in security and defence contexts although institutional oversight mechanisms (e.g. commissioners and parliamentary committees) still exist.

body.name: Information Commissioners Office (ICO)

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 22(1) protects individuals from decisions based solely on automated processing producing 'legal effects' or 'similarly significant effects' covering hiring promotion and termination. Recital 71 explicitly references 'e-recruiting practices without any human intervention' and evaluation of 'performance at work.' Article 22(3) mandates safeguards including human intervention and the right to contest decisions. Article 22(4) restricts automated decisions based on special category data including race and ethnic origin. However the framework does not explicitly address 'discrimination' as a concept which falls under separate legislation (Equality Act 2010). It also does not specifically reference 'algorithmic management systems'.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Article 5(1)(a) establishes transparency as a core principle requiring processing to be 'lawful fair and transparent.' Articles 13(2)(f) and 14(2)(g) mandate controllers provide 'meaningful information about the logic involved as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences' of automated decision-making. Article 15(1)(h) grants workers the right to access information about 'the existence of automated decision-making including profiling' and its logic. Recital 71 references employment contexts including 'performance at work' and the right to 'obtain an explanation of the decision reached.' Article 12 requires information to be provided in 'concise transparent intelligible and easily accessible form.'

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS): Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The ATRS establishes mandatory public disclosure of government algorithmic systems. Section 1 (Summary) mandates publication of ATRS records on GOV.UK. Section 3 (Organisations in scope) defines covered entities: ministerial departments non-ministerial departments and arm's-length bodies providing public services. Section 4 (Algorithmic tools in scope) requires disclosure for tools with 'significant influence on decision-making with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the public.' The framework requires proactive transparency through a standardised template capturing purpose data risks and human oversight.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The ATRS Mandatory Scope and Exemptions Policy explicitly provides for national security exemptions stating that 'situations where no information can be safely published are expected to be unusual (e.g. in cases where even the existence of a tool cannot be made public for security reasons).' The policy also notes that national security was a key consideration in finalising the detailed scope of the mandatory requirement.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: The ATRS addresses all aspects. Public registry: Section 2 (Introduction) establishes 'proactive publication of information on algorithmic tools in the public sector' via a repository at gov.uk/algorithmic-transparency-records. Purpose: Section 4.2 requires disclosure for tools with 'significant influence on decision-making with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the public' capturing each tool's purpose. Description of function: Section 4.1 requires information on how tools 'support or solve a specific problem using complex algorithms.' Responsible agency: Section 3 (Organisations in scope) mandates identification of responsible organisations; records must identify the owner department and team.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: High-risk systems are covered in Section 4.2 (pages 7-8) which targets tools with 'significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect' or that 'directly interact with the general public.' Rationale for use is addressed in Section 5.3 (page 12) stating the ATRS focuses on 'the use case that a tool is deployed into and the steps taken to ensure that a tool is appropriate in that context.' Data for training is partially covered:Section 5.2 (page 11) shows a 'Dataset purposes' field exists in the template but provides limited detail on specific disclosure requirements. However the document contains no provisions requiring disclosure of impact assessment results; there are no references to impact assessment frameworks.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The document provides a framework for distinguishing public disclosure from protected information though it offers broad recommendations rather than detailed guidelines. Section 2 (page 3) establishes that 'Transparency...should be our default position.' For national security Section 5.1 (page 9) addresses cases 'where even the existence of a tool cannot be made public for security reasons' ' For privacy Section 5.1 (page 10) notes the ATRS captures 'tool-level information rather than personal information'. However rather than providing specific disclosure criteria the document broadly aligns exemptions with Freedom of Information Act 2000 and offers guidance on documenting exemptions.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Guidelines for AI procurement (United Kingdom)
items.justification: AI-specific guidelines beyond IT requiring bias/risk checks vendor transparency (avoid ‘black box’) and lifecycle accountability. ‘Top 10 Considerations’ covers data assessment iterative AI impact assessment SME/VCSE-friendly market engagement governance/info assurance and avoiding ‘Black Box’ algorithms/vendor lock-in. In ‘AI-specific considerations’: Publication asks bidders to address data quality/bias and disclose algorithms/models (incl. possible independent audits); Selection/Evaluation lists robust practices (accountability non-discrimination reproducibility testing); Contract Implementation/Ongoing Management requires lifecycle monitoring and end-to-end auditability.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The guidance is AI-specific and goes beyond IT procurement by embedding ethical/social and technical safeguards. “Top 10 Considerations” covers data ethics bias/non-discrimination transparency/explainability governance and avoiding “black box” and vendor lock-in. “AI-specific considerations within the procurement process” adds Data Protection Impact Assessment/data governance data quality and bias checks robust evaluation (testing/reproducibility) and contract-stage monitoring/auditability.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines require vendors to evidence bias fairness and robustness through multiple stages of the procurement process. In “Publication” bidders must explain how they mitigate bias/discrimination and manage data quality and governance; in “Selection Evaluation and Award” authorities are advised to assess testing verification reproducibility and accountability; and in “Contract Implementation” suppliers must ensure ongoing monitoring auditability and lifecycle assurance.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: The Guidelines explicitly warn against “black box” AI and recommend requiring vendor transparency on how systems work. “Top 10 Considerations” includes “Black Box AI systems” and advises obtaining sufficient information from suppliers about the model/algorithm and how it uses data and flags independent assurance/audits. In “Publication” and “Selection Evaluation and Award” it advises setting transparency/explainability requirements in the Invitation to Tender and evaluating suppliers’ ability to explain models and data use. This is intended to prevent procuring opaque systems.

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.justification: The document addresses public sector skills development through capacity building initiatives and training programs for civil servants. Principle 9 (p.14) establishes the competency requirement that civil servants gain skills to 'use design build and maintain AI solutions.' The Acquiring Skills and Talent section (pp.30-31) operationalises this through five learning pathways targeting different civil service roles from beginners to senior leaders. Training programs include free AI courses on Civil Service Learning covering AI fundamentals generative AI machine learning deep learning NLP and computer vision. The Digital Excellence Programme provides specialised AI training for senior civil servants while sandboxes enable practical e
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes a government-wide strategy for upskilling civil servants but excludes the judiciary. Principle 9 (p.14) requires civil servants gain skills to 'use design build and maintain AI solutions' and understand 'risks and opportunities of AI.' The Acquiring Skills and Talent section (pp.30-31) provides a comprehensive strategy with five learner pathways covering foundational AI understanding. Learning Resources (p.31) include courses on 'fundamentals of AI and generative AI including their capabilities and limitations' and 'understanding AI ethics.' However the framework exclusively targets 'civil servants' with no provisions for judges or judicial training.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The document addresses all three aspects. For dedicated AI roles the Governance section (pp.96-97) recommends 'AI governance boards' or 'AI expert representation on an existing governance board' providing oversight and strategic guidance. Ethics committees (p.97) assess ethical implications with specialized experts. For expert guidance the AI community of practice (p.32) offers 'monthly meetings for people working on or interested in AI in the public sector' to share best practices. For fostering responsible AI culture the Leaders pathway (p.31) targets senior civil servants 'responsible for creating an AI-ready culture in government' focusing on governance ethics and strategy.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes clear ongoing professional development requirements. Principle 9 (p.14) states civil servants should 'proactively keep track of developments in the field.' The Acquiring Skills section (p.30) mandates 'Every civil servant can take up to 5 days of learning per year' and emphasises that 'upskilling current digital and data professionals on AI remains crucial.' The Working Collaboratively section (p.32) recommends 'cross-government and industry events that will help your team stay updated on the latest developments and best practices.' The Governance section (p.96) requires frameworks focus on 'continuous improvement through the inclusion of new knowledge methods and technologies.'

items.title: AI Opportunities Action Plan (United Kingdom)
items.justification: In Section 1.3 (“Training retaining and attracting the next generation of AI scientists and founders” pp.10–13) the Action Plan sets an AI skills agenda: it proposes training “tens of thousands” of AI professionals by 2030 (p.11) and expanding pathways into AI careers via further education apprenticeships and employer- or self-led upskilling (Recommendation 17 p.12). It also states the lifelong skills programme must be “ready for AI” ensuring opportunities for workers to reskill into AI and AI-enabled jobs (Recommendation 19 p.12).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Skills England

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Plan covers the objective of reskilling/upskilling for AI-driven labour-market change: it says the lifelong skills programme must be “ready for AI” and that government should ensure “sufficient opportunities for workers to reskill both into AI and AI-enabled jobs” (Recommendation 19 p.12). It also recommends expanding pathways such as further education apprenticeships and employer/self-led upskilling (Recommendation 17 p.12). But it does not set up a specific subsidised programme or funding line in the text.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The Plan supports the idea that employers should upskill workers by recommending expansion of pathways into AI and AI-enabled roles including “employer- or self-led upskilling” (Recommendation 17 p.12) and by calling for sufficient opportunities for workers to reskill ( Recommendation 19 p.12 ). But it does not impose binding requirements on companies to invest in training to mitigate automation-related job displacement (no mandated duties enforcement tools or penalties).

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Code establishes 13 principles across 5 AI lifecycle phases to address cyber security risks specific to AI systems (Introduction). It mandates security obligations including: threat modelling and risk management for AI-specific attacks like data poisoning and model inversion (Principle 3); pre-deployment testing and security assessments (Principle 9); safeguards requiring systems to withstand adversarial attacks and failures (Principle 2); incident management and recovery plans (Principle 6); and monitoring for anomalies and security breaches (Principle 12). The Code applies to all AI supply chain stakeholders including developers system operators and data custodians (Audience section).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: The Code partially addresses this through security-focused provisions but lacks specific quantified thresholds. Principle 2 requires AI systems be 'designed and implemented to withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure' (2.2). Principle 9 mandates security testing before release (9.1). Principle 12 requires monitoring 'to ensure AI models continue to produce desired outputs' and to 'detect anomalies security breaches or unexpected behaviour over time' (12.2). However no specific minimum accuracy requirements quantified performance thresholds or quality benchmarks are established. The focus remains on security robustness rather than accuracy or reliability metrics.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: The Code comprehensively addresses all three aspects. For safeguards Principle 2 (2.2) requires systems 'designed and implemented to withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure.' For fallback procedures Principle 5 (5.3) mandates 'disaster recovery plans to account for specific attacks' and (5.3.1) requires ensuring 'a known good state can be restored.' For emergency protocols Principle 6 (6.5) requires 'an AI system incident management plan and an AI system recovery plan.' Principle 11 (11.1.1) mandates 'contingency plans to mitigate security risks.' Principle 10 (10.3) requires support during incidents 'to contain and mitigate the impacts.'

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: The Code fully addresses all aspects. For pre-deployment testing Principle 9 (9.1) mandates 'all models applications and systems...have been tested as part of a security assessment process' and (9.2) requires 'testing prior to the system being deployed.' For validation Principle 7 (7.3) requires re-running 'evaluations on released models.' For documentation Principle 8 (8.1) mandates 'a clear audit trail of their system design and post-deployment maintenance plans' including 'security-relevant information such as sources of training data intended scope and limitations guardrails...and potential failure modes' (8.1.1). The Scope section confirms lifecycle coverage across all five phases.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: This is the Code's primary focus. The Introduction explicitly addresses AI-specific threats including 'data poisoning model obfuscation indirect prompt injection.' Principle 2 (2.2) requires systems to 'withstand adversarial AI attacks unexpected inputs and AI system failure.' Principle 3 (3.1) mandates threat modelling addressing 'AI-specific attacks such as data poisoning model inversion and membership inference.' Principle 6 (6.2) requires 'controls that mitigate attacks on the AI system via the API' and (6.5) mandates incident management and recovery plans. Principle 12 (12.2) requires monitoring to 'detect anomalies security breaches or unexpected behaviour.'

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (United Kingdom)
items.justification: The Act hard-codes transparency and explainability for automated decision-making. It defines when a decision is 'solely automated' and 'significant' (Art. 22A p. 95) and mandates safeguards (Art. 22C pp. 95–96) that must: provide information about the decision let people make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes. It also amends UK GDPR Articles 13–15 to require information about automated decision-making in notices and access rights (Sch. 6 paras 3–5 p. 198) and ties penalties to breaches of 22B/22C (Art. 83(5) p. 199). In addition restrictions for sensitive data apply (Art. 22B p. 95).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: In the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 defence intelligence and national security are treated as explicit exclusions from the general framework through dedicated exemptions and carve-outs for intelligence services and national security processing (pp. 105–108). These sections remove such activities from the ordinary application of safeguards and rights meaning defence and security are effectively excluded from the framework’s scope for the purposes of this assessment.

body.name: Information Commissioner

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The Act requires controllers to provide information about automated decisions and enable representations human intervention and contesting (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) which promotes clarity for affected individuals. It also amends transparency and access duties so notices and rights requests reflect the new automated decision-making regime (Sch. 6 esp. paras updating Arts 12–15 to reference Arts 15–22D p. 198). However it does not mandate full public disclosure of model internals (e.g. full datasets or comprehensive decision logic documentation).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The Act assigns duties to controllers using solely automated decision-making to give affected individuals information about the decision let them make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) i.e. an explanation focused on the particular decision's basis. It also updates transparency and access duties so privacy notices and access rights reflect automated decision-making use (Sch. 6 updates to Arts 13–15 p. 198). However it does not generally require developers to explain system outputs beyond these automated decision-making contexts.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The Act guarantees safeguards for solely automated decisions that give individuals access to information about the decision and rights to make representations obtain human intervention and contest outcomes (Art. 22C(2)(a)–(d) pp. 95–96) which supports explanation of the result affecting them. It also amends transparency and access duties so notices and access requests reflect automated decision-making use (Schedule 6 updates to Articles 13–15 p. 198). However it doesn't require disclosure of all 'key factors' behind the model beyond these duties focused on automated decision-making.

items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The document directly addresses AI literacy as a core objective. On page 9 Objective (i) explicitly commits to 'Elevate AI literacy and specialized skills' across the workforce. This is to be achieved through inclusive national education and training initiatives including specific skills-building programs focused on AI and data literacy complemented by apprenticeship programs to nurture local talent. This establishes a clear strategic focus on building foundational public understanding and technical capacity in AI.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes a direct recommendation for higher education within the formal system (Pg. 9). Under the objective 'Foster Innovation and R&D' it explicitly proposes to 'Set the foundations for world-class AI university education and applied research by initiating public-private funded programs.' This clearly advocates for the creation and enhancement of advanced specialized AI programs within tertiary educational institutions moving beyond general literacy to establish dedicated centers of excellence and formal advanced learning pathways in the field of artificial intelligence.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: The Personal Data Protection Act (Tanzania)
items.justification: 1. The Act classifies “data related to children” as sensitive personal data (Sec. 3) and prohibits processing without prior written consent (Sec. 30). 2. Since minors cannot consent parents or guardians must provide it (Sec. 30(4)) processing of children’s data. 4. Consent can be withdrawn anytime without cost (Sec. 30(2)). 5. Guardians may also require that decisions affecting the child are not based solely on automated processing (Sec. 36(1)).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Personal Data Protection Commission

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: A data subject including a child’s guardian may demand that decisions significantly affecting the child are not based solely on automated processing (Section 36(1)).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children

items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The document proposes measures to enhance cultural and linguistic diversity. The Diversity and Inclusion guideline (Page 12) suggests AI training data be 'representative of different genders races ethnicities and other diverse factors.'
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: The draft strategy includes provisions to promote AI systems that are representative and culturally responsive. Digital Inclusivity (Paragraph 10.4.1) which aims to integrate diverse human attributes in AI development management and use. It also addresses objectives (Paragraph 11.3.1) by focusing on a Swahili-centered ecosystem ensuring AI responds to local language and cultural contexts. Further specific measures include investment in Swahili resources (Paragraph 11.3.2.4). Additionally the draft establishes technical committees (Paragraph 10.4.2) and promotes media initiatives (Paragraph 13.6.3) to ensure AI development considers inclusivity and cultural relevance.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The draft addresses bias mitigation through data and algorithm design to prevent cultural stereotypes (via Principles 3 & 5 and Guidelines 2 & 6). However it does not explicitly cover preventing the erasure of linguistic diversity or AI tools favoring dominant cultures as no specific provisions target these aspects.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: The draft partially addresses the query through the high-level goal-oriented obligation in Paragraph 10.4.1 to promote inclusivity of diverse human attributes in AI. This applies broadly but is not a specific enforceable rule. The document does not assign explicit mandated obligations to entities to ensure their AI systems are trained on diverse datasets or are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts. Other principles (e.g. 3 5) and guidelines (e.g. 2) on bias and data diversity remain advisory recommendations.

items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The document proposes that fairness and non-discrimination are core principles in AI. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) acknowledges bias risks mandates proactive bias minimization and emphasizes human oversight. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) call for diverse inclusive training data and ongoing vigilance against bias. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline measures such as real-time analysis pre-emptive data checks bias-free design user feedback diverse teams objective mechanisms decommissioning biased systems and early testing. Fairness is linked to Transparency (Pages 10-11 19) Accountability (Page 11) and Safety (Page 10).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document proposes proactive management of bias as a core AI principle. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) mandates that AI must not unjustifiably impair human rights sets standards for bias minimization and emphasizes human oversight. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) focus on diverse inclusive data and ongoing vigilance against bias. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline measures including real-time bias detection bias-free design pre-emptive data checks user feedback diverse teams structural mechanisms decommissioning biased systems and continuous testing.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The document proposes measures to prevent AI from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases. Principle 3: Managed Bias (Page 10) mandates AI must not unjustifiably impair rights and requires bias minimization before deployment. Guidelines 2 and 6 (Pages 12-13) emphasize diverse inclusive data and ongoing vigilance. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) and Recommendation 5 outline real-time bias detection bias-free design pre-emptive data checks user feedback diverse teams and decommissioning biased systems. Transparency (Pages 10-11 19) and Accountability (Page 11) support fairness.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document proposes a proactive duty to manage bias in AI. Principle 3 (Page 10) requires defining bias minimization standards before deployment and assigns humans to spot and correct unintended behaviors. Guidelines 2 3 and 6 (Pages 12-13) address bias across the AI lifecycle covering diverse data ongoing monitoring and careful training analysis. Proposal 5 (Pages 20-21) recommends detailed measures including real-time analysis pre-emptive data checks mitigation via design and multidisciplinary teams continuous testing and mechanisms to eliminate bias. Principle 6 (Page 11) and Proposal 1 (Pages 13-15) reinforce accountability and human oversight for bias management.

items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The document addresses Human Oversight and Determination through Proposal 1: Human  Agency and Control which emphasizes that AI systems must remain under constant human monitoring and control supported by proper documentation (Page 13). It further details steps for implementation (Page 14) including providing technical documentation designing systems for effective monitoring and enabling human choice between AI outputs. Finally it assigns responsibility to system designers requires training of designated personnel and establishes clear criteria for system use and intervention (Page 15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document embeds Human Agency and Control as a core principle (Page 13) requiring AI to remain under constant human monitoring and control. (Pages 13–15) outline concrete safeguards: documenting AI limitations enabling human shutdown designing for oversight and allowing human choice between AI outputs. These apply strongly in critical areas like health justice and education reinforced by principles on safety accountability transparency and risk management (Pages 10–21).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document clearly assigns obligations to designate responsible individuals for AI oversight and accountability. Page 15 Article VII Under Recommendation 1 Principle 1: Human Agency and Control specifies mandates for the clear assignment of obligation for a person who will monitor and control the operations of the AI system. Proposal 6 (Page 22 Article II ) reinforces accountability by requiring defined roles rules and responsibility across the AI lifecycle.

items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The guidelines require developers and deployers to proactively identify and mitigate risks before and during AI deployment. Guideline 9 mandates anticipating risks from data algorithms and system use. Proposal 1 requires early detection of harmful impacts on equality and human rights and Proposal 6 defines risk management as timely identification assessment documentation and minimization of potential harms. Impacts cover societal ethical environmental and economic consequences. Guideline 10 and Proposals 3–5 mandate ethical reviews bias detection data quality checks rigorous testing and thorough documentation with accountability assigned to all responsible parties.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document includes provisions that promote a proactive culture of risk management by requiring evaluation of societal ethical and environmental impacts before AI deployment. Objective (p.9): Calls for ethical AI use through transparency accountability and privacy safeguards. Principles (p.10–11): Require prevention of harm and continuous assessment of impacts. Guidelines (p.12–13): Emphasize anticipating risks and conducting ethical reviews. Recommendations (p.13–22): Call for early detection of harmful impacts and accountability for environmental and societal effects.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: Yes. It assigns obligations to AI developers and users to conduct comprehensive impact assessments for identifying and mitigating risks to individuals and society. Principle 6 (p.10–11) makes developers accountable for system outcomes and their effects on employees. Guidelines 9–10 (p.12–13) require anticipation of risks and regular ethical reviews to detect and address potential harms. Proposals 1 and 6 (p.13–22) call for early detection of harmful impacts documentation and clear accountability while Proposal 3 (p.17–19) mandates data management policies to minimize privacy and societal risks.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document explicitly requires establishing performance thresholds and benchmarks. Page 15 (“Proposal 2: Technical reliability and security”) sets the foundation stating that reliability is achieved when a system “functions as intended” which directly refers to performance benchmarks. Page 14 (Rec. 1.ix) mandates defining metrics and thresholds for system use. Page 16 (Rec. 2.i) details benchmarks such as false-positive and false-negative rates user feedback and validity. Pages 16–17 (Rec. 2.iv) require rigorous testing with quality datasets to confirm reliability.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: On p. 14 there are recommendations for 'technical documentation AI system designs its subsystems and components & mechanisms for monitoring and control of its operation including ex-post analysis of the processing results against the input data' and 'early detection of harmful impacts or side effects to equality and human rights.' To ensure technical reliability and security (p.15) 'Rigorous testing'(p. 16) 'and real-time system monitoring @ p. 17. to mitigate and prevent harm p. 20-21.

However the guideline is not specific on pre-deployment testing.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Yes the document includes specific provisions and recommendations related to protecting AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference. It details specific adversarial risks like training data poisoning avoidance attacks model theft and adversarial attacks (p. 16). items.title: Guidelines for the Secure and Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence in Tanzania (Draft Version 2.0)
items.justification: The document proposes the following AI principles and guidelines. Principle 5: Transparency (Pages 10-11) encourages users to know when AI is used understand its functions and receive clear explanations. Principle 7: Explainable and Interpretable (Page 11) emphasizes technical traceability and the right to explanation. thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document proposes measures and recommendations to promote clarity in AI operations and foster public trust. Proposal 1 (Page 13) suggests documenting AI functionalities use scenarios limitations and areas where the system is not designed to operate. Guideline 5 (Page 12) proposes transparency regarding data sources.  Traceability and Explainability are also discussed in pages 19 & 20. Principle 7 (Page 11) and Proposal 4 (Page 19) recommend explainable outputs and traceable decision logic with Recommendation 4 (Page 20) focusing on clarity at the algorithm and process levels.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications

Principle 6 (Page 11) proposes accountability for designers and deployers emphasizing shared responsibility. Recommendation 1 (Pages 14-15) and Proposal 4 (Page 19) recommend technical documentation ex-post analysis and extra measures for “black box” models to support explainability.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Yes. The document proposes provisions establishing the right for individuals to receive explanations for AI-driven decisions affecting them. Principle 7 (Page 11) states that individuals must be 'meaningfully informed' and have access to the reasons and logic behind decisions presented in an understandable manner. Principle 5 (Pages 10-11) supports this by requiring affected persons to understand how decisions are made.

items.title: Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth
items.justification: The document addresses AI literacy primarily in Section 1 (Background.) noting to equip students with essential AI skills and competencies it frames AI literacy as essential for preparing youth to “understand use and help develop AI technologies.” Section 2 (Policy) establishes AI literacy and proficiency as national priorities emphasizing early exposure critical thinking and ethical understanding of AI systems. Section 4 (Developing an AI-Ready Task Force) and Section 5-7 (Supporting Educators) direct the Department of Education to expand K-12 AI literacy resources integrate AI concepts across subjects and prioritize teacher training and professional development using federal grants.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: White House Task Force on AI Education

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes systemic integration of AI literacy across the education system. Section 2 (Policy) emphasizes early exposure to AI for “America’s youth” indicating primary and secondary (K–12) education while Section 4 references postsecondary pathways such as certifications and Registered Apprenticeships extending AI education into tertiary education and workforce preparation. Together these provisions outline curriculum integration across all educational levels.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
