thematicElements.justification: The document addresses this area partially. In Section 4 (Developing an AI-Ready Workforce) it promotes the expansion of AI-related courses certifications and Registered Apprenticeships and encourages partnerships to increase student exposure to AI. Section 3 establishes a White House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence Education to coordinate such initiatives. However it does not explicitly establish new dedicated AI institutions or formal degree programs.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document clearly includes provisions on teacher training and resources. Sections 5-7 (Supporting Educators) directs the Secretary of Education to prioritize the use of federal discretionary and formula grant programs to support professional development and training for educators so they can integrate AI fundamentals across subjects and offer stand-alone AI and computer science courses. It also emphasizes equipping educators with the skills and tools needed to teach AI literacy effectively.

items.title: Public Law 119-21 'Take it down Act' (USA)
items.justification: The TAKE IT DOWN Act targets AI-enabled harms mainly via “digital forgeries” (AI/ML-generated intimate images) and treats them as a driver of abuse/harassment and coercive threats. It (1) defines “digital forgery” as content created using “machine learning” or “artificial intelligence” (p.1 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); (2) criminalizes knowing publication of such forgeries intended to cause or causing harm and for minors where intent is to “abuse humiliate harass or degrade” (pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); (3) covers threats made to intimidate/coerce/extort or cause “mental distress” (p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); (4) requires platform removal within 48 hours and efforts to remove.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Federal Trade Commission

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: It prevents certain AI-enabled harms by targeting harassment/abuse via nonconsensual intimate images (including AI “digital forgeries”) and related threats plus a takedown mechanism. It does however not address preventing AI tools from creating/amplifying misinformation or hate speech broadly. Relevant provisions: p.2 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); pp.6–7 Sec.3(a).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The Act assigns content-handling obligations to “covered platforms” via a notice-and-removal process required on-platform notice and mandatory removal within 48 hours plus reasonable efforts for identical copies (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(1)–(3)). It does not set comparable obligations for AI developers nor does it require broader transparency reporting on how systems moderate harmful content beyond the notice/process disclosure (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(2)).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: The Act gives targeted individuals a protection/takedown pathway by allowing a notice from an affected person (or representative) and requiring “covered platforms” to remove the content within 48 hours and address duplicates (pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)(1)–(3)). It also provides redress via criminal penalties against perpetrators (pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3)) and FTC enforcement for platform noncompliance (p.7 Sec.3(b)). However the provisions focus specifically on AI-generated intimate forgeries and related harassment and do not establish broader rights covering misinformation or all forms of tech-facilitated violence nor do they provide a comprehensive redress framework against platforms.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The framework addresses a major form of gender-based harassment/violence—nonconsensual intimate visual depictions including AI-enabled “digital forgeries” plus related threats and a platform takedown process. It does not cover gender-based harassment/violence beyond this NCII/deepfake context. (p.2 Sec.2(h)(1)(B); pp.3–4 Sec.2(h)(3); p.5 Sec.2(h)(6); pp.6–7 Sec.3(a)).

items.title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
items.justification: On p. 17 it states that under 'Offer Consistent Remedies or Appeals' that Agencies must ensure that individuals affected by AI-enabled decisions have access to a timely human review and a chance to appeal any negative impacts when appropriate. If an agency already has an appeals or human review process in place such as appeals of adverse actions it may extend or adapt that process to cover decisions made with AI consistent with applicable law. Any remedy process should be designed to avoid placing unnecessary burdens on the individual and should follow established guidance for minimizing administrative burdens.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Appendix §1(c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p.5) states: “This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (as defined in 44 U.S.C. §3552(b)(6)). Additionally Appendix §1(a) (p.4) says it applies to “agencies” per 44 U.S.C. §3502(1) which excludes certain national defense GOCO facilities.

body.name: Chief AI Officer Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Partially because M-25-21 strengthens existing administrative (state-based) pathways but does not create a new ombuds/tribunal/regulator. It requires agencies for high-impact AI to offer remedies/appeals—including timely human review and an opportunity to appeal adverse outcomes and it allows agencies to extend existing review/appeals processes to AI-enabled decisions (Sec. 4(b)(vi) p.17). It also mandates channels to receive public feedback/concerns about high-impact AI use cases (Sec. 4(b)(vii) p.17).

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems

items.title: Children´s Online Privacy Protection Rule Amendments (USA)
items.justification: The document addresses children's rights in the context of AI by expanding the definition of 'Personal information' (p.7) to include biometric identifiers (such as facial templates voiceprints and gait patterns) that can be used for automated or semi-automated recognition (pp.33-35). This change is a direct response to the rapid advancement of technologies like facial recognition and machine learning intended to strengthen the protection of this sensitive immutable data (p.7). The Commission noted concerns about AI/ML tools being used for mass profiling targeted advertising and engagement-maximizing techniques (pp.8 17).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: COPPA includes specific provisions measures and objectives aimed at protecting children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems. The 2025 amendments to COPPA introduce enhanced requirements relevant to AI such as - (a) Verifiable Parental Consent (b) Data Minimization and Retention Limits (c) Transparency and Clear Privacy Notices (d) Prohibition on using children's data for targeted advertising or marketing (e) Security Measures and (f) Restrictions on third-party sharing (pp.7-8 33-35). The Commission shares concerns about practices operators employ to maximize children's engagement with online services (often using AI/ML techniques) and notes it may pursue enforcement under Section 5 of the FTC Act (pp. 8 17).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Yes particularly concerning data collection targeted advertising and sensitive biometric information. Separate Consent for Disclosure: Operators must obtain separate verifiable parental consent for disclosures to third parties and disclosures for advertising purposes are not integral to the service.§312.5(a)(2) on Page 63 (Rule Text) and discussion in Part II.D.1.b on Page 30-33. Definition of 'Support for the internal operations of the website or online service' in §312.2 on Page 61-62. Definition of 'Personal information' in §312.2 on Page 61 (Rule Text). The discussion of this as a response to AI's ability to misuse this data is in Part II.B.3.b on Page 7-8. Contextual advertising Discussion in Part II.B.4.e on Page 19

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers of AI to design systems that are safe age-appropriate and beneficial for children
thematicElements.justification: It was pointed out that profile-based personalization can be beneficial in contexts such as‘‘delivering age-appropriate contentrestricting display of adult contentrestricting contact by adults serving content that is relevant to the user [and]enriching the functionality for a user.’’  (p.18) although the commission decided against this amendment. Nevertheless services - including AI - being age appropriate is being actively discussed (p.47) although not to the level of the assignment of obligations.

items.title: Algorithmic Accountability Act 2025 (USA)
items.justification: The bill operationalizes fairness/non-discrimination by mandating impact assessments for “covered algorithms” used in “critical decisions.” It requires testing for differential performance by protected and other characteristics (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19) and identifying needed resources to improve “fairness including bias and non-discrimination” (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) pp. 24-25). It also mandates consultation with civil-rights and impacted communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) and mitigation of material harms (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11). FTC must publish aggregated findings and a public repository (Sec. 6 pp. 31–36).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The bill includes explicit provisions to promote fair and equitable AI outcomes. It requires algorithmic impact assessments to evaluate differential performance and outcomes across protected classes (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19) directly addressing biased results. Covered entities must identify and implement measures to improve fairness including bias and non-discrimination (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25). It also mandates mitigation of material harms arising from algorithmic decision-making (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11) and consultation with civil rights experts and affected communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) reinforcing equitable treatment objectives.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The bill explicitly aims to prevent AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying societal biases and discrimination. It requires algorithmic impact assessments to test for disparate outcomes and performance across protected characteristics such as race sex age and other legally protected classes (Sec. 4(a)(4)(E) pp. 18–19). Covered entities must document and implement measures to reduce bias and advance fairness and non-discrimination (Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25) and mitigate material harms linked to discriminatory impacts (Sec. 3(b)(1)(H) p. 11). The requirement to consult civil rights experts and affected communities (Sec. 3(b)(1)(G) pp. 9–11) further reinforces bias-prevention objectives.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The bill assigns proactive obligations across the AI lifecycle to entities that develop or deploy covered algorithms. It requires algorithmic impact assessments that identify risks stemming from training data design and deployment contexts (Sec. 4(a)(1)–(4) pp. 16–19). Entities must test for biased or discriminatory outcomes document data sources and limitations and assess how design choices affect outcomes (Sec. 4(a)(3)(B)–(D) pp. 17–18). They must also identify and implement mitigation measures to improve fairness and prevent discrimination before and after deployment (Sec. 4(a)(9)(C) p. 24; Sec. 4(a)(11)(B) p. 25).

items.title: Executive Order 14110 Safe Secure and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligene
items.justification: Gender Equality is addressed through its equity/civil rights mandate: AI must not “disadvantage” groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d) pp.2-3/36). It directs action against algorithmic discrimination and unlawful discrimination in hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3 pp.21–24/36). In health it requires “equity principles” using disaggregated data and monitoring bias across population groups (Sec.8(b)(i)(C) p.25/36). It also requires agencies to assess/mitigate disparate impacts and provide human remedies (Sec.10.1(b)(iv) p.29/36). Under Sec10.2(a) the Director of the Gender Policy Council among others is also tasked with identifying priority mission areas for increased Federal Government AI talent.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: The Attorney GeneralAssistant Attorney General in charge of the Civil Rights DivisionHeads of Federal civil rights officesDepartment of Justices Civil Rights Division

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: The document explicitly requires action against algorithmic discrimination and unlawful discrimination including in contexts such as hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3). It further mandates that AI systems must not disadvantage groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d)) and requires agencies to assess and mitigate disparate impacts and provide remedies where harms occur (Sec.10.1(b)(iv)). However these provisions address discrimination broadly under civil rights protections and gender equality is not explicitly singled out as a distinct category.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns responsibilities to agencies and entities using AI to prevent discrimination and uphold equality. It requires that AI systems must not disadvantage groups denied equal opportunity (Policy & Principles Sec.2(d)) and directs action against algorithmic and unlawful discrimination in areas such as hiring and housing/tenant screening (Sec.7.1–7.3). It also obliges agencies to assess and mitigate disparate impacts and provide human remedies when harms occur (Sec.10.1(b)(iv)). While these obligations cover discrimination generally gender equality is implied rather than explicitly specified as a targeted requirement.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce

items.title: Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights MAKING AUTOMATED SYSTEMS WORK FOR THE AMERICAN PEOPLE
items.justification: The framework explicitly operationalizes human oversight as a core principle of AI governance through its “Human Alternatives Consideration and Fallback” section which establishes that individuals must have access to human review (p. 8) and the ability to contest automated decisions (p. 7). It further requires that automated systems especially in sensitive domains such as employment healthcare and criminal justice incorporate human oversight mechanisms and ensure “human consideration before any high-risk decision” (p. 50–51)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: 'These principles are not intended to and do not prohibit or limit any lawful activity of a government agency including law enforcement national security or intelligence activities.' p. 2

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: Advancing Governance Innovation and Risk Managment for Agency Use of AI (USA)
items.justification: M-24-10 makes AI Impact Assessments a pre-use gate for “safety-impacting” and “rights-impacting” AI: agencies must complete and periodically update an “AI impact assessment” documenting purpose/expected benefit (metrics or qualitative analysis) risks/mitigation stakeholders & failure modes and data quality/provenance/representativeness (§5(a)(iv)(A) pp.17–18). It pairs AI with real-world performance testing (§5(a)(iv)(B) pp.18–19) and independent evaluation using the IA + test results integrated into release/ATO processes (§5(a)(iv)(C) p.19). For rights-impacting AI agencies must record equity/fairness issues and algorithmic discrimination in the AI (§5(a)(v)(A)(1) p.21).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The memo explicitly excludes national-security/defense use: “Applicability to National Security Systems. This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (§2(c) p.4). It also carves out defense/security actors from specific requirements—for example agencies must publish annual AI use-case inventories “except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community” (§3(c)(iv) p.5) and some requirements “do not apply to elements of the Intelligence Community” (§2(a) p.3).

body.name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) with defined governance/risk-management duties

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: M-24-10 requires pre-deployment risk management for “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” AI including completing an AI impact assessment documenting purpose/benefit risks mitigations stakeholders and data issues (§5(a)(iv)(A) PDF pp.17–18) and real-world testing/independent evaluation before release/ATO (§5(a)(iv)(B)–(C) PDF pp.18–19). It also covers societal/ethical aspects via equity/fairness and discrimination duties (§5(a)(v)(A) PDF pp.21–22) and consultation (§5(a)(v)(B) PDF p.22). However it does not require environmental impact evaluation.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: It assigns mandatory obligations to federal agencies (as users/procurers and sometimes developers) to complete and periodically update an AI impact assessment for covered “rights-impacting” and “safety-impacting” AI documenting purpose/benefits risks mitigations stakeholders and data issues (§5(a)(iv)(A) PDF pp.17–18) and to test/evaluate the system before release/ATO (§5(a)(iv)(B)–(C) PDF pp.18–19). It does not impose direct standalone IA duties on all private-sector developers/users (only when acting “on behalf of” an agency) so this obligation only arises in a very specific case as an exception.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: It requires some public-facing disclosure but not a general right to obtain AI Impact Assessment findings. Agencies must post a public AI Use Case Inventory online (§3(a)(iv) “AI Use Case Inventories” p.5) and ensure inventory entries provide plain-language public notice/documentation (§5(a)(v) item “I. Provide public notice…” p.21). For high-risk determinations/waivers agencies must publicly release a summary with justification (§5(a)(ii) “Certification and Publication of Determinations and Waivers” p.14). It does not require publishing the full AI impact assessments.

items.title: Bipartisan House Task Force Report on Artificial Intelligence (USA)
items.justification: According to the document labour protections are addressed in “Education and Workforce” under “Labor Laws for Modern Needs”: employers using AI must comply with anti-discrimination and labor laws and Congress should consider workplace AI transparency to protect workers’ rights (p.104). It states workplace AI must respect NLRA rights (noting NLRB work on emerging tech and protected activity) and calls for OSHA to monitor/update standards as AI enters workplaces (p.104). It also recommends: “Monitor the interaction of labor laws and worker protections with AI adoption” (p.110).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: In Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” (p.104) the Report states employers using AI in the workplace must still comply with anti-discrimination and labor laws and it urges Congress to consider workplace AI transparency to protect workers’ rights. It also recommends monitoring how labor laws and worker protections interact with AI adoption (Recommendation p.110). But it does not provide explicit protections spanning hiring/promotion/termination and does not clearly name non-contract/gig workers under algorithmic management as a specific category.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: The Report explicitly raises the need for “workplace AI transparency” as a way to protect workers’ rights when AI is used by employers (Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” p.104). This supports transparency as an objective/recommendation.But it does not spell out specific obligations to explain AI use for performance monitoring employment decisions or effects on access to benefits nor does it set a defined disclosure standard or enforcement mechanism in that section.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
thematicElements.justification: In Education & Workforce – “Labor Laws for Modern Needs” (p.104) the Report notes that AI-driven workplace practices remain subject to labor laws and points to the relevance of NLRA/NLRB protections as emerging technologies affect workers’ protected activity/rights. This acknowledges organizing and/or collective-rights frameworks in the AI workplace context.But it does not propose concrete AI-specific measures to strengthen collective bargaining and it does not specifically address gig-dominated sectors in this section.

items.title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
items.justification: M-25-21 advances public disclosure mainly through proactive publication requirements: Each agency (except for the Department of Defense and the Intelligence Community) must inventory its AI use cases at least annually submit the inventory to OMB and post a public version on the agency's website. Agencies are encouraged to update the public versions of their inventories on an ongoing basis to reflect their current use of AI. OMB will issue detailed instructions to agencies regarding the inventory and its scope (pp. 12-13).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The memo draws a hard boundary around defense/security uses that qualify as National Security Systems (NSS): in the Appendix Section 1 “SCOPE” subsection (c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p. 4) it states the memo “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System.” It also clarifies NSS AI is governed “through other policy” (footnote 8) reinforcing that this framework’s transparency/governance duties don’t apply to NSS contexts.

body.name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) agency AI Governance Board Chief AI Officer Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: The memo mandates a public inventory: agencies “must inventory [their] AI use cases… and post a public version on the agency’s website” (Appendix §3(b)(v) “Update AI Use Case Inventories” p.12). It implicitly identifies the responsible entity (each agency publishes its own inventory). However it covers AI “use cases” not “all AI systems” and it does not itself require the public inventory to include purpose function description and responsible office—it defers scope/details to OMB: “OMB will issue detailed instructions… regarding the inventory and its scope” (p.13).

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: It sets high-level boundaries but not detailed disclosure-vs-exemption rules. It explicitly excludes National Security Systems: “does not cover AI…component of a National Security System” (Appendix §1(c) p.4). For privacy/disclosure it requires agencies “must inventory [their] AI use cases… and post a public version on the agency’s website” (Appendix §3(b)(v) “Update AI Use Case Inventories” p.12).

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

items.title: Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government (USA)
items.justification: M-25-22 is a federal AI acquisition/procurement framework: it sets scope/applicability to contracts for “AI systems or services” (§2 pp.2–4) mandates agency-level procurement controls (privacy terms IP/lock-in mitigation limits on use of government data for training and documentation/transparency needs) (§3(d)–(f) pp.5–6) and gives AI acquisition lifecycle guidance—cross-functional teams market research product demos/tests performance-based acquisition and ongoing performance/risk management—so agencies buy AI that is fit-for-purpose and preserves public trust (§4(a)–(c) pp.6–8).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The memo excludes national-security/defense acquisition by stating it “does not apply to AI acquired for use as a component of a National Security System” (§2(d) Applicability to National Security Systems p.4). It also notes it does not apply to elements of the Intelligence Community (§2(a) Covered Agencies p.2) reinforcing the security carve-out.

body.name: Senior Agency Officials for Privacy

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: M-25-22 creates AI-specific acquisition guidance beyond standard IT buying by adding ethical/social safeguards (privacy protections and limits on use of govt data for training: §3(d)–(f) pp.5–6; risk controls for high-impact AI: §4.D p.10) and technical requirements (documentation/transparency expectations; testing & evaluation; and ongoing monitoring: §4(b)–(c) pp.7–8 and §4.E pp.10–11).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: Safety/performance testing is addressed: agencies are told to include product demos and testing before award (§4(c) pp.7–8) and contracts must enable ongoing testing/monitoring to evaluate performance risks and effectiveness at set intervals (§4.E pp.10–11). High-impact AI must follow minimum risk-management practices (§4.D p.10). But the memo does not mandate a universal vendor “proof” of bias/fairness testing as a standalone requirement for all procurements.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
thematicElements.justification: It requires/encourages documentation and transparency to support explainability and tracking performance (“Documentation Transparency and Accessibility” §3(e)(v) p.6) and tells agencies to set reasonable transparency/documentation requirements on vendors for (potential) high-impact AI (“Solicitation Development – AI Use Transparency Requirements” §4(c)(1) pp.7–9). It also references data/model portability and pricing/licensing transparency to avoid lock-in (§4(c) p.9–10).

thematicElements.text: Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
items.justification: M-25-21 embeds public-sector skills development in three places: (1) “Agency AI Strategies” requires agencies to plan to “recruit hire train retain… an AI-ready workforce” and achieve “AI literacy for non-practitioners” (p. 6). (2) “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce” links training/upskilling to responsible AI adoption and prioritizes developing and retaining AI talent (p. 9). (3) Minimum practice “Ensure Adequate Human Training and Assessment” requires periodic system-specific training for AI operators (p. 17).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: The memo draws a hard boundary around defense/security uses that qualify as National Security Systems (NSS): in the Appendix Section 1 “SCOPE” subsection (c) “Applicability to National Security Systems” (p. 4) it states the memo “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System.” It also clarifies NSS AI is governed “through other policy” (footnote 8) reinforcing that this framework’s transparency/governance duties don’t apply to NSS contexts.

body.name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO) Agency AI Governance Board

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: M-25-21 establishes government-wide expectations to build an AI-ready federal workforce and foundational understanding through training/upskilling (civil service) but it does not cover the judiciary. It requires Agency AI Strategies to plan to “recruit hire train retain… an AI-ready workforce” and achieve “AI literacy for non-practitioners” (p.6 Agency AI Strategies). It also includes a dedicated section on “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce” (p.9). Scope is limited to covered executive agencies (p.4 §1 Scope).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: M-25-21 makes the CAIO and Agency AI Governance Board responsible for advancing an AI-ready workforce. The CAIO’s duties include advising agency leadership and helping drive the agency’s transformation toward an “AI-ready workforce” (p.10 Sec. 3(a) Agency Governance Roles and Bodies). The Governance Board provides cross-office oversight and coordination for AI governance (which includes workforce readiness activities tied to the memo’s training/upskilling expectations) (p.11 Sec. 3(a)) aligning with the memo’s workforce/training provisions (p.9 “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce”).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: For public-sector skills development M-25-21 explicitly requires ongoing training: under the Minimum Practices “Ensure Adequate Human Training and Assessment” states agencies must ensure “sufficient and periodic training assessment and oversight” for AI operators and that “Training should be conducted on a periodic basis … and should be specific to the AI system” (p.17 Sec. 4(b) practice iv). It also promotes continuous upskilling by urging agencies to “leverage AI Trainings and Resources to Upskill Existing Staff” (p.9 “Enabling an AI-Ready Federal Workforce”).

items.title: America´s AI Action Plan
items.justification: In “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI” (pp. 6–7) the Plan calls for a “serious workforce response” including DOL funding for rapid retraining for AI-related displacement and guidance so states can use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk; it also proposes pilots under WIOA to address AI-driven workforce challenges (p.7). In “Train a Skilled Workforce for AI Infrastructure” (pp. 17–18) it recommends skills frameworks/competency models industry-driven training CTE and Registered Apprenticeships and partnerships with community/technical colleges to transition the existing workforce into critical AI roles (pp.17–18).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: AI Workforce Research Hub (under the US Department of Labor DOL)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: In “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI”; “Recommended Policy Actions” (pp. 6–7) the Plan calls for government-funded/subsidized reskilling/upskilling by directing DOL to (1) fund rapid retraining for workers affected by AI-related job displacement and (2) enable states to use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk (pp. 6–7). It also recommends piloting workforce approaches under WIOA to address AI-driven labor-market challenges (p.7).

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: The Plan supports financial support pathways through public workforce funding mechanisms—e.g. in “Empower American Workers in the Age of AI” (pp. 6-7) it recommends DOL use Rapid Response funds to proactively upskill workers at risk and fund rapid retraining for AI-related displacement (pp. 6-7). However it does not consistently specify direct worker-facing benefits like paid leave or individual grants; many incentives are routed via programs/states/employers rather than support to workers themselves directly.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation
thematicElements.justification: The Plan encourages and incentivizes employer investment in training but it does not create mandate for companies to fund reskilling. In “Train a Skilled Workforce for AI Infrastructure” (pp. 17–18) it promotes industry-driven training and employer involvement to transition the existing workforce into critical AI roles (pp.17–18). It also points to incentive-based approaches (e.g. employer-supported training/education assistance mechanisms) rather than compulsory company obligations.

items.title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
items.justification: M-25-21 links AI Safety/Security to “high-impact AI” and requires “minimum risk management practices” prioritizing AI that is “safe secure and resilient” and mandates a plan to discontinue non-performing high-impact AI or cease use if risk mitigation isn’t possible (Main memo pp.2-3). In the Appendix it requires processes to measure monitor and evaluate ongoing performance (p.10) and mandates termination of non-compliant AI (Sec. 4(a)/4(b) pp.13–14) plus pre-deployment testing and risk mitigation plans (Sec. 4(b)(i) pp.14–15).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: M-25-21 explicitly states: “Applicability to National Security Systems. This memorandum does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (Appendix Section 1 ‘SCOPE’ subsection (c) p. 4).

body.name: Chief AI Officer Council

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
thematicElements.justification: M-25-21 requires use-case metrics and testing/validation—e.g. for high-impact AI it mandates pre-deployment testing reflecting “expected real-world outcomes” and AI impact assessments with benefits “supported by specific metrics” (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(i)–(ii) pp. 14–15). It also requires processes to “measure monitor and evaluate… performance and effectiveness” (Sec. 3(a)(i)(F)(2) p. 10). While it also necessitates to implement minimum risk management practices for AI (pp. 2-3) it does not set a universal minimum accuracy/quality threshold applicable across systems so this remains quite broad and unspecific.

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: For high-impact AI M-25-21 requires agencies to implement safeguards including human oversight and contingency planning: it calls for a plan to “discontinue” high-impact AI that is not performing as intended and to “cease use” when risks can’t be mitigated (main memo pp.2-3).  In the Appendix it requires human review/oversight mechanisms and procedures to manage failures/harms and implement remedies/appeals where relevant (minimum practices for high-impact AI Sec. 4(b)(v)–(vi) pp. 15–16).

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: For high-impact AI M-25-21 requires pre-deployment testing and risk mitigation plans reflecting “expected real-world outcomes” (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(i) pp. 14–15). It mandates an AI Impact Assessment before deployment to be updated periodically throughout the AI lifecycle and documented (Appendix Sec. 4(b)(ii) p. 15). It also requires agencies to document implementation of minimum practices and be ready to report them (Appendix Sec. 4(a)(1) p. 13).

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: M-25-21 recognizes adversarial evasion/manipulation as an AI risk factor (Appendix Sec. 7 “Methods of Understanding AI Risk Management” p. 23). It also requires agencies to test and periodically review high-impact AI to detect adverse impacts to the “performance and security of AI functionality” and to design monitoring to detect changes post-deployment (Appendix minimum practices p. 16). However it does not prescribe detailed technical cybersecurity controls; it instead directs agencies to update internal policies on “cybersecurity and privacy” (Consolidated Table of Actions p. 24).

items.title: Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation Governance and Public Trust (USA)
items.justification: OMB Memorandum M-25-21 embeds Transparency and Explainability as core governance requirements for federal AI use.Transparency is mandated through public disclosure mechanisms including publicly released AI Strategies (Section 2(a) pp. 5–6) AI Use Case Inventories (Section 3(b)(v) pp. 12–13) and public reporting of high-impact AI determinations and waivers (Section 4(a)(iv) p. 15).Explainability is operationalized via documentation and traceability duties requiring agencies to document AI capabilities limitations intended use data provenance and model performance (Section 2(d)(ii) p. 9; Section 4(b)(ii) pp. 16–17). Agencies are also encouraged to favor models that are “inherently more explainable” (Section 3(b)(iii) p. 12).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Defence and security are explicitly excluded from the scope of OMB Memorandum M-25-21. The Appendix states that the memorandum “does not cover AI when it is being used as a component of a National Security System” (Appendix §1(c) p. 5). It further clarifies that elements of the Intelligence Community are exempt from multiple obligations including minimum risk management practices and public reporting (Appendix §1(a) p. 4; Sections 3(b)(v) and 4 pp. 12–15). Additionally agencies are directed to rely on separate defense- and intelligence-specific AI policies for such systems confirming a clear exclusion from this framework’s scope

body.name: Chief AI Officer (CAIO)Agency AI Governance BoardChief AI Officer Council (interagency chaired by OMB)Office of Management and Budget (OMB) (oversight coordination reporting authority)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: The document includes explicit provisions promoting clarity on how AI systems operate to foster public trust. It requires agencies to document AI purpose capabilities limitations intended use data sources and data provenance as well as to conduct and document AI impact assessments (Sections 2(d)(ii) and 4(b)(ii) pp. 9 and 16–17). It also mandates public transparency measures including publicly available AI Strategies AI use case inventories and public reporting on high-impact AI determinations (Sections 2(a) 3(b)(v) and 4(a)(iv) pp. 5–6 12–13 and 15). These measures directly advance clarity explainability and public trust. It also advocates for using AI models that are inherently more explainable where possible (p. 12).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses AI-facilitated misinformation through Line 1.2 Action F (p. 38) which explicitly commits to addressing the impacts of AI on disinformation and the integrity of democratic processes in a manner consistent with freedom of expression through a holistic and systemic approach. Line 1.2 (p. 37) more broadly commits to developing risk-based regulatory frameworks that protect human rights democracy and the rule of law throughout the AI lifecycle. The Strategy does not address gender-based AI-facilitated violence hate speech deepfakes platform content moderation obligations or redress mechanisms for victims of AI-facilitated harm.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content

The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Principle 4 (p. 30) requires proactive measures to prevent gender-based discriminatory stereotypes and biases from being reproduced in AI systems. However this addresses bias and discrimination in AI design broadly — it does not specifically target AI-facilitated gender-based harassment or violence.

items.title: Law No. 18331: Personal Data Protection Law (Uruguay)
items.justification: Article 16 of Law 18.331 protects individuals from decisions made solely on the basis of automated decision-making that significantly affects them granting the right to demand human intervention review and explanation. It is mentioned in the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2024-2030 as part of the legal basis for regulating the automated processing of personal data. The Strategy explains that the Personal Data Regulatory and Control Unit (URCDP) is empowered to “establish the criteria and procedures that must be observed by those responsible and in charge in the automated processing of personal data indicated in Article 16 of the aforementioned Law.”
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: Article 3 lit. b) of Law 18.331 explicitly excludes from the law's scope databases whose purpose is public security national defence State security and activities related to criminal investigation and repression of crime. Accordingly the rights established under the law — including the automated decision-making right under Art. 16 and the Habeas Data remedy under Art. 37 — don't apply to databases operated by armed forces police or intelligence bodies for these operational purposes. Note that administrative data held by these bodies & personal background data provided to judicial or administrative authorities remain subject to the law under Art. 25.

body.name: Personal Data Regulatory and Control Unit (URCDP)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 37 establishes the Habeas Data process by which any person who needs to enforce the rights granted by the Personal Data Protection Law can go to court including the right under Article 16 not to be subject to automated decisions with significant legal effects. Note that this judicial remedy does not extend to databases explicitly excluded from the law's scope under Article 3 lit. b) namely those operated by armed forces police or intelligence bodies for public security national defence or criminal investigation purposes.

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Article 63 of Law 20.075 (2022) amended Article 34 of Law 18.331 to empower the URCDP to establish criteria and procedures for automated processing of personal data under Article 16. As the body responsible for enforcement of Law 18.331 URCDP has sanctioning powers and receives complaints from data subjects regarding violations of their rights including rights related to automated decision-making. Note that as of the assessment period URCDP has not yet published specific criteria or guidance on automated processing and the same exclusion applicable under Article 3 lit. b) limits URCDP's jurisdiction over security and defence operational databases.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 16 of Law 18.331 requires data controllers to provide individuals with information about the criteria and programs used in automated decisions affecting them implying an obligation to respond to individual requests. However it does not mandate companies to establish formal accessible grievance mechanisms or proactive human review processes for AI-related harm.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses cultural diversity in AI through three provisions. Principle 4 (p. 29-30) requires AI actors to prevent ethnic-racial and national-origin biases in AI systems mandates diversity in AI development teams and calls on the public sector to address structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups in training data. Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) explicitly requires generating training datasets reflecting Uruguay's culture and social diversity. In p. 15 cite as a milestone the Montevideo Declaration which establishes cultural and geographical diversity as a guiding principle for responsible AI. Linguistic diversity is not addressed.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
thematicElements.justification: Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) mandates generating training datasets reflecting Uruguay's culture and social diversity. However there is no mention of linguistic diversity or responsiveness to a wide range of languages.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: Principle 4 (p. 30) requires AI actors to prevent ethnic-racial and national-origin biases from being reproduced in AI systems and addresses algorithmic and automation bias. However there are no specific provisions against erasure of linguistic diversity or dominance of specific cultures.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts
thematicElements.justification: principle 4 (p. 30) requires the public sector to address structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups in training data. Line 2.2 Action a (p. 43) mandates culturally representative datasets. However obligations are limited to cultural diversity; linguistic and contextual adaptability are not addressed.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Principle 4 of the Strategy addresses'Equity and non Discrimination' setting the standard for this issue. (Page 29). It requires AI systems to respect equality and explicitly address both algorithmic bias and automation bias recognizing risks of reproducing gender racial social and disability-based inequalities (pp. 29–30). The Strategy promotes proactive measures such as improving training data quality fostering diversity in development teams and ensuring equitable access to AI benefits (p. 30). 'This principle covers both discrimination based on algorithmic bias and discrimination based on automation bias—the human tendency to rely excessively on the support of algorithms even when they make mistakes.' (p.30)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: mainly under the guiding principle of Equity and Non-Discrimination and in Section 5. It explicitly requires preventing discriminatory stereotypes and biases based on gender ethnicity social status or disability and calls for improving data quality and diversity in design teams to reduce biased results (pp. 29–30). In Axis 3 (Sustainable Development) it mandates instruments such as indicators protocols and good-practice guidelines to measure social impacts and address differentiated effects on vulnerable groups (p. 48).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy requires proactive measures to avoid reproducing discriminatory stereotypes and structural inequalities based on 'gender ethnic or racial identity social status national origin or disability' throughout the AI lifecycle (pp. 29–30). It also promotes improving training data quality fostering diversity in development teams and using open public data to reduce underrepresentation and algorithmic bias (p. 30).

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: Page 29 of the Strategy covers this point partially because it establishes a general duty of AI actors to adopt proactive measures to prevent discrimination and reduce unwanted biases but it does not impose detailed enforceable technical obligations. It requires stakeholders to consider all phases of the AI lifecycle and to adopt measures to improve data quality promote diversity in design teams and avoid discriminatory outcomes (p. 29). However these obligations are framed as principles and guidelines rather than as concrete requirements such as mandatory bias impact assessments auditing duties or lifecycle monitoring mechanisms.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Principle 4 'Equity and Non-Discrimination' (pp. 29-30) mandates public & private sector actors to adopt proactive measures to address AI's impact on gender equality & other structural inequalities throughout the entire AI system lifecycle preventing discriminatory stereotypes & biases based on gender ethnic-racial identity social status & national origin from being reproduced in AI systems. It further requires all AI actors to reduce undesired biases in training data & models & obliges the public sector to promote AI models using quality data to overcome the structural underrepresentation of diverse social groups. Line 2.4 Action d (p. 45) promotes women's enrolment in technology & STEM careers to strengthen their participation in AI.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development and use of AI systems and tools that perpetuate gender discrimination and bias
thematicElements.justification: Principle 4 (pp. 29-30) explicitly addresses gender discrimination and bias requiring all AI actors to adopt proactive measures to prevent gender-based discriminatory stereotypes from being reproduced in AI systems throughout their lifecycle. It further mandates measures to ensure training data quality to overcome the structural underrepresentation of diverse groups. The principle covers both algorithmic bias and automation bias. However these remain guiding principles rather than specific binding provisions or procedural requirements targeting gender discrimination.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations and responsibilities to entities developing and using AI systems to ensure Gender Equality and prevent discrimination
thematicElements.justification: Principle 4 (p. 30) assigns responsibilities to public sector actors to promote equitable access to AI benefits and address digital divides and encourages private sector civil society and academia to contribute to this goal. The public sector is further required to promote AI models using quality data to overcome structural underrepresentation. However these are framed as responsibilities to be encouraged rather than binding legal obligations assigned to specific entities.

thematicElements.text: Initiatives to increase women representation in the AI industry workforce
thematicElements.justification: Line 2.4 Action d (p. 45) explicitly commits to continuing through various initiatives the fostering of women's enrolment in technology and STEM careers to strengthen their participation in the AI ecosystem. This constitutes a named objective and concrete action within the Strategy's implementation plan directly targeting women's representation in the AI workforce.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Action 3 of the Strategy focuses on “Respect for Dignity and Human Rights” requiring AI systems to be developed and used in accordance with ethical principles human dignity and internationally protected human rights including autonomy privacy equality and non-discrimination (p. 27). The Strategy warns that the use of AI in decision-making poses significant risks to these rights if decisions are not fair transparent and accountable. As emphasized on page 29 meaningful human oversight and human decision-making are essential particularly in high-risk applications through controls over data and systems monitoring outcomes and ensuring the reliability of AI outputs before decisions are made.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy includes recommendations related to the promotion of meaningful humancontrol over AI systems. Under Action 3 (page 29) it explicitly states that human oversightand decision-making are essential to prevent AI from negatively impacting human rights. Itrecommends that whenever AI is used to make or support decisions particularly in highrisksystems there must always be human oversight over AI outputs including monitoringtheir reliability and establishing controls over data and systems. These recommendationsensure that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replace human judgmentaddressing all aspects of the question.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy includes provisions related to preventing full automation particularly in highrisksystems where human oversight is essential (Action 3 page 29). However it does notexplicitly specify sensitive sectors such as law enforcement or medicine. Therefore whilethe recommendation addresses the need for human intervention and ethical judgment incritical contexts it only partially covers the aspects mentioned in the question.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Under the guiding principle of 'Respect for Human Dignity and Human Rights' the State is required to maintain or adopt frameworks and procedures to identify assess prevent and mitigate adverse impacts on human rights according to the risk and intended use of AI systems (p. 28). In employment the document mandates studies and projections on labor impacts monitoring mechanisms and retraining policies (p. 51). Línea 3.2 includes a specific action to investigate the social economic and environmental impact of AI and develop measurement instruments protocols and good practice guides (p. 48). The Strategy also includes indicators to evaluate economic impact and public services (Línea 3.4 action e p. 50).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Principle 1 (Page 25) “AI for people’s well-being and sustainable development” where the Strategy states: “…and the continuous evaluation of the social economic and environmental repercussions involved in the development and application of AI systems.” In page 28 it refers explicitly to the need for ex ante impact assessments:”These measures should include frameworks and procedures that make it possible to identify assess prevent and mitigate as appropriate ex ante or iteratively throughout the lifecycle of AI systems adverse impacts on human rights based on the risk and intended use involved.'

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy’s section on “Respect for dignity and human rights” establishes that private actors must implement due diligence processes to identify prevent mitigate and account for how they address their impacts on human rights (Page 27-8).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Although the Strategy does not explicitly establish a public right to access impact assessment findings the principle of 'Strengthening Democracy' calls for transparency public accountability and access to information in the context of AI governance (p. 26). Additionally Línea 3.4 calls for implementing indicators and monitoring mechanisms to evaluate AI processes and public policy which implies a degree of public accountability (p. 50). However the Strategy does not explicitly define a right for the public to access the findings of impact assessments.

items.title: Law 20.396/2025 on Minimum Protections for Workers Performing Tasks through Digital Platforms
items.justification: Law 20.396/2025 establishes minimum protections for digital platform workers. Article 4 requires companies to respect equality and non-discrimination in algorithm implementation and mandates disclosure of automated monitoring and decision-making systems. Article 5 requires disclosure of key parameters used in automated decisions. Article 7 grants workers the right to a written explanation within 48 hours of any automated decision affecting their working conditions including account suspension or termination. Article 8 guarantees digital reputation portability and data access. Article 10 requires risk assessment of automated systems. Article 19 upholds collective bargaining rights for autonomous workers.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: Ministry of Labour and Social Security - General Labour and Social Security Inspectorate

thematicElements.text: The protection of workers from AI-driven discrimination in hiring promotion and termination decisions — including those who  lack an employment contract but are subject to algorithmic management systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 4 requires companies to respect equality and non-discrimination in algorithm implementation and mandates disclosure of automated decision-making systems affecting working conditions including account suspension or termination. Article 7 grants the right to a written explanation for automated decisions. However the law covers only platform delivery and transport workers not broader hiring or promotion decisions across sectors.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for transparency in the management process including obligations to explain how AI systems are used to monitor performance make employment-related decisions and interact with or affect workers’ right to access workplace benefits
thematicElements.justification: Articles 4 and 5 require disclosure of automated monitoring and decision-making systems including the parameters used. Article 7 mandates a written explanation within 48 hours for any automated decision significantly affecting working conditions. Article 10 requires risk assessment of automated systems for worker health and safety.

thematicElements.text: The reinforcement of workers' rights to organise and collectively bargain in the context of AI-driven changes in the workplace including in sectors dominated by gig work
thematicElements.justification: Article 19 explicitly guarantees autonomous platform workers the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining enabling them to negotiate conditions more favourable than the legal minimums.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 31) requires public sector entities that use AI whether in service delivery or decision-making support to guarantee public access to information about those systems in accordance with Law 18381/2018 (Uy's Access to Information law). It further mandates public sector compliance with Law 19179/2013 (regulated by Decree 44/2015) on open software & the use of open AI models as mechanisms to ensure transparency of AI systems developed used & acquired by the State. These provisions establish a government-specific disclosure obligation grounded in existing access to information law directly addressing public accountability for government algorithmic systems rather than general AI transparency principles.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: In the Axis of Governance the Action Line 1.2 (Regulatory Frameworks) establishes the need to Generate frameworks for transparency and accountability in developmentActions and use of AI establishing requirements appropriate to the contexts intended uses and specific risks associated with this technology. Although it does not discriminate specifically about high risks the intention is the same as the premise.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: The document does include provisions and recommendations related to distinguishing between information that can be made public and information that must be protected particularly for privacy reasons.Specifically it states that AI actors (public or private) must ensure that the data they collect and use comply with current regulations on the protection and privacy of personal data and with the guidelines of the Personal Data Regulatory and ControlUnit (URCDP).It explicitly refers to compliance with Law No. 18331 (Personal Data Protection Law)and Law No. 20212 which establish the principles of legality purpose consent data security confidentiality and proactive responsibility.  (PP 30 and 42).

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon
thematicElements.justification: The document states that AI stakeholders must ensure transparency and explainability by providing “meaningful information appropriate to the context and the specific situation”. The goal is to make results intelligible and to allow people to challenge decisions that affect them.Although it does not specifically mention avoiding “technical jargon” the emphasis on making information meaningful intelligible and appropriate to the context implies that explanations should be clear and understandable to the public in general rather than overly technical.(PP 31).

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Uruguay's National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 38 Axis 1 Action G) calls for the establishment of a public procurement policy specifically covering the development use acquisition and implementation of AI solutions incorporating principles of ethical responsible and safe use. However this remains a prospective commitment — no AI-specific procurement guidelines vendor requirements or accountability mechanisms are yet in force.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of AI-specific procurement guidelines that go beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical social and technical considerations
thematicElements.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 38 Axis 1 Action G) calls for establishing a public procurement policy specifically covering the development use acquisition and implementation of AI solutions incorporating principles of ethical responsible and safe use of this technology and considering necessary regulatory adjustments. This explicitly goes beyond traditional IT procurement to include ethical and technical considerations.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for vendors to demonstrate that their AI systems have undergone thorough testing for bias fairness and safety
thematicElements.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 30 Principle 4) requires AI stakeholders to collaboratively reduce unwanted biases in data and models promoting training data quality team diversity and openness of public data. While this implies testing for bias and fairness it does not specifically require vendors to demonstrate their systems have undergone such testing prior to procurement.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of a mandate to require transparency from vendors regarding the data and models used in their products to prevent 'black box' systems
Procurement mechanisms that include elements or conditions for prioritising local AI developments as a strategy for enhancing AI sovereignty

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Uruguay's National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (p. 49 Section 3.4 'Public Management') explicitly addresses AI capacity-building for public servants. Action d mandates the design and implementation of a comprehensive training plan in collaboration with AI experts targeting technical specialised and operational roles across all levels of government including the legislative body justice system and regulatory agencies. Action e introduces monitoring mechanisms to assess the effectiveness of these training initiatives. Source: National AI Strategy 2024-2030 p. 49.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: Page50: Action D of Line 3.4: Design and implement a comprehensive training plan in collaboration with AI experts from different sectors aimed at people involved in technical specialized and operational roles across all sectors and at all levels of government decision-making.This plan will include specific actions aimed at those in the legislative body the justice system and regulatory agencies.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
thematicElements.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 (pp. 42–44 Axis 2) supports the creation of specialised AI governance roles and expert teams within government to strengthen internal capacity for responsible AI deployment. However the Strategy stops short of mandating dedicated AI champion roles in every agency or establishing a formal cross-government expert network making this a partial rather than full commitment.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 mandates comprehensive training plans for all State personnel across technical specialised and operational roles at all government levels including the legislature justice system and regulatory bodies (Axis 2 Line 2.4 Action F p. 45; Section 3.4 Actions D and F p. 50). The Strategy further commits to strengthening Uruguay's government AI community to develop ongoing institutional capabilities supporting a culture of continuous professional development in AI.

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: The National AI Strategy 2024-2030 addresses reskilling and upskilling through two dedicated lines of action. Line 2.4 (Talent Management pp. 44-45) commits to incorporating AI training across all educational levels and mandates that all labour training plans include content on AI's impact on work strengthening occupational re-conversion. Line 3.5 (Impacts of AI on Employment p. 51) establishes a specific line of action to address AI-driven job displacement including studies on labour market impacts programmes to maintain employability for both active and inactive workers and engagement with employers and workers' organisations to identify human capital development opportunities.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: Line 2.4 (pp. 44-45) commits to generating instruments and incentives to strengthen university capacity for AI talent and designing a comprehensive training plan for all State personnel. Line 3.5 (p. 51) includes implementing training programmes for both active and inactive workers. These actions imply institutional support and public funding but stop short of explicitly establishing government-funded or subsidised reskilling programmes.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
thematicElements.justification: Page 51: Design tools to maintain the employment status of individuals and implement training and capacity buildingprograms for those currently or not currently employed.
