Does not explicitly says that will provide financial support but to 'design tools' a broad concept.

thematicElements.text: Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Uruguay’s National AI Strategy explicitly incorporates the principles of safety security reliability and responsible innovation. The Strategy dedicates guiding principles to “Reliability and Security” (p. 32) and “Responsible and Safe Innovation” (p. 33) establishes a governance framework to ensure ethical responsible and secure AI (p. 21–22) and contains a cybersecurity section (p. 44). These provisions collectively align with the accuracy reliability and risk-management mechanisms.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of performance thresholds or quality benchmarks to ensure AI systems operate reliably and accurately under stated conditions
The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Onpage 32 it states that “AI systems must be reliable secure and resilient capable ofrecovering from failures or attacks” but no specific implementation requirements orprocedural measures are provided.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Principle 9 (p. 33) establishes that responsible and safe innovation requires incorporating security and privacy measures from design and throughout the entire AI system lifecycle and continuously evaluating and adjusting innovations based on feedback. However no specific pre-deployment testing validation protocols or documentation requirements are established.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference
thematicElements.justification: Principle of Reliability andSecurity (p. 32) requires that:“ AI must be reliable secure and resilient capable of recovering from failures or attacks and generating consistent outcomes and actions. ... function properly and do not pose security risks and that they comply with information-security principles by design.”It further states that actors must adopt “measures and procedures to ensure robustness and resilience of systems … and security against potential cyberattacks” Under “Cybersecurity” (44 the document establishes concrete measures and actions including: “Establish specialized areas for AI cybersecurity… to develop response mechanisms to the threats posed by AI for early threat detection...

items.title: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy of Uruguay 2024-2030
items.justification: Principle 6 is Transparency and Explainability: (page 31)Transparency and explainability play a crucial role in ensuring the effectiveness of all the above principles. AI stakeholders must ensure transparency and explainability in relation to AI systems. This involves providing meaningful information appropriate to the context and the specific situation balanced with the protection of other rights that may be involved. The information disclosed must make the results intelligible and must be appropriate to enable people to challenge them when they are affected. In addition transparency is specifically linked to strengthening democracy (page 26) regulatory frameworks (page 37) and public management (page 49).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: In the specific case of the public sector the implementation of this principle also implies that public entities that use AIwhether in the delivery of public services or in supporting decision-making guarantee access to the respective public information in accordance with the provisions of Law No. 18381 of October 2008 and its regulatory decrees (Access to Public Information Law). The implementation by public sector actors of Law No. 19179 of December 27 2013 regulated by Decree No. 44/015 ofJanuary 30 2015 (Free Software Law and Decree)  and the use of open AI models are also fundamental elements to ensure the transparency and explainabilityof the systems developed used and acquired by the State. Pp. 39 and 40.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy requires AI actors to ensure transparency and explainability of systems (p.31) providing meaningful intelligible and context-appropriate information that allows individuals to challenge decisions affecting them (p.31). It also mandates human oversight in AI-supported decision-making especially for high-risk systems (p.29) and requires decisions to be fair transparent and accountable (p.29). These obligations apply to any AI system whose outputs may impact people However it does not assigns specific obligations to entities and does not explicitly mentions loan applications or hiring.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy requires AI actors to provide meaningful intelligible and context-appropriate information that allows individuals to understand and challenge decisions that affect them (p.31). It mandates transparency and explainability for all AI systems (p.31) and requires that AI-supported decisions be fair transparent and accountable (p.29). Together these provisions ensure that people can know the key factors behind AI outputs and contest adverse outcomes. However it does not establish a right to receive and explanation or to understand key factors.

items.title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: Chapter 3 section 5 promotes enhancing knowledge and skills of the population and developing human resources. Chapter 3 par.3 introduces game-based and experimental learning for early ages.  promotes AI learning “for youth and across all segments”. Par. 5 of Chapter 3 includes measures to improve teacher/professor skills (foreign training upskilling programmes); establish AI labs at universities; provide online courses with foreign experts; build training systems for school and university staff. However it provides no specific measures targeting  measures targeting: rural schools low-income students gender gaps people with disabilities.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy covers tertiary-level curriculum reforms only. Chapter 2 states that AI-focused subjects were introduced in 15 higher education institutions and that 572 students were admitted to new AI degree programmes in 12 universities.  Target Indicators for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 includes establishing  AI laboratories in major universities and expand specialized training. For primary and secondary levels the Strategy mentions early interest-building and programming for schoolchildren but does not mandate curriculum reforms.

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education

items.title: Draft Law on the protection of the rights of users of online platforms and websites (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The draft addresses AI-facilitated misinformation and violence through Article 12 (content moderation) which obliges online-platform owners to: (1) strengthen content-moderation systems and (2) ensure AI technologies operate in compliance with the Law. These duties directly target AI-driven harms by requiring platforms to improve detection/removal workflows and to govern their AI tools accordingly.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: Article 13 (Grounds for Illegal Content): On online platforms and users should prevent distributing “Illegal content” that includes:  false information threatening public order/safety;  incitement of national/racial/ethnic/religious hatred; obscene content showing disrespect to society/state/symbols; drug propaganda; pornography cruelty incitement to suicide; inducement (incl. of minors) to actions threatening life/health; other content advocating criminal/administrative offenses. This article defines takedown grounds that also apply when such content is created/amplified by AI (e.g. deepfakes inciting violence or coordinated harm) giving platforms a legal basis to remove AI-driven illegal content.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: The draft assigns obligations to platforms: Article 12 (Content moderation) requires online-platform owners to improve content-moderation systems and ensure their AI technologies operate in compliance with the Law—a clear duty to implement robust moderation. Chapter 4 / Article 13 defines categories of prohibited content guiding moderation practice. However no explicit transparency duties (e.g. reporting on how systems handle harmful content) and no direct obligations on AI developers apart from platform use is available.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
thematicElements.justification: Art. 10 grants users a right to file complaints to platform owners about harmful content or platform (in)action requires an accessible mechanism and a response within 15 days. Coupled with Art. 12 (platform moderation duty) and Art. 13 (prohibited content) this enables users to seek takedown. However no explicit rights to protection measures appeal/escalation to a regulator compensation/damages or platform liability or remedies against AI developers available.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The Strategy does not contain any direct references to cultural or linguistic diversity multilingual AI localization or the protection of minority languages. However the Strategy outlines framework for the development of a National AI Language Model that takes into account the linguistic characteristics of the region. Par. 4 states 'forming specialized datasets for tasks such as voice video and communication analysis in the Uzbek language'.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy

thematicElements.text: The promotion of the development of AI systems that are representative of and responsive to a wide range of cultures and languages
The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to ensure their systems are trained on diverse datasets and are adaptable to various cultural and linguistic contexts

items.title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The Draft ethical rules addresses Fairness and Non-discrimination by defining key risks and required safeguards. It explains that AI systems must avoid biased or discriminatory outcomes noting that algorithmic bias arises from underrepresented or flawed data and can disproportionately harm protected groups (p.1–2) . It highlights the human-rights basis for non-discrimination and stresses preventing AI from amplifying societal inequalities (p.2–3). The document identifies measures such as bias audits fairness metrics mitigation duties and rights to explanation and redress (pp.3–5).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: Section 4.5 (Fairness and Non-Discrimination) explicitly requires that AI systems be developed implemented regulated and used without discrimination based on gender race nationality language culture religion belief social origin or social status — directly supporting fair and equitable outcomes for all groups.Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers) mandates assessments and tests to identify and mitigate potential biases ensuring AI systems do not produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups.Section 10 (Risk Assessment) requires a preliminary analysis of AI’s impact on human rights including the prevention of bias and discrimination reinforcing the commitment to equitable outcomes.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Section 4.5 (Fairness and Non-Discrimination) prohibits any discrimination in the development implementation regulation and use of AI systems based on gender race nationality language culture religion belief social origin or social status. This directly targets the risk of AI reinforcing societal biases.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The framework includes explicit actionable obligations requiring developers and implementers to address bias:Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers):obliges them to “organize assessments and tests to identify and mitigate potential biases” — a direct requirement to proactively detect and address bias;requires transparency documentation of limitations and regular updates — all elements of lifecycle bias-mitigation practices.Section 10 (Risk Assessment): mandates a pre-deployment risk assessment including analysis of “prevention of bias and discrimination” — confirming obligations across data collection model development and deployment stages.

items.title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The document treats Impact Assessments mainly as pre-deployment and ongoing checks. P.4 §6 Rights & Obligations of AI Developers/Implementers requires developers to “organize assessments and tests” to detect/mitigate bias and to document system limits/potential impacts. On p.5 Part III it §8 Internal Control & Monitoring implies risk identification + safety-measure effectiveness recommended. §9 annual External Audit recommended and §10 Risk Assessment before implementation; includes human-rights impact bias/discrimination safety privacy/security threats.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: Clause 4.2. Prioritization of the Interests of Individuals Society the State and the Environment. AI systems must be developed implemented regulated and used without harming human rights and freedoms the lives and health of citizens state and public security and the environment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns duties that developers and implementers must organize assessments tests to detect or mitigate risks (p.4 §6) and must conduct a risk assessment before implementation covering human-rights impacts bias discrimination safety privacy security (p.5 §10). It also adds internal control and monitoring with recommended external audit (p.5 §§8–9). But it doesn’t clearly require comprehensive impact assessments for all users nor set a detailed impact assessment methodology.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The Strategy addresses public-sector skills development by requiring government bodies to strengthen AI competencies among civil servants. Chapter 3 sets the objective to enhance skills in the use of AI technologies digital skills data analytics and big data for specialists and public employees. Paragraph 5 of Chapter 3 expands training through AI laboratories programming and machine-learning modules and professional retraining programmes for personnel involved in digital-government tasks. Appendix 2 assigns ministries concrete tasks to deliver AI training for staff.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Ministry of Digital Technologies

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy establishes a government-wide plan to enhance AI competencies among public-sector employees. Chapter 3 sets nationwide objectives to improve skills in AI technologies digital skills data analytics and big data for specialists and ministry personnel. Appendix 2 assigns AI-training tasks to multiple ministries confirming a whole-of-government approach. However no section references the judiciary or judicial training so the provision does not extend to members of the judiciary.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The document emphasizes continuous upgrading of knowledge and skills for public administration employees and those responsible for digitalization and calls for specialized AI training programs (Chapter 3 5-§; Appendix 2 assigns ministry implementation responsibilities). However it does not establish a binding or explicit requirement for ongoing professional development (eg mandatory continuing training cycles).

items.title: On Measures to Radically Improve the System of Training Highly Qualified Personnel in the Field of Justice
items.justification: The decree addresses public-sector skills development in the judiciary by embedding AI-related competencies into judicial training. Section I(1)(d) requires candidates judges and court staff to acquire skills in the “practical application of modern information technologies and the capabilities of artificial intelligence.” Section III(6)(i) expands professional retraining through virtual court modules and classes on using AI technologies. Section VI(18) authorises use of the Adolat digital systems complex to support AI-enabled learning and research
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Academy of Justice

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a government-wide strategy for upskilling and reskilling public servants and members of the judiciary to build a foundational understanding of AI its applications and its risks
thematicElements.justification: The decree creates an AI-related upskilling framework exclusively for the judiciary. Section I(1)(d) mandates training in modern technologies and AI capabilities for judicial personnel and Section III(6)(i) requires virtual-court and AI-technology modules in retraining programmes.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of dedicated roles and teams within government to act as AI champions providing expert guidance and fostering a culture of responsible AI innovation
The requirement for ongoing professional development and training to keep pace with the rapid evolution of AI technology
thematicElements.justification: The decree clearly promotes continued skills-building in AI within the judiciary by mandating that candidates judges and court staff develop competence in the practical use of modern information technologies and AI (Section I(1)(d)) and by strengthening retraining through virtual court modules and dedicated classes on AI technologies (Section III(6)(i)) supported by the Adolat digital systems complex for AI-enabled learning and research (Section VI(18)). However it does not set out a formal recurring continuing-professional-development obligation (eg periodic mandatory refresher training).

items.title: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies until 2030 (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The Strategy addresses reskilling and upskilling by prioritizing AI-skills development across education and the workforce. Chapter 3 sets the objective to “enhance the knowledge and skills of the population in the use of AI technologies” and expand human-resource capacity . It calls for teaching programming and AI technologies to students and improving the competencies of teachers and specialists. Chapter 5 introduces AI labs at universities and foreign training programs and expands access to online AI courses and professional retraining to prepare workers for an AI-driven economy.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Coordination Commission for the Implementation of the Digital Uzbekistan 2030 Strategy

thematicElements.text: The establishment of government-funded or subsidized reskilling and upskilling programs to help workers adapt to new job market demands created by AI
thematicElements.justification: The Strategy sets out state-supported measures to expand AI-related skills. Chapter 3 establishes the objective to enhance the population’s competencies in AI technologies and develop human-resource capacity. Chapter 5 and Appendix 2 (Action Plan) include government-led actions such as creating AI laboratories expanding training programmes in universities providing online AI courses and supporting professional development and retraining—constituting government-funded or supported reskilling and upskilling initiatives.

thematicElements.text: The provision of financial support or incentives for workers who participate in reskilling programs
Requirements for companies to invest in the training and development of their existing workforce to mitigate job displacement caused by automation

items.title: Draft Ethical Rules for Artificial Intelligence Development and Usage (Uzbekistan)
items.justification: The Rules directly addresses transparency and explainability through Section 4.6 which requires AI systems to produce clear understandable and explainable outcomes and obliges developers to ensure transparency of training databases including sources limitations and potential biases.Section 6 further obliges developers to ensure transparency and understandability of AI algorithms and provide detailed documentation on functionality and risks. Section 7 grants users the right to receive explanations about AI system algorithms.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

thematicElements.text: The promotion of clarity regarding how AI systems operate including their purpose data sources and decision-making logic to foster public trust
thematicElements.justification: Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) explicitly requires that AI systems be developed to provide “clear understandable and explainable outcomes” and that users be informed about their interaction with AI systems. It further requires developers to ensure transparency regarding the databases used to train AI models including their sources limitations and potential biases which directly supports clarity about system purpose data origins and logic.Section 6 obliges developers to ensure the transparency and understandability of AI system algorithms and to provide documentation describing system functionality and risks—reinforcing public trust by making AI operations more comprehensible.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities developing and using AI to provide meaningful explanations of their systems' outputs especially in high-stakes contexts like hiring or loan applications
thematicElements.justification: Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) requires that AI systems deliver clear understandable and explainable outcomes establishing an obligation for developers to ensure meaningful explanations of outputs.Section 6 (Obligations of Developers and Implementers) further mandates developers to ensure the transparency and understandability of AI algorithms and to provide comprehensive documentation describing functionality limitations and risks upon request.Section 7 grants users the right to receive explanations regarding AI system algorithms reinforcing the expectation of meaningful output explanations including in high-stakes use cases.

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals to receive an explanation for a decision made by an AI system that affects them and to understand the key factors that led to that outcome
thematicElements.justification: Section 7 (Rights of AI Users) explicitly grants individuals the right to “receive explanations regarding AI system algorithms.” This provision ensures that users can understand how an AI system produced an outcome that affects them.Additionally Section 4.6 (Transparency and Openness) requires AI systems to provide clear understandable and explainable outcomes obliging developers to make key factors—such as data sources limitations and potential biases—available. Together these sections establish a right to explanation and insight into the factors influencing AI decisions.

items.title: Resolution of the Politburo on breakthroughs in education and training development (Resolution No. 71-NQ/TW)
items.justification: The document stresses the importance of redefining a new vision and strategy for the education system that contextualizes digital technology and artificial intelligence (P12). It set the objective of II.1 (p3) pursuing universalization of technological capacity artificial intelligence and English proficiency at the 12-K school level. This objective shall be achieved by III.4 (p7) Comprehensive universal digital transformation and strong application of digital technology and artificial intelligence in education and training; 7 (p10) Strongly renovating training programs according to international standards; integrate content on data analytics and artificial intelligence and entrepreneurship.
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

body.name: Party Committee of the National Assembly

thematicElements.text: Curriculum reforms including at primary secondary tertiary levels
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes curriculum reforms across multiple levels of the education system. It calls for introducing knowledge of digital competencies and artificial intelligence into the general education program covering primary and secondary education (p.8). It also promotes modernization of higher education curricula by integrating content on data analytics artificial intelligence entrepreneurship and innovation into training programs (p.10). These reforms are part of a broader strategy of digital transformation and modernization of education including new teaching methods and updated program standards (pp.7–8).

thematicElements.text: Establishment of educational institutions or programs offering AI-related courses within the formal education system
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes the development of AI-related education within the formal education system. It calls for introducing digital competencies and artificial intelligence knowledge into the general education curriculum (p.7–8) and for improving technological and AI capacity across the school system by 2030 (p.3). In higher education it directs institutions to modernize training programs by integrating content on data analytics and artificial intelligence to support research innovation and the development of high-level human resources (p.10). These measures support the establishment and expansion of AI-related courses within formal education programs.

thematicElements.text: Provision of teacher training and resources for AI education
thematicElements.justification: The document includes measures to support teacher training and resources for AI education. It calls for improving digital and artificial intelligence competencies for both learners and teachers and incorporating these competencies into educational programs (pp.7–8). It also encourages policies that mobilize enterprises and higher education institutions to participate in training and fostering teachers and learners in digital capacity and AI. These initiatives are part of a broader strategy for comprehensive digital transformation and the application of AI in teaching learning and educational management (p.7).

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is listed as one of the prohibited cases of AI applications with the potential of causing serious harm to social order safety and national security (Art 11.7 p7). Therefore AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is perceived as a threat to information security and social order security and lies under the responsibility of the Ministry of Public Security (Art 66.2 p36). Moreover AI-facilitated Misinformation and Violence is also referred in the context of AI applications in journalism publishing media and cultural and social fields as AI-generated content that violates the law and lies within the monitoring responsibility of the Ministry of Culture Sports and Tourism (Art 66.3 p36).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI tools from being used to create amplify or disseminate misinformation and hate speech or to facilitate harassment and violence
thematicElements.justification: The document includes provisions aimed at preventing the misuse of AI systems to generate and disseminate harmful or misleading content. Article 11 explicitly prohibits the production or dissemination of AI-generated fake content that is likely to cause serious harm to social order safety or national security (Art. 11(7)). In addition Article 10 requires transparency and labeling measures to clearly identify AI-generated or deepfake content when published publicly (Art. 10(1)–(2)). Together these provisions establish safeguards aimed at and intended to prevent AI tools from being used to create or spread harmful or deceptive content.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to platforms and AI developers to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent about how their systems handle harmful content
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because the obligation to implement robust content moderation policies and to be transparent is mentioned but not explicitly linked to Ai-facilitated misinformation and violence. According to Article 15 on General Obligations for High-Risk AI Systems Providers and implementers of high-risk AI systems have the following obligations: 1. Establish maintain and operate a risk management system throughout the life cycle of the system. 5. Ensure a level of accuracy safety and cybersecurity appropriate to the declared purpose of use. 6. Implement transparency obligations to affected persons including notification of the nature of the system decision-making mechanisms and the right to request human review (p9 10).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for individuals and groups targeted by misinformation or tech-facilitated violence to receive protection and to seek redress against the perpetrators and the platforms that enabled the harm
The prevention of the use of AI tools to facilitate gender-based harassment and violence

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: Article 60 (p33). Liability for compensation for damages in the artificial intelligence value chain. 1. Organizations and individuals who violate the law in artificial intelligence activities and cause damage to the legitimate rights and interests of other organizations and individuals must compensate according to the provisions of the Civil Code and the provisions of this Chapter. Article 61 (p34). Liability for damages in the artificial intelligence value chain. Article 62 (p3435). Civil liability in cases where artificial intelligence systems cause damage. Article 63. Right to request the Court to force the disclosure of evidence. (pages 33-35)
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The establishment or reinforcement of judicial mechanisms that allow individuals or groups to seek remedy for harms caused by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Article 62. Civil liability in case of damage caused by artificial intelligence systems. 2. In order to ensure fairness in determining the causal relationship the Court has the right to request the defendant the supplier or the party implementing the artificial intelligence system to provide information documents and technical data necessary to clarify the system's operating mechanism the risk management measures applied and the factors related to the case. Article 63. Right to request the Court to force the disclosure of evidence (pages 34-35)

thematicElements.text: The creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms (e.g. ombuds institutions regulators tribunals or consumer bodies) to handle AI-related grievances
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because there is no explicit reference to creation or use of state-based non-judicial complaint mechanisms yet Art 17.2 page 11 and Art 23.2 page 15 mention that 'Based on collective complaints serious incidents or information from reliable sources competent state management agencies have the right to request a reassessment or temporarily apply management measures corresponding to a higher level of risk. The Government shall specify in detail the procedures time limits criteria for applying temporary measures and inter-agency coordination mechanisms.' However it does not detail mechanisms to submit and respond to collective complaints.

thematicElements.text: Requirements or incentives for companies or developers to establish accessible grievance or complaints mechanisms for individuals harmed by AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because Art 44.4 (page 25) on Ethics and responsibility in the use of AI in the public sector demands government agencies to establish mechanisms for receiving feedback and complaints from citizens. This however applies to the public sector only.

items.title: A national program on 'Protecting and supporting children's healthy and creative interaction in the online environment 2021 - 2025' (Vietnam)
items.justification: The document outlined a comprehensive package of activities to protect children's rights in cyberspace. As for AI specifically the document mentioned the need to establish CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material) database to contribute to research and monitoring of negative AI applications in this regard.
items.scope: Vertical approach (the framework targets specific sectors specific types of data or  AI technologies.

body.name: There are many entities in the implementation plan as listed above

thematicElements.text: The protection of children's personal data and privacy when they interact with AI systems
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because the overarching goal of the Program is to 'Protect children's private information and personal secrets when they access information and participate in activities on the internet environment' (page 1 Section I.1.a). However specific reference to AI is only one paragraph related to building Child Sexual Abuse Material database which constituted only a small part of children's interactions with AI systems (Section II.3).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the use of AI to exploit manipulate or harm children including through targeted advertising or inappropriate content
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because the document in Section II.3 explicitly aims to prevent sexual exploitation of children based on the application of modern technologies such as artificial intelligence but limits it to that specific area. thematicElements.justification: The document promotes the development of AI systems responsive to diverse languages and cultural contexts. In addition the National Artificial Intelligence Development Fund supports research and development of linguistic AI models particularly those designed for Vietnamese and ethnic minority languages (Art. 38(3)(a)) reinforcing inclusive and culturally representative AI development.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of the development of AI tools that perpetuate cultural stereotypes erase linguistic diversity or favor dominant cultures
thematicElements.justification: The document promotes linguistic and cultural inclusivity in AI development but does not explicitly address the prevention of cultural stereotyping. Article 35 directs the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy to prioritize AI solutions suitable to Vietnam’s conditions particularly technologies for processing Vietnamese and ethnic minority languages (Art. 35(2)(c)). In addition the National Artificial Intelligence Development Fund supports research and development of linguistic AI models for Vietnamese and ethnic minority languages (Art. 38(3)(a)). However the provisions do not explicitly prohibit AI systems that perpetuate cultural stereotypes or favor dominant cultures.

The No.1 priority of the National AI Development Fund is to research develop and apply AI linguistic models especially those for Vietnamese and ethnic minority languages (Art 38.3.a). However there is no explicit assignment of obligations to any entity. This is just encouragement.

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: The document refers to Fairness and Non-discrimination as a key principle that all activities related to AI systems in Vietnam must comply with (Article 4.2&4.4 p.3). Article 11 (p6) lists prohibited AI cases including (3) 'Large-scale social credit scoring of individuals by state agencies leading to unfair or disadvantageous treatment in unrelated social contexts'. Art 44 (p25) emphasized this responsibility in AI applications to provide public services. Art 45.3 (p26) obliges AI systems classified as high-risks or having systemic risks to undertake impact assessments on fairness and discriminatory bias. Administrative penalties can be imposed(Art 56.2.b p.32) & also a subject of state inspection Art 54 p.31
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of fair and equitable outcomes from AI systems ensuring they don't produce biased results that disproportionately affect certain groups
thematicElements.justification: The document refers to Fairness and Non-discrimination as a key principle that all activities related to AI systems in Vietnam must comply with (Article 4.2&4.4 p.3). Article 11 (p6) lists prohibited AI cases including (3) 'Large-scale social credit scoring of individuals by state agencies leading to unfair or disadvantageous treatment in unrelated social contexts'. Art 44 (p25) emphasized this responsibility in AI applications to provide public services. Art 45.3 (p26) obliges AI systems classified as high-risks or having systemic risks to undertake impact assessments on fairness and discriminatory bias.

thematicElements.text: The prevention of AI systems from perpetuating or amplifying existing societal biases and discrimination based on race ethnicity gender religion age or other protected characteristics
thematicElements.justification: Yes the key preventative method is through mandatory AI impact assessments as stated in Art 45.3 (p26) which obliges AI systems classified as high-risks or having systemic risks to undertake impact assessments on fairness and discriminatory bias. Failures to comply with mandatory impact assessment and prevention of bias and discrimination might result in administrative penalties (Art 56.2.b p.32). This prevention is heavily stressed in the public sector as Art 44 (p25) emphasized fairness and non-discrimination in AI applications in public services provision.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and deployers to proactively identify measure and mitigate sources of bias throughout the AI lifecycle from data collection to deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns explicit obligations to developers and deployers to identify measure and mitigate bias throughout the AI lifecycle. Article 15 requires suppliers and implementers of high-risk AI systems to implement data governance measures ensuring the origin quality and representativeness of training testing and operational data while limiting and minimizing bias (Art. 15(2)). Article 45 further mandates  Impact Assessments that identify risks of bias or discrimination and propose technical and managerial mitigation measures (Art. 45(3)(b–c)). These obligations are reinforced by overarching principles requiring AI systems to operate in a non-discriminatory manner (Art. 4(2)) and to minimize bias and discrimination(Art. 42(1)(a)

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: The document establishes multiple safeguards ensuring human oversight of AI systems. Article 4(1) sets a human-centered principle requiring AI to support humans remain under human supervision and not replace humans in important decisions (p.3). Article 15 requires providers of high-risk AI systems to establish mechanisms for human monitoring intervention and control ensuring final human decision-making authority where required (Art. 15(4) p.10). In the public sector Article 44 prohibits fully automated decisions that affect individuals’ rights and requires final decisions to remain subject to human supervision and accountability (Art. 44(2) p.25).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of meaningful human control over AI systems ensuring that AI remains a tool to assist humans rather than replacing human judgment particularly in critical areas where AI-enabled decisions or actions can have broad and systemic implications
thematicElements.justification: The document establishes meaningful human control as a core principle of AI governance. Article 4 requires AI systems to be human-centered serving and supporting humans not replacing them in important decisions and remaining under human supervision and ultimate responsibility (Art. 4(1) p.3). For high-risk systems Article 15 mandates mechanisms for human monitoring intervention and control ensuring final human decision-making authority (Art. 15(4) p.10). In the public sector Article 44 further prohibits fully automated decisions affecting individuals’ rights without human oversight (Art. 44(2) p.25).

thematicElements.text: The prevention of full automation in sensitive sectors where human intervention and ethical judgment are necessary such as in law enforcement or medicine
thematicElements.justification: Yes because Art 14 (p9) lists out 2 mechanisms for managing high-risk AI systems: a) Post-audit; b) Pre-audit which is enforced based on the assessed level of the AI system's autonomy in reducing human control. Art 15 (p10) obliges the supplier and the deployer of high-risk AI systems to 3. Maintain detailed technical documentation including human monitoring mechanisms; 4. Establish human monitoring mechanisms; ensuring that the final decision-making power belongs to humans. In law enforcement sector Art 44.2 p25 specifically says 'State agencies are not allowed to use artificial intelligence systems to make fully automated decisions in cases that directly affect the legitimate rights and interests of organizations and individuals.'

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to entities using AI to designate responsible individuals who can oversee intervene in and ultimately be accountable for the decisions made by the system
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns obligations ensuring human oversight and accountability for AI system decisions. Article 15 requires suppliers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to establish mechanisms for human monitoring intervention and control and to maintain technical documentation including human monitoring mechanisms and operational logs (Art. 15(3)–(4) p.10). In addition Article 4 establishes the principle that AI systems must remain under human control supervision and ultimate responsibility (Art. 4(1) p.3) ensuring that identifiable persons oversee and remain accountable for AI-driven decisions.

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: The document establishes a formal Artificial Intelligence Impact Assessment requirement. Article 45 defines it as a process for identifying analyzing predicting and mitigating potential negative impacts of AI systems on human rights and social values (Art. 45(1)). Developers or deployers of high-risk AI systems or systemic-risk models must conduct the assessment before market release or use (Art. 45(2)). The report must evaluate impacts on human rights privacy equality safety and risks of bias or discrimination and propose mitigation measures including protections for vulnerable groups (Art. 45(3)(a–d)). The government will issue detailed procedures and templates (Art. 45(4)).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

defenceAndSecurity.justification: As mentioned in Article 2.1 (page 1) this Draft Law applies to activities related to artificial intelligence systems taking place in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam or having artificial intelligence system products and services that affect the market users national security social order and safety and the legitimate rights and interests of Vietnamese organizations and individuals. The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The promotion of a culture of proactive risk management by requiring that the potential societal ethical and environmental impacts of AI systems are evaluated before their deployment
thematicElements.justification: The document requires proactive evaluation of potential risks before AI deployment through a mandatory Artificial Intelligence Impact Assessment. Article 45 obligates organizations developing or deploying high-risk AI systems or systemic-risk models to conduct this assessment before bringing the system to market or putting it into use (Art. 45(2)). The assessment must analyze impacts on human rights privacy equality and safety identify risks such as bias or discrimination and propose mitigation measures including protections for vulnerable groups (Art. 45(3)(a–d)). This establishes a structured approach to assessing societal and ethical risks prior to deployment.

thematicElements.text: The assignment of obligations to developers and users of AI to conduct comprehensive Impact Assessments that identify and mitigate potential risks to individuals and society
thematicElements.justification: The document assigns explicit obligations to developers and deployers to conduct impact assessments. Article 45 requires organizations and individuals developing or deploying high-risk AI systems or systemic-risk multi-purpose models to perform an Artificial Intelligence Impact Assessment before market release or use (Art. 45(2)). The assessment must analyze impacts on human rights privacy equality and safety; identify risks such as bias or discrimination; and propose technical and managerial mitigation measures including protections for vulnerable groups (Art. 45(3)(a–d)).

thematicElements.text: The establishment of rights for the public to access the findings of these assessments ensuring that they can hold organizations accountable for the impacts of their AI systems

items.title: Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
items.justification: The document considers Public Disclosure of Gov Algorithmic Systems a top mandatory responsibility and gov agencies must embrace the leadership in setting a bright example in ensuring transparency and accountability when applying AI systems (Art 44.1 p25). The document stresses the far-reaching impacts of public services delivery and administrative decisions and consequently obliges gov agencies to conduct AI Impact Assessment disclose information about the purpose and scope of AI applications in the public sector and most importantly establish a mechanism for receiving feedback and complaints from citizens which is not even an obligation for private companies (Art 44.3 & 4 p25).
items.scope: Horizontal approach (the framework applies across multiple sectors or applications and is not limited to a particular domain or  AI technology type).

The only explicit exclusion regards AI applications developed deployed and used exclusively for defense security and intelligence purposes (in Article 2.3 page 1)

thematicElements.text: The establishment of a public registry or inventory of all AI systems used by the government including their purpose a general description of their function and the agency responsible for their operation
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because while Art 22.1 does mention the establishment of a public registry of AI systems for state management purposes this does not require registration of all AI systems used by the government and is mandatory for AI systems identified with high risks only (p1415 Art. 22.2). By words this means only AI systems with high risks used by the government shall be registered on that public registry.

thematicElements.text: The requirement to disclose key information about high-risk systems such as the data used for training the rationale for their use and the results of any impact assessments
thematicElements.justification: Partially is selected because Art 44.4 (p25) does require gov agencies to disclose information about purpose and scope of all AI applications (not just high-risk ones). However the extent of disclosure is limited to 'basic information on the purpose (rationale for their use) and scope' of the AI applications rather than being substantial about sharing results of AI impact assessments (which is mandated in Art 44.3 p25) or origins of data used for training so the disclosed information is quite limited in scope and does not include these things.

thematicElements.text: Clear guidelines on what information is subject to public disclosure versus what must be protected for reasons of national security or individual privacy
thematicElements.justification: Art 44.4 (p25) does require gov agencies to disclose information about purpose and scope of all AI applications ( 'basic information on the purpose (rationale for their use) and scope' of the AI applications). Art 22.4 (p25) demands (specifically for high-risk AI) that basic information be made public & ensuring a balance between transparency and the requirement to protect state secrets business secrets and personal data. It further notes that the government regulates the scope extent and form of information disclosure.

thematicElements.text: The provision of a clear and accessible explanation for the public on how an AI system works and how it might affect them avoiding technical jargon

items.justification: The strategy promotes workforce upskilling and reskilling in AI through training certification and career-transition programs. It calls for implementing and popularizing basic skills in AI and data science to promote innovation among young people and supports short-term and medium-term certification training in AI for students and workers seeking career changes (Strategic Orientation – Human Resource Development pp.4–5). It also encourages short-term AI training programs for research technical and management staff (Ministry of Information and Communications tasks p.7) and provides AI and data science counseling and training for workers changing careers (Ministry of Labour tasks p.11).

For artificial intelligence systems with risks it is important to ensure transparency accountability and clearly define legal responsibilities for damages caused.'

thematicElements.justification: Article 40 on Technical standards and regulations on artificial intelligence says that 1. The State shall develop promulgate and update the national system of technical standards and regulations on artificial intelligence' and that 2. the national AI standards and regulations must ensure safety reliability and transparency (pages 23-24). This means the government will establish thresholds or quality benchmarks upon which developers and producers of AI systems shall comply in accordance with requirements by their level of identified risks (Art 15.3&5 Art 16 in pages 9 10 11 for high-risk AI systems; Art 19-21 in pages 12-14 for low-risk & systematic-risk AI systems)

thematicElements.text: The implementation of safeguards fallback procedures or emergency protocols to mitigate harm in case of AI system failure or unexpected behavior
thematicElements.justification: Partial is selected as the Draft Law only mentioned a general requirement for documentation of mitigation procedures. However the question requires specific safeguards/emergency protocols in case of AI failure/unexpected behavior which goes beyond mere documentation procedures for Mitigation. Art15 (p910) requires high-risk AI systems to establish maintain and operate risk management throughout the system's lifecycle; create and maintain complete technical documentation (description of functionality scope; algorithm design and architecture; risk assessment report and mitigation plan; operational and incident logs ...); maintain automated operational logs. Art 19 (p.12) sets out requirements for low-risk ones.

thematicElements.text: The requirement for pre-deployment testing validation or documentation to ensure technical robustness throughout the AI system lifecycle
thematicElements.justification: Yes is selected as Art 15 (p.910) requires high-risk AI systems to establish maintain and operate risk management throughout the system's lifecycle; create and maintain complete technical documentation (description of functionality scope and intended use; algorithm design and architecture; source of training and test data; test results and performance evaluation; risk assessment report and mitigation plan; human monitoring mechanism; security policy; operational and incident logs); maintain automated operational logs. Art 19 (p.12) requires low-risk ones to conduct model evaluations using standardized processes and tools including conducting and documenting counter-testing to proactively continuously identify & mitigate system risks.

thematicElements.text: The introduction of security obligations to protect AI systems against cyberattacks manipulation or adversarial interference

Art19.2. d (p12) demanded suppliers of general-purpose artificial intelligence models to ensure adequate cybersecurity for both AI model and its physical infrastructure.
