This institutional framework is intended to include an AI development coalition involving multiple actors including companies labour unions and CSOs in the development of AI-related policies (p. 86).

items.title: Rwanda’s National AI Policy: Stakeholder Workshop
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: The Ministry of ICT and Innovation (MINICT) and the Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Agency (RURA) supported by GIZ FAIR Forward and The Future Society (TFS) have partaken in a multi-stakeholder process to develop a National AI Policy framework and implementation plan for the Republic of Rwanda. Members of civil society participated in the consultations.

items.title: Workshop to formulate the national Artificial Intelligence strategy
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: It allowed the stated CSO called IPAR to express itself on the current state of AI in senegal on possible priority sectors for use and development of AI and they also proposed a roadmap for use of AI in the agricultural sector. Moreover IPAR a Senegalese CSO/think tank participated as a stakeholder in two government working groups on the national AI strategy: one on AI innovation (infrastructure funding; clusters priority use cases) and one on trusted ethical and responsible AI.

items.title: Public Debate Period on the Draft Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia for the Period 2024-2030
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: The draft Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (2024–2030) was subject to a public consultation (which got extended until July 2024) process organized by the Ministry of Science Technological Development and Innovation which invited citizens experts organizations and other stakeholders to review the draft and submit feedback. The consultation allowed participants to provide comments objections and suggestions through Serbia’s eConsultation portal by email and during public discussion events; thereby enabling broad participation from the professional community civil society organizations and the wider public in shaping the strategy’s final content.

items.title: Permanent Committee for Ethics and regulation of AI
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: Permanent Committee for Ethics and regulation of AI (CERAI) is an independent committee established by the Ministry of investment in 2020 and is made up of various experts including from the CSO sector. CERAI is responsible for assessing ethical social and legal issues related to the research development deployment and use of AI technologies and systems. There are no news about the activities of the Committee beyond 2024 however so it is unclear if it has been active recently.

items.title: AISLOVAKIA
items.justification: AISLOVAKIA is a National Platform for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in Slovakia. Originally created by a partnership between private and the academic/cso sector the government is now amongst members of the partnership. One of the projects created and supported through the platform was https://web.archive.org/save/https://aipoint.sk website which aimed to provide access to relevant legislation documents and initiatives in the field of artificial intelligence. This was part of the implementation of measures in the Action Plan for the Digital Transformation of Slovakia 2023-2026. However seems inactive beyond 2024.

items.title: Inter-ministerial Working Group for the Preparation of the National AI Programme 2030
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: The Ministry of Digital Transformation established the Inter-ministerial Working Group (MDS NpUI) on March 24 2025 to include representatives from civil society academia and the private sector. This multi-stakeholder body served as the primary advisory mechanism for drafting the NpUI 2030. CSOs including the umbrella organization CNVOS were formally invited in August 2025 to participate in the strategic drafting process. This involvement culminated in the NpUI 2030 Consultation on September 16 2025 where CSOs participated in thematic workshops. Their input on ethics regulation and sovereign infrastructure was formally consolidated in the group's third meeting on September 25 2025.

items.title: Multi-stakeholder advisory council including CSOs
items.justification: The NpUI 2030 explicitly establishes a governance structure for monitoring and review in Section 5. A key mechanism is the Permanent Forum for AI (Stalni forum za UI) defined in Section 5.2 as an advisory body to the Government. The program emphasizes that successful implementation necessitates an 'inclusive dialogue with civil society'. Additionally Section 5.3 creates the AI Observatory (UI observatorij) to monitor indicators and propose measures based on identified social needs. These formal bodies ensure that stakeholders including civil society have a role in the ongoing oversight and adaptation of the strategy

items.title: Inter-ministerial Working Group for the Preparation of NpUI 2030 (MDS NpUI)
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: As of September 30 2025 the primary operational mechanism is the Inter-ministerial Working Group for the Preparation of NpUI 2030 (MDS NpUI). Formally appointed on March 24 2025 this multi-stakeholder body explicitly includes representatives from civil society. Throughout 2025 this group held multiple sessions (April July and September) to advise on the national AI roadmap. Additionally the NpUI 2030 framework formally establishes the Permanent Forum for AI (Stalni forum za UI) and the AI Observatory (UI observatorij) as the ongoing operational bodies for stakeholder-led monitoring and advice.

items.title: SA National AI Policy Framework Open Call for Comments and Inputs
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: The South African National AI Policy Framework was published on the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies website with an open call for inputs and comments. Stakeholders including CSOs could email comments on the Framework. According to a general internet search many CSOs did email comments. South Africa is currently developing the AI Policy which will hopefully take into account statements submitted from CSOs and other stakeholders.

items.title: Public Consultation on Sri Lanka’s Draft National AI Strategy
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: On 9 January 2025 the MODE in collaboration with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Sri Lanka Citra Social Innovation Lab and Sri Lanka–based ICT policy think tank LIRNEasia held the first public consultation meeting following the release of the draft AI Strategy. The meeting saw participation from the public sector private sector civil society academia and development partners. The core components of the strategy were discussed alongside the importance of introducing safeguards for AI adoption and addressing the ethical use of AI and its associated risks.

items.title: Supporting the development of the National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Strategy for Sri Lanka
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: Citra Social Innovation Lab supported the Committee on Formulating a Strategy for Artificial Intelligence (CFSAI) by providing coordination expert input and drafting support for Sri Lanka’s National AI Strategy. Additionally UNDP Sri Lanka staff and representatives from the private sector academia and civil society were part of the committee as noted in the acknowledgments section of the draft strategy (pp. 62–63). Their involvement enabled non-government participation in the multi-stakeholder working process allowing CSO expertise to inform policy development.

items.title: Multi-stakeholder advisory council including CSOs
items.justification: The aim of the Digital Switzerland Strategy is for the population as a whole to benefit from a digital transformation that is responsible and sustainable (ecologically economically and socially). This is being driven forward jointly by the authorities at all federal levels as well as by stakeholders from civil society business academia and politics. Gender equality is also taken into account. (cited from website)

items.title: Digital Switzerland Advisory Board
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: Meetings of the Digital Switzerland Advisory Committee bring together Federal Council members and representatives from business academia politics public authorities and civil society to address digital transformation issues. Held several times a year and chaired by a Federal Council member or the Federal Chancellor they complement the work of the Federal Council’s Digitalisation and ICT Committee and are organised by the Federal Chancellery’s DTI unit. A meeting with focus on AI is planned for 10 February 2026.

items.title: Other
items.justification: The strategy mentions civil society as a source of alternative statistics to be used to monitor and evaluate the results of measures taken within the implementation process. Section 5 provision 117

items.title: Drafting : National Artificial Intelligence Action Plan for the Development of Thailand for Six-Year Period (2022–2027) (or NAIS)
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: The Artificial Intelligence Association of Thailand (AIAT) was part of the drafting committee of the NAIS. All participating organisations are listed at the bottom and AIAT is one of them.

items.title: For Public Comment: Draft Voluntary National Standard related to Information Technology – Artificial Intelligence
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: TTBS operates a national standardization participation mechanism where all stakeholders—including CSOs—can: Access draft technical AI standards submit written feedback participate in national adoption of AI governance norms. This mechanism is directly AI-related making it one of the clearest CSO-inclusion channels in current AI governance.

items.title: White Paper on Artificial Intelligence Regulation in Ukraine: Vision of the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: The White Paper open public consultations available for all stakeholders whereas relevant CSOs were directly contacted by the Ministry for Digital Transformation with an invitation to provide feedback and recommendations to the substance of the White Paper (p.30).

items.title: Expert Committee on Development of AI in Ukraine under the Ministry for Digital Transformation of Ukraine
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: Civil society experts (including Tetiana Avdieieva (DSLU) and Olga Petriv (CEDEM)) participate in drafting legislative and soft law regulations as well as advise Ukrainian Ministry for Digital Transformation on the matters related to AI governance. Where needed experts provide opinions on compliance of the initiatives with international standards.

items.title: Expert Committee on Development of AI in Ukraine under the Ministry for Digital Transformation of Ukraine
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: As a part of the Expert Committee on Development of AI civil society experts (including Tetiana Avdieieva (DSLU) and Olga Petriv (CEDEM)) participate in drafting legislative and soft law regulations as well as advise Ukrainian Ministry for Digital Transformation on the matters related to AI governance. Where needed experts provide opinions on compliance of the initiatives with international standards.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: AI regulation: a pro-innovation approach - Government response to consultation
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: The Department for Science Innovation and Technology (DSIT) conducted a 12-week public consultation on its AI regulation white paper. Section 6 (p.42) confirms 409 written responses from organizations and individuals plus 364 individuals engaged through roundtables and workshops. The Ministerial foreword by Secretary of State Michelle Donelan notes that 'leading voices in academia and civil society' supported the approach (p.4). DSIT commits to working 'closely with civil society industry and international partners' on future policy development (p.7) including targeted consultations on the cross-economy AI risk register and monitoring framework (p.8).

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Other
items.justification: The “central function for AI regulation” is described in Section 3.1 as a mechanism to support implementation and build “feedback loops with… civil society.” It will coordinate regulators assess risks and engage stakeholders across sectors. This constitutes a formal structure for inclusive ongoing participation.

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Government Digital Service Responsible AI Advisory Panel
items.type: Oversight advisory policy monitoring and evaluation bodies where CSOs have a seat
items.justification: The GDS Responsible AI Advisory Panel is an external body set up by the Government Digital Service to “bring together views from across the public sector industry academia and civil society on the responsible use of AI.” Civil-society experts sit as panel members and give strategic advice plus “constructive challenge and scrutiny” of government AI products and approaches providing an ongoing channel for CSO oversight of public-sector AI use.

items.title: Federal Registration. Request for information on the development of an Artificial Intelligence Action Plan
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: SUMMARY: On behalf of the Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP )the NITRD NCO requests input from all interested parties on the Development ofan Artificial Intelligence (AI) Action Plan (‘‘Plan’’) (p. 1). The RFI enabled CSO participation by opening an inclusive public consultation: it “seeks input from the public… and any other interested parties” (SUMMARY p.1). It provides clear submission channels (email/mail) and rules (=15 pages; one submission) (ADDRESSES/Instructions p.1). It also commits that “Comments received will be taken into consideration” (Supplementary Information p.2) and notes responses may be posted online/FOIA-releasable (p.2).

items.title: Public Consultation on the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy
items.type: Open public consultation (e.g. online comments public hearing)
items.justification: According to the Strategy: 'Stage 4 - Public Consultation. The document was published for public consultation from September 16 to October 21 2024 through the Digital Citizen Participation Platform allowing all interested parties to contribute.We received 28 proposals from 4 national and international civil society organizations 6 private sector organizations 1 multilateral organization and 6 individuals. These proposals resulted in 78 contributions 63% of which were incorporated in full or in part into the document while others will be included in the Roadmap that will be developed.' (p.54)

items.title: Dialogue table “Artificial Intelligence: opportunities and challenges of a national strategy”
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: According to the Strategy: 'Stage 2 - Proposals. Seven dialogue and working groups were held to gather proposals related to the potential objectives and actions to be integrated into the new strategy along with discussion groups with children and adolescents.The dialogue groups included the participation of more than 300 representatives from over 40 government institutions 11 civil society organizations 45 private sector organizations academia and various stakeholder groups who contributed diverse perspectives. All reports detailing each contribution are available on the Agesic website. (p. 53).

items.title: D? th?o Online - Noi nhân dân tham gia vào ho?t d?ng l?p pháp c?a qu?c h?i (Online Draft Legislations - Where people participate in the legislative activities of the National Assembly)
items.justification: The platform publishes public consultations. Anyone and any organization (including CSOs) can submit their comments online and have their comments published on the platform. This platform enables: 1) right of access to information on the Draft law (and other AI policies); 2) right to speak up and share comments on the Draft Law. Even though the platform has not yet published the responses and inclusion of CSO' feedback I know that there is a response mechanism in which the National Assembly and relevant agencies must consider and reply to all comments provided (as I have received many Draft law full packages). The platform has been active since 21st January 2007 and will continue to be active for following AI related laws.

items.title: Stakeholder Consultation
items.type: Participation in multi-stakeholder working groups or advisory committees
items.justification: The strategy’s Stakeholder Analysis (Page 17 3.2 Assessment and Goal Setting) identifies civil society as a key stakeholder and describes a co-creation process with government academia private sector and civil society to design an inclusive AI strategy. It mentions “broad consultations with representatives from civil society” and “iterative input” from stakeholders. However specific CSOs consulted are not listed and no formal submissions or feedback summaries are provided. This Evidence supports partial involvement.

items.title: Security Risk Assessment Tool (SRAT) for immigration detainee risk scoring
items.justification: Security Risk Assessment Tool (SRAT) developed by the global corporation Serco used for visa processing and immigration detention in Australia assigns detainees algorithmic risk scores that determine housing restraints movement and access to activities. Evidence shows inflated data systemic errors and no ability for detainees to view or challenge their scores (Guardian 12 Mar 2024; AHRC Use of Force inquiry). This functions as a government social-scoring system with severe impacts on liberty fairness and human rights.

items.title: AI-powered video surveillance
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Advanced video surveillance systems supplied by companies such as ZTE Corporation enable real-time AI-driven monitoring through centralized command platforms. Page 16 of the document identifies  AI-powered video surveillance systems with facial recognition likely procured. These systems are linked to ZTE Corporation on pages 22 and 47 which describe AI-enabled IP cameras biometric surveillance kits capable of  facial recognition and iris scanning as well as vehicle tracking and crowd analysis. The document also notes covert tools such as under-door viewing kits and the use of drones for video surveillance. These technologies enable pervasive monitoring posing severe risks to privacy freedom of movement and democratic participation.

items.title: The Belarusian government uses the 'Kipod' facial recognition software to track identify and detain peaceful protestors journalists and opposition figures
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The AI-powered surveillance system Kipod enables real-time facial recognition across thousands of public cameras without legal safeguards or public oversight. Sources indicate that the Kipod video-surveillance system was first tested in 2014 (https://news.zerkalo.io/life/9802.html). This technology has been used to identify and detain peaceful protestors (https://www.biometricupdate.com/202212/synesis-to-appeal-eu-sanctions-over-misuse-of-its-facial-recognition-software + https://data.europa.eu/apps/eusanctionstracker/subjects/126887). Such surveillance suppresses freedom of expression and assembly by creating mass surveillance. It poses an unacceptable risk by enabling automated targeting and undermining democratic participation.

items.title: Belarusian state-backed Silovik (controlled by Belarus’ GUBOPiK agency) Influence network on Telegram and X using AI
items.type: AI weapons or the use of AI in armed conflicts
items.justification: Debunk.org (Disinformation analysis center) confirms the use of inauthentic accounts posting AI-created content to spread state propaganda and discredit Ukraine. This state-led influence operation misleads the public distorts discourse and erodes trust in democratic institutions through deception and AI-generated content.

items.title: Belarus Deploys AI-Enabled Combat Drones 'Chekan V' and 'Berkut-3' and unveils AI-driven Hunter helicopter to target marine drones
items.type: AI-driven cyberattacks disinformation or influence operations
items.justification: Belarus has introduced AI-enabled combat drones 'Chekan V' and 'Berkut-3' into military service. The Chekan V system passed all types of testing and was accepted into service with the Armed Forces of the Republic of Belarus in July 2024. Demonstrated to President Lukashenko these autonomous weapon systems can identify and strike targets without human intervention raising concerns about potential future harm from their deployment in armed conflict.

items.title: Facial recognition camera systems installed in educational centers
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: According to a video from the Autonomous Government of Santa Cruz (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YAvYIkuxjvE) in 2023–2024 the Municipal Government of Santa Cruz implemented an AI-based surveillance system in 126 public educational institutions. The system uses facial recognition on underage students including real-time tracking and a biometric database.Supreme Decree No. 1436 mandates the installation of security cameras in public educational institutions but does not authorize biometric identification facial recognition or automated tracking. Therefore the system constitutes a government use of AI classified as an unacceptable risk.

items.title: RecFaces live facial recognition used for security during 2024 Brazilian Carnival
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Cameras using Id-Guard from RecFaces a Dubai-based facial recognition software developer were used to secure Brazil Carnival 2024 according to a company release. The cameras were used at mobile control checkpoints. ID-Guard’s real-time biometric identification would immediately notify security if barred individuals were present in the audience. The deployment has been confirmed by ReFaces themselves who documented their use on their website: https://recfaces.com/articles/facial-recognition-from-recfaces-for-security-during-brazilian-carnival-2024

items.title: Brazilian pension system utilisation of AI systems and automation in the delivery of social benefits at the National Institute of Social Security (INSS) - Research report
items.justification: A research report assessed Brazilian pension system especially focusing on the utilisation of AI systems and automation in the delivery of social benefits at the National Institute of Social Security (INSS) concluding that in fact its results are unfair and biased against certain groups. They further note that discrimination against these groups is not because of bias in the system but rather from the inadequate structuring of information. As a result many citizens are misled by the way the information is presented. However this tends to be more present in the profile of low-income workers who tend to work in multiple jobs and companies throughout their lives.

items.title: Babel X under Project Wide Awake
items.justification: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police deployed Babel X under Project Wide Awake to collect and analyze large volumes of personal data from social media the dark web geolocation services and private databases for policing purposes. This is a verified deployment as confirmed by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada in its 2024 report. The OPC found that the RCMP’s ongoing collection of personal information was not adequately assessed for legality or compliance and may contravene privacy law with the matter remaining unresolved. The system was in use from at least 2016 and expanded in 2021 continuing into 2024.

items.title: SITIA and Calle Segura
items.justification: Chile’s systems described in Chile AI policing systems overview fit criminal justice and law enforcement misuse because they integrate invasive AI practices into policing decisions and surveillance workflows. Systems like SITIA and Calle Segura combine camera networks facial recognition capabilities and data-sharing platforms to support detection of suspects and monitoring of public spaces (although not fully in real-time but policing and incident based). They enable authorities to aggregate and analyze large volumes of data influencing operational responses and policing priorities.

items.title: ‘Sharp Eyes’ Surveillance Program
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The Sharp Eyes and SkyNet programs qualify as real-time remote biometric identification for law enforcement purposes in publicly accessible spaces. Sharp Eyes (launched in 2015) with the goal of achieving 100% coverage of public spaces by 2020 integrating automated facial recognition algorithms into networks of 200+ million cameras. SkyNet (since 2005) which focuses on installing cameras connected to facial recognition algorithms uses facial recognition data from building complexes shared with local police to build population databases. Both projects are ongoing and fully operational utilizing facial recognition algorithms to capture analyze and process visual and behavioral data in real-time.

items.title: AI-Powered Anti-Corruption Drive
items.justification: This case qualifies as an unacceptable risk because it automates legal investigation undermining due process and privacy. According to the report the system uses algorithmic profiling to map social networks and hidden equity nesting flagging individuals based on patterns (section 'AI and the Future of Anti-Corruption in China'). It fits individual risk assessment by using dynamic risk modelling to predict graft creating a digital panopticon where officials are judged by a black-box system.

items.title: AI deployment in the credit reporting by the People's Bank of China
items.justification: The report confirms that the central government via the People's Bank of China (PBOC) actively promotes the use of AI in credit scoring. The PBOC states its intent to 'deepen the application of big data artificial intelligence blockchain and other new technologies in the credit reporting field' to fully unleash data value and achieve high-quality development and security. By licensing and regulating private agencies like Baihang and Pudao to profile individual behaviors using 'big data' algorithms the state creates a standardized system where social and financial conduct determines an individual's access to critical services and life opportunities.

items.title: AI-orchestrated cyber espionage campaign
items.type: AI-driven cyberattacks disinformation or influence operations
items.justification: Anthropic reported disrupting an espionage campaign that used their AI tool. Anthropic claims that the actor was 'a Chinese state-sponsored group' with high confidence (p.3). It states that the actor manipulated the Claude Code tool into attempting to infiltrate global targets. It was able to leverage AI to execute 80-90% of tactical operations independently at physically impossible request rates (p.3). The actor was reported succeeded in roughly 30 cases before Anthropic disrupted it (p.3). (In the report Anthropic said that this event was in mid-September).

items.title: Algorithmic Video Surveillance for Transport Security
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: This case qualifies as an unacceptable risk of mass biometric surveillance. Although the government sought to extend the 'Olympic experiment' until 2027 via the Transport Security Law the Constitutional Council (Decision n° 2025-878 DC) censored the extension. Amnesty International argues VSA performs 'biometric processing' by analyzing gaits and gestures to flag 'abnormal' behavior which inherently suppresses the right to anonymity in public spaces. It also demonstrated a discriminatory impact by disproportionately flagging marginalized groups (homeless) as 'suspicious objects' violating the principles of equality and non-discrimination.

items.title: Algorithmic Fraud Detection System of the National Family Allowance Fund (Caisse nationale des allocations familiales - CNAF)
items.justification: The French Social Security Agency’s National Family Allowance Fund (CNAF) uses an AI system to identify suspected welfare fraud and overpayments. The algorithm assigns risk scores to approximately 32 million benefit recipients based on personal and socio-economic characteristics including low income unemployment disability and residence in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Amnesty International notes that the system disproportionately targets marginalized groups and therefore violates the rights to equality non-discrimination and privacy. As the AI system is deployed by a public authority in the administration of essential social welfare services it constitutes a discriminatory AI-enabled public service system.

items.title: Biometric Internet Matching (The 'Security Package' / Sicherheitspaket)
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Following a series of security incidents the German government passed legislation authorizing federal police and migration authorities to use AI for matching biometric data (facial images/voice) against images scraped from the open internet including social media platforms like Instagram and LinkedIn. Civil rights organisations (e.g. AlgorithmWatch Chaos Computer Club) labeled this as biometric mass surveillance. While the government argues it avoids a central database technical experts state that such large-scale matching effectively treats the entire internet as a biometric database a practice specifically prohibited as an 'unacceptable risk' under Article 5 of the EU AI Act which Germany bypassed via national security exemptions.

items.title: Palantir/VeRA (Automated Data Analysis Platform)
items.justification: After a 2023 Federal Constitutional Court ruling set strict limits on 'data mining' the Bavarian government pushed through state-level legislation to make the VeRA platform (powered by Palantir Gotham) fully operational by December 25 2024. The system aggregates vast previously separate police datasets to identify 'behavioral patterns' and 'at-risk' individuals for preventive policing. The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) has challenged this as a violation of the right to informational self-determination. The system allows for automated profiling of individuals not suspected of any crime creating a high risk of 'black box' discrimination and lack of accountability in law enforcement.

items.title: The  State of deployment of surveillance technologies in Africa. Ghana - Overview of Surveillance Technologies Deployment
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: There is much reported evidence that the government uses technology to monitor the population against the principles and rights guaranteed in the Constitution such as QuaDream spyware that exfiltrates user data (without authorization) (pp. 94-98). Regarding AI since 2019 the government has created a 'safe cities' project deploying Huawei cameras in three cities and planning to expand the installations. With the 2020 cybersecurity law it became legal for the government to conduct surveillance on citizens. This has boosted the use of the Chinese company's AI for surveillance via facial recognition (p. 95).

items.title: KENTAUROS
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: KENTAUROS constitutes a system of large-scale biometric surveillance in asylum facilities relying on AI-enabled behavioural analytics and biometric data processing. According to the Greek DPA’s April 2024 decision the system was implemented in breach of core GDPR requirements notably without a prior Data Protection Impact Assessment and without clear information on its automated functions or interoperability with law-enforcement databases. These deficiencies create a high risk of disproportionate and continuous surveillance of asylum seekers with serious implications for privacy and other fundamental rights. Despite the regulator’s findings no public evidence suggests that KENTAUROS has been deactivated.

items.title: HYPERION
items.justification: HYPERION deploys AI-driven behavioural analytics and biometric processing within asylum facilities targeting a highly vulnerable population. The Greek Data Protection Authority’s April 2024 decision identified serious GDPR violations including the absence of a Data Protection Impact Assessment and insufficient transparency regarding automated decision-making functions. These shortcomings heighten the risk of discriminatory treatment and unequal access to rights for asylum seekers particularly given the lack of clear safeguards against bias in behavioural analysis systems. There is no publicly available evidence that HYPERION has been suspended following the DPA’s findings. Potentially discriminatory practices may still be ongoing.

items.title: Predictive Policing
items.justification: The PIB release confirms that AI is “now being leveraged” and “integrated” in Indian law enforcement including for predictive analytics surveillance and investigative support. These uses involve processing large-scale personal data and influencing policing decisions which raises concerns regarding opacity potential bias and impacts on fundamental rights. In particular applications such as predictive policing and facial recognition may affect individuals without clear safeguards or accountability.

items.title: Facial recognition in Poshan Tracker app
items.justification: The document mentions that the Ministry of Women and Child Development mandated the use of facial recognition in to ensure that only genuine beneficiaries (infants pregnant and lactating women) receive Take Home Ration (THR). While the doc doesn't mention any negative impacts civil society organisations state that this system has led to a loss of flexibility in allowing family members to collect rations when a mother cannot adverse impact on right to food making it a conditional privilege based on access to a smartphone a national ID (Aadhaar) linked phone number and FRS effectiveness. Link: https://internetfreedom.in/face-recognition-in-poshan-tracker-what-the-government-told-us-and-what-it-didnt/

items.title: Mass Surveillance System for the West Bank - (Not official name)
items.justification: Based on publications this system implemented the use of cameras (and maybe other elements such as drones) located around the occupied territories and combined algorithmic system to allow both for online and archival retrieval of identities based on facial recognition. This mass surveillance system being used by the IDF for all the West Bank (Occupied territories) caused Microsoft to disconnect the IDF from its online services.

items.title: The Artificial Intelligence System for Detention and Drug Searches at Ben-Gurion Airport
items.type: AI weapons or the use of AI in armed conflicts
items.justification: The Israel Police implemented an algorithmic system that was aimed at recommending probable drug smugglers at the International Airport based on a secretive algorithmic process. According to the petition there was a high risk that the system included data as to sexual preferences (proxy if not direct). A petition was handed and the court was later updated that use of the system was stopped. No reason was given.

items.title: The Gospel
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: According to foreign press releases the IDF is using an AI based system to select target for bombing during the Gaza War. There are no details if this is an unacceptable use as such but the number of targets it has produced is directly linked to a rise in civilian casualties.

items.title: Abnormal Behavior Detection System to Snare Criminals Before They Commit Crime
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: During the Tokyo election law-enforcement authorities deployed AI-enabled behavior-detection cameras. The deployment followed recent violent incidents involving Japanese politicians. The system was used to scan crowds in real-time and generate immediate alerts based on predefined movement patterns including actions such as drawing a handgun and other movements classified by the system as suspicious marking it as real-time surveillance in a public space. The article confirms both the use of the system in an election setting and its functionality as a crowd-scanning and alert-generation tool. No information is provided regarding on-site public notice individual notification or mechanisms to contest alerts generated by the systems.

items.title: AI tools used in Kenya to discredit protesters and allege Russian connections
items.type: AI-driven cyberattacks disinformation or influence operations
items.justification: This article articulates how the Kenyan government used content creators and influencers to promote online campaigns on twitter (X) in support of the controversial finance bill that was widely protested against by the whole country. The government using a network of X accounts appeared to operate in coordination amplifying several hashtags that attacked protestors and boosted support for the President and the government. The accounts aimed at spreading disinformation and controlling political narratives flooded X with similar or identical posts often shared within a short period of time and used images that appeared to be AI-generated.

items.title: mass facial and fingerprint data collection
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: it started in march 2024  and still going on this process include mass facial and finger prints data collection with a lot of restriction for non compiling to those collection process (see the last paragraph of 1st link )  and it is the first step to install the surveillance cameras with mass facial recognition and huge debate about privacy data leakage .If you did not submit it you can not travel and your bank account may get suspended .

items.title: AI-Enabled National Police Facial Recognition Surveillance System
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The deployment of AI-enabled facial recognition cameras by the Interior Ministry launched in June 2023 (https://web.archive.org/save/https://akipress.com/news:714362) qualifies as an unacceptable-risk use of AI because it enables mass biometric surveillance in public spaces without clear legal safeguards transparency or oversight. Although authorities claim the cameras recognise only wanted criminals continuous 24/7 facial scanning in public areas inherently captures biometric data of all passersby posing risks of privacy violations unlawful data processing and potential misuse that could chill freedom of movement expression and assembly.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Court Sentencing (AiCOS)  - ONE CASE UNDER THE SYSTEM FLAGGED BY OECD AS 'INCIDENT'
items.justification: The AI sentencing system produced a recommended imprisonment percentage referenced during sentencing directly affecting an individual's liberty. The deployment raised concerns regarding individual criminal offence risk assessment by AI in high-stakes judicial contexts. The underlying model feature weighting and output interpretation weren't publicly disclosed at the time limiting the ability of affected parties to understand or contest the system's influence on the proceedings pp.129–131.

items.title: With Artificial Intelligence Michoacán accelerates searching for criminales and missing persons: Bedolla
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The state of Michoacán deployed a live facial recognition system (SAFR platform) connected to public cameras across urban areas rural zones and roads generating real-time alerts to law enforcement via the C5 center (See as well: https://ssp.michoacan.gob.mx/cerca-de-3-mil-camaras-del-c5-michoacan-vigilan-zamora-morelia-y-uruapan/). This constitutes remote real-time biometric tracking in public spaces meeting the EU AI Act-aligned threshold for mass biometric surveillance.

items.title: 'Better Tomorrow' facial recognition surveillance system – Ministry of Interior of Montenegro
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The Ministry of Interior deployed the Better Tomorrow facial recognition system in public spaces in Podgorica Bar and Budva. AZLP found this violated citizen's rights confirming the presence of biometric facial-recognition functions (page 4) and unlawful deployment across these cities (page 1). The system processed biometric data without consent notification or safeguards (page 3) enabling real-time identification. Cameras were removed only after inspection and oversight was obstructed by classified withheld documentation (page 2). AZLP ordered deactivation on 30 May 2024 (pages 3 and 4). This constitutes an unacceptable-risk AI under the EU AI Act threatening privacy freedom of movement and democratic oversight.

items.title: Myanmar’s repressive use of AI  to counter “terrorism” report
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Pages 2–4 outline Myanmar’s AI system as a “human-rights-violation multiplier” automating repression. Pages 5–9 show biometric and surveillance databases eliminating anonymity. Pages 4–6 detail AI-powered censorship and “Safe City” facial recognition.

items.title: Surveillance Cameras and Face-reading cameras
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The report reads Nepal police deploying multiple technologies to investigate crime.Among them- Face reading cameras have been installed in 10 places and cameras with video management based on AI have been installed at 150 places for effective traffic management. Apart from this ten 'Automatic Number Plate Recognization Cameras' are in use in the Kathmandu valley along with other 170 CCTV cameras.

items.title: Camera Surveillance at Peaceful Protests in the Netherlands
items.justification: Amnesty International published a research that reported drones and video-surveillance cars with facial-recognition capability were used to monitor peaceful protests in the Netherlands(p.8) . It causes a 'chilling effect' discouraging protest through fears of ID logging and databases like 'Catch Aliens' (P. 4 26). This violates privacy by collecting data on political beliefs (P. 11 18). Risks for migrants are severe fearing impacts on residence status or future jobs (P. 26-27). The government published a policy response addressing Amnesty’s recommendations(https://web.archive.org/web/20251208153911/https://www.rijksoverheid.nl/documenten/rapporten/2025/01/20/bijlage-6-beleidsreactie-rapport-camerasurveillance-bij-vreedzaam-protest)

items.title: Preselect Recidivism algorithm
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: This poses an unacceptable risk due to discriminatory profiling and lack of oversight. First raised by FTM article summary here https://web.archive.org/web/20260301115253/https://cybernews.com/news/police-algorithm-labels-kids-future-criminals/. In its official response (attached doc) the govt confirmed that the algorithm calculates risk using immutable traits such as gender and inputs like the police history of “housemates” (pp. 2 8) creating a risk of “derivative guilt.” Used since 2013 relying on an outdated model with acknowledged “decreased predictive power”  was omitted from the public Algorithm Register blocking necessary transparency (pp. 3–46). Families were never informed and the government confirmed no way to object.

items.title: The Child Benefits Agency (Dienst Toeslagen)
items.justification: The childcare allowance is a govt benefit to reimburse parents for childcare costs. https://www.rekenkamer.nl/actueel/nieuws/2025/05/21/privacyproblemen-bij-algoritmes-dienst-toeslagen-en-belastingdien; in the scandal risk-classification algorithms were used to detect alleged fraud and reclaim payments. The Court of Audit in its 2024 accountability report found that the algorithm used to identify parents for support does not comply with the GDPR (p.56) sensitive data of a vulnerable group aren’t properly protected and privacy risks are insufficiently managed . It is also concerned that data from assistance could later be used for surveillance or fraud checks risking discrimination loss of privacy and trust and unequal treatment.(p.58).

items.title: DUO's approach to fraud found to be discriminatory and illegal
items.justification: The DUO case qualifies as an unacceptable risk because it functioned as a discriminatory public service system directly violating the fundamental right to non-discrimination. The Dutch Data Protection Authority (AP) ruled the system illegal because the algorithm used 'risk indicators' such as education type and distance to parents that lacked objective justification and served as proxies for migration background. Consequently students with a non-Western background were disproportionately targeted for invasive fraud inspections. This undermined democratic processes by automating bias without scientific evidence subjecting vulnerable citizens to unjustified state surveillance based on a flawed 'risk score'.

items.title: Safe City Islamabad
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The important parts the research paper in the drive titled “AI-Driven Policing in Pakistan: Potential Pitfalls and Privacy Concerns” (Page 342 last line and Page 345 second para) raises concerns regarding deployment of Safe City Islamabad without any legal authority. Pakistan does not have a data protection law so no formal requirements to obtain informed consent or warrants by judicial authorities to surveil and data minimization requirements. AI in policing presents serious implications to privacy civil liberties democratic governance and institutional integrity. It has potential usage of facial recognition to target people at political rallies religious events with little or no transparency or safeguarding procedures in place.

items.title: AI Surveillance Cameras Aid Crime Reduction in Bulgarian Resorts
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The deployment of AI-powered surveillance cameras in Bulgarian resorts such as Nessebar and Sunny Beach constitutes real-time surveillance because the system continuously monitors public spaces and performs live tracking of individuals and vehicles. Using facial and vehicle recognition the cameras process video feeds instantly allowing authorities to identify and follow movements as they occur. This enables the immediate detection of suspects and the tracking of their location across the monitored area having lead to the resolution of at least 5 crimes.

items.title: NEOM
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: the document shows that NEOM’s large-scale deployment of facial recognition creates pervasive continuous surveillance that abolishes anonymity and collapses the distinction between public and private life. The system converts individuals into constantly monitored data points enabling pre-emptive behavioral control rather than accountable law enforcement. This undermines privacy autonomy freedom of expression and political subjectivity while normalizing automated governance without meaningful consent or democratic oversight. The authors argue this “negation of privacy” and data-driven governance erode individual agency and democratic deliberation replacing them with totalizing surveillance justified by efficiency and security pp.2-6

items.title: 22000 Units of AI-based intelligent CCTV to be installed in Seoul
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Seoul Metropolitan Government announces that the city will install 22000 additional “intelligent CCTV” units in 2025 raising the share of AI-enabled cameras to more than half of all public CCTV and that these upgraded systems will use AI to classify objects detect “abnormal” behaviors and trigger automated alerts across parks streets and other public spaces. Because this deployment enables wide-area real-time monitoring and automated behavioral analysis in places accessible to the public it resembles the types of untargeted public-space surveillance that the EU AI Act classifies as an unacceptable risk.

items.title: RisCanvi has been fully deployed at the regional level in the Catalan prison system since 2010
items.justification: RisCanvi has been fully deployed at the regional level in the Catalan prison system since 2010 and is regularly used in all centers managed by the Generalitat de Catalunya. In Catalonia ‘RisCanvi’ is an algorithm used by prison administration to calculate the risk of an inmate committing a reoffence based on a series of weighted characteristics. The algorithm was initially intended to target reoffending among particular crimes such as murder or sexual offences but it has been expanded to include several types of offenders.

items.title: Intelligent Transport Management System (ITMS)
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The government launched the Intelligent Transport Management System (ITMS) which installs digital tracking chips in all automobile number plates registered in the country to resolve motor-vehicle-related criminality. This was building on the country’s existing traffic surveillance system with a network of surveillance cameras.The Human Rights Watch noted that the Ugandan government has limited public scrutiny of the technical system and its capabilities and the contract with the system provider a Russian company had not published plans for oversight & human rights mitigation. More information here: http://web.archive.org/web/20251119140928/https://www.hrw.org/news/2023/11/14/uganda-rights-concerns-over-license-plate-tracking

items.title: Clearview AI
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Uncontrolled biometric surveillance based on scraping of personal data. Quote: Since the start of the full-scale invasion Ukrainian law enforcement agencies have been using Clearview AI’s facial recognition system. The program helps to enhance security at checkpoints and checkpoints. It is also a powerful tool for identifying war criminals.

items.title: AI-driven drones
items.type: AI weapons or the use of AI in armed conflicts
items.justification: AI-driven drones are deployed to safeguard Ukrainian territory against Russian aggression. Many of them are equipped with automated target capture and high-resolution intelligence systems.

items.title: Dubai Oyoon (Eyes)
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The Executive Council Resolution No. (34) of 2021 approves the deployment of intelligent camera surveillance systems using AI to establish an integrated security system capable of helping entities predict and proactively respond to incidents (Art.3). This AI-driven surveillance overseen by the Dubai Police & the State Security Authority in Dubai poses a profound risk to rights & freedoms. The system enables mass surveillance & potential erosion of privacy and freedoms due to constant monitoring & predictive policing capabilities(Art.2). Further risk arises as the system requires developing policies on the use of security AI (Art.4) and references rules governing the confidentiality of information (Art. 8).

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Metropolitan Police Live Facial Recognition (LFR) Surveillance
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: Per House of Commons Library report CDP 2024/0144: the Lords Justice and Home Affairs Committee called for 'a clear foundation in law' and 'independent scrutiny' (p.6). Studies show 'Black men being more likely to be incorrectly matched' due to 'bias in computer learning' (p.5).  The Equality and Human Rights Commission (Aug 2025) declared the Metropolitan Police's use incompatible with European Convention on Human Rights Articles 8 10 11. This is real-time remote biometric identification used by the police https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/met-polices-use-facial-recognition-tech-must-comply-human-rights-law-says-regulator

country.name: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

items.title: Department for Work and Pensions Universal Credit Advances Fraud Detection Algorithm
items.justification: The Department for Work and Pensions uses machine learning to risk-score almost one million Universal Credit Advances claims yearly. A February 2024 fairness analysis revealed 'statistically significant' bias against older claimants non-United Kingdom nationals disabled people and those with certain marital statuses . No analysis was conducted for race sex religion or other protected characteristics. Amnesty International (July 2025) found the Department for Work and Pensions' 'unchecked use of tech and artificial intelligence systems' causes 'exclusion of people with disabilities and other marginalized groups.'.This constitutes a biased algorithm in welfare with discriminatory impacts on vulnerable populations.

items.title: First Step Act Annual Report: PATTERN: a government risk-prediction tool
items.justification: Over the past year (2024) the Federal Bureau of Prisons FBOP continued to implement PATTERN version 1.3 the current version of the tool. PATTERN qualifies as unacceptable because it is an individual criminal-risk prediction used to shape liberty-related outcomes. The report links PATTERN levels to time-credit eligibility and pre-release custody (Medium/High can apply credits only with warden approval) (Section I.B.2 pp.19–20; I.B.1 p.18). It also reports racial/ethnic overprediction (higher predicted risk than outcomes for Black Hispanic Asian people) raising discrimination and due-process concerns (Section I.A.1 pp.10–11).

items.title: The Civil Rights Implications of the Federal Use of Facial Technology
items.justification: Facial Recognition Technology is used by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) (p. 4) to control access to public/assisted housing (a public service) (p. 8). Documented demographic error-rate disparities can cause unequal denial of entry/services. GAO reports concerns that higher error rates for some groups—especially Black women—can lead to repeated access denials (GAO-25-107196 p.15 “Error rates”). GAO also flags privacy/consent harms and possible data sharing with law enforcement increasing rights and due-process risks (GAO-25-107196 p.15 “Privacy and consent”; p.20 guidance gaps on consent/data sharing).

items.title: The Ministry of the Interior applies artificial intelligence to detect homeless people.
items.type: Mass biometric surveillance (e.g. facial recognition in public spaces)
items.justification: The Uruguayan Ministry of the Interior through its Unified Command Center (CCU) deploys an AI-based video surveillance system that conducts real-time remote monitoring of individuals in publicly accessible spaces. The system applies automated behavioural analysis to identify patterns associated with people remaining or sleeping on the streets generating real-time alerts that trigger police deployment. While framed as a humanitarian response to cold weather emergencies the system constitutes real-time AI-powered surveillance of a vulnerable population in public spaces without a clear legal basis or publicly documented safeguards.
